records.title: International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945)
records.text: A company does not need an office in a state to be sued there. If it sends salesmen into the state year after year and the lawsuit grows out of that business, it has enough ties that being sued there is fair. Courts look at what the company actually did, not at where it is said to be present.

The opinion supplies the starting framework. Later cases in the course specify purposeful availment, claim relatedness, general jurisdiction, and independent routes such as consent. Its historical examples should be read alongside those later decisions.

records.title: World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson (1980)
records.text:
Evaluate each defendant separately. The opinion does not hold that an automobile manufacturer serving Oklahoma would receive the same result, and it does not make a low percentage of forum sales automatically insufficient.

Justice White wrote for a 6–3 Court; Justice Brennan dissented alone, Justice Marshall dissented joined by Justice Blackmun (a retailer joining a national network can expect its product to cause injury elsewhere), and Justice Blackmun dissented separately (automobiles are inherently mobile). The Robinsons bought the Audi from Seaway in 1976 and were driving to Arizona in 1977 when another car struck them.

The often-quoted test is whether the defendant's conduct and connection with the forum are such that it should reasonably anticipate being haled into court there; the manufacturer (Audi) and importer (Volkswagen of America) were not petitioners before the Supreme Court; only the regional distributor and the retail dealer sought review.

records.title: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court (2021)
records.text:
The decision’s reasoning concerns the combination of facts actually present. Do not reduce it to “any local sales plus any local accident,” or treat the opinion as a decision about all-purpose jurisdiction.

The plaintiffs were the estate of Markkaya Gullett, killed in Montana when a tire on her Ford Explorer failed, and Adam Bandemer, injured in Minnesota as a passenger in a friend's Crown Victoria; Justice Kagan wrote for the Court, which was 8–0 (Justice Barrett not participating).

Rule statement: the 'arise out of or relate to' formulation has two halves; the first asks about causation, but the second contemplates that some relationships will support jurisdiction without a causal showing, though 'relate to' incorporates real limits.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text:
A forum-selection clause is an agreement designating the court or place where specified disputes are to be litigated. Its scope, enforceability, and procedural effect require separate questions.

Read whether the clause is exclusive, which claims and parties it covers, and what law governs enforcement. Compare Bremen and Carnival on enforcement and Atlantic Marine on how a valid clause affects transfer in federal court.

A forum clause differs from a choice-of-law clause. Agreement also does not create missing federal subject-matter jurisdiction. Carnival’s notice concession must not be converted into a general holding that every passenger had adequate notice.

records.title: Determining what the agreement requires
records.text:
Begin with the language and the issue in dispute. A disagreement about meaning is different from a claim that an additional agreement should be included. The parol evidence rule addresses the effect of a final written agreement on earlier or contemporaneous terms. Rules about extrinsic evidence address what may be considered in interpreting the words that remain.

Pacific Gas and Trident examine a context-sensitive approach and its consequences. W.W.W. Associates and Greenfield emphasize the written language where it is unambiguous under their approach. Frigaliment and Hurst show the importance of commercial meaning. Nanakuli, Figgie, and Columbia Nitrogen address established practices that may explain or supplement an agreement. These decisions cannot be reduced to a universal instruction either to ignore context or to admit all context.

The case index includes relevant decisions from formation and performance because interpreting a commitment also determines whether a promise exists, how discretion is constrained, and whether conduct amounts to breach.

records.title: Interpreting legislation: enacted text and statutory context
records.text:
The approach protects the terms on which legislation actually secured enactment and resists substituting unenacted intentions or general policy aspirations. In Katzmann’s account, modern textualism uses context, established terms, ordinary usage, and conventions rather than treating dictionary definitions as invariably decisive. Criticism of legislative history also rests on bicameralism, presentment, and concerns about who speaks for the legislature.

Thomas’s Dolan and Small dissents illustrate disagreements over whether ordinary meaning already supplies a clear answer. Katzmann argues that excluding legislative history can discard useful evidence; textualists argue that using it can empower selective or unrepresentative statements. The existence of these disagreements does not mean every textualist always reaches one result, as Scalia’s vote in Dolan illustrates.

Katzmann’s competing account of legislative purpose

Identify the problem Congress addressed, the means it enacted, and the level of generality at which a claimed purpose operates. Katzmann’s version generally respects unambiguous text and uses reliable context to resolve uncertainty. The Hart-and-Sacks account limits interpretation to meanings the words can bear and recognizes clear-statement rules.

Holy Trinity is the source’s historical example of purpose narrowing broad coverage. Raila tests a proposed reading against the tort statute’s purposes and neighboring provisions. The Murphy litigation shows a disagreement about whether expert-fee reimbursement implements Congress’s intended scheme or exceeds the enacted authorization. A broad policy goal alone does not answer how Congress resolved a particular compromise, and the reading expressly acknowledges difficulty identifying a single purpose.

records.title: Reading the whole statute and related provisions
records.text:
Compare definitions, exceptions, related grants of authority, and the consequences of proposed readings across the scheme. In Raila and Dolan, differently worded Federal Tort Claims Act exceptions helped establish the chosen postal exception’s relative scope. In Gayle and Small, the explicit federal-or-state business-offense exception created an anomaly if the general any-court prohibition included foreign convictions.

An anomaly is evidence to evaluate, not a license to repair every asymmetry. Congress may choose uneven rules or a compromise with limited reach. The interpreter must explain why the structural difference supports the proposed meaning and consider a plausible competing explanation, as the Small dissent does.

records.title: UCC § 2-207 — formation and unmatched terms
records.text:
Subsection (1) recognizes a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance or timely written confirmation despite additional or different terms, unless acceptance is expressly conditioned on assent to those terms. Subsection (2) treats additional terms as proposals and supplies the between-merchants rule and its exceptions. When the writings do not establish a contract, subsection (3) recognizes one through both parties’ conduct and supplies agreed terms plus applicable supplementary Code terms.

Dorton, C. Itoh, Bayway, and Northrop examine different parts of this sequence. Northrop preserves disagreement over different terms; Hill and Klocek disagree about later-delivered consumer terms and Hill’s one-form argument. Identify the formation route before deciding which clause controls. The complete assigned text and comments remain in the Contracts Selections.

records.title: Assignment 01 · Overview
records.text:
Hawkins v. McGee: A physician’s sufficiently definite guarantee can create a contractual obligation. Compensation measures the promised result against the actual result, subject to the limits explained in the opinion.

Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow: Test data for a differently configured boat and general promotional praise did not establish the specific speed warranty asserted for Crow’s boat.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 1–13.
Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 2–8.

records.title: Hawkins v. McGee
records.text: If a doctor truly guarantees a result, breaking that guarantee is a contract claim. Damages are the gap between the hand you were promised and the hand you got, not the pain that any such operation would have involved.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 2–3.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hawkins v. McGee
records.text: When a physician guarantees a specified result, damages for breach are the difference between the value of the promised condition and the value of the actual condition, plus incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation, and not the pain ordinarily incident to the agreed operation.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 2–3.

records.title: Hawkins v. McGee
records.text:
Court: Supreme Court of New Hampshire (1929).

C&M pp. 2–3 contain the promise analysis; pp. 11–13 contain the damages analysis. The editors’ later statutory-override example on p. 4 concerns another jurisdiction and another case. It does not retroactively change the holding in Hawkins.

The graft of chest skin caused thick hair to grow on Hawkins's palm, which is why the case is known as the "hairy hand" case (Hawkins v. McGee, 84 N.H. 114, 146 A. 641 (1929)).

Procedural detail: the jury found for Hawkins, but the trial court set the verdict aside as excessive when Hawkins refused to accept a remittitur to $500, and the Supreme Court's ruling on the damages instruction sent the case back for a new trial.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 2–3.

records.title: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow
records.text: Precise numbers only create a warranty if they describe the thing you actually bought. Figures for a differently equipped boat and general sales praise do not promise how your boat will perform.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 4–8.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow
records.text: A seller's statement creates an express warranty only if it is an affirmation, promise or description relating to the goods actually sold that forms part of the basis of the bargain; statements about differently configured goods and general commendation do not.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 4–8.

records.title: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow
records.text:
Court: Supreme Court of Virginia (1999).

The implied-warranty part of the opinion is expressly omitted by the editors at C&M p. 8. The historical references to Article 2 and its enactment belong to this casebook’s account.

257 Va. 121, 509 S.E.2d 499 (1999). The boat reached only 13 mph on delivery (about 17 mph after repairs) against the 30 mph shown in the prop matrixes; the trial court had awarded Crow $135,000 plus prejudgment interest, and the Supreme Court of Virginia reversed on the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness as well as on the express warranty.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 4–8.

records.title: Assignment 02 · Introduction to remedies
records.text: Introduction to remedies. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 02 · Introduction to remedies
records.text:
Sullivan v. O’Connor: A patient recovered for expenses, worsened appearance, and an additional operation after a promised cosmetic result failed. The parties’ appellate waivers limited the court’s need to choose between expectation and reliance measures.

United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications, Inc.: Contract damages compensated the publisher’s lost hardcover profits; the licensee’s separate profits were not recoverable merely because its early paperback sales breached the agreement.

Morris v. Sparrow: A horse that the claimant had personally trained had sufficiently distinctive value to justify delivery of that horse rather than an award of its market price.

White v. Benkowski: Actual inconvenience supported modest compensatory damages for deliberate water interruptions, but malice alone did not support punitive damages on the contract claim presented.

records.title: Sullivan v. O’Connor
records.text: A patient can sue on a surgeon's clear promise of a specific result even when the surgery was done without negligence. The recovery can cover the money spent, the worsening of the condition and the extra pain and distress the broken promise caused.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Sullivan v. O’Connor
records.text: A patient may recover on a physician's clearly proved promise of a specific result even without negligence, and the damages may include out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of the patient's condition, and pain and mental distress beyond what the promised treatment would have entailed.

records.title: Sullivan v. O’Connor
records.text:
Court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts (1973).

Sullivan was a professional entertainer, and the trial judge's instruction let the jury compensate her out-of-pocket expenses, the disfigurement, related emotional distress in light of her profession, and the pain and suffering of the third operation (363 Mass. 579, 296 N.E.2d 183, decided May 9, 1973).

records.title: United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications, Inc.
records.text: Contract damages make up the injured party's own loss. The breaching publisher's profits can be evidence of that loss, but profits that do not match what the plaintiff lost are not simply handed over.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications, Inc.
records.text: Contract damages ordinarily compensate the injured party's own loss; the breaching party's gains can sometimes help measure that loss, but gains that do not correspond to it are not automatically recoverable in an ordinary contract action, and a supported estimate of the loss suffices despite uncertainty.

records.title: United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications, Inc.
records.text:
Court: Second Circuit (1991).

The editors flag a possible numerical misprint in the opinion’s monthly hardcover-sales discussion.

records.title: Morris v. Sparrow
records.text: Usually a disappointed buyer of goods gets money, not the goods. But when the item is one of a kind to the buyer, like a horse he personally trained, a court can order it delivered because money would not replace it.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Morris v. Sparrow
records.text: Although specific performance is ordinarily not the remedy for an agreement to sell personal property, equity may order delivery of a specific chattel when special circumstances give it a peculiar and unique value that makes damages inadequate.

records.title: Morris v. Sparrow
records.text:
Court: Supreme Court of Arkansas (1956).

The decision is Morris v. Sparrow, 225 Ark. 1019, 287 S.W.2d 583 (1956); Morris refused to deliver Keno on the ground that Sparrow had not done a good job, and the court's rule is that equity may order specific performance of a contract for a chattel when the chattel is unique or damages would be inadequate.

records.title: White v. Benkowski
records.text: Even a deliberate, spiteful breach of contract does not bring punitive damages unless a separate tort is proved. A small award is still real compensation when the loss, like interrupted household water, is real but hard to price.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: White v. Benkowski
records.text: Punitive damages are not available for breach of contract, even a willful and malicious one, where no tort is pleaded or proved; and actual damages need not be proved with mathematical precision to support a modest compensatory award.

records.title: White v. Benkowski
records.text: Court: Supreme Court of Wisconsin (1967). The contractual payment and termination details and the two damages rulings were checked against the page image at printed p. 31.

records.text: Consideration and formalities. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 9–10.

records.title: Assignment 03 · Consideration and formalities
records.text:
Hamer v. Sidway: Requested surrender of lawful freedom can supply consideration even when the promisee benefits from abstaining and the promisor receives no measurable economic gain.

Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.: An invalid claim can still support a settlement through good-faith forbearance. Whether Dyer honestly held the claim remained a factual question, so summary judgment was premature.

Tolosa v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.: The alleged oral promise to delay foreclosure fell within the Texas loan-agreement writing requirement, and the pleaded reliance did not satisfy the specific estoppel exception applied by the court.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement §§ 71, 79, 81; N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1105; CISG Article 11.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 9–10.

records.title: Hamer v. Sidway
records.text: Giving up something you had a legal right to do, because someone promised to pay you for it, is enough to make the promise enforceable. It does not matter whether the promisor gained anything and that quitting was good for you.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hamer v. Sidway
records.text: A promisee's surrender of a legal right at the promisor's request is sufficient consideration, even if the forbearance benefits the promisee and no benefit to the promisor is shown.

records.title: Hamer v. Sidway
records.text:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1891).

Names for the exam: the promisor was William E. Story, the promisee his nephew William E. Story 2d, Sidway was the executor of the uncle's estate, and Louisa Hamer sued as the assignee of the nephew's claim; the case is Hamer v. Sidway, 124 N.Y. 538, 27 N.E. 256 (1891).

Rule in one line: forbearance from a lawful right at the promisor's request is consideration even if the promisor derives no benefit; it is enough that something is promised, done, forborne or suffered by the promisee as consideration for the promise.

records.title: Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.
records.text: Dropping a legal claim can be a real price for a promise even if the claim turns out to be worthless, so long as it was genuinely doubtful or you honestly believed it might win. Settlements made in good faith are protected.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.
records.text: Good-faith forbearance from asserting a claim that later proves invalid can be consideration if the claim was objectively doubtful or the surrendering party honestly believed it might fairly be determined valid.

records.title: Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.
records.text: Court: Supreme Court of Iowa (1986).

records.title: Tolosa v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.
records.text: In Texas, a bank's promise to delay foreclosure on a large loan has to be in a signed writing. Saying you relied on an oral promise does not get around that unless the bank also promised to sign the paperwork.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Tolosa v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.
records.text: Under Texas law, a loan agreement over $50,000, including a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, must be in a signed writing, and promissory estoppel avoids that requirement only if the promisor promised to sign a complying written document.

records.title: Tolosa v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.
records.text: The suit (S.D. Tex., 2011) pleaded fraud, wrongful foreclosure, slander of title, promissory estoppel, unreasonable collection and an accounting; HSBC's motion argued that every claim rested on the alleged oral promise and so was barred by the Texas statute of frauds for loan agreements.

records.title: Assignment 04 · Consideration and interpretation
records.text:
Mattei v. Hopper: A purchaser’s satisfaction condition did not make his promise illusory because he had to exercise his judgment about the proposed leases in good faith.

Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. v. Zoltek Corp.: A requirements contract remained enforceable despite uncertain quantity and purchasing flexibility because exclusivity, a matching right, and good faith constrained the buyer’s choices.

Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon: The exclusive agency agreement carried an implied promise to use reasonable efforts, drawn from its structure and compensation terms, so it was not unenforceable for want of an undertaking by Wood.

Additional assigned materials: UCC § 2-306; Agreement in Wood (SEL).

records.title: Mattei v. Hopper
records.text: A promise that depends on the promisor being satisfied is not an empty promise, because the law requires satisfaction to be judged honestly and in good faith. That duty is enough to make the deal binding on both sides.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Consideration and interpretation big brief, pp. 1–2

records.title: Mattei v. Hopper
records.text: A promise conditioned on the promisor's own satisfaction is not illusory, because the promisor must judge satisfaction honestly and in good faith, and that enforceable duty supplies consideration.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Consideration and interpretation big brief, pp. 1–2

records.title: Mattei v. Hopper
records.text:
Court: Supreme Court of California (1958).

The decision is Mattei v. Hopper, 51 Cal.2d 119, 330 P.2d 625 (Cal. 1958); Mattei was a real-estate developer planning a shopping center on a tract adjacent to Hopper's land, and the rule is that a promise conditioned on the promisor's satisfaction is not illusory because the promisor must exercise that judgment in good faith.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Consideration and interpretation big brief, pp. 1–2

records.title: Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. v. Zoltek Corp.
records.text: A promise to buy all you need from one seller is a real commitment even if you currently need nothing, because the Code requires you to order your actual needs in good faith. That obligation is the price that holds the contract together.

records.title: Assignment 05 · Promissory estoppel and restitution
records.text: Promissory estoppel and restitution. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 05 · Promissory estoppel and restitution
records.text:
Ricketts v. Scothorn: A foreseeable, induced change of position supported enforcement of a gift promise even though quitting work was not the price the grandfather required in exchange.

Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.: The pension lacked bargained-for consideration, but Feinberg’s retirement in reliance on it supported enforcement under promissory estoppel.

Cohen v. Cowles Media Company: The Minnesota court rejected ordinary contract liability in this news-source setting but later upheld a damages award through promissory estoppel after constitutional review.

D & G Stout, Inc. v. Bacardi Imports, Inc.: An at-will distributorship assurance could support recovery for a foregone sale opportunity even though it did not guarantee future distributorship profits.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement § 90.

records.title: Ricketts v. Scothorn
records.text: A grandfather's gift promise had no price attached, so it was not a bargain. But because he meant his granddaughter to quit her job in reliance on it and she did, his estate could not take the promise back for want of consideration.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 1–2

records.title: Ricketts v. Scothorn
records.text: A promisor who intentionally induces the promisee to change position for the worse in reasonable, foreseeable reliance on a gratuitous promise is equitably estopped from asserting lack of consideration.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 1–2

records.title: Ricketts v. Scothorn
records.text: Court: Supreme Court of Nebraska (1898).

records.text: A company's promise of a pension was not paid for by past work or by any promise to keep working. It bound the company anyway, because the employee retired in reliance on it, just as the company should have expected.

records.title: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.
records.text: A promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial action or forbearance, and that does induce it, is binding under Restatement (First) § 90 when injustice can be avoided only by enforcement, even without bargained-for consideration.

records.text: A source who was promised confidentiality and then named in print can sue the newspaper for breaking that promise under promissory estoppel. A general law that applies to everyone does not become unconstitutional because a newspaper is the one who broke the promise.

records.title: Cohen v. Cowles Media Company
records.text: A promise that is not enforceable as a conventional contract may still be enforced under promissory estoppel when it is clear, induces intended and actual detrimental reliance, and must be enforced to avoid injustice; the First Amendment does not bar applying that generally applicable doctrine to the press.

records.title: Cohen v. Cowles Media Company
records.text: 479 N.W.2d 387 (Minn. 1992), after Cohen v. Cowles Media Co., 501 U.S. 663 (1991). On remand the court resolved four questions: Cohen's failure to plead promissory estoppel did not bar the theory, the state constitution's free-press guarantee did not bar it, public policy did not bar enforcement, and the $200,000 compensatory verdict could be reinstated without retrial.

records.text: A promise to keep an at-will relationship going cannot earn you the future profits you hoped for, because it could end at any time. It can still make the promisor pay for a real opportunity you gave up in reliance on it.

records.title: D & G Stout, Inc. v. Bacardi Imports, Inc.
records.text: Under promissory estoppel, a promise of a continuing at-will relationship cannot support recovery of expected future profits, but it can support reliance damages for an existing opportunity the promisee foreseeably surrendered in reliance on it.

records.title: D & G Stout, Inc. v. Bacardi Imports, Inc.
records.text:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1991), applying Indiana law.

923 F.2d 566 (7th Cir. 1991), decided January 31, 1991. After Bacardi withdrew, National's renewed offer was $550,000 lower than its earlier one; the Seventh Circuit held that this lost opportunity could support reliance damages but not lost profits, because an at-will promise cannot be reasonably relied on for future profits, and remanded for trial.

records.text: Assent and intention to be legally bound. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 06 · Assent and intention to be legally bound
records.text:
Lucy v. Zehmer: The sellers’ words and conduct reasonably conveyed a serious land sale, so an undisclosed intention to joke did not defeat enforcement.

Balfour v. Balfour: A husband’s promise of a temporary living allowance while the spouses remained amicably married did not establish the contractual obligation the wife sought to enforce.

Specht v. Netscape Communications Corp.: Downloading free software did not manifest assent to license terms hidden below the download button without reasonably conspicuous notice.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 2(a), (c).

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 11–20.

records.title: Balfour v. Balfour
records.text: Everyday arrangements between a husband and wife living together, like a promised allowance, are not contracts. Courts presume the couple did not intend legal consequences unless the party suing proves otherwise.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 11–20.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Balfour v. Balfour
records.text: An ordinary domestic arrangement between spouses living in amity, such as a promised allowance during a temporary absence, is not an enforceable contract unless the party asserting it proves a contract, expressly or by necessary implication, intended to have legal consequences.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 11–20.

records.title: Balfour v. Balfour
records.text: [1919] 2 K.B. 571 (C.A.), reported as 24 and 25 June 1919. Atkin L.J. reasoned that agreements between spouses living in amity are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations, and that enforcing them would flood the courts; Warrington L.J. rested on the absence of any bargain by the wife, and Duke L.J. warned that enforcing such domestic promises would be a fruitful source of dissension.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 11–20.

records.title: Assignment 07 · Offer and acceptance
records.text: Offer and acceptance. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 07 · Offer and acceptance
records.text:
Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store: A definite advertisement identifying the item, price, time, and first person entitled to buy could be accepted by the requested conduct; an unannounced restriction could not then be added.

Wucherpfennig v. Dooley: A statement of readiness to proceed, coupled with unresolved questions about the price, did not unequivocally accept the land-sale offer.

International Filter Co. v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Co.: The purchaser’s order specified executive approval as sufficient acceptance. The seller’s approval created the contract without a separate notification requirement.

White v. Corlies & Tifft: Uncommunicated preparations using materials equally suitable for other jobs did not accept an offer inviting an agreement to complete the work.

records.title: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store
records.text: An advertisement becomes a binding offer when it is definite enough that nothing is left to negotiate: this item, this price, first come first served. Once a customer meets those terms, the store cannot add new conditions.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Offer and acceptance briefs, pp. 2–3

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store
records.text: A public advertisement is an offer when it is sufficiently definite and leaves no further negotiation necessary to complete the transaction, and the advertiser may not impose new conditions after the offer has been accepted.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Offer and acceptance briefs, pp. 2–3

records.title: Assignment 08 · Irrevocability and formation under Article 2
records.text:
Drennan v. Star Paving Co.: Reasonable reliance on a subcontractor’s bid protected the general contractor’s opportunity to accept it after winning the main contract, even though using the bid was not itself acceptance.

Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp.: A form stating that acceptance was “subject to” its terms did not clearly make the transaction depend on the buyer’s assent to those terms. Whether its added arbitration clause entered the contracts required further findings.

C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. v. Jordan International Co.: An expressly conditional acknowledgment prevented formation through the writings; subsequent performance formed a contract whose terms excluded the unmatched arbitration clause.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement §§ 45, 90; UCC §§ 2-204–2-207; N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1109.

records.title: Assignment 09 · Battle of the forms and later-delivered terms
records.text:
Bayway Refining Co. v. Oxygenated Marketing & Trading A.G.: The buyer failed to establish that an added, customary tax-allocation clause materially altered this merchant contract, so the clause became part of it under § 2-207(2).

Northrop Corp. v. Litronic Industries: The court predicted that Illinois would apply the knockout approach to conflicting warranty terms, although it preferred another interpretation of § 2-207.

Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc.: The Seventh Circuit treated retention beyond the stated return period as acceptance of the seller’s package terms, including arbitration, under its deferred-formation approach.

Klocek v. Gateway, Inc.: Gateway failed to show assent to its package arbitration terms. The court treated the consumer’s order as the offer and the later terms as proposals requiring agreement.

Additional assigned materials: UCC § 2-207; Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 2(b), (c).

records.title: Bayway Refining Co. v. Oxygenated Marketing & Trading A.G.
records.text: Between merchants, UCC § 2-207 has three exceptions to including extra terms: the offer limits acceptance, the term materially alters the deal, or timely objection occurs. Bayway concerns material alteration: the opponent bears that burden, and personal surprise did not suffice against unrebutted industry practice.

records.text: Between merchants under UCC section 2-207(2), additional terms in an acceptance become part of the contract unless an exception applies, and the party opposing inclusion bears the burden of proving that the term materially alters the contract.

OMT lacked the tax-exempt registration that would have avoided the federal excise tax, so Bayway paid it; the court, following the weight of authority elsewhere, held that the party opposing an additional term bears the burden of proving material alteration, defined as surprise or hardship.

records.title: Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc.
records.text: A seller may propose a contract whose written terms arrive with the product and invite acceptance by retention; a buyer who keeps the product beyond the stated return period after an opportunity to read the terms accepts them, including an arbitration clause.

records.title: Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc.
records.text:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1997).

The case’s use of Carnival Cruise should be read with the separate Carnival entry: the Supreme Court treated notice as conceded there, so it did not decide every question about undisclosed later terms.

Judge Easterbrook wrote for a unanimous Seventh Circuit panel, which reversed the district court's refusal to compel arbitration; the Hills' underlying complaint alleged that the computer's defects made Gateway a racketeer under RICO, with mail and wire fraud as predicate offenses (Hill v. records.title: Enforceable promise and sources of contract law
records.text: An enforceable promise is a commitment for which the law supplies a remedy when it is broken, or otherwise recognizes a duty to perform.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 1–10. Open assigned page 1.

records.title: Enforceable promise and sources of contract law
records.text:
Identify the exact commitment, its maker, and the governing law. Common-law decisions, enacted statutes, and persuasive restatements have different authority; Article 2 governs within its sales scope, with ordinary law supplementing it unless displaced. Consideration and promissory estoppel supply different possible grounds for enforcing a promise. A writing requirement, a defect in bargaining, or public policy can still bar enforcement, and a valid obligation does not guarantee an order to perform.

Restatement § 1 supplies the introductory definition. The course separates identifying a promise, establishing its enforceability, and choosing a remedy. It introduces reasons for enforcement and breach remedies before formation, without treating one philosophical account as the entire law.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 1–10. Open assigned page 1.

records.title: Promise, prediction, description, and commendation
records.text: A promise communicates a commitment to bring about a result or take an action. A prediction communicates an expectation about what is likely to happen.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 2–8. Open assigned page 2.

records.title: Promise, prediction, description, and commendation
records.text: Read the statement in its actual setting. In Hawkins, the doctor’s specific guarantee and repeated solicitation could support a commitment, while estimates of recovery time remained predictions. In Bayliner, performance figures concerned a differently equipped boat and promotional praise did not warrant a particular speed. Specificity, connection to the actual subject, and place in the transaction matter. A disappointing result alone does not establish a promise; identify what a reasonable recipient understood the speaker to undertake and the supporting evidence. The textbook’s theories then ask why an identified assurance should receive legal enforcement.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 2–8. Open assigned page 2.

records.title: Expectation interest
records.text: The expectation interest places the injured party in the position performance of the promise would have produced, subject to the rules limiting recovery.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 11–26. Open assigned page 11.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 34–36. Open assigned page 34.

records.title: Expectation interest
records.text:
Identify the promised position, the actual position, avoided costs, and other qualifying losses before adding figures. Hawkins compares the promised and actual hand; ordinary pain of the contemplated operation belonged to the performance the patient agreed to undergo. Naval Institute estimates lost hardcover profits rather than automatically transferring the breacher’s gains. Sullivan shows how different remedial interests can share components.

The early chapters introduce these distinctions. Later cases develop completion cost, lost profits, mitigation, foreseeability, certainty, and agreed remedies. Those limits must be applied before selecting a dollar measure.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 11–26. Open assigned page 11.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 34–36. Open assigned page 34.

records.title: Reliance interest and opportunities forgone
records.text: The reliance interest concerns losses caused by changing position in reliance on a promise or agreement, measured against the position without that reliance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 13–21. Open assigned page 13.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 120–130. Open assigned page 120.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 138–143. Open assigned page 138.

records.title: Reliance interest and opportunities forgone
records.text:
Compare the claimant’s position with the position without the induced change, including provable opportunities forgone. D&G Stout concerns a lost opportunity to sell the business, distinct from hoped-for distributorship profits; Sullivan concerns expenses and physical or emotional injury associated with surgery. Hayes asks whether retirement decided before a pension promise was actually induced by it.

Promissory estoppel is a possible basis of liability; reliance is also a possible measure of relief. Connect the change to the assurance. The doctrinal basis alone does not settle the amount or permit recovery twice for the same loss.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 13–21. Open assigned page 13.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 120–130. Open assigned page 120.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 138–143. Open assigned page 138.

records.title: Restitution as a remedial interest
records.text: The restitution interest concerns restoration of benefits conferred on another party, rather than the full value of expected performance or every loss incurred in reliance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 18–21. Open assigned page 18.
Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 12–13

records.title: Restitution as a remedial interest
records.text:
Identify the benefit, its recipient, and the legal reason for restoring it. In the surgery example, the doctor’s fee benefits the doctor; a hospital payment may be a reliance expense without benefiting that defendant. Algernon Blair later concerns the reasonable value of work and equipment supplied to a contractor. Mobil Oil illustrates restitution following breach despite doubts about the venture’s profitability.

Restitution can accompany a breached agreement or arise independently from unjust enrichment, introduced at pp. 145–146. It does not automatically reimburse every preparation expense or confer the full expected performance value.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 18–21. Open assigned page 18.
Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 12–13

records.title: Disgorgement and defendant’s gains
records.text: Disgorgement asks about gains attributable to the wrong rather than solely about the injured party’s loss.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 20–26. Open assigned page 20.

records.title: Disgorgement and defendant’s gains
records.text: The text presents it alongside expectation, reliance, and restitutionary interests. Naval Institute limits the attempt to turn a licensee’s breach into a copyright-profits recovery. The hypothetical possibility of a more profitable alternative use does not itself transfer all those profits to the original promisee. The legal basis for gain recovery must be identified before selecting a defendant-profit number.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 20–26. Open assigned page 20.

records.title: Specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text: Specific performance is a court order requiring the promised performance. An injunction may similarly restrain conduct that violates a contractual obligation.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 26–30. Open assigned page 26.

records.title: Specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text:
The assigned cases ask whether damages adequately protect the claimant and whether the requested order can be administered. Morris concerns a horse the claimant personally trained; Klein concerns an aircraft with available substitutes; Walgreen concerns difficult-to-measure competitive injury from violating a lease restriction. The notes compare attachment to a pet and a cannery’s inability to obtain enough tomatoes in time. Uniqueness matters through difficulty of substitution, not merely a category label.

Specific relief depends on the transaction and equitable considerations. An enforceable contract does not automatically entitle its claimant to it. Personal services raise distinct concerns: restraining competing performance differs from affirmatively compelling service.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 26–30. Open assigned page 26.

records.title: Nominal and actual damages
records.text: A nominal award recognizes breach without proven actual loss; a small actual loss remains compensatory.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 30–34. Open assigned page 30.

records.title: Nominal and actual damages
records.text: White v. Benkowski distinguishes a $1 nominal award from the jury’s $10 for actual inconvenience. Size alone does not determine the category. Pecuniary proof is not the only possible evidence of actual harm. Neither a nominal nor a compensatory award automatically supplies a basis for punitive damages.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 30–34. Open assigned page 30.

records.title: Punitive damages and independent torts
records.text: The assigned materials distinguish compensatory contract relief from punishment and from separately actionable tort conduct.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 30–34. Open assigned page 30.

records.title: Punitive damages and independent torts
records.text: White rejects punishment for the malicious contract breach presented. The accompanying notes discuss exceptional tort settings and evolving decisions, including insurance and alleged bad-faith denials of contractual obligations. Those historical examples should not be compressed into either “punitive damages always follow bad faith” or a statement that no conduct connected to a contract could ever support punitive relief.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 30–34. Open assigned page 30.

records.title: Economic analysis of breach and remedies
records.text: The assigned introduction tests how damages affect the allocation of a promised resource.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 34–36. Open assigned page 34.

records.title: Economic analysis of breach and remedies
records.text: In the machine example, a seller’s cost is $300, the price $600, and the original buyer’s value $1,000. A second buyer willing to pay $1,200 changes the allocation question. Paying the original buyer’s $400 expectation can leave the seller better off while protecting that buyer’s modeled value. These are stipulated values in an example, not measured welfare in real litigation. Distinguish a gain with actual compensation from potential compensation, and account for the institutional costs discussed in Remedies in Action. The later pages of this economic discussion are not assigned until a later unit.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 34–36. Open assigned page 34.

records.title: Remedies in action: cost, institutions, and nonlegal enforcement
records.text: The practical value of an entitlement depends on the cost and means of enforcing it.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 44–48. Open assigned page 44.

records.title: Remedies in action: cost, institutions, and nonlegal enforcement
records.text: Litigation costs, attorney fees, delay, collectability, and bargaining position can separate legal damages from net recovery. The text considers business reputation, repeat dealings, and private dispute institutions as additional enforcement mechanisms. Macaulay’s business observations, Galanter’s repeat-player analysis, Mentschikoff’s arbitration discussion, and Bernstein’s private-ordering work approach different parts of this problem. A source’s descriptive observation is distinct from a recommendation to substitute a private system for courts.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 44–48. Open assigned page 44.

records.title: Consideration: bargained-for exchange
records.text: Consideration is a performance or return promise that the parties bargain for in exchange for the promise whose enforcement is sought.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 49–68. Open assigned page 49.

records.title: Consideration: bargained-for exchange
records.text:
Identify what each promisor sought and what the other party gave or promised in exchange. The return may be an act, forbearance, or a change in a legal relationship. Hamer concerns requested surrender of lawful freedoms; Dyer concerns forbearance of a disputed claim. A benefit or detriment identifies a possible object of exchange, but reciprocal inducement is still required.

In Feinberg, past work and continued work not required as the pension’s price did not establish the bargain. Action caused by a promise may instead support reliance. Generosity or other motives can coexist with an exchange; adequacy, nominal recitals, and formal substitutes present separate questions.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 49–68. Open assigned page 49.

records.title: Legal detriment and surrender of freedom
records.text: A legal detriment occurs when a person gives up a legal freedom or assumes an obligation as part of an exchange. It can exist even when the choice benefits that person.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 54–60. Open assigned page 54.

records.title: Legal detriment and surrender of freedom
records.text: In Hamer, abstaining from drinking and tobacco could improve the nephew’s health while restricting his legal freedom. Consideration therefore did not depend on whether he became financially or physically worse off. Identify the surrendered right or assumed obligation and connect it to the requested exchange. A detriment merely occurring after a promise, without being sought as its price, requires a separate reliance analysis.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 54–60. Open assigned page 54.

records.title: Adequacy, nominal consideration, and sham exchange
records.text: Adequacy concerns the comparative value of the things exchanged. The existence of consideration concerns whether the parties actually bargained for an exchange.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 58–68. Open assigned page 58.

records.title: Adequacy, nominal consideration, and sham exchange
records.text:
Restatement § 79 separates the value of an exchange from its existence under § 71. A genuinely desired item of slight value may be consideration; a token transfer or recital masking a gift raises the distinct question whether there was any real exchange. The first and second Restatements’ nominal-dollar examples prevent treating form alone as decisive.

Unequal value, lack of exchange, unconscionability, and public policy are different objections. Public-gift restrictions discussed in the notes also raise constitutional questions that ordinary consideration doctrine does not resolve.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 58–68. Open assigned page 58.

records.title: Motive and reciprocal inducement
records.text: A party’s personal reason for contracting can differ from the performance or promise that serves as the agreed exchange.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 58–61. Open assigned page 58.

records.title: Motive and reciprocal inducement
records.text:
Restatement § 81 and Holmes’s reciprocal-inducement formulation distinguish why a party desires an outcome from what it requests as the price. Someone may paint for money while also seeking reputation, enjoyment, or friendship. Affection or generosity can likewise coexist with a bargain; exchange need not be either party’s only motive.

A benefit or induced act not sought in exchange does not become consideration merely because it helps explain the transaction. Identify the agreed return rather than every consequence of the promise.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 58–61. Open assigned page 58.

records.title: Forbearance of claims and settlement
records.text: Giving up or delaying a legal claim can be consideration for a settlement promise, subject to limits concerning the claim and the claimant’s belief in it.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 62–68. Open assigned page 62.

records.title: Forbearance of claims and settlement
records.text:
Dyer concerns a claim assumed legally invalid. Under the Iowa court’s approach, invalidity alone did not defeat consideration if the claimant honestly believed it could be valid; good faith remained for determination on remand. Restatement § 74 distinguishes doubt about a claim from honest belief in a claim that proves invalid. The casebook records more demanding formulations in other jurisdictions.

Identify the surrendered claim, the promised return, and the claimant’s belief when bargaining. Fiege supplies a paternity comparison. Settlement policy does not protect knowingly baseless harassment, and litigation certification duties or other limits may apply separately.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 62–68. Open assigned page 62.

records.title: Past action and the requirement of exchange
records.text: An act completed before a later promise ordinarily cannot be the bargained-for return for that promise, because the later promise did not seek the completed act in exchange.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 69–74. Open assigned page 69.
Fall 2026 supplement, p. 9: N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1105.

records.title: Past action and the requirement of exchange
records.text:
Feinberg’s earlier service explained gratitude but could not have been induced by the later pension promise. Her additional eighteen months of work were also not demanded as the resolution’s price; retirement required separate promissory-estoppel analysis. The benefactor/naming problem varies timing and separate promises. Mills introduces moral obligation on its opening assigned page, while the remaining opinion lies outside those ranges.

New York General Obligations Law § 5-1105 supplies a distinct signed-writing route for specified past-consideration promises. Read its requirements in the supplement rather than assuming that mentioning past services always suffices.

records.title: Illusory promises and constrained discretion
records.text: An illusory promise appears to commit its maker while leaving the maker unrestricted freedom to perform nothing. Such words may fail to provide consideration for the other party’s promise.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 101–117. Open assigned page 101.

records.title: Illusory promises and constrained discretion
records.text:
Examine the obligation imposed by the language, context, and governing law. Mattei limits satisfaction by honest judgment; Structural Polymer constrains requirements through good faith and the supply/price-matching arrangement; Wood implies reasonable efforts from exclusivity and revenue sharing. A conditional or flexible obligation can therefore supply a real commitment.

Identify the limit on choice before calling a promise illusory. A termination right, condition, or uncertain quantity does not automatically leave the maker free to perform nothing.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 101–117. Open assigned page 101.

records.title: Satisfaction conditions: reasonableness and good faith
records.text: A satisfaction clause makes a party’s duty to perform depend on being satisfied with a specified performance or circumstance. The applicable standard limits how that judgment may be exercised.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 102–107. Open assigned page 102.

records.title: Satisfaction conditions: reasonableness and good faith
records.text:
Mattei distinguishes commercial quality or mechanical utility, ordinarily assessed through reasonableness, from taste or judgment requiring honest good-faith dissatisfaction. Evaluating proposed leases involved rent, tenant quality, duration, restrictions, and other interdependent business considerations; dissatisfaction with them differed from regretting the purchase price. Gibson later concerns a portrait.

Identify the subject of satisfaction and the standard the decision actually applies. The distinction does not make every commercial judgment objectively reviewable.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 102–107. Open assigned page 102.

records.title: Requirements and output contracts
records.text: A requirements contract measures quantity by the buyer’s needs; an output contract measures quantity by the seller’s production. The agreed arrangement and good-faith limits constrain those quantities.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 107–113. Open assigned page 107.

records.title: Requirements and output contracts
records.text: Structural Polymer explains why small or temporarily zero requirements do not necessarily make an agreement illusory: good faith, exclusivity, and the price-matching arrangement constrained choice. UCC § 2-306 supplies further limits concerning stated estimates and disproportionate demands. A later claim of manipulated quantities concerns performance of an obligation, distinct from whether one existed at formation. The breadcrumb-output problem asks whether shutting production after losses is consistent with the bargain.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 107–113. Open assigned page 107.

records.title: Implied efforts in exclusive dealings
records.text: An implied efforts obligation requires a party to take steps toward the contract’s objective even though the agreement does not state that obligation in an express sentence.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 113–117. Open assigned page 113.

records.title: Implied efforts in exclusive dealings
records.text:
Wood reads exclusive control, contingent compensation, the agent’s organization, accounting, and related provisions together to imply reasonable efforts. The court does not insert an obligation merely because the arrangement seems unfair. The casebook compares the sales provision’s “best efforts” with Wood’s “reasonable efforts” and links the full agreement in the Selections.

Bloor later examines an express best-efforts promise to promote a beer brand. Determine what the particular agreement requires and which conduct complies; exclusivity does not automatically demand unlimited spending or maximum possible performance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 113–117. Open assigned page 113.

records.title: Good faith in the early enforceability cases
records.text: Good faith constrains the exercise of a contractual choice or the performance of an obligation in ways connected to the parties’ agreement. Its content depends on the issue and governing law.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 102–117. Open assigned page 102.

records.title: Good faith in the early enforceability cases
records.text:
Good faith helps identify the obligation that exists for consideration purposes: genuine satisfaction or dissatisfaction in Mattei and constrained requirements in Structural Polymer. The later Good faith and Contractual discretion entries examine promised evidentiary review in Dalton, commercial conduct in Market Street, and promotion in Bloor.

Keep those applications and their governing law distinct. Good faith does not authorize invention of any term considered fair, and the supplement includes jurisdictions resisting a general implied duty. These early cases are not a complete outline of the later performance unit.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 102–117. Open assigned page 102.

records.title: Formalities and substitutes for consideration
records.text: A formality can have evidentiary, cautionary, channeling, clarifying, or managerial functions.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 49–53. Open assigned page 49.

Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 371–383. Open assigned page 371.

records.title: Formalities and substitutes for consideration
records.text: The seal’s historical force and its later limits differ from a modern writing used as evidence. The notes compare proposals to enforce written promises, statutory presumptions, and the Pennsylvania written-obligations approach described by the book. A signature does not everywhere eliminate the bargain requirement. Conversely, a writing requirement such as a statute of frauds can limit enforcement even where there is a genuine bargain. The specified jurisdiction and provision matter.

records.title: Promissory estoppel
records.text: Promissory estoppel can make a promise binding when it foreseeably induces action or forbearance and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice. The remedy may be limited as justice requires.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 120–130. Open assigned page 120.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 135–144. Open assigned page 135.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 252–259. Open assigned page 252.

records.title: Promissory estoppel
records.text:
Identify the promise, the action it could reasonably be expected to induce, the action actually induced, and why leaving it unenforced would produce injustice. Ricketts concerns leaving work, Feinberg retirement, Cohen confidentiality, and D&G Stout a lost business-sale opportunity. Drennan protects an opportunity to accept a subcontractor’s bid rather than treating reliance as completed acceptance.

The two Restatement § 90 formulations differ, including the later language allowing relief limited as justice requires. Distinguish enforceability from the amount recovered. D&G Stout does not guarantee indefinite future profits, and case-specific holdings and jurisdictional formulations remain separate.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 120–130. Open assigned page 120.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 135–144. Open assigned page 135.

records.title: From equitable to promissory estoppel
records.text: Equitable estoppel can prevent a person from asserting a position inconsistent with an earlier representation or conduct on which another person reasonably relied to their detriment.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 121–126. Open assigned page 121.
Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 10–11

records.title: From equitable to promissory estoppel
records.text:
Traditional equitable estoppel often concerns representations about existing facts; promissory estoppel concerns future commitments. Ricketts uses the older terminology when a gift promise induces the granddaughter to leave employment, then prevents reliance on the absence of consideration.

The notes trace protection of reliance through family land improvements, gratuitous bailments, and charity. Modern § 90 makes the future promise explicit. Preserve the court’s historical language without treating those labels alone as a complete account of modern elements.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 121–126. Open assigned page 121.

records.title: Charitable subscriptions and reliance
records.text: The charitable-pledge materials separate bargained-for duties, actual reliance, and the second Restatement’s special provision.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 124–130. Open assigned page 124.

records.title: Charitable subscriptions and reliance
records.text: Allegheny College finds an implied undertaking associated with a named memorial fund and is treated as a consideration case despite its important estoppel discussion. The first § 90 formulation required definite and substantial induced conduct. The second adds a provision for charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements without proof that the promise induced action or forbearance. The book’s decisions and questions do not establish uniform state adoption of that exception.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 124–130. Open assigned page 124.

records.title: At-will relationships and reliance loss
records.text: A relationship that either party may end can still produce a separate reliance injury when a specific assurance induces the other party to give up an identifiable opportunity.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 138–143. Open assigned page 138.

records.title: At-will relationships and reliance loss
records.text:
D&G Stout distinguishes a concrete lost business-sale opportunity from profits hoped for over an indefinite distributorship. Its employment comparison separates moving costs and old wages forgone while preparing to move from new wages expected after the job begins. The appellate ruling permitted the claim to proceed and left reasonable timing and proof for trial; the later trial result is reported separately.

Identify the specific assurance and opportunity surrendered. Reliance protection does not make an at-will relationship permanent or compensate every disappointment following termination.

records.title: Restitution as an independent basis of liability
records.text: Unjust enrichment concerns a benefit that a defendant has received at another person’s expense and that the law regards as unjust to retain without payment or return.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 145–146. Open assigned page 145.
Brief · Promissory estoppel and restitution big brief, pp. 12–13

records.title: Restitution as an independent basis of liability
records.text:
Identify who received what benefit, why it was supplied, and why retention would be unjust. The introduction compares mistaken payments, mistakenly performed services, and property improvements with services deliberately forced on an unwilling recipient. Where bargaining is feasible, an officious provider ordinarily cannot make the recipient pay merely by supplying a benefit. Emergency intervention presents a different issue.

This liability can arise without an enforceable promise. Restitution following breach separately depends on an existing agreement and its termination. Cotnam begins on the last assigned page; its full reasoning is outside the assignment.

records.title: Quasi-contract, quantum meruit, and restitution
records.text: Quantum meruit is a claim measured by the reasonable value of services for which payment is legally due. Its application depends on the basis of the claim and the parties’ circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 145–146. Open assigned page 145.

records.title: Quasi-contract, quantum meruit, and restitution
records.text:
Algernon Blair permits recovery of the reasonable value of labor and equipment furnished before justified cessation, although completing the subcontract would have produced a loss. The measure concerns services received by the defendant, not every expense the claimant incurred.

The casebook notes imprecise usage: quasi-contract concerns recovery without a true contractual undertaking, quantum meruit historically the worth of services, and quantum valebant the worth of goods. State whether the basis is a promise, actual agreement, or unjust enrichment before choosing contract price, market value, or expenditures as the measure.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 145–146. Open assigned page 145.

records.title: Assent, consent, and legal enforceability
records.text: Mutual assent concerns what the parties communicated as their agreement. Voluntary consent and an intention concerning legal enforceability raise related but distinct questions.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 169–173. Open assigned page 169.

records.title: Assent, consent, and legal enforceability
records.text:
Separate communicated agreement to an exchange, voluntary participation, and manifested intention concerning legal enforcement. A coerced exchange can be understood by both parties yet remain defective; capacity and impermissible pressure concern consent. Restatement § 21 generally does not demand affirmative intent to incur legal obligation, but manifested intent to remain unbound can matter. Courts sometimes use “mutual assent” for more than one issue.

Lucy concerns seriousness, Specht notice and downloading, and the later fraud and duress cases bargaining defects. Interpretation asks what the agreement means. The course index connects these distinct applications without treating them as identical assent holdings.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 169–173. Open assigned page 169.

records.title: Objective interpretation of assent
records.text: Objective interpretation of assent asks what a party’s words and conduct reasonably communicated in their actual context, including relevant knowledge shared by the parties.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 171–187. Open assigned page 171.

records.title: Objective interpretation of assent
records.text:
Lucy protects a genuine, reasonable understanding of a serious land sale despite a claimed private joke. Keller involves shared knowledge of a joke; Leonard concerns what a reasonable viewer would understand an advertisement to mean. Specht asks what downloading communicates when terms are hidden.

Context, notice, and relevant shared knowledge matter. The scholarly debate concerns how far an objective account should exclude evidence of actual intention; it does not establish that subjective knowledge never affects the communication’s meaning.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 171–187. Open assigned page 171.

records.title: Social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text: Intention concerning legal enforceability asks whether the parties’ undertaking belongs to a relationship the law will treat as contractually binding in the circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 183–187. Open assigned page 183.

records.title: Social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text:
The readings distinguish moral or social seriousness from legal enforceability. Balfour’s judges give distinct reasons about a domestic allowance; its opinion is in supplement pp. 11–20 and its own brief. Cohen’s earlier decision rejects ordinary contract liability in the source-reporter setting, while the later decision permits promissory-estoppel recovery.

Social rides, family arrangements, medical reassurance, and unmarried partners’ ability to contract raise different contextual questions. Identify the particular court’s ground rather than treating moral importance, marriage, or informality as a complete answer.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 183–187. Open assigned page 183.

records.title: Preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text: A preliminary agreement records commitments while parties still anticipate further negotiation or a later document. Its legal effect depends on what they have already agreed to undertake.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 187–191. Open assigned page 187.
Brief · Definiteness and preliminary agreements briefs, pp. 1–2

records.title: Preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text:
The Tribune discussion distinguishes a settled transaction awaiting documentation from a limited commitment to negotiate remaining terms in good faith within an agreed framework. The latter does not guarantee a final deal. Relevant factors include an express reservation of execution, settled terms, partial performance, and whether that transaction usually receives a signed writing.

A letter of intent can disclaim the ultimate bargain while binding a negotiating process. Channel Home later examines withdrawal of property from the market; Dixon and Cyberchron concern reliance before a final transaction. Identify whether the claim seeks the final bargain, performance of the process, or protection of a narrower assurance.

records.title: Offer and the power of acceptance
records.text: An offer communicates willingness to enter a bargain in a way that reasonably gives the recipient the power to conclude it by accepting.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 191–192. Open assigned page 191.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 198–205. Open assigned page 198.

records.title: Offer and the power of acceptance
records.text:
Under Restatement § 24, ask whether the recipient’s assent would finish the bargain or whether further assent by the proposer remains necessary. Read specific language, audience, context, and unresolved decisions; a quotation, order, advertisement, or document titled “proposal” has no automatic legal effect.

Lefkowitz’s definite first-come advertisement differs from an invitation for orders. International Filter shows that drafting the form does not necessarily make its drafter the offeror. Identify the actual offeror because the offer determines the response capable of acceptance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 191–192. Open assigned page 191.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 198–205. Open assigned page 198.

records.title: Advertisements, quotations, catalogs, and offers
records.text: Specific limitations can make an advertisement an offer, while many advertisements invite further orders.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 198–205. Open assigned page 198.

records.title: Advertisements, quotations, catalogs, and offers
records.text: Lefkowitz specifies an item, a price, and a first-come mechanism that leaves nothing open. The Moulton note asks how an unbounded quantity affects a quotation’s apparent commitment. The coin-allocation problem tests whether receipt or confirmation of an order is acceptance. Geismar illustrates that a consumer statute may supply relief even if ordinary offer-and-acceptance analysis supplies no contract.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 198–205. Open assigned page 198.

records.title: Auction formation and reserve terms
records.text: The bidding and closing mechanism determines which act creates the sale.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 203–205. Open assigned page 203.

records.title: Auction formation and reserve terms
records.text: The textbook discusses the ordinary role of bids as offers, the auctioneer’s completion of the sale, and limits on withdrawal in an auction without reserve. It distinguishes the owner’s withdrawal question from a bidder’s ability to retract before completion. An analogy to a land auction is not a direct application of Article 2 to land. The Foley problem asks about an agent’s mistaken listing of a reserve auction as no-reserve.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 203–205. Open assigned page 203.

records.title: Rewards: knowledge and invited performance
records.text: A reward claimant’s awareness of an offer differs from the claimant’s motive for performing.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 205. Open assigned page 205.

records.title: Rewards: knowledge and invited performance
records.text: Broadnax is used for the need to act in response to a known reward offer. Knowledge can allow an acceptance even if the performer has other motives. The notes ask what happens when a claimant learns of the offer after beginning the requested activity and point to Restatement § 51. They do not invite dispensing with notice merely because the advertiser benefited.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 205. Open assigned page 205.

records.title: Acceptance and invited method
records.text: Acceptance is the offeree’s manifestation of agreement in the manner invited or required by an offer while the power to accept remains open.

Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 227–229. Open assigned page 227.

records.title: Acceptance and invited method
records.text:
Identify the offer, the invited return promise or performance, the responsive act, any notice requirement, and the time of effectiveness while the power to accept remains open. Wucherpfennig finds further negotiation, International Filter stipulated executive approval, White insufficient communicative preparation, and Ever-Tite commencement expressly invited by the form.

For goods, the UCC changes some common-law rules about acceptance methods and nonmatching terms. Neither readiness to proceed nor any expenditure automatically supplies the acceptance the offer invites.
