records.title: Acceptance and notification
records.text: Notice of acceptance communicates to the offeror that the invited response has occurred. Whether notice is required, and when, depends on the offer and the method of acceptance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 217–225. Open assigned page 217.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 227–229. Open assigned page 227.

records.title: Acceptance and notification
records.text:
An offer seeking a promise ordinarily requires an appropriate communication unless it dispenses with notice. International Filter makes executive approval the accepting act without further notice, although its later letter would have sufficed. White requires a manifestation placed in a reasonable course of communication.

For performance-only offers, distinguish completing the act from notifying the offeror. Carlill dispenses with advance notice; Bishop requires notice where the offeror would not promptly learn of the act. Keep acceptance, notification, and their effective times separate.

records.title: Beginning performance and mere preparation
records.text: Beginning the performance invited by an offer can have a different legal effect from merely preparing to perform. The wording of the offer and the actual conduct determine the distinction.

records.title: Beginning performance and mere preparation
records.text:
White’s work on ordinary materials usable for other jobs did not adequately communicate acceptance. Ever-Tite’s loading and dispatch began performance under a form expressly inviting commencement. The offer’s wording and the conduct determine whether work is acceptance or preparation.

Restatement § 45 protects beginning or tendering invited performance of a performance-only offer. Section 87(2), discussed through Drennan, separately addresses preparatory reliance on an offer seeking a return promise. These routes do not make every expenditure an acceptance.

records.title: Silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
records.text: Silence ordinarily does not accept an offer. Prior dealings, knowingly accepted services, or other circumstances can give silence a different significance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 235–236. Open assigned page 235.
Brief · Offer and acceptance briefs, pp. 10–11

records.title: Silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
records.text:
An offeror ordinarily cannot impose acceptance by declaring that failure to reject counts as assent. Hobbs examines retained eel skins after similar transactions; American Bronze examines a longstanding ordering-and-production practice. These differ from unsolicited goods and from a negative-option subscription already authorized by the recipient.

Silence about additional goods-contract terms can have a statutory effect distinct from accepting an offer. Under Klocek’s formation account and record, retention did not establish express agreement to the newly supplied consumer terms.

records.title: Contract formation and civil-rights claims
records.text: The legal significance of formation can extend beyond a claim for breach.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 236–238. Open assigned page 236.

records.title: Contract formation and civil-rights claims
records.text: Perry’s procedural remand examined when a salon appointment became a contract under the then-existing interpretation of § 1981. The book immediately explains that the 1991 amendment extended the provision to performance, modification, termination, and enjoyment of contractual benefits. That historical limitation must not be taught as the later statute’s coverage. The Barfield change-making example asks whether the bank transaction contained consideration; the assigned passage presents the question without a full resolution.

records.text: The chapter separates lapse, revocation, rejection, and death or incapacity, then considers communication timing.

records.title: Termination of the power of acceptance
records.text: An offer can expire by its stated limit or a reasonable time. Revocation is the offeror’s withdrawal and normally requires communication; public offers create a publicity problem. Rejection is the offeree’s act and is distinct from mere inquiry. Death and incapacity have specified effects for ordinary offers, with an option-contract qualification. The mailbox rule addresses when an otherwise proper acceptance becomes effective, rather than whether the response contains assent.

records.title: Lapse and reasonable time
records.text: An unstated acceptance period is measured in the transaction’s circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 238–240. Open assigned page 238.

records.title: Lapse and reasonable time
records.text: A face-to-face offer ordinarily ends with the conversation, as the Akers discussion illustrates. Rapid changes in market price can shorten reasonable time. Loring’s reward responded to a past emergency, whereas Carr’s reward concerned possible future crimes. The settlement-countdown problem varies procedural circumstances and the timing of acceptance. A later unfavorable verdict does not itself supply an agreed expiration term.

records.title: Revocation: communication and public offers
records.text: Revocation withdraws an ordinary offer before effective acceptance, subject to limits such as an option.

Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 246–248. Open assigned page 246.

records.title: Revocation: communication and public offers
records.text: Hoover’s words could communicate unwillingness without the technical word “revoke.” For public rewards, equivalent publicity can serve where personal communication to every reader is infeasible. The notes ask whether removal of a posted notice achieves that purpose and whether the underlying offer was continuing. A stated period and an enforceable promise to hold open are different inquiries; the firm-offer and option provisions address the latter.

Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 246–248. Open assigned page 246.

records.title: Option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text: An option contract protects an offeree’s opportunity to accept an offer by limiting the offeror’s power to revoke it. It is distinct from acceptance of the underlying transaction.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 242. Open assigned page 242.
Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 246–259. Open assigned page 246.

records.title: Option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text:
The course presents four routes: consideration for holding an offer open, a merchant firm offer, beginning performance under § 45, and qualifying reliance associated with § 87(2), illustrated by Drennan. Each has its own predicates and duration. A stated deadline may establish expiry without preventing earlier revocation.

Identify why the power to accept is protected and whether it has been exercised. Keep the underlying terms, holding-open obligation, acceptance, and later breach remedies separate. Ordinary death or rejection rules should not automatically be transferred to an option.

records.title: Merchant status and the particular UCC provision
records.text: A merchant is a person whose dealings, occupation, or attributed professional knowledge meet the UCC’s definition for the provision being applied.

records.title: Merchant status and the particular UCC provision
records.text:
Read § 2-104 with the particular provision: the relevant expertise may concern goods, business practices, or both. Firm offers and the § 2-207 between-merchants rule have distinct requirements. A business buying equipment for its own use is not classified solely by whether it resells that product; Hill also cautions that commercial use of retail software does not itself establish software-merchant status.

Article 2 can govern a consumer sale even when a merchant-only provision does not. Outside the between-merchants incorporation rule, additional terms instead raise a proposal-and-assent question.

records.title: Scope of Article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text: Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code supplies statutory rules for transactions in goods. Identifying its scope determines which formation, interpretation, and remedial rules govern.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 248–250. Open assigned page 248.

records.title: Scope of Article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text:
Identify movable goods and examine any accompanying services or other property. The readings compare a sale with installation, a navigation device with continuing services, and a radio business with mixed assets. Bonebrake uses predominant purpose, Foster separates portions, and Anthony Pools examines the gravamen of the claim.

The book reproduces 2022 hybrid-transaction amendments and describes enactment as early-stage in April 2023; that publication-time account does not establish 2026 adoption. Section 1-103 permits supplemental law unless displaced, and the CISG can govern qualifying international sales. Merchant status is a separate inquiry affecting particular provisions.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 248–250. Open assigned page 248.

records.title: Death and incapacity: ordinary offers and options
records.text: The book reports termination of an ordinary power of acceptance on death or incapacity, with a qualification for option contracts.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 259. Open assigned page 259.

records.title: Death and incapacity: ordinary offers and options
records.text: Restatement § 48 is discussed as applying even without the offeree’s knowledge. The commentary criticizes the rule’s conceptual fit with objective assent and explains the drafting history. The offeror’s death does not terminate the offeree’s power under an option contract. Death after a contract already exists raises a separate question about performance, which is reserved for a later chapter. The funeral-promise problem begins here but continues beyond the assigned page.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 259. Open assigned page 259.

records.title: Mailbox rule and overtaking communications
records.text: A properly invited acceptance may take effect on dispatch, while revocation ordinarily takes effect on receipt.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 261–263. Open assigned page 261.

records.title: Mailbox rule and overtaking communications
records.text: The book traces the rule to Adams v. Lindsell and explains the dependable basis it gives the offeree. A medium not invited by the offer can change the result. Dispatch can also end the offeree’s power to reject, producing the problem of a rejection arriving before a previously mailed acceptance. The commentary raises estoppel where the offeror relies on the earlier-arriving rejection. The opening of U.S. Life v. Wilson is assigned, but its complete reasoning on the payment mechanism is not.

records.title: Mirror-image rule and counteroffers
records.text: The traditional approach treats a qualified acceptance as rejection and a new offer, subject to interpretation of the actual response.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 269–272. Open assigned page 269.

records.title: Mirror-image rule and counteroffers
records.text: Ardente makes the buyer’s request about furnishings a condition. The notes contrast terms already implied in the offer and unqualified acceptance accompanied by a merely precatory request. State v. Rios distinguishes inquiry about a better offer from rejection of the existing one. Different language does not mechanically mean a counteroffer; ask whether the response makes agreement dependent on the proposed change.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 269–272. Open assigned page 269.

records.title: Last-shot analysis
records.text: Under traditional counteroffer analysis, subsequent performance can appear to accept the last communicated set of terms.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 270–274. Open assigned page 270.

records.title: Last-shot analysis
records.text: The rule can favor the party whose form comes last, even though the recipient never read its boilerplate. Mid-South Plant Services illustrates factual disagreement over whose proposal performance accepted. The majority and dissent differ about whether that inference was suitable for summary judgment. Section 2-207 changes the sales analysis by separating contract formation from incorporation of unmatched terms.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 270–274. Open assigned page 270.

records.title: Boilerplate, dickered terms, and the battle of forms
records.text: Boilerplate consists of standard terms reused across transactions, often while the parties separately negotiate price, quantity, or other transaction-specific matters.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 272–276. Open assigned page 272.

records.title: Boilerplate, dickered terms, and the battle of forms
records.text:
Macaulay’s account describes quotations, purchase orders, and acknowledgments whose operating personnel check item, quantity, price, and delivery while overlooking clauses prepared by lawyers or copied from other forms. Section 2-207 responds to some resulting differences without dispensing with a definite acceptance or making radical commercial changes irrelevant.

Consumer cases separately address notice, reasonable expectations, and unconscionability. A standard term may bind, fail for lack of agreement, or be limited by another rule; repetition across transactions alone determines none of those outcomes.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 272–276. Open assigned page 272.

records.title: Contract formation versus selection of terms
records.text: Contract formation asks whether an agreement has become a contract. Term identification asks what obligations that contract contains. The two questions can require different evidence and rules.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 274–304. Open assigned page 274.

records.title: Contract formation versus selection of terms
records.text:
Under § 2-207(1), an acceptance may form a contract despite nonmatching forms; subsection (2) then addresses additional terms. Where the writings fail but the parties perform, subsection (3) supplies a different route to both formation and terms. Hill and Klocek disagree earlier about whether formation had already occurred when package terms arrived.

Later interpretation materials ask what an existing agreement means and whether other terms supplement it. Identify which question the court decides before generalizing its conclusion about assent or validity.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 274–304. Open assigned page 274.

records.title: Expressly conditional acceptance
records.text: An expressly conditional response makes the responder’s willingness to contract depend on the offeror’s assent to additional or different terms. Under § 2-207(1), that can prevent the response from operating as acceptance.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 276–284. Open assigned page 276.

records.title: Expressly conditional acceptance
records.text:
Dorton requires a clear indication that the offeree will not proceed without assent to new terms; merely saying “subject to” its form did not suffice. C. Itoh satisfies that condition, but subsequent performance creates a subsection (3) contract without the unmatched arbitration clause. Klocek finds an inadequate showing under the possible standards it considers.

A condition blocking formation through the writings does not itself incorporate the desired term. Distinguish assent to transact from assent to that term, and conditional acceptance under subsection (1) from an offer limiting acceptance to its own terms under subsection (2)(a).

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 276–284. Open assigned page 276.

records.title: Additional terms under § 2-207(2)
records.text: An additional term addresses a matter added by an acceptance or confirmation to the offer or agreement. Section 2-207(2) determines whether such a proposed term becomes part of a contract.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 284–290. Open assigned page 284.

records.title: Additional terms under § 2-207(2)
records.text:
Outside transactions between merchants, additions are proposals requiring agreement. Between merchants, § 2-207(2) includes them unless the offer expressly limits acceptance, the addition materially alters the bargain, or timely objection occurs. Bayway places the burden of establishing material alteration on the party opposing inclusion; Klocek emphasizes the nonmerchant distinction.

A conflicting clause raises Northrop’s different-terms problem. Identify the term’s classification and formation route, then assess materiality under the governing approach rather than payment size alone.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 284–290. Open assigned page 284.

records.title: Material alteration: surprise and hardship
records.text: A material alteration is an added term whose incorporation without express awareness would cause the kind of surprise or hardship addressed by § 2-207(2)(b) and its commentary.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 284–290. Open assigned page 284.

records.title: Material alteration: surprise and hardship
records.text:
Bayway places the burden on the merchant resisting inclusion and examines personal awareness as well as what a reasonable merchant should anticipate. Industry practice defeated objective surprise there. The court leaves open whether hardship is independently sufficient because the evidence failed either way; Union Carbide treats hardship as a consequence rather than a separate criterion.

Some courts classify particular clauses as material categorically, while Dorton treats its arbitration issue as fact dependent. Preserve those differences. Neither invoice size nor saying a form went unread answers the materiality question.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 284–290. Open assigned page 284.

records.title: Industry practice in term incorporation
records.text: Evidence of customary allocation can affect whether an added term objectively surprises a merchant.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 285–289. Open assigned page 285.

records.title: Industry practice in term incorporation
records.text: Bayway uses trader testimony and sample contracts rather than the buyer’s personal reaction alone. A form bundling tax into the price can reflect the same allocation as one separately billing it; a silent form does not necessarily contradict an otherwise established practice. The party capable of avoiding the tax supplies part of the court’s reasoning. This is the assigned application, not the complete later course unit on usage of trade and course of dealing.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 285–289. Open assigned page 285.

records.title: Different terms and the three § 2-207 approaches
records.text: Different terms conflict with terms addressing the same matter in the other party’s offer or response. The wording of § 2-207 leaves their treatment disputed.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 290–294. Open assigned page 290.

records.title: Different terms and the three § 2-207 approaches
records.text:
Northrop compares knocking out both conflicting clauses, retaining the offeror’s clause after dropping the offeree’s, and treating the response’s clause as an additional term under subsection (2). It predicts Illinois would use the first despite preferring the third. The buyer’s more generous warranty therefore did not survive the knockout.

The applied rule depends on jurisdiction and the formation analysis. Do not mistake the court’s policy preference for its holding.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 290–294. Open assigned page 290.

records.title: Knockout and gap-filling
records.text: Under the knockout approach, conflicting clauses are removed and applicable supplementary rules supply the resulting contractual terms.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 281–294. Open assigned page 281.

records.title: Knockout and gap-filling
records.text:
Northrop’s treatment of conflicting terms in a subsection (1) contract is an interpretive issue distinct from C. Itoh’s subsection (3) contract by conduct. The latter’s text supplies agreed terms plus applicable supplementary law; an unagreed arbitration clause cannot return as a supposed gap-filler.

Identify the formation route, excluded clauses, and actual source filling each gap. The notes also ask whether Code defaults are neutral and how they influence drafting incentives.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 281–294. Open assigned page 281.

records.title: Pay now, terms later and rolling formation
records.text: Rolling formation describes an approach in which a seller supplies detailed terms with a product and invites acceptance by retaining or using it after an opportunity to review and return it.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 294–304. Open assigned page 294.

records.title: Pay now, terms later and rolling formation
records.text:
Hill treats retention beyond a review-and-return period as acceptance of the vendor’s package offer and puts its one-form transaction outside § 2-207. Klocek rejects a textual two-form prerequisite and assumes on its record that the consumer offered and the vendor accepted earlier, making later terms proposals requiring agreement.

The cases differ in governing law, procedural posture, notice, offeror identity, and formation timing as well as the return period. That period is relevant, but it does not resolve every later-terms transaction.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 294–304. Open assigned page 294.

records.title: Arbitration provisions as contract-formation questions
records.text: Before enforcing an arbitration clause, a court must determine whether the parties agreed to that clause under the applicable rules of contract formation and term inclusion.

records.title: Arbitration provisions as contract-formation questions
records.text:
Specht examines notice and manifested assent; Dorton whether arbitration was agreed or materially added; C. Itoh its exclusion from a conduct contract; Hill and Klocek competing accounts of later terms; and Anderson attempted adoption of changed terms. Graham separately examines unfairness despite an expected arbitration arrangement.

Identify agreement, scope, enforceability, and the procedural request separately, with the applicable law and evidentiary posture. Resolving arbitration does not itself decide the underlying merits.

records.title: Statute of Frauds: coverage, writing, and exceptions
records.text: A statute of frauds requires particular agreements to be supported by a qualifying written record before they may be enforced. Its scope and exceptions depend on the governing statute.

atlasSources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 371–383. Open assigned page 371.

records.title: Statute of Frauds: coverage, writing, and exceptions
records.text:
Identify the agreement, the governing statute’s coverage, the record’s content and form, whose signature is needed, and any exception or defense. A writing barrier differs from absence of agreement; waiver and other uses of the agreement may matter.

Tolosa applies Texas’s loan-agreement provision to delaying foreclosure and rejects the pleaded estoppel theory. It supplies no universal rule for oral promises. The historical English categories and modern state comparisons demonstrate variation; CISG Article 11 supplies a different form rule within its own scope. The full later units on satisfying writing requirements and exceptions are outside the early assigned ranges.

records.text: The consideration inquiry requires a performance or return promise bargained for.

records.title: Restatement § 71 — exchange requirement
records.text: The assigned chapter explains reciprocal exchange and uses Hamer to distinguish a requested act from a gratuitous promise. § 71: a performance or return promise is consideration only if it is bargained for, that is, sought by the promisor in exchange for the promise and given by the promisee in exchange for it. The full section with comments and illustrations is in the Contracts Selections, linked above.

records.title: Restatement § 90 — first and second formulations
records.text: The first formulation at p. 126 requires action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character on the part of the promisee. The second at p. 128 includes the promisee or a third person, omits that phrase, and states that the remedy may be limited as justice requires. Both include a promise, reasonably expected inducement, actual induced conduct, and the requirement that injustice be avoidable only by enforcement. The second adds a charitable-subscription and marriage-settlement provision dispensing with proof of induced conduct. Both formulations are reproduced in the casebook pages; the full section with comments is in the Contracts Selections, linked above.

records.text: § 2-205: an offer by a merchant to buy or sell goods, in a signed writing that by its terms gives assurance it will be held open, is not revocable for lack of consideration during the time stated or, if none, a reasonable time, in no event longer than three months; a firm-offer term on a form supplied by the offeree must be separately signed by the offeror. records.title: N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1109 — written irrevocable offers
records.text: The quoted provision excepts offers governed by UCC § 2-205 and otherwise addresses an offer in a writing signed by the offeror or agent that states it is irrevocable for a period or until a time. Absence of consideration for that assurance does not make the offer revocable during the period. A writing stating irrevocability without a period is construed to use a reasonable time. This is the text reproduced by the 2023 casebook, not a current legislative verification.

Drennan’s protection depends on justified reliance and prompt action, and it limits shopping or reopening the bargain. Holman rejects an automatic reciprocal duty based only on using the bid. records.title: What a Statute of Frauds does and does not do
records.text: The chapter separates formation, statutory coverage, compliant evidence, and exceptions. A defense may be waived; a signature may bind one party without the same evidence against the other. The agreement can have consequences for restitution, property, defenses, or interference even when an action to enforce it is barred. The precise consequence depends on the claim and the provision, not the word “void” used loosely.

records.title: Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts (RLCC) §§ 1–10
records.text:
Each section opens at its own page from the source buttons. Sections 4, 6, 8 and 9 also have their own entries on the Contracts map, in the subtopic of the assignment that lists them.

§ 2. Adoption of standard terms (Assignments 6, 9). (a) A standard term is adopted if the business shows the consumer manifested assent to the transaction after reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review it. (b) For terms available only after assent: reasonable advance notice that terms will follow, of the opportunity to review and terminate, and that not terminating adopts them; a reasonable opportunity to review afterwards; and a reasonable opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value or personal burden, not exercised. (c) A contract is not unenforceable because some standard terms were not adopted; its terms are those adopted, any unadopted standard terms the consumer elects, terms both parties agreed to, and terms supplied by law.

§ 3. Modification of standard terms (Assignment 11). (a) In an ongoing relationship a proposed modification is adopted only if the business shows reasonable notice of the modified term and opportunity to review it; a reasonable, noticed opportunity to reject it and continue under the existing term; reasonable notice that continuing without rejecting adopts it; and either assent or continued use after the rejection period. (b) The contract may set a reasonable modification procedure, which may substitute a reasonable opportunity to terminate for the opportunity to reject, but may not otherwise exclude (a) to the consumer's detriment. (c) The modification must be proposed in good faith, be fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated at contracting, and not undermine an affirmation or promise that was part of the basis of the original bargain. (d) Standard terms may not be modified once the contract has been substantially performed by at least one party.

§ 4, § 6, § 8, § 9: see their own entries.

Not assigned: § 1 (definitions and scope), § 5 (discretionary obligations), § 7 (deception), § 10 (derogation from mandatory provisions).

The 2019 Tentative Draft reprinted in the Contracts Selections is superseded by the 2024 text.

Court: New York Court of Appeals (1923), 139 N.E. 470. This is a pre-UCC case. The notes separately discuss modern UCC §§ 2-204 and 2-305, trade usage, implied terms, and the distinction between missing terms and a failure to plan for future contingencies. The majority’s refusal to fill this agreement is not a statement that every open price term defeats formation.

29 N.Y.2d 124 (1971), decided July 6, 1971 by a 4-3 vote: Chief Judge Fuld wrote for the majority (Burke, Scileppi and Gibson concurring), and Judge Bergan's dissent was joined by Judges Breitel and Jasen.

records.text: Evidence of a collateral oral agreement is admissible unless the writing was intended as the complete embodiment of the bargain; a collateral term may be proved if similarly situated parties might naturally have made it separately and it does not contradict the writing.

records.title: Masterson v. Sine
records.text:
After the 1958 conveyance Dallas Masterson went bankrupt; the plaintiffs seeking a declaration of the right to exercise the option were his bankruptcy trustee and Rebecca Masterson, and Medora Sine was Dallas's sister, so the Sines' evidence went to whether the option was personal to the Mastersons and beyond the trustee's reach.

records.title: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.
records.text: Under California’s approach, apparently clear words do not end the inquiry. A court provisionally considers outside evidence and admits it if relevant to a meaning the language can reasonably bear. The court reversed the exclusion here without deciding what coverage the parties actually intended.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.
records.text: The test for admitting extrinsic evidence to explain a written contract is not whether the writing appears plain on its face, but whether the offered evidence is relevant to prove a meaning to which the language is reasonably susceptible.

records.title: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.
records.text: Chief Justice Traynor wrote the opinion (69 Cal.2d 33, 442 P.2d 641, decided July 11, 1968); the 1960 contract was for removing and replacing the upper cover of PG&E's steam turbine, and the trial court had excluded the extrinsic evidence on a 'plain meaning' rationale.

records.title: W.W.W. Associates, Inc. v. Giancontieri
records.text: New York's answer to Pacific Gas: a complete and clear written contract means what it says, and a party cannot use outside evidence to manufacture an ambiguity or add terms the writing does not contain.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: W.W.W. Associates, Inc. v. Giancontieri
records.text: A complete, clear and unambiguous written contract is enforced according to its terms, and extrinsic evidence of what the parties intended may not be used to create an ambiguity in it or to add to or vary it.

records.title: Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.
records.text: A contract that transfers ownership of recordings without limit covers new uses the parties never mentioned. Silence about a particular use does not create an ambiguity, so the artists could not read in a reserved right.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.
records.text: Under New York law, a clear, complete writing is enforced according to its terms, and silence about a particular use does not make an unconditional transfer of ownership ambiguous or reserve that use to the grantor.

records.title: Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.
records.text:
The plaintiffs were the Ronettes (Ronnie Greenfield, formerly Veronica Bennett, with Estelle Bennett and Nedra Talley); the 1963 agreement ran five years, produced recordings including "Be My Baby," and the disputed licensing for film and television began in the 1980s (Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc., 98 N.Y.2d 562 (2002)).

Rule in one line: an unambiguous grant of full ownership of master recordings permits every use by the owner unless the contract expressly limits specific uses, and the artists cannot use extrinsic evidence to read in a limitation.

records.title: Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.
records.text: Even when the documents seem to leave no room for a borrower's reading, California law requires the court to at least hear the borrower's outside evidence of what the parties meant before ruling it out.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.
records.text: Under California law as stated in Pacific Gas & Electric, a party must be allowed to offer extrinsic evidence that an integrated contract means something other than what it appears to say, even where the writing seems clear on its face.

records.title: Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.
records.text: Judge Kozinski's opinion (847 F.2d 564, 9th Cir. 1988) held three things: the note's terms did not entitle Trident to prepay; under Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co. Trident could nevertheless offer extrinsic evidence to vary the unambiguous documents; and the district court's Rule 11 sanctions were improper and were reversed. Trident was a partnership formed by an insurance company and two large law firms, and the loan was made in 1983.

records.title: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
records.text: When a word like chicken has two trade meanings, the party claiming the narrower one has to prove it. Newcomers to a trade are bound by its usage only if they knew it or it was so settled they should have.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
records.text: A party who asserts that an ambiguous contract term was used in the narrower of two possible senses bears the burden of proving that meaning, and a trade usage binds a newcomer only if actually known or so established that knowledge is chargeable.

records.title: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
records.text: The transaction predates the CISG. Its international parties do not make the historical court’s analysis a CISG holding. The notes compare trade usage with the rules for interpreting writings and ask which party should bear uncertainty about unfamiliar terminology.

records.title: Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.
records.text: Numbers that look exact can carry a special trade meaning. Evidence that horse-meat traders treat 49.5 percent protein as meeting a 50 percent minimum could be used to read the written contract, even though it seemed unambiguous.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.
records.text: Evidence of a trade usage is admissible to show that parties in the trade used words or figures in a written contract with a special trade meaning, even though the terms appear unambiguous in their ordinary sense.

records.title: Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.
records.text: The surrounding notes distinguish usage of trade from a course of dealing between particular parties. They also examine whether a newcomer must know a usage before it can affect the contract.

records.title: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.
records.text: Under the Code, trade practice and the parties' own past performance are part of the contract. A posted-price term could be qualified by the paving trade's practice of price protection, with no need to first find the writing ambiguous.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.
records.text: Under the UCC, trade usage and course of performance are part of the parties' agreement and may qualify an express term, such as a posted-price term, so long as they can reasonably be construed as consistent with it, without any showing of ambiguity.

records.title: Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.
records.text:
The editors compare Naval Institute: industry practice cannot simply erase an agreed restriction on early paperback sales. They also ask whether a comparable usage could explain irrevocability of a subcontractor’s bid in Drennan. That latter question is an editorial comparison, not a Nanakuli holding.

The dispute arose from Shell's 1974 price increase, which it announced with no advance notice, by a letter dated December 31 that Nanakuli received January 4; the Ninth Circuit (664 F.2d 772 (9th Cir. 1981)) held that the jury could find price protection was a usage of the Hawaiian asphaltic paving trade, a practice the court traced to government paving contracts that allowed no escalation clauses.

records.title: Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.
records.text: Evidence of trade usage and past dealings comes in to explain a written sales contract unless it flatly cannot be squared with the express terms. The old rule that the writing first had to be ambiguous is gone under the Code.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.
records.text: Under the UCC, evidence of trade usage and course of dealing is admissible to explain or supplement a written contract without a finding of ambiguity, unless it cannot reasonably be construed as consistent with the express terms or is carefully negated.

records.title: Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.
records.text: 451 F.2d 3 (4th Cir. 1971). The test of admissibility is not whether the contract appears on its face to be complete in every detail, but whether the proffered evidence of course of dealing and trade usage reasonably can be construed as consistent with the express terms; the court also affirmed the district court's rejection of Columbia's antitrust claims.

records.title: Dalton v. Educational Testing Service
records.text: A party that promises to use its discretion has to actually use it, and not arbitrarily. The testing service had to genuinely consider the student's evidence, though it did not have to prove he cheated, and the court ordered a real review rather than releasing the score.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dalton v. Educational Testing Service
records.text: The implied covenant of good faith requires a party to actually exercise discretion it has promised to exercise and to do so neither arbitrarily nor irrationally, but it cannot create obligations inconsistent with the contract's terms.

records.title: Dalton v. Educational Testing Service
records.text: 87 N.Y.2d 384, 663 N.E.2d 289 (1995). The dissenters were Judge Levine, joined by Judge Simons, who pointed to concrete evidence that ETS had considered Dalton's submissions; the trial court had found ETS failed to make even rudimentary efforts to evaluate or investigate the information.

records.title: Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg
records.text: Federal airline law preempted this Minnesota good-faith claim because it concerned prices and services and imposed duties beyond the airline’s voluntary promises. The Court did not reject every airline contract claim or every good-faith claim; the statutory connection and source of the duty matter.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg
records.text: The Airline Deregulation Act preempts a state-law implied covenant of good faith claim that relates to airline prices, routes or services when the covenant is a state-imposed obligation that enlarges the airline's voluntarily adopted contractual undertakings.

records.title: Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg
records.text:
The book asks how the UCC Permanent Editorial Board’s account of good faith would affect the characterization. That is a comparison of sources and theories of obligation, not a finding that this frequent-flyer agreement was a sale of goods.

The Supreme Court decided the case on April 2, 2014 (572 U.S. 273), Justice Alito writing for a unanimous Court; Ginsberg had sued as a class action in the Southern District of California, the district court dismissed, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded.

The Court's stated rule: the Airline Deregulation Act preempts a state-law implied-covenant claim if it seeks to enlarge the contractual obligations that the parties voluntarily adopted, which the Minnesota claim did because Minnesota law does not let parties contract out of the covenant.

records.title: Market Street Associates v. Frey
records.text: Good faith in performing a contract does not require you to look after the other side's interests, but it forbids deliberately taking advantage of a mistake they are making about their own contract rights.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Market Street Associates v. Frey
records.text: The duty of good faith in performance does not require altruism or general candor, but it forbids deliberately exploiting the other party's oversight about its rights under the existing contract.

records.title: Market Street Associates v. Frey
records.text: The later finding reported at C&M p. 735 was that Orenstein initially expected the trust to review the lease, then realized it was not doing so and continued sending ambiguous requests until invoking the option. The editors report denial of specific performance on that later record. That later finding is separate from the Seventh Circuit's remand, which decided only that the question needed a trial.

records.title: Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.
records.text: Best efforts did not require bankruptcy or substantial losses merely to promote this brand, but pursuing overall profit did not excuse ignoring the promised sales volume. Falstaff breached its brand-specific duty. Ordinary effort and expense cannot be dismissed merely because they reduce profit.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.
records.text: A promise to use best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales does not require the promisor to incur bankruptcy or substantial losses, but it is not discharged by pursuing overall profit while disregarding the promised volume.

records.title: Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.
records.text:
The opinion connects the royalty arrangement to Wood v. Lucy: even without the express best-efforts language, a good-faith effort to generate royalty-producing sales would matter. The casebook quotes the operative provisions of the separately assigned Bloor agreement. The notes offer several competing accounts of what “best” efforts require.

601 F.2d 609 (2d Cir. 1979), affirming 454 F. Supp. 258 (S.D.N.Y. 1978). The royalty ran from April 1972 to March 1978, and the two clauses at issue were the promise to use best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales and the liquidated payment triggered if Falstaff substantially discontinued distribution under the Ballantine name.

records.title: Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.
records.text: A take-it-or-leave-it contract is still enforceable, but its terms must fit the weaker party's reasonable expectations and not be oppressive. An arbitration clause that let the other side's own union judge the dispute failed that test.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.
records.text: A contract of adhesion is enforceable unless a term falls outside the adherent's reasonable expectations or is unduly oppressive or unconscionable; an arbitration clause naming a body whose interests are effectively identical to one party's as sole arbitrator will not be enforced.

records.title: Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.
records.text:
The famous phrase: the "minimum levels of integrity" required of a contractual arrangement for nonjudicial dispute resolution are not met by designating the union of one party as arbitrator, especially where the arrangement is the product of adhesion (Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc., 28 Cal.3d 807, 623 P.2d 165 (1981)).

The two-step California test for adhesion contracts stated in the opinion: enforcement is denied (1) if a provision falls outside the reasonable expectations of the weaker party, and (2) even if within those expectations, if the term is unduly oppressive or unconscionable.

The performer was Leon Russell, whose corporation Scissor-Tail, Inc. contracted with promoter Bill Graham.

records.title: Klar v. H. & M. Parcel Room, Inc.
records.text: Handing someone a claim check does not prove they agreed to the fine print on it. A parcel room that wants to limit its liability has to show the customer was reasonably told about the limit and accepted it.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Klar v. H. & M. Parcel Room, Inc.
records.text: A bailee for hire relying on a liability limitation printed on a claim check must show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent; accepting a ticket issued to identify property does not establish that assent as a matter of law.

records.title: Doe v. Great Expectations
records.text: Applying New York’s 2005 dating-service statute, the court found Great Expectations’s forms unlawful and awarded recovery for those contracts. The decision concerned the then-applicable price, duration and referral requirements. Current § 394-c includes specific online-service exceptions, so the 2005 case does not supply the entire current regime.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Doe v. Great Expectations
records.text: Under New York General Business Law § 394-c as applied in 2005, a dating-service contract that does not promise a specified number of referrals per month may charge at most $25, and an injured consumer may recover actual damages or $50, whichever is greater.

records.title: Doe v. Great Expectations
records.text: The book distinguishes individual restitution, public civil penalties, and punitive damages. The $25 cap and the $50 minimum recovery are the figures in General Business Law § 394-c as the court applied it in 2005.

records.title: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
records.text: A court can refuse to enforce a contract that was unconscionable when it was made: one side had no real choice and the terms were grossly one-sided. The court set out the test and sent the case back, without itself striking the contracts down.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
records.text: A court may refuse to enforce a contract that was unconscionable when made, meaning that one party lacked meaningful choice and the terms unreasonably favored the other party.

records.title: Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.
records.text: The editors discuss how allocating payments to the earliest purchases would have allowed ownership of many items to clear. They also present later social and economic accounts of the store’s practices and debates over paternalism; those accounts are not facts found by the appellate court in 1965.

records.title: Stoll v. Xiong
records.text: A hidden clause that forced land buyers who could not read English to supply chicken litter worth far more than the land price was unconscionable. No meaningful choice plus shockingly one-sided terms means the clause will not be enforced.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Stoll v. Xiong
records.text: A contract term is unconscionable and unenforceable when, judged at formation, an absence of meaningful choice combines with terms so one-sided that they oppress or unfairly surprise a party; the question is one of law for the court.

records.title: Stoll v. Xiong
records.text: The printed price description contains an internal words-and-numerals inconsistency. The editors ask how the outcome might differ if the litter value had actually been reflected in a negotiated discount on the land.

records.title: Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.
records.text: A seller normally gets paid even if the buyer plans to misuse the goods, but not when the seller actively helps the misuse. A supplier that knowingly furthered the cheese maker's improper use of its product could not collect the price.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.
records.text: A seller who has performed does not ordinarily lose the right to payment merely because the buyer plans an improper use of the goods, but a seller who acts to further that improper use may be denied enforcement on public-policy grounds.

records.title: Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.
records.text: 133 Wis. 2d 386, 395 N.W.2d 619 (Ct. App. 1986). Blossom sued on an open account for $138,306 owed for Kasson's last purchase; Kasson had bought roughly 100 times the quantity a starter use would require, and mislabeling let it charge about twice as much for the product.

records.title: X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.
records.text: For this New York antitrust defense, a facially lawful contract was not automatically unenforceable because of an alleged bid-rigging conspiracy. The issue was whether judgment would enforce the prohibited conduct itself. Factual questions remained, so the court refused dismissal rather than awarding the unpaid price.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.
records.text: A contract that is lawful on its face is not unenforceable merely because it arose from an antitrust conspiracy; enforcement is refused only if the judgment would itself enforce the precise conduct the antitrust laws prohibit.

records.title: X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.
records.text: 83 N.Y.2d 513 (1994). Supreme Court dismissed the complaint as illegal; the Appellate Division reinstated it; the Court of Appeals (Ciparick, J.) affirmed, so Rivergate, not X.L.O., was the appellant before the Court of Appeals.

records.title: Hassler v. Circle C Resources
records.text: In 2022, the Wyoming Supreme Court refused to rewrite an unreasonably broad noncompete to save it. That decision is historical guidance on judicial redrafting. Wyoming’s 2025 statute separately governs noncompetes entered on or after July 1, 2025, with a ban and specified exceptions.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hassler v. Circle C Resources
records.text: A noncompetition covenant is prima facie invalid and the employer must prove it reasonable; a court will not rewrite an unreasonable covenant into a reasonable one, so a covenant with unreasonable duration or geography is void.

records.title: Hassler v. Circle C Resources
records.text:
The precedent overruled was Hopper v. All Pet Animal Clinic, Inc. (Wyo. 1993), which had adopted the liberal blue-pencil rule; the decision is Hassler v. Circle C Resources, 2022 WY 28, issued 25 February 2022, and under it a noncompete with an unreasonable duration or territory is void in its entirety as against public policy.

The covenant's territorial term as written barred competition for 24 months in any geographic area in which Circle C marketed or had marketed its services during the year before separation, which is why the district court thought narrowing was needed before it could enforce.

records.title: Luttinger v. Rosen
records.text: When a purchase depends on getting a mortgage on stated terms and the only available loan has a higher rate, the condition has failed and the buyers get their deposit back. The seller offering to make up the difference does not change that.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Luttinger v. Rosen
records.text: A condition precedent is an event the parties intend to occur before a right to performance arises, and when an express condition does not occur on its stated terms the conditional duty does not arise.

records.title: Luttinger v. Rosen
records.text: The notes ask whose performance the condition protects and whether a buyer choosing to pay cash could insist on completion. They also invite comparison with the risk of dealing with an individual financier rather than a bank. Those questions should be analyzed separately from the holding.

records.title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
records.text: The Florida court read these ambiguous owner-payment clauses as setting a reasonable payment time, rather than shifting the owner’s nonpayment risk to the subcontractor. Transferring that risk required unambiguous language. The result depends on the clause and governing law; not every “pay after payment” clause has the same effect.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
records.text: An ambiguous subcontract clause making final payment due after the owner pays the general contractor is construed as fixing a reasonable time for payment, not as a condition precedent; shifting the risk of owner nonpayment to the subcontractor requires unambiguous language.

records.title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
records.text:
The following notes describe later Florida clarification and other jurisdictions’ public-policy limits. Their jurisdictional rules must not be collapsed into the holding of Peacock.

Peacock was the general contractor on a condominium project; the two subcontractors were Modern Air Conditioning and Overly Manufacturing, and the Florida Supreme Court (353 So.2d 840 (Fla. 1977)) reasoned that such clauses are presumed to fix a reasonable time for payment because small subcontractors cannot afford to bear the risk of the owner's nonpayment absent clear language shifting it.

records.title: Gibson v. Cranage
records.text: If you agree to paint a portrait that the customer may reject unless it satisfies him, his honest dissatisfaction ends the matter. It does not help that other people think the portrait is good.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Gibson v. Cranage
records.text: Where a buyer expressly reserves the right to reject and decline to pay for a portrait that is not satisfactory to him, and the seller accepts those terms, the buyer's own dissatisfaction defeats the seller's claim to the price.

records.title: Gibson v. Cranage
records.text:
The notes connect Gibson to Mattei, commercial satisfaction, third-party certificates, and forfeiture. They do not establish a general permission to invoke satisfaction dishonestly.

Citation and rule: Gibson v. Cranage, 39 Mich. 49 (1878); where parties agree that payment depends on the buyer's personal satisfaction and the agreement is neither fraudulent nor against public policy, the court will hold them to it, so the buyer's honest dissatisfaction defeats the price claim.

records.title: Kingston v. Preston
records.text: Whether one party must perform before the other depends on the sense of the deal, not the order of the clauses. Because providing security was plainly meant to come before handing over the business, the buyer could not sue without first providing it.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Kingston v. Preston
records.text: Whether covenants are independent, dependent or concurrent depends on the evident sense and meaning of the parties and the order of performance the transaction requires, and a party is not liable on its covenant until a condition precedent to it has been fulfilled.

records.title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
records.text: A builder who innocently used a different brand of equally good pipe did not forfeit payment for the house. Trivial departures are compensated in damages, measured by the drop in value when tearing out the work would cost far more than it is worth.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
records.text: A trivial and innocent departure from a construction contract does not forfeit the builder's right to the price but is compensated in damages, measured by diminution in value when the cost of replacement is grossly and unfairly disproportionate to the benefit.

records.title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
records.text: The editors reproduce additional contract specifications at p. 853, including prior written approval for substitutions, architect decision clauses, and replacement language. Those provisions sharpen the question whether the majority’s interpretation respected the bargain. The notes also explain that Restatement § 241 treats good faith as a factor rather than making every deliberate deviation categorically fatal.

records.title: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.
records.text: When a contract prices each item separately, a party can be paid for each item it fully delivered even though it did not finish the whole job. It gets nothing for items only partly carried out.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.
records.text: A contract is severable when the consideration is apportioned among distinct performances, so the performing party may recover the stipulated price for each item fully performed, but nothing for an item only partly performed.

records.title: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.
records.text: Citation and rule statement: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co., 151 Pa. 534, 25 A. 120 (1892); a contract is severable (divisible) when one party's performance consists of several distinct items and the price is apportioned to each item, so payment is due per unit actually delivered.

records.title: Nelson v. Hazel
records.text: A contractor whose work fell short of substantial performance still cannot be made to hand over the value of the work for free. He recovers whatever the benefit to the owner exceeds the owner's damages.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Nelson v. Hazel
records.text: A building contractor whose defective work falls short of substantial performance may still recover in quasi-contract the amount by which the benefit conferred on the owner exceeds the owner's damages.

records.title: Nelson v. Hazel
records.text: The action began as Nelson's suit to foreclose a mechanic's and materialman's lien for remodeling the Hazels' home; the Idaho Supreme Court's earlier decision is reported at 89 Idaho 480 and the accounting appeal is Nelson v. Hazel, 91 Idaho 850, 433 P.2d 120 (1967), applying the principle that a builder whose defective performance falls short of substantial performance but confers benefits exceeding the owner's injury may recover that excess in quasi-contract.

records.title: McKenna v. Vernon
records.text: The owner repeatedly paid without demanding the architect’s certificate, then tried to use its absence as a complete defense to the final payment. On these facts, that conduct prevented forfeiture for honestly and substantially performed work. It does not mean that every ignored condition is permanently waived.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: McKenna v. Vernon
records.text: An owner who repeatedly makes payments without demanding the architect's certificate the contract requires cannot rely on the missing final certificate as a defense to payment for work honestly and substantially performed.

records.title: McKenna v. Vernon
records.text: The case is McKenna v. Vernon, 258 Pa. 18, 101 A. 919 (1917); the builder sued for the $2,750 balance (recovering $2,500), and the architect testified that the theatre was substantially completed and that he withheld certificates only because no one asked him for them.

records.title: Stees v. Leonard
records.text: The 1874 court held that latent soil problems did not excuse the builders’ unconditional promise: the building remained possible with suitable foundations or drainage. This historical strict-performance rule is part of the background to later impossibility, impracticability and risk-allocation doctrines.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Stees v. Leonard
records.text: A party who makes a positive, express promise must perform it despite unforeseen hindrance or hardship unless performance is prevented by an act of God, the law or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility is no excuse.

records.title: Stees v. Leonard
records.text: The editors contrast United States v. Spearin and distinguish a specification requiring a result from a detailed design that may imply a warranty of adequacy. That later contrast qualifies the use of Stees as a general construction-risk rule.

records.title: Renner v. Kehl
records.text: The shared mistake about water for a jojoba farm allowed rescission. Restitution covered the down payment and the value added to the returned land, minus its rental value; it did not reimburse all development spending. The amounts still had to be determined on remand.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Renner v. Kehl
records.text: A contract is voidable for mutual mistake about a basic assumption material enough to upset the exchange, but absent fraud or misrepresentation the rescinding party recovers only restitution of benefits conferred, not consequential damages for reliance expenditures.

records.title: Taylor v. Caldwell
records.text: The parties’ bargain depended on this music hall’s continued existence, which the owners had not guaranteed. Its faultless destruction excused the promised concert performance, and the promoters could not recover their preparation losses. An express allocation of the destruction risk could produce a different result.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Taylor v. Caldwell
records.text: Where the nature of a contract makes the continued existence of a particular person or thing fundamental to performance, and its existence is not warranted, the law implies a condition excusing performance if that person or thing perishes without the contractor's default.

records.title: Taylor v. Caldwell
records.text: The agreement was made on May 27, 1861 for the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall on June 17, July 15, August 5 and August 19; the hall burned on June 11, 1861; Blackburn J.'s opinion (3 B. & S. 826, 122 Eng. Rep. 309) reads an implied condition that the parties are excused when performance becomes impossible through the perishing of the thing without fault of either side, the origin of the common-law impossibility/frustration doctrine.

records.title: Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States
records.text: Closing Suez made the planned voyage more expensive, but sailing around Africa remained commercially practicable on this record. The shipper could not shift the extra cost to its customer. Impracticability examines the contingency, allocation of risk and severity of the burden; expense alone did not suffice here.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States
records.text: Performance is excused for impossibility or commercial impracticability only if an unexpected contingency occurred, the risk of it was not allocated by agreement or custom, and the contingency made performance commercially impracticable; added expense alone did not suffice on this record.

records.title: Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States
records.text: Judge J. Skelly Wright's opinion (363 F.2d 312, D.C. Cir. 1966) states the three-part impracticability test: (1) something unexpected must have occurred, (2) the risk of that occurrence must not have been allocated by agreement or custom, and (3) the occurrence must have rendered performance commercially impracticable; the vessel was the SS Christos carrying wheat from a Gulf port to Bandar Shapur, Iran, and the shipowner sued in quantum meruit for the added Cape expense.

records.title: Krell v. Henry
records.text: The cancelled coronation procession defeated the shared foundation of this room-rental agreement: both parties understood that viewing it was the rental’s purpose. The court excused the unpaid balance. A disappointed personal motive alone is different; the event must be fundamental to the bargain and its risk must not have been allocated otherwise.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Krell v. Henry
records.text: Where a state of things assumed by both parties is the foundation of a contract, and an event that could not reasonably have been contemplated prevents performance of the substantial contract, the parties are discharged even though literal performance remains physically possible.

records.title: Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.
records.text: A court may enforce a shopping-centre exclusivity clause with an injunction rather than damages when damages would be hard to measure. The choice turns on weighing the costs and benefits of each remedy in the particular case.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.
records.text: A permanent injunction against breach of contract is proper when the plaintiff shows that damages are an inadequate remedy, which the court decides by comparing the costs and benefits of damages and injunctive relief in the particular case.

records.title: Plante v. Jacobs
records.text: A builder who substantially completed a house gets the price minus the cost of fixing defects. For a misplaced wall that did not change the home's value, the measure is the lost value, because tearing it out would be economic waste.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Plante v. Jacobs
records.text: A builder who substantially performs, judged by the essential purpose of the contract, recovers the contract price less damages for defects, measured by cost of repair for defects that can reasonably be corrected and by diminution in value where correction would cause unreasonable economic waste.

records.title: Plante v. Jacobs
records.text: The accompanying notes question whether market price measures a particular homeowner’s actual loss. They discuss proof of personal value, intended repairs, and the owner’s likely use of an award. Those questions qualify the use of Plante as a universal market-value rule.

records.title: Groves v. John Wunder Co.
records.text: The Minnesota court selected completion cost for the contractor’s deliberate failure to level the land, despite the smaller increase in land value. It remanded to determine the promised work and award. This contrasts with Peevyhouse’s Oklahoma approach; deliberate breach does not establish one national damages rule.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Groves v. John Wunder Co.
records.text: When a contractor deliberately fails to perform a construction obligation, the owner's damages are the reasonable cost of performing the promised work, even if that cost exceeds the value of the completed land; economic waste concerns only destroying a completed or substantially completed structure.

records.title: Groves v. John Wunder Co.
records.text:
The editors report a later $55,000 settlement and subsequent limited grading and sale of part of the land. Those later events inform the policy questions in the notes; they are not the court’s damages judgment or facts that supplied its original rationale.

The number that drives the debate: had Wunder graded the land as promised, the property would have been worth only $12,160, against a restoration cost above $60,000 (Groves v. John Wunder Co., 205 Minn. 163, 286 N.W. 235 (1939)).

The majority's rule: the proper measure of damages is the reasonable cost of performing the part of the contract that the defendant wilfully failed to complete; the dissent objected that a $60,000 award would enrich Groves beyond the value of his bargain.

records.title: Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.
records.text: The opposite outcome to Groves: a coal company that skipped the promised restoration of a farm paid only the small drop in the land's value, not the large cost of the work, because restoration was incidental to the lease's main purpose.

records.title: Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.
records.text: Reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures damages for omitted remedial work under a coal lease, but where the breached provision is merely incidental to the main purpose and the economic benefit of performance is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to diminution in value.

records.text: The notes report Schneberger’s later adherence to Peevyhouse and present competing readings of economic waste. The separately assigned lease is in the Contracts Selections (PDF page 699; retyped at page 703), linked below.
