records.title: United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.
records.text: A subcontractor driven off the job by the other side's serious breach can ask for the value of the work it did instead of contract damages. That value is not capped by the contract price, even if finishing the job would have lost money.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.
records.text: A subcontractor who justifiably stops work after the other party's material breach may elect restitution for the reasonable value of the performance conferred, less payments received, without deduction for the loss it would have suffered by completing and without the contract price as a ceiling.

records.title: United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.
records.text: The notes identify disagreement over using the contract price as a ceiling. They contrast Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 373 with Restatement (Third) of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment § 38(2)(b), and separately discuss the limitation after full performance. The case’s rule should not erase those qualifications.

records.title: Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.
records.text: Once a county told the bridge builder to stop, the builder could not keep building and bill for it. After a clear repudiation you recover what you had spent plus your expected profit, not costs you could have avoided.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.
records.text: After receiving an absolute repudiation, a contractor may not continue performing and charge the avoidable cost to the repudiating party; recovery is limited to labor, materials and expenses in partial performance before repudiation plus the profit the contract would have produced.

records.title: Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.
records.text: The editors explain that a failure to mitigate generally limits damages rather than creating independent liability to the breaching party. The notes raise uncertainty about repudiation and contrast a performance-only offer under Restatement § 45; those textbook problems remain questions rather than decided extensions of this holding.

records.title: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.
records.text: The studio could not reduce the actress’s recovery by pointing to a substitute role that was different and inferior. The employer had to prove reasonably available comparable employment; she did not have to accept that particular substitute. The court upheld her guaranteed-pay award.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.
records.text: A wrongfully discharged employee recovers the agreed compensation less what the employer proves was or could reasonably have been earned in other employment, but only comparable or substantially similar work counts; different or inferior work need not be accepted.

records.title: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.
records.text: The plaintiff was the actress Shirley MacLaine (Parker was her married name); the decision is 3 Cal.3d 176, 474 P.2d 689 (Cal. 1970), and Justice Sullivan's dissent argued that jobs must be of different kinds, not merely different, and that comparability was a fact question unsuited to summary judgment.

records.title: Hadley v. Baxendale
records.text: Recoverable losses arise naturally from breach or were reasonably contemplated at formation as its probable result, including communicated special circumstances. The court treated the carrier as unaware that the mill would remain idle without this shaft, so it excluded those lost profits and ordered a new trial.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hadley v. Baxendale
records.text: Damages for breach of contract are limited to losses that arise naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or that both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as its probable result, including losses made ordinary by communicated special circumstances.

records.title: Hadley v. Baxendale
records.text:
The notes compare later approaches, including assumed responsibility, Restatement § 351, and Article 2. They question the opinion’s application to its own facts. Those distinctions should remain alongside the rule rather than be collapsed into a statement that every foreseeable loss is always recoverable.

The parties: the millers (Hadley) sent the shaft through Pickford & Co., the carrier firm of which Baxendale was managing partner, to Joyce & Co. in Greenwich to serve as the model for a new shaft, after being told that a shaft delivered before noon would reach Greenwich the next day (Hadley v. Baxendale, 9 Exch. 341, 156 Eng. Rep. 145 (1854)).

The two-branch rule as usually stated: recoverable damages are those arising naturally, according to the usual course of things, from the breach itself, or those that may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting as the probable result of a breach.

records.title: Kenford Co. v. County of Erie
records.text: Unusual losses, like the rise in value of land around a stadium that was never built, are recoverable only if the breaching party could be seen to have taken on that risk when it made the contract. Foreseeing a loss is not the same as agreeing to pay for it.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Kenford Co. v. County of Erie
records.text: Unusual or extraordinary damages are recoverable only if liability for them was contemplated at or before contract formation as a probable consequence of breach, judged by the contract's nature, purpose and circumstances and the liability the defendant consciously assumed or reasonably led the plaintiff to believe it assumed.

records.title: Kenford Co. v. County of Erie
records.text: The editors emphasize that the tacit-agreement test has not generally been accepted and that UCC § 2-715 Comment 2 rejects it. The earlier refusal of the operator’s twenty-year profits involved both contemplation and reasonable certainty; that was a distinct claim from the land-appreciation award at issue here.

records.title: Fera v. Village Plaza, Inc.
records.text: A new business is not automatically barred from recovering the profits it never got to earn. It needs a reasonable basis for estimating the loss, not mathematical certainty, and the jury may not simply guess.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Fera v. Village Plaza, Inc.
records.text: A new business is not automatically barred from recovering lost anticipated profits; it may recover them if the evidence gives a reasonable basis for estimating the loss, without absolute or mathematical certainty, though the jury may not guess.

records.title: Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.
records.text: Trade custom can make a limited remedy, such as repair, replace or refund, part of a sales contract even where it is unclear that the written terms were ever delivered. The remedy did not fail of its purpose when the refund alternative was actually carried out.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.
records.text: Under the UCC, a trade usage may supply an exclusive limitation of remedies as part of the parties' agreement, and a limited remedy that includes return and refund does not fail of its essential purpose merely because repair attempts were unsuccessful.

records.title: Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.
records.text: The printed standard-terms language is awkward. The court’s analysis consistently identifies the operative alternatives as repair, replacement, or return with repayment. The notes separately question broad exclusions of incidental and consequential damages and the distinction between commercial and consumer losses; they do not establish that every disclaimer is enforceable.

records.title: Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State
records.text: A per-day charge for finishing a highway late was enforceable because delay damages were genuinely hard to measure and the graduated amounts were a fair estimate. Actual loss became irrelevant once the clause was valid.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State
records.text: A stipulated damages clause is enforceable liquidated damages, not a penalty, when at formation the harm was difficult to estimate, the parties made a reasonable effort to fix fair compensation, and the stipulated sum is reasonably related to probable damages.

records.title: Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State
records.text:
The notes ask whether an independently delayed bridge would change the result and compare legitimate alternative performances with penalty labels. The hypothetical bridge was not a fact of Gustafson itself.

83 S.D. 160, 156 N.W.2d 185, decided February 13, 1968. The October 1963 contract recited that time was essential because of the costs and public inconvenience of delay, and the graduated schedule set $210 per day for contracts between $500,001 and $1,000,000.

records.title: Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.
records.text: A clause that guaranteed the bagging company its full revenue without deducting the costs it saved by not working was a penalty, not a reasonable estimate of damages, so Illinois law would not enforce it.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.
records.text: Under Illinois law a liquidated damages clause must be a reasonable estimate, at formation, of likely damages that are difficult to measure; a formula awarding unearned gross revenue without deducting the costs the promisee avoids is an unenforceable penalty.

records.title: Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.
records.text: The source rounds numerical examples. They illustrate the formula’s operation rather than a final damages computation. The last opinion page was checked as an image because its searchable text omits the paragraphs preserving ordinary damages and ordering remand.

records.title: Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown
records.text: A stipulated damages clause between commercial parties of equal strength is presumed reasonable and the challenger must prove otherwise. But a clause keyed to gross receipts can still be a penalty, and the court sent that question back for findings.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown
records.text: A stipulated damages clause is enforceable if it is reasonable under the circumstances as a fair estimate of compensation; in commercial contracts between parties of comparable bargaining power it is presumptively reasonable, and the challenger bears the burden of showing it is unreasonable.

records.title: Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown
records.text: The printed total has a one-cent variation between the narrative and arithmetic display. The court expressly reserved consumer-contract enforcement rather than generalizing its commercial presumption to all parties.

records.title: Lawrence v. Fox
records.text: This landmark New York decision allowed the intended creditor beneficiary to enforce a promise supported by consideration from the debtor, although the beneficiary paid nothing. Six judges affirmed, but they did not share one rationale. It illustrates an early beneficiary-enforcement route, rather than the origin of all third-party-beneficiary law.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Lawrence v. Fox
records.text: A third person for whose benefit a promise is made, on valuable consideration moving from the promisee, may sue the promisor to enforce it, even though the third person was not a party to the agreement and furnished no consideration.

records.title: Lawrence v. Fox
records.text: The editors’ historical account questions the reported name “Holly” and explores the loan’s gambling background.

records.title: Seaver v. Ransom
records.text: A niece could enforce her uncle's promise to his dying wife to leave the niece money. A promise made for a close family member's direct benefit is enforceable by her even though no one owed her a debt.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Seaver v. Ransom
records.text: A beneficiary may enforce a promise made on valid consideration for her direct benefit when the promisee's relationship to her falls within the principle of the close-family beneficiary cases; degree of kinship is not an absolute limit, and no pecuniary debt to her is required.

records.title: Seaver v. Ransom
records.text: The notes question the proposition that only the beneficiary can enforce such a promise. They discuss a promisee’s possible specific-performance action under Restatement § 307. The case should therefore not be read as announcing that a promisee necessarily loses all enforcement rights.

records.title: Sisney v. State
records.text: An inmate could not sue on the prison's food-service contract because the contract was made for the State's benefit and any benefit to inmates was incidental. Government contracts are presumed not to give private people enforceable rights.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Sisney v. State
records.text: A third person may enforce a contract only if the contracting parties clearly manifested at formation an intent to benefit that person; for government contracts there is a presumption against private beneficiary rights unless plain contractual language indicates an intended private enforcement right.

records.title: Sisney v. State
records.text: The editors expressly question how recipients of promised kosher food can be classified as incidental and ask about the consequences of allowing suit against different defendants. The court’s characterization is therefore presented as its contested reasoning, not as a self-evident description of the contract’s purpose.

records.title: Sisney v. Reisch
records.text: The South Dakota court allowed Sisney’s contract claim to survive dismissal: the State’s agreement could waive immunity for its contractual obligations, and he plausibly alleged an intended benefit for inmates. That did not prove breach or establish that every government contract waives immunity.
records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Sisney v. Reisch
records.text: A contract expressly made to benefit an identifiable class of third persons may be enforced by a member of that class, and the State, by entering a contract, waives immunity to the extent a party or beneficiary sues to enforce its undertaking.

records.title: Sisney v. Reisch
records.text: The edited opinion does not reproduce the full immunity analysis. Its reported conclusion is retained without reconstructing omitted reasoning. The editors emphasize that available relief can differ with the defendants and their immunity positions.

records.title: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.
records.text: Applying New York law, the court held that the releases specifically disclaimed reliance on the subject of the alleged Borat deception, defeating the necessary reasonable reliance. The peculiar-knowledge exception did not apply on this record. A disclaimer’s wording and applicable exceptions matter; the court did not find that no misrepresentation occurred.

records.title: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.
records.text: Under New York law, a specific disclaimer of reliance on representations about the very subject of the alleged fraud ordinarily bars a fraudulent-inducement claim, and the peculiar-knowledge exception does not ordinarily protect someone who could have insisted on a written assurance.

It illustrates the form; it should not be represented as the exact signed document of every plaintiff in this case. The appellate ruling is identified in the supplement as a summary order not selected for publication in the Federal Reporter.

records.title: Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.
records.text: When a writing completely covers its subject, an earlier oral promise on that subject ordinarily cannot add a term that would naturally have appeared in the writing. Pennsylvania treated this lease as complete on the disputed sales rights, so Gianni’s claimed oral exclusivity promise was excluded.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 37–39.

records.title: Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.
records.text: When a writing is the complete agreement on a subject, an alleged prior or contemporaneous oral term that parties would naturally and normally include in that writing is barred by the parol evidence rule, even if sued on as a separate contract.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 37–39.

records.title: Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.
records.text:
The court's much-quoted statement of the rule: "Where parties, without any fraud or mistake, have deliberately put their engagements in writing, the law declares the writing to be not only the best, but the only evidence of their agreement." (Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., 281 Pa. 320, 126 A. 791 (1924)).

The test the court applied: if the subject of the alleged oral agreement is one that would naturally and normally have been included in the written contract, evidence of the oral agreement is inadmissible to add to or vary the writing absent fraud, accident or mistake.

records.text: Under the international sales convention there is no parol evidence rule, so a merger clause excludes earlier oral understandings only if both parties actually meant it to. Evidence of the negotiations had to be considered.

records.title: TeeVee Toons, Inc. v. Gerhard Schubert GmbH
records.text: Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause bars evidence of prior oral understandings only if both parties shared the intention to be bound by it, so negotiations must be considered under Article 8 even when they contradict the writing.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 40–45.

records.title: TeeVee Toons, Inc. v. Gerhard Schubert GmbH
records.text:
The decision denies part of the seller’s summary-judgment motion; it is not a final award to the buyer.

The case (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 23, 2006, 2006 WL 2463537) is usually taught for the point that, unlike the UCC parol evidence rule, CISG Article 8 lets a court consider evidence of the negotiations that contradicts the written terms, so a merger clause and warranty disclaimer do not automatically control.

records.title: Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others
records.text: Singapore's court implies a term only when necessary to make the contract work, and declined to imply a general duty of good faith into every contract. An entire-agreement clause shuts out implied terms only if it says so clearly.

records.title: Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others
records.text: A term is implied in fact only where necessary, tested by business efficacy and the officious bystander together, and the court declined to imply a general duty of good faith in law; an entire-agreement clause excludes implied terms only by clear language.

records.title: Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others
records.text:
The supplement’s editorial note at page 73 reports later Canadian and English developments, including Wastech, Braganza, and Yam Seng. Those are later editorial comparisons, not holdings of the 2009 Singapore court.

The decision is Ng Giap Hon v Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd [2009] SGCA 19; Ng was a remisier claiming commission on IPO placement shares allocated to two of the firm's customers, and the Court of Appeal declined to imply a duty of good faith as a matter of law, citing the need to protect the sanctity of contract and the unsettled content of a general good-faith duty in the authorities.

records.title: Swiss Federal Supreme Court: contractual penalty decision of September 24, 2024
records.text:
The December 2020 agreement restricted use of specified names and trademarks to compete or suggest continued affiliation, while permitting necessary information to third parties and limited historical references. It stipulated CHF 100,000 for each violation. A later letter to candidates described a takeover of operational business and advertised Arkadium as a leading headhunter, using protected names and branding. The courts accepted that some notice of the transferred placement processes was permissible, but found that the disputed promotional wording exceeded that purpose.

The breach occurred once, was minor, and was not expected to recur. The claimant failed to substantiate damage or a risk of damage; a cited email did not show the alleged confusion. The financially significant underlying transaction and the clause’s punitive function nevertheless supported some penalty rather than complete elimination.

records.text:
The translated Swiss rule permits parties to stipulate a penalty while requiring judicial reduction of an excessive amount. Courts exercise restraint in recognition of contractual freedom, but assess gross disproportion by reference to the creditor’s legitimate interest at breach, the seriousness and fault of the violation, the relationship, and the parties’ circumstances. The debtor generally must raise and prove the basis for reduction.

Here, the claimant could not merely assert the value of its trademarks or the parties’ sophistication without answering the substantiated account of a minor, nonrecurring breach. The court could consider lack of damage in assessing amount while recognizing that a penalty can become due without compensable damage. The continued CHF 10,000 award reflected the punitive function and the significance of the transaction. The analysis therefore differs from the domestic rule that invalidates a penalty and leaves ordinary breach damages.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement, pp. 130–138.

records.title: How contract law fits together
records.text: Contract law determines which commitments create legal duties, what those duties require, and what relief follows when they are broken. The governing source of law must be identified before applying a formation checklist.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 1–8.
Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 40–45: TeeVee Toons and CISG Articles 8 and 11.

records.title: How contract law fits together
records.text:
Begin with the transaction. The common law consists of rules developed through judicial decisions; the relevant jurisdiction’s cases matter. The Restatement collects and organizes general common-law principles. It is persuasive authority rather than an enacted statute. The Uniform Commercial Code is a model whose enacted state version supplies statutory rules. Article 2 principally governs transactions in goods, while Article 1 supplies shared definitions and background rules. Under § 1-103(b), principles of law and equity supplement the Code unless a particular Code provision displaces them.

The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, abbreviated CISG, is a treaty governing qualifying international sales. It has its own rules of formation, interpretation, and remedies. It is not simply another name for Article 2 or for the Restatement. TeeVee Toons illustrates why a court may consider negotiations and intent under CISG Articles 8 and 11 even though a domestic parol-evidence approach might treat a writing differently. The precise scope, exclusions, declarations, and any effective choice require checking the applicable text. The treaty text is in the Contracts Selections (CISG Article 11 at PDF page 615).

Once the governing law is identified, ask what was communicated and agreed; what supports legal enforcement; whether sufficient certainty and required form exist; and whether a defense limits enforcement. After that, identify the terms, conditions, performance, any excuse, and the remedy. These questions interact: interpretation can establish an implied promise, and a statutory form requirement can prevent enforcement even where an agreement exists. The sequence is a study framework synthesized from the cited readings, not a single rule announced by one court.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 1–8.
Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 40–45: TeeVee Toons and CISG Articles 8 and 11.

records.title: Contractual discretion
records.text: Contractual discretion is a party’s power to make a choice affecting performance, such as whether a result is satisfactory, how much to order, or how strongly to promote a product. The question is what limits govern that choice.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 65–75: Ng Giap and the limits on implying duties.

records.title: Contractual discretion
records.text:
A contract can leave room for judgment without leaving a party free of all obligation. In Mattei, the buyer could evaluate proposed leases but had to be genuinely dissatisfied rather than use the condition to escape an unwanted bargain. In Structural Polymer, uncertain requirements were constrained by good faith and the agreed purchasing arrangement. In Wood, the exclusive agency and revenue-sharing structure implied reasonable efforts even without an express sentence saying so.

Later cases ask how discretion is exercised after formation. Dalton examines a testing service’s obligation to consider evidence within its promised review process. Bloor examines efforts to market a brand where royalties depended on sales. Market Street addresses the use of a contractual procedure and possible exploitation of the other party’s oversight. Ng Giap cautions that a broad good-faith obligation cannot simply be assumed across jurisdictions or used to rewrite express rights.

To analyze discretion, identify the exact choice, the person entitled to make it, the contractual purpose, and the relevant standard. A reasonableness standard asks whether the choice meets an external benchmark. A subjective good-faith standard asks whether the stated judgment is genuine within the agreed undertaking. Express terms and governing law determine which applies. A judge’s discretion over procedure or remedies is a different issue.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 65–75: Ng Giap and the limits on implying duties.

records.title: Using cases and precedent
records.text: A case explains a court’s resolution of a dispute under particular law and facts. Its usefulness depends on the issue decided, the governing jurisdiction, and the procedural posture.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 2–4.

records.title: Using cases and precedent
records.text:
Extract the rule together with the facts that make it operate. A court may decide only that a claim can proceed, leaving facts for trial. A remand for findings is different from a final decision that a disputed contract term applies. The same opinion may discuss another rule without adopting it. Northrop makes this especially visible: the court preferred one treatment of different terms but predicted that Illinois would use another.

A statute can also change the legal landscape reflected in an older opinion. The casebook’s medical-promise notes illustrate legislative responses to judicial decisions. The Restatement provides a useful organization and persuasive formulation, but the court’s actual adoption or rejection of that formulation matters.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 2–4.

records.title: International sales and the CISG
records.text: The CISG is the United Nations treaty on contracts for qualifying international sales of goods. Its own provisions can govern a sale instead of the domestic sales rules a reader might otherwise assume apply.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 40–45 (TeeVee Toons).

records.title: International sales and the CISG
records.text:
The assigned TeeVee Toons dispute concerned a buyer and a German machinery supplier. The court used the Convention’s treatment of intent and interpretation, including negotiations and conduct, to examine whether disputed printed terms and a merger clause were actually accepted. This matters because the parol evidence rule cannot simply be imported into a Convention case as though domestic law automatically controlled.

CISG Article 11 generally removes a writing requirement for the sales contract within its operation; that does not remove the need to establish agreement. Article 8 provides the interpretive framework discussed in the assigned supplemental opinion. These are distinct questions: how an agreement may be proved, what the parties meant, and whether they adopted a particular term.

Use the applicable treaty text to determine coverage and qualifications in a real problem. The CISG articles are in the course Selections, which open from the Article 11 entry.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 40–45 (TeeVee Toons).

records.title: Liability during negotiations
records.text: Negotiations can create limited legal obligations before the parties form the final contract they are discussing. The obligation may arise from a specific assurance or an agreement about how to negotiate.

records.title: Liability during negotiations
records.text:
First determine whether a complete agreement already exists, with a writing intended only as a later record. If it does not, identify the narrower undertaking actually made. Dixon concerns assurances and alleged reliance during loan-modification discussions. Cyberchron concerns work performed while major commercial terms remained unresolved. Channel Home Centers examines a letter promising withdrawal from the market and good-faith negotiation.

A duty to negotiate in good faith does not guarantee that negotiations will succeed. A reliance claim likewise does not automatically entitle the claimant to the profits of the hoped-for final bargain. The assurance, reasonable induced action, causation, and applicable remedy must each be established. The assigned French Civil Code provision supplies a comparative rule protecting freedom to negotiate while requiring good faith and limiting recovery for faulty negotiations. Keep that provision’s jurisdiction and remedy limits distinct from the American cases.

records.title: Definiteness and open terms
records.text: Definiteness concerns whether the parties’ commitment is clear enough for a court to identify the obligation, determine breach, and provide a remedy. An open term can sometimes be supplied without defeating the agreement.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Definiteness and preliminary agreements briefs, pp. 1–2

records.title: Definiteness and open terms
records.text:
The significance of a missing term depends on what the parties left open and what they intended. In Sun Printing, both future price and the period for which a price would apply remained unresolved. The court declined to impose the ongoing bargain urged by the buyer; the dissent offered a different reading. In Oglebay, a long relationship, a stated duration, and evidence of intended commitment supported supplying a price after specified pricing mechanisms failed.

Distinguish an agreement to agree later from a present commitment with a workable method for completing details. An external benchmark, established practice, course of performance, or governing gap-filler can make an obligation manageable. Those tools cannot automatically override an express decision to remain unbound until further agreement. The transaction’s purpose, wording, and history must justify the completion.

atlasSources.label: Brief · Definiteness and preliminary agreements briefs, pp. 1–2

records.title: Changing an existing contract
records.text: A modification changes duties under an existing contract. Identify the proposed change and the governing law before deciding whether new consideration, good faith, a writing, or assent is required.

records.title: Changing an existing contract
records.text:
Alaska Packers applies the pre-existing-duty rule to a demand for increased pay for the same work after the workers had reached a remote location. Watkins examines the parties’ response to unexpected excavation conditions and their subsequent agreement. Austin addresses a price increase obtained through a threat to withhold urgently needed goods when practical alternatives were unavailable. These cases ask different questions: whether an exchange supports the change, whether the agreement was genuinely voluntary, and whether an asserted adjustment responds fairly to circumstances.

UCC § 2-209 removes a new-consideration requirement for a covered modification, while the assigned discussion retains limits involving good faith, form, and assent. A no-oral-modification clause raises another inquiry; a failed modification may have consequences as a waiver. The New York signed-writing provision in the supplement supplies a separate statutory route. Keep those routes distinct rather than treating “both agreed” as the whole analysis.

records.title: Duress and economic pressure
records.text: Duress asks whether an improper threat induced agreement when the affected party lacked a reasonable alternative. Severe commercial pressure requires examination of its source, timing, and available responses.

atlasSources.label: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 176 · Contracts Selections, PDF page 94 of 713
Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 175 · Contracts Selections, PDF page 93 of 713

records.title: Duress and economic pressure
records.text:
In Austin, a supplier threatened to stop deliveries of components needed for the buyer’s naval commitments unless it received price increases and additional business. The buyer’s unsuccessful attempts to obtain timely replacements, its exposure on the main contracts, and the inadequacy of simply suing later were central. A party’s eventual written agreement does not itself settle whether the agreement was obtained through duress.

Distinguish this inquiry from ordinary hard bargaining and from the pre-existing-duty rule. The latter asks what consideration supports a new promise; duress asks about the legitimacy of the pressure that induced assent. The assigned Restatement §§ 175 and 176 are cross-referenced in the syllabus, and their complete text and illustrations are in the Contracts Selections (PDF pages 93–94), linked below.

atlasSources.label: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 176 · Contracts Selections, PDF page 94 of 713
Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 175 · Contracts Selections, PDF page 93 of 713

records.title: Misrepresentation and induced assent
records.text: Misrepresentation concerns a false or misleading representation that affects a party’s decision to agree. Analyze what was represented, why it was misleading, how it induced assent, and whether reliance was justified under the applicable rule.

records.title: Misrepresentation and induced assent
records.text:
A statement can be misleading through what it says, what it implies, or an omission that makes a partial account deceptive. Swinton and Kannavos distinguish mere silence in the circumstances presented from statements that create a false impression unless completed. Speakers of Sport separates predictions or promotional confidence from actionable factual commitments, while Vokes examines flattering opinions given by a party with superior knowledge to an inexperienced customer.

Contract avoidance for misrepresentation, damages in tort for fraud, and breach of an express warranty are related but distinct routes. Psenicska adds the problem of a specific no-reliance clause and what the plaintiffs agreed they were not relying on. A general merger clause and a specific disclaimer of reliance need not have the same effect. Preserve the jurisdiction, procedural stage, and precise representation before drawing a result.

records.title: Silence, disclosure, and half-truths
records.text: Disclosure rules determine when a party must reveal information rather than remain silent. A party that chooses to speak may need to supply enough information to keep its statements from becoming misleading.

records.title: Silence, disclosure, and half-truths
records.text:
Swinton declined to impose liability for undisclosed termite damage under the rule and allegations before that court. Kannavos involved an advertised multi-family use that was unlawful: the seller’s partial description created an impression that required correction. The distinction turns on the communication and circumstances, not merely whether one party possessed information the other lacked.

Questions about active concealment, special relationships, reasonable investigation, and known mistakes may require additional doctrines. The assigned cases and notes present competing policy reasons for protecting information-gathering and for preventing deception. They do not support a single rule that buyers must discover everything or that sellers must disclose everything.

records.title: The parol evidence rule
records.text: The parol evidence rule determines how a final written agreement affects alleged earlier or contemporaneous agreements. It addresses the legal effect of a writing, not simply whether a witness may speak about it.

records.title: The parol evidence rule
records.text:
Ask whether the writing was intended as a final expression of the terms it addresses, and whether it was also intended as a complete expression of the agreement. A partially integrated writing can preclude inconsistent earlier terms while leaving room for consistent additional ones. A complete integration can exclude those additional terms as well. The governing approach determines what evidence the court considers in deciding completeness.

Gianni treats an alleged exclusivity promise as one that would naturally have been included with the lease’s other business restrictions. Masterson takes a different view of whether a claimed family restriction on assignment would naturally be omitted from a deed. Bollinger concerns a claimed mutual mistake in reducing the agreement to writing. Later modifications, fraud, mistake, and interpretation must be identified separately; their treatment is not resolved merely by calling evidence “oral.”

For goods, examine UCC § 2-202 and the role of trade usage and prior dealings. For a CISG contract, TeeVee Toons shows why domestic parol-evidence assumptions cannot automatically be applied. The assigned Selections provisions open from their own entries (Restatement §§ 209–216, UCC § 2-202, CISG Article 8).

records.title: Final and complete writings
records.text: An integrated writing is intended as a final expression of some or all agreed terms. A complete integration is also intended to contain the entire agreement within its scope.

records.title: Final and complete writings
records.text:
Finality and completeness answer different questions. A writing may finally settle the price while leaving another consistent undertaking outside its scope. Determining what the parties intended requires the jurisdiction’s method for evaluating the writing and surrounding evidence. Gianni and Masterson illustrate different assessments of whether an alleged collateral agreement belongs inside the written instrument.

A merger clause states that the writing represents the whole agreement. It is evidence relevant to integration, but its legal effect depends on the governing rule and circumstances. A clause cannot be assumed to settle its own disputed adoption, as the CISG analysis in TeeVee Toons illustrates.

records.title: Trade usage and the commercial setting
records.text: A trade usage is a sufficiently established practice in a business that helps determine what parties in that setting reasonably understand their agreement to mean or require.

records.title: Trade usage and the commercial setting
records.text:
Frigaliment asks what “chicken” meant in the relevant transaction and who had proved the narrower meaning. Hurst asks whether a numerical protein specification carried an established trade tolerance. Nanakuli examines price protection as a practice relevant to an asphalt supply agreement. Bayway uses industry evidence to assess whether an added tax term would objectively surprise a merchant.

Identify the practice precisely, establish the evidence supporting it, and explain its relationship to the disputed term. Trade usage is different from a course of dealing between these particular parties and from a course of performance under this very agreement. The readings show that practice may explain, supplement, or qualify language in some circumstances; it is not a license to disregard every express term.

records.title: Course of dealing between the parties
records.text: A course of dealing is the parties’ pattern of conduct in previous transactions, used to understand their expectations in a later agreement.

records.title: Course of dealing between the parties
records.text:
A recurring way of placing, confirming, and filling orders can give a later communication significance that it would not have between strangers. American Bronze’s order-processing history is an early formation example. The later commercial-context readings examine how established dealings bear on obligations and the inclusion of terms.

Keep the time periods distinct: prior transactions supply a course of dealing; repeated conduct under the disputed contract supplies a course of performance. Both differ from practices of a wider trade. A conclusion about either requires evidence of the actual pattern and its relevance, not simply that the parties have known each other for a long time.

records.title: Good faith in performance
records.text: Good faith limits the way a party performs or exercises rights under an existing contract. Its content depends on the bargain, the governing law, and the particular choice or conduct at issue.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 65–75: Ng Giap and the limits on implying duties.

records.title: Good faith in performance
records.text:
Dalton required the testing service to carry out its promised review process meaningfully; it did not authorize a court to replace the service’s assessment with its own. Market Street examines whether a party deliberately exploited the other’s oversight of a contractual procedure. Bloor asks whether the brewer made the effort required by an express best-efforts clause despite its own commercial pressures.

The casebook also presents different explanations of good faith, including excluding bad-faith conduct and limiting recapture of opportunities surrendered in the bargain. Those theoretical accounts help ask what the alleged opportunism consists of, but the legal duty still needs to be tied to the agreement. Northwest and Ng Giap show important limits, including preemption and reluctance to imply a broad obligation inconsistent with express rights.

Good faith is not an independent permission to impose whatever outcome seems fair, and it does not always require sacrificing all self-interest. Ask which benefit or procedure was promised, how the party’s conduct affected it, and what the governing authority actually requires.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 65–75: Ng Giap and the limits on implying duties.

records.title: Adhesion and standardized contracts
records.text: An adhesion contract is a standardized agreement presented by a party with superior bargaining power on terms the other party can generally accept or reject rather than negotiate.

records.title: Adhesion and standardized contracts
records.text:
Graham shows that even an experienced businessperson may face an adhesive form when industry arrangements leave no realistic alternative. The label begins the inquiry; it does not itself decide that every term is unenforceable. The court separately considered reasonable expectations and an arbitrator’s structural bias.

Other readings examine notice of terms, the duty to read, consumer statutes, and substantive unfairness. Klar turns on the meaning and notice of a claim check. Doe applies a statute regulating a particular service. Anderson addresses attempted adoption and retroactive use of changed online terms. These are separate legal mechanisms for assessing standardized contracting. The course-wide index preserves those differences.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: Unconscionability examines whether the circumstances of agreement and the substance of its terms make enforcement impermissibly unfair under the governing rule.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text:
Williams considers meaningful choice together with terms unreasonably favorable to the seller. The purchase documents allowed earlier purchases to remain subject to repossession through a cross-collateral arrangement, and the court remanded for the relevant assessment rather than itself awarding final relief. Stoll examines a transaction involving language difficulties and a chicken-litter provision whose consequences dwarfed the nominal land-price adjustment.

Procedural concerns include how terms were presented and the parties’ opportunities to understand and choose. Substantive concerns include the obligations and risks imposed. Their required relationship and the remedy depend on governing law. Graham separately evaluates a biased arbitration arrangement. A harsh term, unequal bargaining position, or disappointing result should be connected to the particular legal standard rather than treated as self-proving.

The supplied Anderson opinion is assigned alongside these materials, but its actual analysis of notice, amendment, and accrued claims should be preserved rather than rewritten as a generic unconscionability holding.

records.title: Public policy and enforceability
records.text: Public-policy rules can limit enforcement of an agreement because of interests the law protects beyond the parties’ private exchange.

records.title: Public policy and enforceability
records.text:
Identify the policy’s source and the connection between that policy and the promise being enforced. A licensing violation, illegal performance, or restraint on work may present different questions. Blossom Farm examines the consequences of unlawful conduct connected with a sale; X.L.O. considers an agreement connected with an alleged antitrust violation. The existence of wrongdoing does not automatically answer which party may enforce which obligation or obtain restitution.

Hassler addresses an overbroad employment restraint and whether a court should rewrite it. The supplementary FTC materials concern a dated federal rule-removal history, not a conclusion that every private noncompete is valid. State statutes and judicial standards remain separate questions. Policy analysis should identify the protected interest, the effect of enforcement or nonenforcement, and the remedy appropriate to the case.

records.title: Restrictive employment covenants
records.text: A noncompetition covenant limits a worker’s or business seller’s ability to compete after a relationship ends. Its enforceability requires the particular governing restrictions and the scope of the restraint to be examined.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 102–107.

records.title: Restrictive employment covenants
records.text:
Hassler analyzes the employer’s asserted interests, the duration and geography of the restraint, and the court’s approach to overbreadth. The consequences of an excessive clause may differ depending on whether the governing law permits partial enforcement or rewriting. An agreement supported by consideration and signed voluntarily can still encounter these limits.

The Fall 2026 supplement separately reproduces federal materials removing an FTC rule after litigation. They are a specific source history as supplied for class. Their inclusion does not establish that all noncompete agreements are enforceable or replace the state-law inquiry.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 102–107.

records.title: Consumer legislation and contract terms
records.text: Consumer-protection statutes can impose requirements and remedies even when ordinary rules of assent and consideration would recognize a contract.

records.title: Consumer legislation and contract terms
records.text:
Doe applies New York’s dating-services legislation to contracts that attempted to describe the service as something outside the statute. The court examined what the service actually did and the mandatory terms and price rules governing it. The agreement’s own characterization did not determine the statute’s coverage.

The casebook compares judicial review, legislation, administrative enforcement, and European controls on unfair terms. Those approaches may regulate disclosure, substantive terms, or remedies. Keep each source’s coverage and remedy separate; a rule requiring readable disclosure does not necessarily decide whether a clearly disclosed term is substantively fair.

records.title: Express conditions to performance
records.text: An express condition is an event the parties specify must occur before a duty becomes due, or whose occurrence affects that duty as the agreement provides.

records.title: Express conditions to performance
records.text:
Luttinger’s financing condition made the buyers’ duty depend on obtaining a qualifying mortgage after the required effort. Gibson’s satisfaction condition concerned the buyer’s judgment of a portrait. Peacock asks whether a clause tied payment to an event as a true risk-shifting condition or merely fixed payment timing. The wording and transaction determine the difference.

A condition is distinct from a promise. Failure of a condition may mean that a duty never becomes due without itself being a breach. A person can also promise to bring about the condition, in which case failure may have both effects. Interpretation, excuse, waiver, and prevention must be analyzed before concluding that nonoccurrence defeats recovery.

records.title: Constructive conditions of exchange
records.text: A constructive condition is a dependency the law recognizes between the parties’ performances even when the agreement does not expressly use conditional language.

records.title: Constructive conditions of exchange
records.text:
Kingston shows the significance of the order of performance: provision of security was required before the other party had to turn over the business. More generally, an exchange may require simultaneous performance or performance by one side before the other must act. A breach does not automatically excuse every remaining duty; its materiality and the governing dependency matter.

Substantial-performance and divisibility doctrines can soften the consequences of incomplete performance. Jacob & Youngs distinguishes a minor, innocent departure in construction from a failure that defeats the exchange. Identify whether the disputed condition is express or supplied by law, because the governing degree of required compliance may differ.

records.title: Substantial performance and minor defects
records.text: Substantial performance can permit recovery of the contract price, with an adjustment for defects, where the party has performed the essential undertaking and the remaining departure does not justify treating the exchange as failed.

records.title: Substantial performance and minor defects
records.text:
Jacob & Youngs involved pipe from manufacturers other than the specified brand, discovered after a house was complete. The quality and function of the installed pipe, the character of the omission, the purpose of the specification, and the destructive cost of replacement mattered. The decision distinguished the right to payment from the measure of damages for the defect.

Substantial performance does not make every deviation harmless or erase express risk allocations. A deliberate or material departure can lead to a different result. Plante, Groves, and Peevyhouse later ask related but distinct questions about the cost of completion and loss in value. The materiality of breach, the payment condition, and the damages measure should each be addressed.

records.title: Divisible exchanges
records.text: A divisible contract separates agreed performances into corresponding parts, so a party’s right to payment for one completed part may be assessed independently of unperformed parts.

records.title: Divisible exchanges
records.text:
Gill considers whether payment for delivered logs could be separated from duties concerning the remaining timber. The relevant question is whether the agreement pairs portions of performance with corresponding compensation. A price expressed by units is evidence to interpret, not a complete answer by itself.

Distinguish dividing an exchange from merely measuring damages in units. Divisibility affects whether a condition of full performance must occur before any payment becomes due. The parties’ language, purpose, and apportionment of obligations determine whether that treatment fits.

records.title: Forfeiture and the consequences of a condition
records.text: Forfeiture occurs when a party loses a promised entitlement despite having already supplied substantial performance or incurred substantial reliance, often because a condition was not met.

records.title: Forfeiture and the consequences of a condition
records.text:
The concern is the relationship between the condition’s purpose and the loss caused by enforcing it strictly. Nelson and the waiver materials consider circumstances in which a party’s conduct or the governing doctrine prevents reliance on a condition. Jacob & Youngs raises a related concern about withholding the entire contract price after substantial construction.

Avoiding forfeiture is not a universal power to disregard conditions. Determine whether the event was material to the agreed exchange, whether the condition was waived or its occurrence prevented, and what the applicable doctrine permits. The reason for relief and its limits belong in the analysis.

records.title: Waiver of a contractual requirement
records.text: Waiver concerns a party’s decision or conduct giving up the right to insist on a contractual requirement, including a condition placed for that party’s protection.

records.title: Waiver of a contractual requirement
records.text:
A party may act in a way that communicates it will accept performance despite an unmet requirement. The question is what right was relinquished, what the conduct reasonably meant, and whether the other party relied or the governing rule otherwise makes that relinquishment effective. Waiver is distinct from an agreed modification supported by the requirements applicable to changing the bargain.

The assigned mitigating-doctrines materials use waiver alongside estoppel and prevention. Those doctrines can overlap in consequences, but their reasons differ. Preserve the specific facts showing why the party could or could not later insist on strict compliance.

records.title: Prevention and hindrance of performance
records.text: A party’s interference with an event or performance it later invokes as a condition can affect its ability to rely on that event’s nonoccurrence.

records.title: Prevention and hindrance of performance
records.text:
McKenna examines the consequences of conduct affecting a certification requirement. The surrounding materials ask when one party’s obstruction, failure to cooperate, or control of a needed step excuses a condition or constitutes breach. Identify the promised cooperation, the actual interference, and the causal connection to the missing event.

The doctrine does not eliminate every condition merely because one party could influence it. The agreement may allocate relevant risks or discretion. Interpretation and good faith therefore remain important in deciding which actions the parties were entitled to take.

records.title: Mistake about the bargain’s basic assumptions
records.text: Mistake concerns an erroneous belief about facts existing when the agreement is made. Relief depends on the significance of that assumption and who bears the risk that it is wrong.

records.title: Mistake about the bargain’s basic assumptions
records.text:
Renner involved land and water conditions essential to the parties’ intended agricultural use. The court treated the mistaken basic assumption as grounds for rescission and then addressed restitution separately. Stees illustrates a different treatment of an undertaking to achieve a construction result despite unexpected difficulty.

Ask what fact was mistaken, whether the mistake was shared, whether it materially affected the exchange, and whether the contract or governing rule allocated the risk. A mistaken prediction about later profitability is not automatically the same as a mistake about an existing basic fact. The remedy also requires care: unwinding the exchange and compensating every expenditure are not identical.

records.title: Allocation of contractual risk
records.text: Risk allocation determines which party must bear the consequences when a relevant assumption proves wrong or an event makes performance more difficult or less valuable.

records.title: Allocation of contractual risk
records.text:
Allocation may be expressed through conditions, warranties, fixed prices, or force-majeure clauses. It may also follow from the undertaking interpreted in context and the governing legal rules. Stees, Taylor, Transatlantic, and Krell illustrate different relationships among the promised result, the disrupted circumstances, and the claimed excuse.

Foreseeability is relevant, but asking whether an event could have been imagined does not finish the inquiry. A party may know a risk exists without clearly assuming every consequence; conversely, an unconditional undertaking may place a risk on that party. Explain the language, commercial purpose, alternatives, and burden rather than using “risk” as an unexplained label.

records.title: Impossibility and impracticability
records.text: Impossibility and impracticability doctrines address circumstances in which an event prevents or severely disrupts the promised performance and the governing law may excuse it.

records.title: Impossibility and impracticability
records.text:
Taylor concerns destruction of the specific music hall essential to the performances. Transatlantic concerns closure of the Suez Canal when the ship could still complete the voyage by a longer route. That contrast makes the promised performance and available alternatives central. Increased cost or difficulty does not automatically establish an excuse.

Identify the event, its effect on the actual undertaking, the assumption on which the parties contracted, the allocation of risk, and any fault or contractual clause affecting the analysis. The casebook also discusses more recent disruptions as applications to test; their treatment depends on the particular contract. Keep impossibility of the performance distinct from a decline in the value the recipient expects to obtain.

records.title: Frustration of contractual purpose
records.text: Frustration concerns an event that destroys the principal purpose of the exchange for a party even though the promised performance may remain physically possible.

records.title: Frustration of contractual purpose
records.text:
In Krell, rooms could still be supplied, but cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared purpose for which the particular daytime use had been arranged. The court considered the transaction’s setting and the parties’ understanding rather than requiring an express sentence naming that purpose.

A party’s private hope or ordinary loss of profit does not necessarily define the bargain’s principal purpose. Determine whether the purpose was sufficiently shared or known, whether the disruption was fundamental, and whether the party claiming excuse bore the risk. Distinguish frustration from impossibility: the former asks what performance would now achieve, while the latter asks whether the undertaking can be performed.

records.title: Force-majeure clauses
records.text: A force-majeure clause allocates the consequences of specified events that disrupt performance. Its wording can determine whether a party receives more, less, or different protection than a background excuse doctrine would provide.

records.title: Force-majeure clauses
records.text:
Identify the listed events, any general catchall, the required effect on performance, notice requirements, mitigation duties, and the stated consequence. A clause may permit delay, suspension, or termination rather than erase all obligations. Causation matters: occurrence of an event does not by itself show that the event prevented the performance in dispute.

The syllabus calls for a force-majeure clause alongside the excuse cases. The casebook’s discussion supplies the conceptual setting. The clause assigned for class 21 was handed out in class.

records.title: Cost of completion and loss in value
records.text: These measures compare the cost of obtaining the promised performance with the reduction in the property’s value caused by the defect. The governing rule decides which better protects the contractual entitlement in the circumstances.

records.title: Cost of completion and loss in value
records.text:
Plante evaluates substantial construction and the cost of correcting particular deficiencies. Groves and Peevyhouse reach different results about restorative work whose cost greatly exceeded the resulting market-value increase. The significance of the promise, the character of the breach, proportionality, and the court’s understanding of the contract matter.

Cost of completion is not automatically a windfall merely because the owner has not yet done the work. Loss in value is not automatically adequate merely because it is cheaper for the breacher. Identify the interest the promise protected, the evidence of valuation and cost, and the legal limits the relevant court applied. Preserve dissents and procedural outcomes rather than converting these cases into a single arithmetic formula.

records.title: Avoidable loss and mitigation
records.text: Mitigation limits recovery for loss the injured party could reasonably have avoided after breach. It ordinarily concerns the recoverable amount rather than imposing a separate duty to perform for the breacher’s benefit.

records.title: Avoidable loss and mitigation
records.text:
Rockingham asks why a contractor continued construction after learning that the county repudiated. Parker asks whether a discharged performer had to accept a different proposed role to reduce her damages. Avoidance may require reasonable steps, but not every alternative is sufficiently comparable or reasonable. The breacher’s burden of proving avoidable loss and the factual posture matter.

Identify when the injured party learned of the breach, what alternatives were actually available, their costs and risks, and whether accepting them would sacrifice a protected interest. Distinguish replacement income that truly substitutes for the lost transaction from income that could have been earned in addition to it. The assigned materials also consider arguments about the breacher’s equal opportunity to prevent loss; they do not state a universally accepted exception.

records.title: Foreseeability of contract loss
records.text: Foreseeability limits which consequences of breach can be charged to the breaching party by reference to the circumstances and information at the time of contracting.

records.title: Foreseeability of contract loss
records.text:
Hadley distinguishes loss arising ordinarily from breach from loss depending on special circumstances communicated to the other party. Its facts and application require careful reading: the editors identify a discrepancy between the reported trial account and the circumstances the appellate court treated as established. Kenford examines whether the county assumed responsibility for the developer’s anticipated increase in surrounding land value.

Ask which loss is claimed, how it follows from breach, what the defendant knew when agreeing, and whether the governing formulation also requires an undertaking of responsibility. Mere causal connection after the event is insufficient. Do not collapse this concept into foreseeability of reliance under promissory estoppel or foreseeability in tort; the time, purpose, and legal consequences differ.

records.title: Proof and reasonable certainty of damages
records.text: The certainty requirement asks whether evidence supports the existence and amount of the claimed loss sufficiently for an award. It does not always require exact arithmetic or an established business history.

records.title: Proof and reasonable certainty of damages
records.text:
Fera concerns projected profits of a new business, supported by testimony that the jury could evaluate. The majority and dissent disagreed about the evidence and the weight of uncertainty. The broader materials distinguish uncertainty about whether loss occurred from difficulty measuring a loss known to have occurred.

Identify the assumptions behind projections, the available market or operating evidence, causation, and the standard of review. The fact that a business is new is relevant to proof but should not be used as a substitute for examining the evidence under the applicable rule. Naval Institute supplies an earlier example of a supported counterfactual estimate.

records.title: Agreed damages and penalty limits
records.text: A stipulated remedy specifies consequences of breach in advance. Courts distinguish enforceable compensation arrangements from penalties under the governing law, and the parties’ label is not conclusive.

records.title: Agreed damages and penalty limits
records.text:
Dave Gustafson considers a daily delay amount. Lake River examines a minimum-quantity shortfall formula that could recover the bagging contractor’s full contract charges for the unshipped quantity without subtracting costs saved. Wasserman’s separates compensation for improvements from a gross-receipts-based cancellation amount requiring further examination. Figgie concerns an agreed refund or replacement arrangement and its interaction with limitations on liability.

Ask what event triggers the clause, what losses it was designed to address, the difficulty of estimating those losses, the relation between the amount and compensable harm, and the applicable timing of that evaluation. A limitation on recovery is not the same as a clause imposing liquidated damages. The Swiss supplement provides a distinct comparative approach permitting reduction of an excessive penalty; that approach should remain attributed to Swiss law rather than silently merged with the American rules.

records.title: Rights of intended third-party beneficiaries
records.text: A third-party beneficiary is someone who may claim a benefit under a contract made by other people. The key question is whether the agreement and governing law give that person an enforceable right rather than merely an incidental advantage.

records.title: Rights of intended third-party beneficiaries
records.text:
Lawrence concerns a promise to pay another person’s debt. Seaver concerns a promise to provide for someone in a will. Those cases explore why the person benefited may sue despite not making the bargain. The two Sisney cases involve distinct arrangements and different evidence about an intention to create enforceable rights. A contract serving the public or benefiting an identifiable group does not automatically give every member a private contract action.

Identify the promisor, promisee, proposed beneficiary, precise performance promised, and evidence of intended enforceability. The beneficiary’s interest must be tied to that contract. Questions about vesting and later modification arise only after identifying a right capable of vesting.

records.title: When a beneficiary’s rights become protected
records.text: Vesting concerns when contracting parties lose some freedom to modify or discharge a benefit promised to a third party without that beneficiary’s consent.

records.title: When a beneficiary’s rights become protected
records.text:
First establish that the person is an intended beneficiary with a right under the contract. Then examine the governing rule about events such as assent, reliance, or suit, and any reservation in the agreement. The assigned introductory materials distinguish the existence of a third-party benefit from the point at which the original parties can no longer freely alter it.

The syllabus assigns an introduction rather than every later case in the chapter. The complete Restatement text is in the Contracts Selections.

records.title: Delegating performance of a duty
records.text: Delegation arranges for someone else to perform a contractual duty. It must be distinguished from transferring the right to receive performance and from releasing the original obligor.

records.title: Delegating performance of a duty
records.text:
Identify who originally owed the duty, what performance was promised, and whether the obligee has an important interest in that particular person’s performance. Personal skill, trust, contractual restrictions, and the governing law may matter. A transfer of performance responsibilities does not automatically prove that the original party was discharged; that is a separate question about the agreement and any substitution accepted by the obligee.

The assigned pages introduce delegation. Their scope should not be mistaken for a complete treatment of all exceptions or of every later case in the chapter.

records.title: Assigning contractual rights
records.text: Assignment transfers a contractual right from its holder to another person. The assignee seeks the transferred benefit, while the underlying agreement determines what the obligor must provide.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., p. 54.

records.title: Assigning contractual rights
records.text:
Hamer begins with a claimant who acquired the nephew’s right through intermediate assignments. Masterson later raises the significance of an alleged restriction on transfer of an option. These examples show why identifying the original parties is not enough: a later claimant may hold a right acquired from one of them.

Distinguish assignment of a right from delegation of a duty. Also ask about any restriction on transfer, the nature of the right, notice, and defenses under the governing law. The final assignment includes only introductory pages on this subject.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., p. 54.

records.title: N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1103: written modification or discharge
records.text: Section 5-1103 prevents specified written, signed modifications or discharges from failing merely for lack of consideration.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, p. 9.

records.title: N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1103: written modification or discharge
records.text:
The provision covers an agreement, promise, or undertaking to change, modify, or discharge a contract, obligation, lease, mortgage, or other security interest described in the text. It requires a writing signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought or that party’s agent.

Place this statutory rule alongside Alaska Packers’ consideration analysis, Watkins’ treatment of a changed agreement, and UCC § 2-209. These are different sources with different conditions. Eliminating a consideration objection does not establish that a modification was free from duress or other defects.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, p. 9.

records.title: Other New York statutory departures from consideration requirements
records.text: The supplement also reproduces provisions concerning written assignments, published rewards, and promises in certain conveyances.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 9–10.

records.title: Other New York statutory departures from consideration requirements
records.text:
Section 5-1107 addresses the effect of a written assignment signed by the assignor or agent. Section 5-1113 addresses written or published promises of a reward for return of lost or mislaid property. Section 5-1115 addresses a grantor’s promise or warranty in a qualifying acknowledged or proved real-property conveyance where no consideration was intended.

These provisions illustrate why statutory scope matters. Their distinct subjects and formal requirements should be examined separately; they do not replace all consideration rules with a universal requirement of a writing.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 9–10.

records.title: French Civil Code Article 1112: negotiations
records.text: The assigned translation combines freedom to initiate, conduct, and end negotiations with a mandatory requirement of good faith.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, p. 21.

records.title: French Civil Code Article 1112: negotiations
records.text:
The translation permits damages where negotiations are at fault but excludes compensation for the benefits expected from the unmade contract and for the lost chance of obtaining those benefits. This makes it useful to separate a freedom to decline a final transaction from responsibility for the way negotiations are conducted.

Compare the provision with Dixon, Cyberchron, and Channel Home. Identify whether liability rests on reliance, an agreed negotiating commitment, or the regulation of negotiating conduct. Then identify the permissible measure of recovery. The translation is presented as comparative material, not as the rule governing a domestic U.S. dispute.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, p. 21.

records.title: Borat: sample participant release
records.text: The sample release illustrates how a written disclaimer of reliance can interact with claims that a participant was induced to sign by misleading statements.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 35–36.

records.title: Borat: sample participant release
records.text:
Examine the provisions describing the project, the rights granted, compensation, releases, and the participant’s disclaimer of reliance on representations concerning the film or its participants. The document gives concrete language against which the Psenicska reasoning can be tested.

The supplied sample is identified with separate litigation; it should not be presented as proof of every fact concerning the Psenicska plaintiffs’ own signing process. Keep the text’s scope, the particular alleged misrepresentation, and the distinction between a general merger clause and a specific disclaimer of reliance in view.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 35–36.

records.title: Hall and Elliot: Can AI Fix Bad Rules?
records.text: The authors examine the relationship between legal interpretation rules, agreement design, and the use of artificial intelligence.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 46–52.

records.title: Hall and Elliot: Can AI Fix Bad Rules?
records.text:
Read the authors’ question, method, and evidence separately from the legal rules discussed in Pacific Gas, W.W.W. Associates, Greenfield, and Trident.

For study, ask what problem the authors attribute to existing rules, which comparisons their design permits, and what remains uncertain about using an automated system in a different setting.

records.text:
Assignment 16 specifically names paragraphs 1, 2(a), and 8(a). Read the asset and proprietary-rights descriptions together with the payment provisions to understand why declining sales could harm the seller even after the transfer. Compare that allocation with the performance evaluated in Bloor.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the supplied reproduction: under “Certain Other Covenants of Buyer,” paragraph 8(a) uses the word “Seller” for the party promising best efforts. That wording is visible on supplement page 59. The Bloor opinion treats the relevant promotional duty as Falstaff’s. records.text: The supplement’s notes compare different approaches to good faith and the review of contractual powers, including Braganza, Yam Seng, and Wastech.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 73–75.

records.title: Comparative limits on contractual discretion and good faith
records.text:
These short extracts and descriptions should be read as comparative authorities with different legal settings. They ask whether a power must be exercised for its contractual purpose, whether an obligation arises by implication in the particular relationship, and how far a court may review discretionary judgment.

The notes are not full opinions. They do not establish that the jurisdictions adopt one interchangeable general rule, or that good faith always requires a party to subordinate its interests. Ng Giap’s resistance to a general implied duty remains distinct from the approaches discussed in the notes.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 73–75.

records.title: Assigned FTC notice removing the Non-Compete Rule
records.text: The assigned February 2026 Federal Register notice removes the FTC’s Non-Compete Rule from the Code of Federal Regulations following court decisions and the agency’s abandonment of appeals.

records.title: Assigned FTC notice removing the Non-Compete Rule
records.text:
The reproduced notice explains the agency’s response to vacatur and distinguishes the Non-Compete Rule from two other rulemaking actions discussed in the same document. Its account concerns federal administrative authority and judicial review of the rule.

Removal of this particular rule is not a holding that every noncompetition agreement is enforceable. The state-law and public-policy inquiries in Hassler remain separate. Use this document to trace which institution acted, the legal basis it described, and the effect of the action. Later developments after February 2026 are not covered here.

records.title: Rowan: specific enforcement in French contract law
records.text: The assigned comparative reading explains French specific enforcement, substitute performance, and limits based on impossibility or manifest disproportion.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 Contracts supplement, pp. 113–123.

records.title: Rowan: specific enforcement in French contract law
records.text:
The reading places the revised Civil Code provisions in the context of earlier French law and distinguishes performance in kind from monetary compensation. It examines Article 1221, including the significance of good faith and the comparison between the cost to the debtor and the creditor’s interest. It also discusses Article 1222’s route for arranging performance by another and the coercive payment mechanism known as an astreinte.

These mechanisms serve different functions. A coercive payment intended to induce compliance is not simply the same measure as damages for loss. Compare the source’s institutional and remedial assumptions with Klein and Walgreen, and preserve its distinctions between versions of the legislation.
