records.text: Under Swiss law a court may reduce an excessive contractual penalty, weighing the considerations relevant to that determination.

records.title: Swiss penalty-clause discussion: 1988 authority
records.text:
The decision distinguishes the parties’ agreement to a penalty from the court’s power to reduce an excessive amount. Its discussion supplies a comparative point of reference for the U.S. cases’ treatment of liquidated damages and penalties.

The later 2024 decision in the same packet is separately indexed because its concrete facts and application should not be attributed to this earlier authority. Only the court’s statement of the reduction power is reproduced; the facts are not.

records.title: Assignment 10 · Definiteness, preliminary agreements, and precontractual liability
records.text: Definiteness, preliminary agreements, and precontractual liability. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 21–21.

records.title: Assignment 10 · Definiteness, preliminary agreements, and precontractual liability
records.text:
Dixon v. Wells Fargo, N.A.: A lender’s specific instructions to default while it considered a loan modification supported a promissory-estoppel claim, although the borrowers had no promise of a particular modified loan.

Cyberchron Corp. v. Calldata Systems Development, Inc.: Assurances to continue producing customized equipment supported reliance damages despite the parties’ failure to agree on weight requirements and penalties.

Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman: A sufficiently definite and supported agreement to negotiate exclusively and in good faith can bind parties before they have agreed on the final lease.

Sun Printing & Publishing Ass’n v. Remington Paper & Power Co.: The majority refused to enforce future paper deliveries because both the future price and the period for which that price would operate remained to be agreed.

Oglebay Norton Co. v. Armco, Inc.: A long-term shipping contract remained enforceable after both pricing mechanisms failed because the evidence showed that the parties intended their underlying commitment to continue.

Additional assigned materials: Tribune preliminary-agreement discussion, C&M pp. 190–191; French Civil Code Article 1112.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 21–21.

records.title: Assignment 11 · Contract modifications
records.text: Contract modifications. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 9–9.

records.title: Assignment 11 · Contract modifications
records.text:
Alaska Packers’ Association v. Domenico: The fishermen’s promise to perform the same work they already owed did not support a midseason promise to double their fixed compensation.

Watkins & Son v. Carrig: The court enforced a voluntarily agreed higher excavation price even though the original contract already required removal of the rock.

Austin Instrument, Inc. v. Loral Corporation: Loral established economic duress when an indispensable supplier withheld precision gears to extract price increases that Loral could not practicably resist.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement §§ 89, 175, 176; UCC § 2-209; Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 3; N.Y. General Obligations Law § 5-1103.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 9–9.

records.title: Assignment 12 · Fraud and misrepresentation
records.text: Fraud and misrepresentation. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 22–36.

records.title: Assignment 12 · Fraud and misrepresentation
records.text:
Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank: The Massachusetts court rejected a damages claim based only on a seller’s silence about a concealed termite infestation, while distinguishing affirmative deception and duties to disclose.

Kannavos v. Annino: Advertising property as an income-producing apartment investment made silence about known zoning violations a misleading half-truth.

Speakers of Sport v. ProServ: A rival sports agent’s optimistic prediction about endorsements did not establish the fraudulent promise needed for the former agent’s interference claim.

Vokes v. Arthur Murray, Inc.: An allegedly deceptive campaign by expert dance instructors could support rescission even though their assurances were framed as opinions about ability and progress.

Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.: The courts enforced specific written disclaimers of reliance on statements about the film and its participants, defeating the pleaded fraud challenges to the Borat releases.

Additional assigned materials: Borat release.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 22–36.

records.title: Assignment 13 · The parol evidence rule
records.text: The parol evidence rule. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 37–45.

records.title: Assignment 13 · The parol evidence rule
records.text:
Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.: A tenant could not prove a separate oral promise of exclusive soft-drink sales where the written lease appeared complete and already addressed what he could sell.

Masterson v. Sine: The court allowed evidence of a family agreement limiting assignment of a repurchase option because the deed was not necessarily the complete expression of the parties’ bargain.

Bollinger v. Central Pennsylvania Quarry Stripping and Construction Co.: Proof of a shared drafting omission supported reformation of the writing to include the promised restoration of topsoil.

TeeVee Toons, Inc. v. Gerhard Schubert GmbH: Under the CISG, a factual dispute about the parties’ intent to exclude printed terms—including their merger clause—prevented summary judgment based on those terms.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement §§ 209, 210, 213–216; UCC § 2-202; CISG Article 8; Restatement of Consumer Contracts §§ 8, 9.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 37–45.

records.title: Assignment 14 · Meaning and extrinsic evidence
records.text: Meaning and extrinsic evidence. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 46–52.

records.title: Assignment 14 · Meaning and extrinsic evidence
records.text:
Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.: California’s contextual approach requires consideration of credible evidence that contract language bears the meaning a party proposes, even when the words initially seem clear.

W.W.W. Associates, Inc. v. Giancontieri: New York enforced a written cancellation right given to either party and refused outside evidence offered to turn it into a right benefiting only the buyer.

Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.: The same decision applied New York’s textual approach to a recording agreement and California’s contextual approach to a separate divorce release.

Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.: A federal court allowed the borrower to present extrinsic evidence under California law despite finding the text clear and criticizing that law’s consequences.

Additional assigned materials: Hall and Elliot, Can AI Fix Bad Rules?.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 46–52.

records.title: Assignment 15 · Commercial context and past dealings
records.text: Commercial context and past dealings. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 15 · Commercial context and past dealings
records.text:
Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.: The buyer failed to prove that “chicken” in these contracts meant only young broilers rather than also including stewing hens.

Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.: A trade practice for rounding protein measurements could explain a contract requiring at least 50 percent protein, despite the apparent precision of the written number.

Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.: The jury could find that established price protection qualified Shell’s posted-price term and that imposing a sudden increase violated commercial standards of good faith.

Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.: Uncontradicted evidence of industry practice supplied an exclusive repair, replacement, or refund remedy; the completed refund prevented that remedy from failing merely because earlier repair efforts had been unsuccessful.

Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.: A detailed written sales contract did not justify excluding trade-usage and prior-dealing evidence without asking whether that evidence could reasonably explain or supplement its terms.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement §§ 20, 200–204; UCC §§ 1-303, 2-202.

records.title: Assignment 16 · Performance in good faith
records.text: Performance in good faith. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 53–75.

records.title: Assignment 16 · Performance in good faith
records.text:
Dalton v. Educational Testing Service: ETS had to consider the relevant information it promised to consider, but the remedy was a good-faith reconsideration of the score rather than automatic certification of its validity.

Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg: The Airline Deregulation Act preempted this Minnesota implied-covenant claim because the obligation it sought to enforce was imposed by state law rather than voluntarily undertaken by the airline.

Market Street Associates v. Frey: Deliberately exploiting a contractual partner’s oversight could violate good faith, but the relevant state of mind could not be decided against the tenant on this summary-judgment record.

Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.: Falstaff’s best-efforts promise required attention to Ballantine’s sales volume; concentrating on Falstaff’s overall profits while allowing that volume to collapse did not satisfy the agreement.

Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others: The Singapore Court of Appeal declined to imply the proposed general good-faith duty into an agency agreement, while distinguishing that issue from narrower terms implied from a particular bargain.

Additional assigned materials: Bloor agreement paragraphs 1, 2(a), 8(a); Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 4.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 53–75.

records.title: Assignment 17 · Standard forms and adhesion
records.text: Standard forms and adhesion. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 76–93.

records.title: Assignment 17 · Standard forms and adhesion
records.text:
Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute: The Supreme Court enforced the Florida forum-selection clause in the cruise ticket under federal admiralty law, treating notice as conceded and preserving scrutiny for fundamental fairness.

Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.: A powerful concert promoter could still be an adherent to an industry form; the arbitration requirement was expected, but selecting the other side’s union as arbitrator was unconscionable.

Doe v. Great Expectations: The dating service had to refund the customers’ payments because its contracts violated statutory requirements and it failed to disclose rights that would have affected their decisions to contract.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement § 211; Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 8; EU Directive and associated Notifications.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 76–93.

records.title: Assignment 18 · Unconscionability
records.text: Unconscionability. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 94–101.

records.title: Assignment 18 · Unconscionability
records.text:
Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.: The court recognized power to refuse an unconscionable bargain and remanded for findings; it did not itself finally decide that the customers’ contracts were unconscionable.

Stoll v. Xiong: A thirty-year right to valuable poultry litter, added to an already substantial land price and accepted without meaningful understanding, was an unconscionable provision.

Anderson v. Binance: The assigned 2026 opinion rejects Binance’s attempt to compel arbitration through later website terms, addressing both lack of constructive notice and the limits on retroactive modification.

Additional assigned materials: Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 6.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 94–101.

records.title: Assignment 19 · Public policy
records.text: Public policy. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 102–107.

records.title: Assignment 19 · Public policy
records.text:
Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.: A lawful sale of an ingredient became unenforceable when the seller knowingly facilitated the buyer’s continuing scheme to mislabel imitation cheese as real cheese.

X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.: A contract connected with an antitrust conspiracy was not automatically unenforceable; the court required a developed record on whether payment would enforce the prohibited arrangement itself.

Hassler v. Circle C Resources: The Wyoming Supreme Court abandoned judicial rewriting of unreasonable noncompetes and directed judgment for the employee because this covenant’s duration and geographical reach were unreasonable.

Additional assigned materials: FTC removal of Non-Compete Rule.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 102–107.

records.title: Assignment 20 · Express and constructive conditions
records.text: Express and constructive conditions. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 20 · Express and constructive conditions
records.text:
Luttinger v. Rosen: A home buyer who diligently sought the specified mortgage could recover the deposit when no qualifying loan was available; the seller’s later offer to subsidize a different loan did not satisfy the condition.

Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.: An ambiguous subcontract payment clause set a time for payment rather than transferring the owner’s insolvency risk to the subcontractors.

Gibson v. Cranage: A buyer who had expressly reserved personal satisfaction with a portrait of his deceased daughter was not required to pay merely because others might regard the portrait as excellent.

Kingston v. Preston: An apprentice had to provide the agreed security for payment before he could compel the transfer of his employer’s business.

Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent: An innocent substitution of equivalent pipe could be substantial performance; the owner’s monetary allowance depended on the significance of the defect and the disproportionate cost of replacement.

Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.: A log-driving contract was divisible by completed deliveries at specified unit prices, but the contractor could not collect a fraction of a delivery price for logs lost partway through the journey.

Nelson v. Hazel: A negligent builder who had not substantially performed could recover the net benefit retained by the homeowner after credit for payments and the cost of correcting defects.

McKenna v. Vernon: An owner who repeatedly paid without the architect’s required certificate could not invoke the absent final certificate to defeat payment for honestly and substantially completed work.

records.title: Assignment 21 · Mistake, impracticability, and frustration
records.text: Mistake, impracticability, and frustration. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 21 · Mistake, impracticability, and frustration
records.text:
Stees v. Leonard: A builder’s undertaking to erect and complete a building placed the burden of overcoming the site’s quicksand conditions on the builder under the court’s strict reading of the contract.

Renner v. Kehl: A shared material mistake about water needed for jojoba cultivation justified rescission, but restitution did not reimburse all development expenditure regardless of benefit to the sellers.

Taylor v. Caldwell: The accidental destruction of the particular music hall essential to the planned concerts excused both sides from future performance.

Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States: Closure of the Suez Canal did not make an available, more expensive Cape route commercially impracticable on this record, and the shipowner could not add the extra expense to its agreed price.

Krell v. Henry: Cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared foundation for hiring particular viewing rooms, excusing payment of the remaining charge.

Additional assigned materials: Force majeure clause.

records.title: Assignment 22 · Specific relief
records.text: Specific relief. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 108–128.

records.title: Assignment 22 · Specific relief
records.text:
Klein v. PepsiCo, Inc.: The aircraft sale was binding, but available substitutes and adequate damages made specific performance inappropriate.

Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.: An injunction enforcing a shopping-center pharmacy exclusivity clause was justified because projecting ten years of competitive losses would be costly and uncertain.

In Commonwealth v. Cosby (Pa. 2021), the majority enforced the former prosecutor’s unconditional nonprosecution decision because it intentionally induced reasonable, detrimental surrender of Cosby’s Fifth Amendment protection in civil depositions. The decision concerns that record and these charges; it does not make every prosecutorial assurance enforceable.

Additional assigned materials: French specific-enforcement reading; Economics of remedies video lecture.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 108–128.

records.title: Assignment 23 · Performance value and losing contracts
records.text: Performance value and losing contracts. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 23 · Performance value and losing contracts
records.text:
Plante v. Jacobs: A substantially performing homebuilder could recover the unpaid price subject to appropriate defect deductions; replacing a misplaced interior wall was too wasteful when the wall caused no loss in market value.

Groves v. John Wunder Co.: A contractor’s deliberate failure to restore gravel land supported damages measured by the reasonable cost of the promised work, even though that cost exceeded the land’s market value; the case returned for a new trial.

Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.: The majority limited recovery for unperformed mine-restoration work to the farm’s $300 diminution in value because it treated restoration as incidental to the lease and its cost as grossly disproportionate to its economic benefit.

United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.: A subcontractor that justifiably stopped after the prime contractor’s material breach could recover the reasonable value of its supplied labor and equipment, even though completing the subcontract would have produced a loss.

Additional assigned materials: Peevyhouse agreement.

records.title: Assignment 24 · Limitations on damages
records.text: Limitations on damages. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 24 · Limitations on damages
records.text:
Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.: After receiving the county’s repudiation, a bridge builder could recover its legitimate breach losses but could not enlarge recovery by continuing to build a bridge the county no longer wanted.

Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.: An actress did not have to accept a different and inferior substitute role to reduce damages after the studio cancelled her promised musical role.

Hadley v. Baxendale: A carrier was not liable for the mill’s lost profits on the facts the court accepted because the exceptional consequences of delay had not been sufficiently communicated when the shipping contract was made.

Kenford Co. v. County of Erie: The county’s knowledge that a stadium would increase surrounding land values did not establish that it assumed liability for Kenford’s lost appreciation if the stadium was never built.

Fera v. Village Plaza, Inc.: A new business could recover projected profits when detailed evidence supported a reasonable estimate; lack of an operating history was not an automatic bar.

records.title: Assignment 25 · Stipulated remedies
records.text: Stipulated remedies. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 129–138.

records.title: Assignment 25 · Stipulated remedies
records.text:
Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.: Uncontradicted evidence of industry practice supplied an exclusive repair, replacement, or refund remedy; the completed refund prevented that remedy from failing merely because earlier repair efforts had been unsuccessful.

Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State: A graduated daily charge for delay in completing a public highway was enforceable as a reasonable advance estimate of losses that were difficult to measure.

Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.: A minimum-quantity damages formula was an unenforceable penalty because it required payment for unperformed services without crediting the service provider’s saved costs; ordinary breach damages remained available.

Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown: A lease-cancellation payment based on gross receipts required factual examination of its reasonableness; the court preserved reimbursement for improvements but did not finally uphold or invalidate the receipts formula.

Swiss Federal Supreme Court: contractual penalty decision of September 24, 2024: The court upheld reduction of a contractual penalty to CHF 10,000 for a minor breach with no demonstrated damage or risk, while preserving a punitive function for the clause.

Additional assigned materials: Swiss penalty-clause readings.

atlasSources.label: Fall 2026 supplement, pp. 129–138.

records.title: Assignment 26 · Third-party rights, delegation, and assignment
records.text: Third-party rights, delegation, and assignment. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.

records.title: Assignment 26 · Third-party rights, delegation, and assignment
records.text:
Lawrence v. Fox: A creditor could enforce a promise made to his debtor for the creditor’s benefit even though the creditor supplied no consideration directly to the new promisor.

Seaver v. Ransom: A niece could enforce the husband’s promise to his dying wife to provide for the niece by will, where the wife signed her own will in exchange for that promise.

Sisney v. State: An inmate was not entitled to enforce the state’s general food-service contract because the court found no clear contractual intent to grant him an individual enforcement right.

Sisney v. Reisch: An inmate sufficiently alleged a right to enforce a settlement promising certified kosher meals to all Jewish inmates who requested them; dismissal was reversed.

records.title: Definiteness, preliminary agreements, and precontractual liability: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Definiteness, preliminary agreements, and precontractual liability: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Dixon v. Wells Fargo, N.A.: Dixon separates an enforceable limited assurance during negotiations from agreement on the final transaction. Read it with Drennan and Cyberchron when identifying exactly what reliance protects.

Cyberchron Corp. v. Calldata Systems Development, Inc.: The case separates three bases of recovery: an agreed contract, restitution for a benefit received, and protection of expenses induced by a promise. Only the third supported this appeal.

Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman: This is a bargained preliminary contract. Compare Dixon and Cyberchron, which use reliance to protect narrower promises without a completed bargain.

Sun Printing & Publishing Ass’n v. Remington Paper & Power Co.: Compare the same judge’s willingness to imply reasonable efforts in Wood and the later willingness to replace failed pricing mechanisms in Oglebay. Identify precisely which open terms matter before treating a contract as indefinite.

Oglebay Norton Co. v. Armco, Inc.: Oglebay connects assent over time, definiteness, reliance-producing investment, gap filling, and specific relief. Its result depends heavily on the established relationship and evidence of continuing commitment.

records.title: Contract modifications: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Contract modifications: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Alaska Packers’ Association v. Domenico: It connects consideration to contract modification and shows why a promise to pay more for unchanged performance can raise both an exchange problem and a coercion problem.

Watkins & Son v. Carrig: It supplies a contrasting judicial response to the pre-existing-duty rule and makes the distinction between an assumed original risk and an enforceable later adjustment explicit.

Austin Instrument, Inc. v. Loral Corporation: It explains what must be shown in addition to a threat of breach: practical inability to replace the promised performance and an inadequate damages remedy.

records.title: Fraud and misrepresentation: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Fraud and misrepresentation: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank: It establishes the baseline that Kannavos qualifies: silence, a half-truth, active concealment, and a special duty to speak are different grounds of analysis.

Kannavos v. Annino: It shows how individually true statements become deceptive in context and how a duty to complete a partial disclosure differs from a duty to volunteer all information.

Speakers of Sport v. ProServ: It helps distinguish a legally assumed risk, an optimistic prediction, and a promise made with fraudulent intent.

Vokes v. Arthur Murray, Inc.: It demonstrates how the speaker’s expertise and the surrounding sales process can change the legal significance of apparently subjective praise.

Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp.: This case links fraud, interpretation, signed releases, and assent. Its result depends on the disclaimer’s specificity and the courts’ account of available precautions.

records.title: The parol evidence rule: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: The parol evidence rule: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.: Gianni supplies the restrictive “naturally included” approach. Compare Masterson’s contextual approach to a collateral term and TeeVee Toons’ CISG analysis of the parties’ intent.

Masterson v. Sine: It illustrates partial integration, contextual evidence of completeness, and the difference between excluding a claimed term and deciding whether that term was proved.

Bollinger v. Central Pennsylvania Quarry Stripping and Construction Co.: It explains why the parol evidence rule does not make a mistaken writing immune from correction.

TeeVee Toons, Inc. v. Gerhard Schubert GmbH: TeeVee Toons makes the choice of legal regime concrete: the same dispute about a written agreement receives a different evidentiary analysis under the CISG than under the restrictive domestic approach in Gianni.

records.title: Meaning and extrinsic evidence: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Meaning and extrinsic evidence: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.: It provides the contextual side of the course’s comparison with New York’s more restrictive treatment of extrinsic evidence.

W.W.W. Associates, Inc. v. Giancontieri: It explains why strong evidence about negotiations may fail to affect a result under a rule that gives a clear writing controlling force.

Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.: It shows concretely why identifying the governing law precedes applying a general statement about contractual interpretation.

Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.: It connects the interpretation debate to the hierarchy of authority: a federal court’s preferred rule does not replace controlling state substantive law.

records.title: Commercial context and past dealings: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Commercial context and past dealings: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.: This case shows how an apparently simple word can require a factual inquiry into negotiations, specialized usage, incorporated standards, and price. It connects the formation-stage question of objective assent to interpretation of an agreement both sides acknowledge.

Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.: Hurst gives a concrete example of contextual interpretation of numbers. Read it with Frigaliment and Nanakuli to separate proof of a usage, the parties’ connection to it, and its consistency with express language.

Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co.: Nanakuli connects interpretation, evidence of prior performance, and good-faith limits on contractual discretion. It shows why the written price clause is the beginning of an inquiry into the agreement rather than the entire inquiry.

Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.: Figgie connects interpretation and remedies: first identify the remedy the parties’ agreement contains, including trade usage, and only then decide whether that remedy remains enforceable. It demonstrates why a case needs to appear in more than one topic index.

Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.: This is a major qualification to the idea that a merger clause excludes all outside evidence. The kind of evidence matters: commercial practices have a distinct place in the Code’s account of agreement.

records.title: Performance in good faith: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Performance in good faith: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Dalton v. Educational Testing Service: Dalton is the clearest worked example of contractual discretion in this course: identify who has the choice, what process was promised, what facts bear on that choice, and how a remedy can enforce the process without dictating the result.

Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg: Read this after Dalton to see why the source of an obligation matters. A court must identify the governing state rule and any controlling federal statute before applying a general account of good faith.

Market Street Associates v. Frey: Market Street explains good faith through a particular misuse of an existing contractual mechanism. It also shows why a case’s procedural stage matters when its outcome depends on a person’s knowledge.

Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.: Bloor explains how a flexible business obligation can still be enforceable. It identifies the promised objective, considers the promisor’s financial capacity, examines concrete decisions, and gives a workable damages method.

Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others: Ng Giap belongs beside Dalton and Market Street as a jurisdiction-specific counterpoint. It also explains why the source and specificity of a proposed limit on discretion matter.

records.title: Standard forms and adhesion: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Standard forms and adhesion: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute: Carnival links assent, adhesion, remedies, and Civil Procedure. Keep the majority’s conceded-notice premise separate from the disputed notice questions in Specht, Hill, Klocek, and Anderson.

Graham v. Scissor-Tail, Inc.: Graham prevents two oversimplifications: sophistication does not establish bargaining freedom, and knowledge of a term does not establish its substantive enforceability.

Doe v. Great Expectations: This case shows how legislation can impose terms and remedies that the printed agreement omits. It connects informed contracting, mandatory consumer protection, and recovery of payments.

records.title: Unconscionability: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Unconscionability: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.: Williams joins formation concerns about meaningful assent to a direct review of oppressive terms. Its remand is crucial: recognition of the doctrine and proof that a particular agreement satisfies it are separate steps.

Stoll v. Xiong: Stoll makes the economic content of a noncash term visible. A clause that looks ancillary can substantially alter the effective price, and the process of understanding that clause matters.

Anderson v. Binance: Although assigned in the unconscionability unit, the reproduced reasoning chiefly concerns assent, modification, choice of law, and good faith. It belongs in all of those indexes.

records.title: Public policy: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Public policy: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.: Blossom shows that formation and performance do not end the enforceability inquiry. A court must also consider the relationship between the requested judgment and public policies implicated by the transaction.

X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.: Compare Blossom Farm to see why “connected to illegality” is an insufficient rule. The relationship between the specific performance sought, the prohibited conduct, and the parties’ relative positions must be explained.

Hassler v. Circle C Resources: Hassler links the substantive limits on a restraint to the remedy for excessive drafting. The choice between rewriting and nonenforcement changes the incentives created by the rule.

records.title: Express and constructive conditions: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Express and constructive conditions: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Luttinger v. Rosen: This case separates a duty to make reasonable efforts from a condition that those efforts must actually produce a particular result. It also demonstrates how conditions allocate financing risk.

Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.: Peacock shows how transactional context and a default interpretation determine whether a clause creates a condition or simply fixes when an existing payment duty must be performed.

Gibson v. Cranage: This is the performance-stage counterpart to Mattei: a satisfaction provision can preserve a genuine choice while the nature of the promised result determines how that choice is judged.

Kingston v. Preston: Kingston supplies the basis for understanding why one party may withhold its performance when the return performance on which it depends has not occurred.

Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent: The case links substantial performance, implied conditions, forfeiture, and the choice between cost-of-correction and value-based damages. It explains why a breach and a continuing duty to pay can coexist.

Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.: Divisibility asks which parts of an exchange the agreement treats as corresponding units. It can reduce forfeiture without rewriting every unfinished task into a payable fraction.

Nelson v. Hazel: Nelson separates a breaching party’s failed claim for contract compensation from its possible restitution claim. A court can deny substantial performance and still prevent the owner from keeping a net benefit for free.

McKenna v. Vernon: Conduct during performance can change whether a party may insist on a condition, even though the written contract originally required it.

records.title: Mistake, impracticability, and frustration: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Mistake, impracticability, and frustration: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Stees v. Leonard: Stees establishes the background expectation that a party bears the risks its promise allocates. It connects the definition of the promised result, parol evidence, modification, and excuse.

Renner v. Kehl: Renner distinguishes avoiding a contract from obtaining damages for its breach. The legal basis of relief determines which losses and benefits enter the calculation.

Taylor v. Caldwell: Taylor identifies a limited setting in which an unexpected event destroys an essential basis of performance, rather than merely making the promised work more costly.

Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States: The case teaches the sequence for evaluating changed circumstances and the difference between predicting a risk, allocating it, and proving that it made performance impracticable.

Krell v. Henry: Krell explains why a contract can be excused even where performing it remains possible: the shared, particular purpose for receiving the performance may have disappeared.

records.title: Specific relief: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Specific relief: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Klein v. PepsiCo, Inc.: Klein demonstrates why formation, breach, and remedy require separate analysis. It also contrasts with Walgreen’s difficult-to-measure long-term injury and Morris’s individually valued horse.

Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.: Walgreen explains the adequacy inquiry through the practical costs of measuring loss, enforcing an order, and negotiating a release. Economic reasoning can support specific relief as well as damages.

Commonwealth v. Cosby: This assigned remedies reading reaches back to reliance and promise enforcement. It illustrates why a course-wide concept index must cross the syllabus’s unit boundaries.

records.title: Performance value and losing contracts: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Performance value and losing contracts: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Plante v. Jacobs: This case separates three questions: whether performance is substantial, which defects are compensable, and how each defect should be valued. It links the conditions doctrine in Jacob & Youngs to the competing damages measures in Groves and Peevyhouse.

Groves v. John Wunder Co.: Groves makes the promised physical result central to expectation damages. Peevyhouse later adopts a different treatment of a similarly disproportionate restoration obligation.

Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.: Peevyhouse connects contractual purpose and bargaining evidence to the measure of damages. Its facts show why a complete remedies analysis must distinguish market value, personal value, and the performance expressly purchased.

United States v. Algernon Blair, Inc.: This case separates restitution from both expectation and reliance. It is especially useful when a plaintiff has partly performed a contract that would have lost money.

records.title: Limitations on damages: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Limitations on damages: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.: Luten Bridge introduces mitigation as a limit on recovery. It also distinguishes the wrongfulness of repudiation from the injured party’s response to it.

Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.: Parker shows that mitigation protects an employee’s substantial nonmonetary interests as well as pay. Its procedural disagreement also warns against treating every difference between two jobs as automatically decisive.

Hadley v. Baxendale: Hadley supplies the organizing distinction between ordinary and special consequential loss. It also illustrates why factual notice and the procedural treatment of that notice matter as much as the verbal rule.

Kenford Co. v. County of Erie: Kenford makes it necessary to ask what risk the defendant assumed, rather than infer responsibility from bare knowledge of possible gain. It belongs beside Hadley and the contrasting Article 2 discussion.

Fera v. Village Plaza, Inc.: Fera contrasts with Kenford’s unsuccessful profit claims and clarifies what reasonable certainty requires. It also separates sufficiency of evidence from appellate disagreement with a jury’s choice.

records.title: Stipulated remedies: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Stipulated remedies: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.: Figgie connects interpretation and remedies: first identify the remedy the parties’ agreement contains, including trade usage, and only then decide whether that remedy remains enforceable. It demonstrates why a case needs to appear in more than one topic index.

Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State: This decision supplies a successful example of advance damages estimation. Compare its size-and-duration formula with the saved-cost problem in Lake River and the gross-receipts problem in Wasserman’s.

Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.: Lake River makes the relationship between revenue, saved expenses, and lost profit concrete. It also illustrates how a federal court separates its policy preferences from its responsibility to apply state contract law.

Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown: Wasserman’s shows why concern about a formula does not always justify deciding its validity on summary judgment. The lease’s economic value and the nature of the loss matter alongside sales figures.

Swiss Federal Supreme Court: contractual penalty decision of September 24, 2024: This comparison prevents the word “penalty” from silently carrying the same legal consequence across jurisdictions.

records.title: Third-party rights, delegation, and assignment: editorial notes and questions
records.text: The casebook's notes and questions around the principal cases.

records.title: Third-party rights, delegation, and assignment: editorial notes and questions
records.text:
Lawrence v. Fox: The three people perform different legal roles. Keeping those roles explicit explains how consideration can support a promise while someone other than its promisee enforces it.

Seaver v. Ransom: Seaver extends beneficiary protection beyond the debt-discharge setting in Lawrence v. Fox. It distinguishes a gift intended for the beneficiary from an unsupported gift promise between the actual contracting parties.

Sisney v. State: The comparison with Sisney v. Reisch is essential. The same inmate and similar food problem produced a different result under a different agreement.

Sisney v. Reisch: Together the two Sisney decisions isolate the importance of identifying the precise contract, its beneficiaries, the defendant’s duty, and the procedural posture.

records.title: Remedies for breach
records.text: Remedies determine what relief follows a breach: compensation, restoration of benefits, an order to perform, or another legally authorized response.

records.title: Remedies for breach
records.text: Begin with the protected interest and the kind of relief requested. Then apply the relevant limits, including adequacy of damages, avoided loss, foreseeability, certainty, and agreed remedies. The case index separates the different remedial questions and retains each case’s procedural result.

records.title: Terms supplied by law or implication
records.text: Gap filling supplies a term that the parties’ agreement leaves open, using applicable law or a justified implication from their transaction.

records.title: Terms supplied by law or implication
records.text: The existence of an omitted term does not always prevent enforcement. Identify the source and limits of the proposed term, the parties’ intention, and whether there is a sufficiently definite agreement to enforce. Northrop and the definiteness cases illustrate different problems; they do not authorize replacing every disagreement with a court’s preferred outcome.

records.title: Proof and procedural limits in Contracts cases
records.text: A case’s procedural posture determines which facts are assumed, which are established, and what the court’s ruling actually resolves.

records.title: Proof and procedural limits in Contracts cases
records.text: A dismissal decision can test pleaded allegations without finding them true. Summary judgment asks whether the relevant record requires a trial. An appellate remand may permit a theory while leaving factual questions unresolved. Read these distinctions alongside D&G Stout, Dorton, and the damages cases; a successful appeal does not necessarily establish ultimate liability or a particular award.

records.title: Contract formation by conduct under § 2-207(3)
records.text: When the writings do not establish a sales contract, both parties’ conduct recognizing a contract may establish one under § 2-207(3).

records.title: Contract formation by conduct under § 2-207(3)
records.text: The subsection then supplies the terms: “those terms on which the writings of the parties agree, together with any supplementary terms incorporated under any other provisions of this Act.” Conflicting terms in the two forms therefore drop out (the knock-out rule) and the Code’s gap-fillers take their place. C. Itoh explains why the unagreed arbitration clause could not return as a supposed gap filler. This route differs from recognizing acceptance under subsection (1) and evaluating additional terms under subsection (2).

records.title: Beneficiaries of government contracts
records.text: A person who benefits from a government contract does not necessarily acquire a private contractual right to enforce it.

records.title: Beneficiaries of government contracts
records.text: Sisney v. State and Sisney v. Reisch examine different agreements and evidence of intended rights. The analysis asks what the contracting parties undertook and whether the intended benefit supports enforceability by this claimant; general public benefit and an individual enforcement right are distinct.

records.title: Rescission and avoidance
records.text: Rescission or avoidance concerns undoing or declining enforcement of an agreement on an applicable ground, with attention to restoration and other legal consequences.

records.title: Rescission and avoidance
records.text: The misrepresentation and mistake readings raise different bases for this remedy. Identify the defect, the party entitled to invoke it, and the effect of later conduct or an allocation of risk. Avoidance is a separate question from how damages for breach would be measured.

records.title: Refusal to perform and avoidable loss
records.text: An announced refusal to perform can require the injured party to decide whether further performance will create avoidable loss.

records.title: Refusal to perform and avoidable loss
records.text: Rockingham County concerns continued construction after a communicated repudiation. Its damages discussion separates loss already caused from expense unnecessarily increased afterward. The syllabus does not assign the casebook’s complete separate chapter treatment of prospective nonperformance.

records.title: Separating lawful and unlawful promises
records.text: Severability asks whether an enforceable part of an arrangement can be separated from a term or undertaking affected by a legal defect.

records.title: Separating lawful and unlawful promises
records.text: The public-policy readings examine the relationship between the challenged conduct, the bargain being enforced, and the consequences of refusal. Identify the actual promises and the governing rule instead of assuming that one unlawful circumstance invalidates every associated obligation.

records.title: Warranties as contractual undertakings
records.text: A warranty concerns an undertaking about a characteristic, quality, or condition of goods or performance, with legal consequences if the undertaking is unfulfilled.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 4–8.

records.title: Warranties as contractual undertakings
records.text: Bayliner examines whether particular statements created an express warranty concerning the boat purchased. Northrop concerns competing warranty periods in exchanged forms. Express and implied warranties, their inclusion, and their exclusion raise distinct questions. The full separate casebook chapter on warranties is outside the assigned reading ranges in this syllabus.

atlasSources.label: C&M, 10th ed., pp. 4–8.

records.title: Capron v. Van Noorden (1804)
records.text: A plaintiff who picked a federal court can still win a reversal by pointing out that the record never showed the court had the power to hear the case. Choosing the forum does not stop you from later attacking its authority.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 29–30

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Capron v. Van Noorden (1804)
records.text: A plaintiff may obtain reversal of a judgment when the record fails to establish the federal court's jurisdiction, even though the plaintiff chose that court.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 29–30

records.title: Capron v. Van Noorden (1804)
records.text:
This very short assigned opinion concerns what the record established. It does not find that the parties in fact shared citizenship or resolve the substantive claim. The casebook’s questions ask why a losing plaintiff might seek reversal that produces no merits victory.

The action was one of trespass on the case in the federal circuit court for North Carolina; the record alleged only that Van Noorden was 'late of Pitt County' and said nothing about Capron's own citizenship, and the plaintiff who had lost on the merits successfully used the jurisdictional defect he himself had failed to plead to obtain reversal.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 29–30

records.title: Tickle v. Barton (1956)
records.text: Fraud by a party or its agent that induces an otherwise unreachable nonresident to enter the state can invalidate personal service there. The West Virginia court held the challenge legally sufficient if the inducement was proved; it did not itself establish fraud or finally quash service.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Tickle v. Barton (1956)
records.text: A party cannot secure personal service on an otherwise out-of-reach nonresident by fraud, trickery, artifice or a wrongful device, used by the party or someone acting for the party, that induces the person to enter the court's territorial jurisdiction; such service will be set aside.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Tickle v. Barton (1956)
records.text:
Keep this West Virginia service doctrine distinct from the constitutional minimum-contacts inquiry and from immunity for witnesses attending court.

Rule stated by the court: when a nonresident is "inveigled, enticed or induced, by fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device for which a party is responsible by virtue of the action of his attorney to come within the jurisdiction for the purpose of enabling such party to obtain personal service of process, service of process which results from such fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device is invalid and does not justify the exercise of jurisdiction by such court over the person so served with process."

Richard Tickle, a minor, sued Raymond Barton, a resident of Austinville, Virginia, in the Circuit Court of McDowell County for injuries inflicted by a motor vehicle on private property; Barton alleged that Tickle's attorney telephoned him and refused to identify himself when asked, while persuading him to attend a banquet in West Virginia.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Pennoyer v. Neff (1878)
records.text: Pennoyer’s 1878 territorial framework invalidated this personal judgment and the later land sale: Neff was absent, had not appeared, and the land had not first been brought under court control. International Shoe and Shaffer later changed the jurisdictional analysis; in-state service is not the only modern basis for suing a nonresident.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 79–90

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Pennoyer v. Neff (1878)
records.text: An ordinary personal money judgment against an absent nonresident requires personal service within the state or voluntary appearance; a state may reach a nonresident's local property only if it is brought under the court's control before judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 79–90

records.title: Pennoyer v. Neff (1878)
records.text:
Read this as the historical framework developed and qualified by International Shoe, Shaffer, and Burnham. It does not supply the complete modern test. “In personam” concerns personal liability; “in rem” and “quasi in rem” describe forms of adjudication involving property.

Mitchell, a Portland, Oregon attorney, won a default judgment for less than $300, including costs, for unpaid legal fees; he bought Neff's land himself at the sheriff's sale and three days later assigned it to Pennoyer, and Justice Field wrote the majority opinion.

Pennoyer's famous rule: every state possesses exclusive jurisdiction over persons and property within its territory and none may exercise direct jurisdiction over persons or property outside it, so a personal judgment against a nonresident who was neither served in the state nor appeared is void.

records.title: Hess v. Pawloski (1927)
records.text: A state can say that driving on its roads counts as agreeing to be served through a state official. So a nonresident driver who causes a crash can be sued there. The law was fair because the driver was told about the suit and had time to defend.

records.title: Hess v. Pawloski (1927)
records.text: A state may treat a nonresident's driving on its highways as appointing a state official to receive service in suits arising from that driving, provided the statute requires actual receipt of notice and affords reasonable time to defend.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 90–93

records.title: Hess v. Pawloski (1927)
records.text:
The syllabus points to page 90; the case begins on printed page 91 after introductory material. This is a specific, activity-linked statutory mechanism, not authorization for every claim against anyone who once drove through Massachusetts.

Hess was a Pennsylvania resident sued by Pawloski in Massachusetts state court; the statute deemed driving on Massachusetts highways an appointment of the state registrar of motor vehicles as agent for service, which the Court upheld against a Fourteenth Amendment due-process challenge.

records.title: McGee v. International Life Insurance Co. (1957)
records.text: One insurance policy sold into a state can be enough to let that state's courts hear a suit over that policy. The insurer's only California tie was a single policy sold by mail, but the suit was about that very policy, so California could hear it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 102–103

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: McGee v. International Life Insurance Co. (1957)
records.text: Due process permits a state to exercise personal jurisdiction over a foreign insurer in a suit on a contract that has a substantial connection with the state, even when that single contract is the insurer's only shown business there.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 102–103

records.title: McGee v. International Life Insurance Co. (1957)
records.text:
Hanson immediately qualifies an expansive reading: a plaintiff’s unilateral relocation is not equivalent to an insurer’s own solicitation into the forum. McGee does not make every contract with a resident sufficient.

Franklin bought the policy in 1944 from Empire Mutual, an Arizona company; International Life, a Texas corporation, assumed its obligations in 1948 and Franklin mailed premiums from California until his death in 1950. McGee, his mother and beneficiary, sued under California's statute permitting service on out-of-state insurers.

records.title: Hanson v. Denckla (1958)
records.text: A state cannot claim power over a company just because someone else moved there. The trust was set up in Delaware, and the settlor later moving to Florida was her own choice. The trustee had done nothing to reach into Florida, so Florida courts had no hold on it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 103–106

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hanson v. Denckla (1958)
records.text: A State may exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant only if the defendant purposefully availed itself of conducting activities in the State, invoking the benefits and protections of its law; the unilateral activity of another person cannot supply the connection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 103–106

records.title: Hanson v. Denckla (1958)
records.text:
Distinguish the person whose conduct supplies the contact from the person who suffers the consequences. Also distinguish personal jurisdiction, property jurisdiction, and the authority to select governing law.

Verbatim rule: 'it is essential in each case that there be some act by which the defendant purposefully avails itself of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State, thus invoking the benefits and protections of its laws'; the unilateral activity of those claiming a relationship with the defendant cannot supply the contact.

Dora Donner, a Pennsylvanian, created the trust with a Delaware trustee (Wilmington Trust Co.) and later moved to Florida, where she exercised the power of appointment and died; the Court (Warren, C.J., 5–4) held Florida lacked both in rem and in personam jurisdiction, reversed the Florida Supreme Court, and affirmed the Delaware Supreme Court's refusal to give the Florida decree full faith and credit; Justice Black's dissent was joined by Justices Burton and Brennan, and Justice Douglas dissented separately.

records.title: Gray v. American Radiator & Standard Sanitary Corp. (1961)
records.text: The Illinois Supreme Court in 1961 allowed suit over a valve that entered ordinary distribution and injured someone in Illinois, where its use was contemplated. That was Illinois’s stream-of-commerce approach; later Supreme Court decisions divided over what additional forum-directed conduct, if any, is necessary.

records.title: Gray v. American Radiator & Standard Sanitary Corp. (1961)
records.text: A tortious act under a long-arm statute includes the injury that completes the tort, and due process permits jurisdiction over a nonresident component maker whose product, placed in ordinary commercial distribution with use in the forum contemplated, causes injury there.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 107–113

records.title: Gray v. American Radiator & Standard Sanitary Corp. (1961)
records.text:
This is an Illinois Supreme Court decision in the developmental sequence. Later Supreme Court cases, especially World-Wide Volkswagen, Asahi, and Nicastro, complicate the stream-of-commerce issue. Do not treat Gray’s formulation as a later unanimous Supreme Court rule.

Phyllis Gray was injured in Cook County when the water heater exploded; Titan sold its valves to American Radiator outside Illinois, which built them into heaters in Pennsylvania; the circuit court dismissed both Gray's complaint and American Radiator's cross-claim against Titan, and the appeal went directly to the Illinois Supreme Court because it raised a constitutional question about substituted service on nonresidents.

records.title: Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc. (1984)
records.text: A magazine that sells thousands of copies in a state every month can be sued there for libel, and the whole nationwide harm can be argued in that one suit. The plaintiff's own lack of ties to the state does not matter. What counts is what the publisher did there.

records.title: Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc. (1984)
records.text: A publisher's deliberate, regular circulation of its magazine in a state supports personal jurisdiction there over a libel claim based on the magazine's contents, even for nationwide damages, and the plaintiff need not have minimum contacts with the forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 124–125

records.title: Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc. (1984)
records.text:
Contrast Walden, where the defendant’s challenged conduct lacked the necessary forum connection, and Bristol-Myers, where the nonresident claims were not linked to the forum conduct.

Keeton, a New York resident, sued Hustler (an Ohio corporation with its principal place of business in California) in the District of New Hampshire because its six-year libel limitations period was the only one still open; the district court dismissed, the First Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed.

records.title: Calder v. Jones (1984)
records.text: California was the focal point of both the allegedly libelous story and its harm. The reporter and editor’s own intentional conduct was expressly aimed there, supporting jurisdiction over them individually. Knowing that a plaintiff lives in a state and will feel harm there, by itself, is insufficient.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 126

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Calder v. Jones (1984)
records.text: A State may exercise personal jurisdiction over nonresident individuals whose own alleged intentional conduct was expressly aimed at the forum and who knew the brunt of the injury would be felt there, with each defendant's contacts assessed individually.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 126

records.title: Calder v. Jones (1984)
records.text:
Walden requires a defendant-created forum connection; knowledge that a plaintiff resides in the forum, by itself, does not recreate Calder’s facts.

The decision was unanimous (Rehnquist, J.); the defendants were National Enquirer reporter John South and president-editor Iain Calder, the Enquirer sold over 600,000 copies a week in California out of about 5,000,000 nationally, and the Court held that First Amendment concerns play no role in the jurisdictional analysis and that the defendants were not mere employees whose contacts are judged by the employer's.

records.title: Kulko v. Superior Court (1978)
records.text: Letting your child live with the other parent in another state is not a choice to enjoy that state's protection. A father who agreed that his children would live in California with their mother could not be pulled into a California court over child support.

records.title: Kulko v. Superior Court (1978)
records.text: A parent who acquiesces in his child's move to live with the other parent in another state has not thereby purposefully sought that state's benefits and protections, so due process bars that state from exercising personal jurisdiction over him in a child-support action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 126–127

records.title: Kulko v. Superior Court (1978)
records.text:
Read alongside McGee and Burger King to see why the kind of relationship and the defendant’s own conduct matter. The note does not support a categorical rule that every noncommercial relationship defeats jurisdiction.

The decision was 6-3: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court and Justice Brennan dissented, joined by Justices White and Powell, concluding the father's California connection was not too attenuated to require him to defend there. The Kulkos had married in California during Ezra's military stopover, lived in New York for 13 years, and signed a separation agreement in New York giving the children to the mother in California for summers and holidays.

records.title: Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court (1987)
records.text: Even when a company has some tie to a state, a court can refuse to hear the case if it would be too unfair. A Japanese valve maker was being asked to defend a leftover indemnity claim in California, which was too burdensome. The justices split on what counts as enough contact.

records.title: Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court (1987)
records.text: Even where a purposeful-contact theory is available, fair play and substantial justice can defeat personal jurisdiction, as where a foreign component maker is sued in a state court on a foreign indemnity claim; no majority resolved the stream-of-commerce test.

records.title: Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court (1987)
records.text:
The factual posture after settlement is essential. This is not a holding that foreign manufacturers can never be sued where their products cause injury, nor a majority endorsement of either stream-of-commerce formulation.

The case began with Gary Zurcher's motorcycle accident; Cheng Shin (Taiwan) impleaded Asahi (Japan), and Justice O'Connor's Part II-A plurality (joined by Rehnquist, Powell and Scalia) required 'additional conduct' directed at the forum beyond awareness, giving as examples designing the product for the forum market, advertising there, establishing channels for advice to forum customers, or marketing through a distributor who agreed to sell in the forum; Justice Brennan's four-Justice group would have found awareness that the product regularly reaches the forum sufficient.

records.text: A foreign manufacturer that sells through a distributor and aims at the whole United States is not automatically open to suit in every state. One machine reaching New Jersey was not enough. No single reasoning won five votes, and the Court did not say which view controls.

records.text: On the judgment in Nicastro, a foreign manufacturer that targets the United States market through an independent distributor is not subject to specific jurisdiction in a state on one isolated sale there without a regular sales flow or forum-specific effort; no rationale commanded five votes.

records.title: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro (2011)
records.text:
The casebook discusses the difficulty of identifying the controlling rule in fragmented decisions. Do not label all of Justice Kennedy’s reasoning “the Court’s holding.”

Nicastro injured his hand on a metal-shearing machine made in England by J. McIntyre, which sold in the United States only through an independent Ohio-based exclusive distributor; the Kennedy plurality was joined by Roberts, Scalia and Thomas, and Breyer's concurrence (joined by Alito) rested on the thin record rather than the plurality's sovereignty theory.

records.title: Walden v. Fiore (2014)
records.text: Your claim against a defendant is not enough just because you live in the state and felt the harm there. The defendant must have made a real connection with the state itself. An officer who seized cash in Georgia was not reachable in Nevada merely because the travelers lived there.

records.title: Walden v. Fiore (2014)
records.text: Specific personal jurisdiction requires that the defendant's own suit-related conduct create a substantial connection with the forum state itself; the plaintiff's forum connections, or an injury the plaintiff feels there, cannot be the only link, even for intentional torts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 159–161

records.title: Walden v. Fiore (2014)
records.text:
The case clarifies the effects analysis rather than abolishing it. Use the actual direction of the defendant’s conduct, not simply an intentional act plus a known forum resident.

Gina Fiore and Keith Gipson, professional gamblers, had about $97,000 seized by Walden, a Georgia police officer deputized to assist a DEA task force at the Atlanta airport; the district court dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court (Thomas, J., unanimous) reversed the Ninth Circuit.

records.text: Indirect tire sales did not make the foreign subsidiaries essentially at home in North Carolina, so they could not face this unrelated accident claim there. Contacts-based general jurisdiction usually belongs at incorporation or the principal place of business. Consent is a separate basis, addressed later in Mallory.

records.title: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown (2011)
records.text: A state may exercise general, all-purpose jurisdiction over a corporation only when its affiliations with the state are so continuous and systematic that it is essentially at home there; products reaching the forum through the stream of commerce do not suffice.

records.text:
The course’s later Daimler and BNSF materials develop the at-home inquiry. Perkins and Helicopteros receive separate indexed accounts here, even though the syllabus assigns them through Goodyear’s discussion.

Two 13-year-old boys from North Carolina died in a bus crash outside Paris attributed to a tire made in Turkey; the defendants were Goodyear USA and its subsidiaries in Turkey, France and Luxembourg, and Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court, framing the paradigm general-jurisdiction forums as the place of incorporation and the principal place of business.

records.text: A company that has moved its real business operations into a state can be sued there even for claims unrelated to that business. The mining company ran its wartime business from Ohio, so Ohio could hear a stock claim. The Constitution allows it but does not force the state to.

records.title: Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co. (1952)
records.text: When a foreign corporation carries on continuous and systematic corporate activities in a state, due process permits, but does not require, that state to exercise jurisdiction over it on causes of action entirely distinct from those activities.

records.title: Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co. (1952)
records.text:
Perkins, herself a nonresident of Ohio, sued for dividends and stock certificates; the company's president ran the business from Ohio during the Japanese occupation of the Philippines (directors' meetings, correspondence, banking, stock transfers, salaries, purchases), and the Court described these as 'continuous and systematic' activities supporting jurisdiction on a claim that did not arise in Ohio.

The Ohio courts had refused jurisdiction; the Supreme Court vacated and remanded, holding that due process neither compelled nor forbade Ohio to hear the case, leaving the choice to Ohio.

records.text: Buying equipment and sending staff for training in a state does not make a foreign company at home there. A Colombian helicopter operator that bought helicopters and trained pilots in Texas could not be sued in Texas over a crash in Peru unrelated to those trips.

records.text: A foreign corporation's purchases and purchase-related training trips in a forum, a single negotiating trip there and receipt of checks drawn on a forum bank are not the continuous and systematic contacts needed for general jurisdiction over a claim unrelated to them.

records.title: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall (1984)
records.text:
Use Perkins as the comparison in character of operations. Use Ford for a later discussion of relatedness; Helicopteros is not a holding that every claim involving goods bought in a state necessarily lacks specific jurisdiction.

The decision was 8-1: Justice Blackmun wrote for the Court and Justice Brennan alone dissented, arguing the Texas contacts were substantial and sufficiently related to the claim; the Court reversed the Texas Supreme Court, which had sustained jurisdiction.

Helicol had bought about 80 percent of its helicopter fleet (roughly $4 million) from Bell Helicopter in Fort Worth, sent pilots and management there for training, and sent its chief executive to Houston to negotiate the Peruvian pipeline contract, which was signed in Peru; the 1976 crash killed four U.S. citizens whose representatives sued in Texas.

records.text: Being big and doing lots of business in a state does not make a company at home there. A German carmaker could not be sued in California over events in Argentina just because its American subsidiary sold cars across California.

records.text: A court may exercise general jurisdiction over a corporation only where its affiliations make it essentially at home, paradigmatically its place of incorporation and principal place of business; a substantial, continuous, and systematic course of business in the State is not enough.

records.title: Daimler AG v. Bauman (2014)
records.text:
Do not turn this into a numerical percentage rule. The Court did not hold that a company is immune wherever its forum sales represent a small proportion of worldwide business.

Procedural history: the Northern District of California dismissed for want of personal jurisdiction; a Ninth Circuit panel first affirmed, then on rehearing reversed and upheld jurisdiction (with en banc rehearing denied); the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J.) reversed the Ninth Circuit.

records.text: A state court may exercise general jurisdiction over a corporation only where it is essentially at home, ordinarily its place of incorporation and principal place of business, and FELA's section 56 governs venue and subject-matter jurisdiction, not personal jurisdiction.

Mallory presents a separate registration-consent route. BNSF’s at-home analysis and Mallory’s due-process treatment of an express registration scheme address different asserted grounds of authority.

Justice Alito wrote for an 8-1 Court; the plaintiffs were 86 California residents and 592 residents of 33 other states, BMS is incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in New York, and the Court rejected the California Supreme Court's 'sliding scale' approach, requiring a connection between the forum and the specific claims at issue while leaving open whether the Fifth Amendment imposes the same limits on federal courts.

records.text:
The doctrine also takes in the later note cases on geographic targeting. Zippo is a federal district court decision. It does not mean that every interactive website is subject to suit wherever a browser can reach it.

Decided by the Western District of Pennsylvania; Zippo Dot Com was a California corporation running a USENET news service that registered zippo.com, zippo.net and zipponews.com, and Zippo Manufacturing sued for trademark dilution, infringement and false designation under the Lanham Act and state law. Two of the seven Pennsylvania access-provider agreements were with providers in the Western District.

records.title: Shaffer v. Heitner (1977)
records.text: A state cannot reach a person just because they own some property there if the property has nothing to do with the dispute. Delaware could not hear a suit against company officers merely because their stock was treated as sitting in Delaware. Property claims face the same fairness test as everything else.

records.title: Shaffer v. Heitner (1977)
records.text: Assertions of state-court jurisdiction over property, whether labeled in rem or quasi in rem, must be evaluated under International Shoe and its progeny; the mere statutory presence of property unrelated to the claim does not supply sufficient contacts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 210–222

records.title: Shaffer v. Heitner (1977)
records.text:
The opinion should not be restated as “property never supports jurisdiction.” Its significance is the required contacts inquiry and the distinction between a dispute about property and the use of unrelated property solely to secure a forum.

Heitner, a nonresident, brought a shareholder derivative suit against 28 present and former Greyhound officers and directors for conduct in Oregon, and used Delaware's sequestration statute to seize the stock and options of 21 of them; Justice Marshall wrote for the Court, Justice Powell concurred, Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, Justice Brennan concurred in part and dissented in part, and Justice Rehnquist did not participate.

Rule statement: all assertions of state-court jurisdiction, including in rem and quasi in rem, must be evaluated under the International Shoe minimum-contacts standard; presence of property in the state is a relevant contact but, where the property is unrelated to the claim, it is not by itself sufficient.

records.title: Burnham v. Superior Court (1990)
records.text: If you are handed court papers while you are voluntarily in a state, even for a short visit, that state's courts can hear the case. A father served while visiting his kids in California could be sued there for divorce. The justices agreed on the result but not on why.

records.title: Burnham v. Superior Court (1990)
records.text: A state court may exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident individual who is personally served while voluntarily present in the state, even though the visit is temporary and the suit is unrelated to his activities there.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 223–231
Brief · Personal jurisdiction briefs, pp. 42–45

records.title: Burnham v. Superior Court (1990)
records.text:
This is an individual’s voluntary presence. It does not decide all cases involving fraudulent inducement, compelled attendance, immunity, or service on a corporation’s agent. Compare Tickle and Wyman before extending the rule to deception.

Dennis Burnham was a New Jersey resident served with his estranged wife's California divorce petition during a brief visit to California; the Scalia opinion reasons that jurisdiction based on physical presence alone satisfies due process because it is one of the continuing traditions of our legal system, while Brennan's concurrence reasons that a visitor knowingly avails himself of the state's benefits and protections and can reasonably anticipate being sued there.

records.title: Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co. (2023)
records.text: Pennsylvania’s express registration-and-consent statute survived this due-process challenge: Pennsylvania Fire remained controlling. The Court did not decide the separate Commerce Clause challenge or treat every state’s registration law as consent. This is a consent route, distinct from the at-home test for jurisdiction based on business contacts.
