records.text: The Due Process Clause does not prohibit a state from exercising general jurisdiction over a foreign corporation that registered to do business under a statute expressly making registration a basis for such jurisdiction; Pennsylvania Fire controls and International Shoe did not overrule it.

The casebook’s earlier discussion at printed page 197 predates this decision.

records.text: Notice must be reasonably calculated to reach interested people and let them object; due process does not guarantee actual receipt. Newspaper publication was inadequate for known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had: they were owed at least ordinary mail. Publication could suffice for interests or whereabouts unascertainable with due diligence.

records.title: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co. (1950)
records.text: Before a proceeding that is to be accorded finality, due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections.

records.title: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co. (1950)
records.text:
Distinguish adequate notice from personal jurisdiction. A state may have a legitimate relationship with a trust or its administration and still use a defective method of informing beneficiaries. Later cases address returned mail, known incapacity, and institutional delivery systems.

Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; Justice Burton dissented, arguing that supplemental notice for state-created common trust funds should be left to state discretion, and Justice Douglas took no part. Mullane was the court-appointed special guardian for beneficiaries who had not appeared, and it was he who objected that publication notice was constitutionally inadequate.

records.title: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent (1964)
records.text: Parties to a contract can agree in advance to be sued in a certain place and can name someone to receive court papers for them. Because the named agent promptly passed the papers along, serving her was valid even though she never promised to do so.

records.title: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent (1964)
records.text: Contracting parties may agree in advance to submit to a court's jurisdiction, and a person a contract designates to receive process is an agent authorized by appointment under the Federal Rule when she promptly accepts and transmits the process, even without an express promise to do so.

records.title: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent (1964)
records.text:
This makes a useful Contracts connection concerning standardized agreements and procedural consent, but the governing service question and the broader fairness of the bargain remain distinct.

The Szukhents, Michigan farmers, leased farm equipment from the New York company on a printed form; the decision was 5-4 with Justice Stewart writing, Justice Black dissenting alone, and Justice Brennan dissenting joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg.

records.title: Wyman v. Newhouse (1937)
records.text: If a person is tricked into entering a state so they can be served, a resulting judgment is void. Wyman lured Newhouse into Florida by claiming her mother was dying and she was leaving the country for good, then had him served at the airport, so Newhouse could later defend against enforcement of that judgment in another state.

records.title: Wyman v. Newhouse (1937)
records.text: A judgment obtained by serving a defendant who was fraudulently induced to enter the state for service is void for want of personal jurisdiction and may be attacked collaterally when its enforcement is sought in another state.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 276–278
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 17–19

records.title: Wyman v. Newhouse (1937)
records.text:
Compare Tickle’s earlier-stage demurrer to a plea with Wyman’s later effort to enforce a default judgment. Also compare Burnham’s voluntary, untainted visit.

Newhouse was met at the Miami airport by Wyman, a deputy sheriff who served him, and a photographer; the Florida claims were for money loaned, money advanced, and seduction under promise of marriage. The Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the New York action on the judgment, reasoning that jurisdiction obtained by fraud is treated as no jurisdiction, so the judgment was void and not entitled to enforcement in another state.

records.title: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. (1969)
records.text: Wisconsin could not freeze earned wages under this procedure without notice and a prior opportunity to be heard. A later chance to recover the money did not cure the interim hardship. The Court reserved extraordinary situations needing special protection; it did not require a full merits trial before every provisional remedy.

records.title: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. (1969)
records.text: Absent an extraordinary situation requiring special protection of a governmental or creditor interest, prejudgment garnishment of wages without notice and a prior opportunity to be heard violates procedural due process, even though the deprivation is temporary.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 279–280
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 25–26

records.title: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. (1969)
records.text:
Family Finance claimed $420 on a promissory note and, under a Wisconsin statute, served a garnishment writ on Sniadach's employer freezing half her wages before any hearing; the Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the procedure and the U.S. Supreme Court reversed 7-1 in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Harlan concurring and Justice Black dissenting.

The Court treated wages as a specialized type of property whose prejudgment garnishment may drive a wage-earning family to the wall, so absent extraordinary circumstances notice and a prior hearing are required.

records.title: Fuentes v. Shevin (1972)
records.text: A state cannot help a seller grab your household goods, such as a stove or a stereo, before you get a chance to tell your side. Getting the items back later does not fix the harm. Sellers must give notice and a hearing first, except in real emergencies.

Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 27–29

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Fuentes v. Shevin (1972)
records.text: Due process requires notice and an opportunity to be heard before a State helps a private claimant seize goods in another person's possession, even temporarily and even where title is disputed, except in extraordinary situations.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 280–283
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 27–29

records.title: Fuentes v. Shevin (1972)
records.text:
Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing refine the significance of prior judicial scrutiny, an existing creditor interest, and prompt procedures to dissolve an attachment. Do not read Fuentes as eliminating every prejudgment remedy.

Margarita Fuentes bought a gas stove and a stereo from Firestone on conditional sales contracts; after a dispute over servicing, with about $200 left, Firestone claimed she had stopped paying, and a sheriff seized the goods on a writ obtained from a court clerk on a double-value bond before she had even received the summons.

Justice Stewart wrote for a 4–3 Court; Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun; Justices Powell and Rehnquist did not participate.

records.title: Connecticut v. Doehr (1991)
records.text: A person cannot lock up your house with a court attachment just by swearing out a claim against you if there is no hearing and no emergency. The court weighs your interest, the risk of mistakes and the claimant's need. Here the claimant had no stake in the house and had no reason to rush.

records.title: Connecticut v. Doehr (1991)
records.text: A prejudgment attachment procedure is tested under a modified Mathews v. Eldridge balance weighing the private interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation and value of added safeguards, and principally the interest of the party seeking the remedy, with any ancillary government interest.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 286–296

records.title: Connecticut v. Doehr (1991)
records.text:
The assigned surrounding notes continue through page 296 and include applications concerning liens, forfeiture, and procedural assistance.

John DiGiovanni sued Brian Doehr for assault and battery and, on an affidavit of five one-sentence paragraphs, obtained an ex parte $75,000 attachment on Doehr's home under a Connecticut statute that required no bond and no pre-attachment notice.

Justice White wrote; Parts I–III (applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, adapted to a private-creditor dispute, and holding the statute unconstitutional) spoke for the Court, while Part IV (that due process would also require a bond) was joined only by Justices Marshall, Stevens and O'Connor; Chief Justice Rehnquist (joined by Justice Blackmun) and Justice Scalia concurred in part and in the judgment.

records.title: Lacks v. Lacks (1976)
records.text: Calling a legal requirement jurisdictional does not make a judgment void when it is broken. The divorce court had the basic power to hear divorces, and the residence rule only governed the claim itself. So the wife could not undo the final divorce on that ground.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 297–303

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Lacks v. Lacks (1976)
records.text: Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns a court's competence to entertain the category of action, not the plaintiff's ability to establish the substantive conditions for relief, so an error about a statutory element of the claim does not render the judgment void.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 297–303

records.title: Lacks v. Lacks (1976)
records.text:
Capron illustrates genuine missing federal jurisdiction. Lacks shows why the label must be justified. Later notes concerning Arbaugh and other statutory requirements develop this distinction in federal law.

The husband's divorce judgment (March 1970) was affirmed by the Appellate Division in 1972; two years later the wife moved to vacate it for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the husband had not met the residence requirement. The Court of Appeals held the residence requirements go to the substance of the cause of action, not the court's competence.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 297–303

records.title: Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806)
records.text: Under the 1789 diversity statute, each person sharing a joint interest had to be able to sue or be sued in federal court, so one shared state on each side defeated jurisdiction. Today's complete diversity rule grew from this reading.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–306

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806)
records.text: Under the statutory diversity grant, where an interest is joint, every person representing that interest must be competent to sue, or liable to be sued, in the federal courts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–306

records.title: Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806)
records.text: Do not use this short note to invent the underlying transaction or a modern exception. Compare statutory interpleader and the Class Action Fairness Act for separately authorized jurisdictional arrangements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–306

records.title: Mas v. Perry (1974)
records.text: For state citizenship in diversity cases, a person must be a U.S. citizen domiciled in that state. Domicile combines residence with intent to remain and persists until a new one is acquired. Judy Mas’s temporary Louisiana graduate study did not change her Mississippi domicile; citizenship was assessed when suit began.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 309–312

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Mas v. Perry (1974)
records.text: For diversity purposes a natural person is a citizen of a state only if a United States citizen domiciled there; domicile persists until the person takes up residence elsewhere intending to remain, and citizenship is determined when the complaint is filed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 309–312

records.title: Mas v. Perry (1974)
records.text:
The syllabus abbreviates this case as “Perry.” Search by Mas or Perry reaches this record. The separate A.F.A. Tours entry addresses the course’s principal amount analysis.

Jean Paul Mas (French citizen) and Judy Mas (Mississippi domiciliary) sued their Baton Rouge landlord for invasion of privacy; the jury awarded $5,000 to Mr. Mas and $15,000 to Mrs. Mas. Perry also argued Mr. Mas's $5,000 award fell short of the jurisdictional amount, and the Fifth Circuit rejected that because the claim exceeding the amount was made in good faith.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 309–312

records.title: A.F.A. Tours, Inc. v. Whitchurch (1991)
records.text: If a plaintiff claims over the federal dollar threshold in good faith, the court accepts that amount unless it is clear beyond doubt the claim is worth less. A judge should not dismiss on the spot but should let the plaintiff show why the claim is worth enough.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–322

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: A.F.A. Tours, Inc. v. Whitchurch (1991)
records.text: The amount a plaintiff claims in apparent good faith controls unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less than the jurisdictional amount, and the court must give the plaintiff a reasonable opportunity to show otherwise before dismissing.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–322

records.title: A.F.A. Tours, Inc. v. Whitchurch (1991)
records.text:
The dollar threshold in the historical litigation was $50,000. The course’s casebook describes the later ordinary diversity threshold separately. Keep the historical amount, the legal test, and the actual damages award distinct.

Whitchurch had worked for A.F.A. as a tour escort for about seventeen years and had escorted roughly 1,500 A.F.A. clients; the district court raised the jurisdictional amount on its own at oral argument on the summary-judgment motion and granted summary judgment for Whitchurch, and the Second Circuit vacated under the rule that the sum claimed by the plaintiff controls if made in good faith unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–322

records.title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908)
records.text: A predicted federal defense does not create ordinary federal-question jurisdiction. The federal basis must appear in the plaintiff’s own properly pleaded claim. The Mottleys’ state contract claim failed that test; later cases explain the separate, narrow route for state claims necessarily raising substantial federal issues.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908)
records.text: For statutory federal-question jurisdiction, the plaintiff's statement of his own cause of action must establish the federal basis; anticipating a federal defense, and pleading a federal answer to it, does not make the suit arise under federal law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908)
records.text:
The existence of a federal question somewhere in a lawsuit does not answer § 1331. Grable supplies a distinct and limited route for a federal issue necessarily embedded in the plaintiff’s own state-law claim. It does not erase Mottley’s defense rule.

The Mottleys were injured in an 1871 railway accident and settled for lifetime free passes; a 1906 federal act forbade free passes and the railroad refused renewal in 1907. They sought specific performance; the trial court overruled the railroad's demurrer and ruled for them, and the Supreme Court raised the jurisdictional defect on its own motion and directed dismissal.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: American Well Works Co. v. Layne & Bowler Co. (1916)
records.text: A claim belongs to the body of law that creates it. A company sued under state law for hurting a business with false statements did not bring a patent case merely because patents might come up as part of the defense.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: American Well Works Co. v. Layne & Bowler Co. (1916)
records.text: A suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action, so a state-law claim for injury to business does not arise under the patent laws merely because a defense may require deciding patent validity or infringement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.title: American Well Works Co. v. Layne & Bowler Co. (1916)
records.text:
This is a short assigned note. It supplies no complete lower-court history or full account of the commercial transactions.

American Well Works sued in Arkansas state court for libel and slander of its title to its pump; Layne removed, the district court dismissed on the theory that the suit arose under patent law, and the Supreme Court (Holmes, J., with Justice McKenna dissenting) reversed, stating the creation test: a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.title: Shoshone Mining Co. v. Rutter (1900)
records.text: Congress allowing a certain kind of lawsuit does not by itself move that lawsuit into federal court. Adverse suits over mining claims go to any court that already has power. The suit must raise a real federal question or meet some other ordinary ground for federal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Shoshone Mining Co. v. Rutter (1900)
records.text: The mere fact that Congress authorized an action, such as an adverse suit to determine the right of possession of a mining claim, does not confer federal-question jurisdiction; jurisdiction requires a genuine federal question or another independent basis under the ordinary rules.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.title: Shoshone Mining Co. v. Rutter (1900)
records.text:
Use the case as the limited exception identified by the assigned materials. The short note does not establish a general rejection of federal jurisdiction over federally created causes of action.

Rutter sued in federal court claiming superior title to a mining claim under the adverse-claim procedure of Revised Statutes §§ 2325-2326; the case went through the federal Circuit Court in Idaho to the Ninth Circuit, but the Supreme Court (7-1, Justice Brewer) reversed because the statutes let possession be decided by local customs, rules of miners and state law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 339–340

records.title: Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co. (1921)
records.text: A shareholder who sued to stop a bank from buying federally issued bonds raised a federal question, because the only reason the purchase would be unlawful was that the federal law behind the bonds was unconstitutional. A real federal issue at the core of the claim can be enough.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–342

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co. (1921)
records.text: A claim created by state law can arise under federal law when a substantial federal question, resting on a reasonable foundation and more than merely colorable, appears in the plaintiff's own statement of the claim and is necessary to the relief sought.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–342

records.title: Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co. (1921)
records.text:
The decision does not make every state claim containing any federal issue jurisdictionally federal. The later cases require necessity, actual dispute, substantiality to the federal system, and consistency with the federal-state division of judicial work.

Smith sued in the Western District of Missouri to enjoin the company from investing in farm-loan bonds issued under the Federal Farm Loan Act of 1916; Missouri law allowed the trust company to invest only in securities authorized by valid law, so the state-law claim turned on the Act's constitutionality, which the Court (Justice Day) then upheld on the merits.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–342

records.title: Grable & Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering & Manufacturing (2005)
records.text: Some state-law claims can still go to federal court when a big, truly disputed federal question sits at the heart of the case. Here the dispute turned on whether the IRS gave proper notice of a tax seizure, which the federal government cares about, and such cases will be few.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 342–347

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Grable & Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering & Manufacturing (2005)
records.text: A state-law claim supports federal-question jurisdiction when it necessarily raises a federal issue that is actually disputed and substantial, and a federal forum can decide it without disturbing the congressionally approved balance of federal and state judicial responsibilities.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 342–347

records.title: Grable & Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering & Manufacturing (2005)
records.text:
The test is conjunctive. Gunn shows that an issue can be necessary and disputed yet lack the required significance to the federal system. Mottley remains the starting rule for locating the issue in the plaintiff’s own claim.

The IRS seized Grable's Michigan property in 1994 for unpaid taxes and sold it to Darue after certified-mail notice; five years later Grable sued to quiet title, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed federal jurisdiction before the Supreme Court (Souter, J., unanimous) did so, clarifying that Merrell Dow's absence of a federal private right of action is a factor, not a bar.

Justice Thomas concurred, suggesting he would be open in a future case to returning to Justice Holmes's test that a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 342–347

records.title: Gunn v. Minton (2013)
records.text: Being a case about a patent in the background is not enough for federal court. A client who sued his lawyer for malpractice over a patent argument raised a patent question, but its answer would not matter to the wider patent system, so the state court kept the case.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 347–351

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Gunn v. Minton (2013)
records.text: Federal jurisdiction over a state-created claim requires a federal issue that is necessarily raised, actually disputed, substantial to the federal system as a whole, and capable of resolution in federal court without disrupting the congressionally approved division of responsibility between federal and state courts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 347–351

records.title: Gunn v. Minton (2013)
records.text:
A necessary federal issue is only one part of the test. Grable’s system-wide concern with federal tax collection differs from the case-specific malpractice counterfactual here.

Minton's TEXCEN trading-software patent was invalidated under the on-sale bar because he had leased the system more than a year before applying; Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a unanimous Court, restating the Grable inquiry as whether the federal issue is (1) necessarily raised, (2) actually disputed, (3) substantial, and (4) capable of federal resolution without disrupting the federal-state balance approved by Congress.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 347–351

records.title: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966)
records.text: If your federal claim is real and a state claim comes out of the same events, the federal court can hear both in one case. Judges look at how the facts connect, not at labels, and they still choose whether to keep the state claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 353–359

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966)
records.text: A federal court has pendent power over a state claim when the federal claim is substantial, both claims arise from a common nucleus of operative fact, and a plaintiff would ordinarily be expected to try them together; exercising that power remains discretionary.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 353–359

records.title: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966)
records.text:
The historical term “pendent jurisdiction” describes the related state claim in this setting. Do not treat Gibbs alone as resolving the later pendent-party questions in Aldinger, Kroger, and Finley.

Justice Brennan wrote the opinion; the case came from the Eastern District of Tennessee, where a jury found for Gibbs, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed before the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court replaced the narrower Hurn v. Oursler test with the 'common nucleus of operative fact' standard, under which the state and federal claims must be ones a plaintiff would ordinarily expect to try in one judicial proceeding.

Despite upholding pendent jurisdiction, the Court reversed the judgment for Gibbs on the merits, so the case is a jurisdictional win and a substantive loss for the plaintiff; pendent jurisdiction was described as a doctrine of discretion, not of plaintiff's right, and state claims should ordinarily be dismissed if the federal claims drop out before trial.

records.title: Aldinger v. Howard (1976)
records.text: Under the statutes and precedent in force in 1976, the county was excluded from § 1983, and the Court would not append the state claim against it. That is a historical statutory holding: later developments changed municipal § 1983 liability, and § 1367 now expressly addresses supplemental claims involving additional parties.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–360

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Aldinger v. Howard (1976)
records.text: Pendent-party jurisdiction requires both that Article III permit it and that Congress has not expressly or implicitly negated it in the jurisdictional statute; a state claim against a county excluded from section 1983 could not be appended to section 1983 claims against its officials.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–360

records.title: Aldinger v. Howard (1976)
records.text:
The book notes later changes concerning municipal liability and Congress’s enactment of § 1367. This is a historical holding, not a freestanding current rule that counties cannot be sued under § 1983.

Aldinger was a clerk in the Spokane County treasurer's office who was fired without a hearing for living with her boyfriend; she sued the treasurer under section 1983 and joined Spokane County on a state-law claim, and the Court (Rehnquist, J.) held that Congress's then-understood exclusion of counties from section 1983 barred pendent-party jurisdiction over the county, a result later addressed by Monell (1978) and by 28 U.S.C. section 1367(a).

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–360

records.title: Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978)
records.text: A plaintiff who sues one defendant and then finds that defendant has dragged in a third party cannot sue that third party directly in federal court if they share citizenship. Related facts do not fix the missing diversity.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 360–361

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978)
records.text: In a diversity action, ancillary jurisdiction does not extend to the plaintiff's direct state-law claim against an impleaded third-party defendant who shares her citizenship, because § 1332 requires complete diversity and Rule 14 cannot supply subject-matter jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 360–361

records.title: Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978)
records.text:
Section 1367(b) later expressly addresses specified claims by plaintiffs in cases founded solely on diversity. Analyze its text rather than treating every later-added claim as automatically excluded.

James Kroger was electrocuted when a crane boom came near a high-tension line in Iowa; his widow sued the Omaha Public Power District (a Nebraska corporation) in diversity, OPPD impleaded Owen under Rule 14, Kroger amended to sue Owen directly, OPPD won summary judgment, and Owen's Iowa principal place of business surfaced only at trial.

Procedurally, the jury returned a verdict for Kroger, the Eighth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed in an opinion by Justice Stewart; Justice White, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented, arguing ancillary jurisdiction should reach the claim because the plaintiff had not tried to evade complete diversity.

Congress codified the Kroger result in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(b), which withholds supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases over claims by plaintiffs against persons made parties under Rules 14, 19, 20 or 24 when that would be inconsistent with § 1332.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 360–361

records.title: Finley v. United States (1989)
records.text: In 1989, the FTCA’s grant over claims against the United States did not authorize related state claims against additional defendants. Finley required statutory authorization, beyond factual overlap. Congress subsequently enacted § 1367, which expressly includes additional-party claims subject to its exceptions; Finley’s restrictive approach is historical.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 361–364

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Finley v. United States (1989)
records.text: Under the statute then governing, a jurisdictional grant covering claims against a particular party, such as the FTCA's grant over claims against the United States, did not authorize federal courts to hear related state-law claims against additional parties lacking an independent jurisdictional basis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 361–364

records.title: Finley v. United States (1989)
records.text:
Do not apply Finley as though § 1367 had never been enacted. Its principal course role is to explain the need for and design of the later supplemental-jurisdiction statute.

Facts and posture: Finley's husband and children died when their plane struck power lines approaching a San Diego airfield; she sued the United States under the FTCA for FAA negligence, then moved to add state-law claims against the City of San Diego and the utility; the district court allowed it under Gibbs, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court (Scalia, J.) affirmed.

The decision was 5–4: Justice Blackmun dissented, and Justice Stevens dissented joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 361–364

records.title: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005)
records.text: In a diversity case, if one named plaintiff meets the dollar threshold, other plaintiffs or class members with smaller related claims can come along. The statute overrode the old rule that each plaintiff had to clear the threshold alone. The parties must still be completely diverse.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–374

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005)
records.text: Where complete diversity exists and at least one named plaintiff's claim satisfies the amount in controversy, § 1367 authorizes supplemental jurisdiction over related claims of additional Rule 20 plaintiffs or Rule 23 class members whose claims fall below that amount.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–374

records.title: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005)
records.text:
Separate claim aggregation from supplemental jurisdiction. The case does not combine small claims into one fictional large claim; it identifies a valid anchor and asks whether the statute supplies authority over additional related claims.

The two consolidated cases were the Exxon dealers' class action (about 10,000 dealers alleging fuel overcharges, where the Eleventh Circuit upheld supplemental jurisdiction after a jury verdict) and Ortega v. Star-Kist (a nine-year-old injured by a tuna can, where only her claim met the amount and the First Circuit rejected jurisdiction over her family's claims); the Court (Kennedy, J.) affirmed the Eleventh Circuit and reversed the First Circuit.

The majority distinguished incomplete diversity, which 'contaminates' the whole action and so is not cured by § 1367, from a single plaintiff's failure to meet the amount in controversy, which does not.

records.title: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets (1941)
records.text: If you start a case in state court and the defendant answers with a counterclaim against you, you do not become a defendant who can remove it. Only the party that was sued can take the case to federal court.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 381–382

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets (1941)
records.text: Under a removal statute authorizing removal by the defendant or defendants, an original state-court plaintiff cannot remove on diversity grounds merely because the defendant asserts an independent counterclaim, and federal courts must keep removal jurisdiction within the limits Congress prescribed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 381–382

records.title: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets (1941)
records.text:
This short assigned note does not provide a complete underlying transaction or litigation history. Its course function is identifying who may remove.

Shamrock, a non-Texas corporation, sued Sheets (doing business as Friona Independent Oil Co.), a Texas citizen, in Texas state court to recover an alleged indebtedness; Sheets counterclaimed for more than $3,000 for breach of a separate contract, and Justice Stone wrote for a unanimous Court that the removal statute's reference to 'defendants' means only the defendants to the original action, so a plaintiff cannot remove on the basis of a counterclaim.

Shamrock is the standard citation for strict construction of removal jurisdiction: due regard for the rightful independence of state governments requires federal courts to scrupulously confine their jurisdiction to the precise limits the statute defines.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 381–382

records.title: Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson (2019)
records.text: A business pulled into someone else's lawsuit by a counterclaim cannot remove the case to federal court, even in a class action. Only the original defendant, the one sued in the plaintiff's own complaint, has that power.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 382–383

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson (2019)
records.text: Neither the general removal statute, § 1441(a), nor CAFA's removal provision, § 1453(b), permits removal by a third-party counterclaim defendant, because the defendant who may remove is the defendant to the original plaintiff's complaint.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 382–383

records.title: Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson (2019)
records.text:
A strong federal interest or substantial class exposure does not itself supply removal authorization. Begin with statutory party status, then analyze original jurisdiction and the remaining removal requirements.

Citibank sued Jackson in North Carolina state court to collect charges on a Home Depot credit card; Jackson counterclaimed against Citibank and added class claims against Home Depot and Carolina Water Systems. The Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit 5-4 in an opinion by Justice Thomas (joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan), reasoning that a third-party counterclaim defendant is a defendant to a claim but not to the 'civil action.'.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 382–383

records.title: Bright v. Bechtel Petroleum, Inc. (1986)
records.text: A plaintiff cannot keep a case in state court by dressing up a federal claim in state-law words. Here Bright attacked federal tax withholding, so the claim was federal underneath and the case could be removed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 383–384

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bright v. Bechtel Petroleum, Inc. (1986)
records.text: Under the artful-pleading doctrine, a plaintiff cannot defeat removal by using state-law terminology to conceal a claim's true federal nature, although a federal question must arise from the claim itself and not merely from an anticipated defense.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 383–384

records.title: Bright v. Bechtel Petroleum, Inc. (1986)
records.text:
The syllabus abbreviates the case as “Bechtel.” The assigned note is short.

Bright filed a W-4 claiming exemption from federal income-tax withholding and then sued in California state court for breach of contract when Bechtel withheld anyway; Bechtel removed, the district court denied remand, dismissed, and awarded attorney's fees, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed and imposed sanctions for a frivolous appeal, invoking the artful-pleading doctrine as a limit on the plaintiff's status as master of the complaint.

records.title: Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc. (2006)
records.text: Removing a case when the defendant is a citizen of the state where it was filed is a mistake you can lose by staying quiet. If the plaintiff does not object within thirty days, the judge cannot send the case back later on that ground.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc. (2006)
records.text: Removal of a diversity action in violation of the forum-defendant rule is a waivable, nonjurisdictional defect: the plaintiff must seek remand on that ground within thirty days, and the district court may not remand for it on its own.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 384–385

records.title: Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc. (2006)
records.text:
Do not infer that parties can waive the absence of complete diversity or another genuine defect in subject-matter jurisdiction.

Lively sued in California state court over a slip and fall in a Wild Oats store; Wild Oats removed on diversity, no remand motion was filed within 30 days, and the Ninth Circuit held the forum-defendant rule is procedural and waivable and so cannot support a district court's sua sponte remand, joining eight of nine circuits to decide the question (456 F.3d 933).

records.title: Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co. v. Owens (2014)
records.text: When a defendant removes a case, it only has to say plausibly that more than the required amount is at stake. It does not have to attach proof unless the plaintiff disputes the number or the judge questions it.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co. v. Owens (2014)
records.text: A notice of removal under section 1446(a) needs only a plausible allegation that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdictional threshold; evidence establishing the amount is required only when the plaintiff contests, or the court questions, the allegation.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 385–386

records.title: Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co. v. Owens (2014)
records.text:
The opinion’s discussion of CAFA does not automatically decide every presumption for ordinary removal. The casebook revisits this decision in the class-action jurisdiction material at pages 871–872.

Facts and posture: Owens filed a Kansas state-court class action over underpaid oil-and-gas royalties; Dart's CAFA removal notice alleged more than $8 million in controversy without evidence; the district court remanded under Tenth Circuit precedent, the Tenth Circuit denied leave to appeal the remand, and the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J.) held that denial an abuse of discretion, vacated and remanded.

The Court also stated that no antiremoval presumption attends cases invoking CAFA, and that when the amount is contested the removing defendant must establish it by a preponderance of the evidence under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(c)(2)(B).

The decision was 5–4: Justice Scalia dissented (joined by Justices Kennedy and Kagan, and by Justice Thomas in part) on the ground that the Court could review only the Tenth Circuit's discretionary refusal to hear the appeal, and Justice Thomas dissented separately.

records.title: Reasor-Hill Corp. v. Harrison (1952)
records.text: Arkansas judges were willing to hear a damages claim for harm to a crop on Missouri land. The court looked at why the old rule existed and refused to let the defendant escape any remedy just because the land was in another state.

records.title: Reasor-Hill Corp. v. Harrison (1952)
records.text: The Arkansas Supreme Court rejected the local-action rule for this interstate controversy, holding that an Arkansas court may hear a damages claim for injury to real property in another state; its central concern was that the defendant could otherwise escape any remedy.

records.title: Reasor-Hill Corp. v. Harrison (1952)
records.text:
The syllabus cites page 395, the beginning of the chapter; the case itself begins at printed page 399. Later federal venue reforms discussed in the chapter should be kept distinct from this state-court decision.

The suit began when Planters Flying Service sued D.M. Barton in Arkansas for crop-spraying fees; Barton answered that the spraying had ruined his Missouri cotton crop and cross-complained against the insecticide's manufacturer, Reasor-Hill, which then petitioned the Arkansas Supreme Court for a writ to stop the trial court from hearing the cross-complaint.

records.title: Bates v. C & S Adjusters, Inc. (1992)
records.text: In a federal debt-collection suit, you can file where the collection letter landed, because getting the letter is a key event behind the claim. The collector did not have to aim the letter at that place on purpose.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 404–407

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bates v. C & S Adjusters, Inc. (1992)
records.text: Under § 1391(b)(2) as amended in 1990, venue lies in any district where a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred, and receipt of a debt-collection notice is such an event even if the collector did not deliberately send it there.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 404–407

records.title: Bates v. C & S Adjusters, Inc. (1992)
records.text:
This is not a rule that a plaintiff may always sue at home. The source identifies a concrete claim-generating event in the district. The case illustrates why venue and personal jurisdiction must be analyzed separately.

Bates incurred the debt while living in the Western District of Pennsylvania and C & S was a local Pennsylvania collection agency doing no regular business in New York; the Postal Service forwarded the unmarked notice to Bates's new Western District of New York address, and the Second Circuit reversed and remanded under the 1990 amendment to 28 U.S.C. section 1391 (a district where a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred), reasoning that the harm from an abusive collection notice occurs on receipt.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 404–407

records.title: Livingston v. Jefferson (1811)
records.text: In 1811, the court treated trespass to Louisiana land as a local action that could not proceed in Virginia merely because Jefferson was there. This is the historical local-action rule. Modern federal venue under § 1391 is determined without the local/transitory distinction, subject to other applicable law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 401–408

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Livingston v. Jefferson (1811)
records.text: An action for trespass to land is a local action that can be brought only where the land lies, and a court does not acquire jurisdiction over it merely because the defendant resides or can be found in its district.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 401–408

records.title: Livingston v. Jefferson (1811)
records.text:
The assigned materials discuss later changes to federal venue law.

Livingston sued former President Jefferson in federal court in Virginia alleging that Jefferson as President had entered land Livingston claimed on the Batture in New Orleans, in the Territory of Orleans, and expelled him; Marshall (sitting with District Judge Tyler) applied the English local-action rule, so the suit could be brought only in Orleans Territory.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 401–408

records.title: Hoffman v. Blaski (1960)
records.text: Under § 1404(a)’s 1960 wording, the destination had to be a district where the plaintiff could originally sue; the defendants’ later consent was insufficient. The current statute adds a separate alternative allowing transfer to a district to which all parties consent, while retaining convenience and justice requirements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–415

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hoffman v. Blaski (1960)
records.text: Under the version of § 1404(a) then in force, a transferee district had to be one where the plaintiff had a right to bring the action when suit began, independently of the defendant's later consent or waiver of venue and personal-jurisdiction objections.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–415

records.title: Hoffman v. Blaski (1960)
records.text:
The casebook notes the later statutory addition permitting transfer to a district to which all parties consent. Preserve the historical holding while reading that later language; the decision is not a prohibition on the all-party-consent route.

Illinois plaintiffs sued a Texas corporation for patent infringement in Texas; the Texas district court transferred the case to Illinois, and the Seventh Circuit issued mandamus because the defendant could not have been served in Illinois and the action could not have been brought there. The Court held 1404(a) permits transfer only to a district where the plaintiff had a right to bring the action, regardless of defendant consent.

Justice Whittaker wrote the majority; Justice Frankfurter dissented, joined by Justices Harlan and Brennan.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–415

records.title: Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981)
records.text: A court can send a case abroad as inconvenient even if the foreign country's law is less generous to the plaintiff. Foreign plaintiffs get less deference for choosing a US court, and Scotland counted as a fair alternative for the aircraft crash claims.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 421–429

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981)
records.text: A foreign forum's less favorable substantive law ordinarily receives neither conclusive nor substantial weight in the forum non conveniens inquiry, a foreign plaintiff's forum choice receives less deference, and a district court's reasonable balancing is reviewed only for clear abuse of discretion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 421–429

records.title: Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981)
records.text:
Forum non conveniens dismisses in favor of another system; § 1404 transfers within the federal system. A foreign forum still must be available and adequate, and conditions on dismissal can matter.

The 1976 crash killed the pilot and five Scottish passengers; Piper built the plane in Pennsylvania and Hartzell Propeller built the propeller in Ohio; Gaynell Reyno, a California legal secretary appointed administratrix, filed in California state court, and the case was removed and then transferred under § 1404(a) to the Middle District of Pennsylvania.

Rule statements: a foreign plaintiff's choice of a United States forum deserves less deference than a resident's, and an unfavorable change in law may be given substantial weight only where the alternative forum's remedy is so clearly inadequate or unsatisfactory that it is no remedy at all; the district court's balancing of the Gilbert private- and public-interest factors is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 421–429

records.title: Atlantic Marine Construction Co. v. U.S. District Court (2013)
records.text: A valid forum clause does not make otherwise proper venue improper. A clause choosing another federal district is enforced through transfer; one choosing a state or foreign court ordinarily through forum non conveniens. The plaintiff’s forum choice and private convenience arguments lose their usual weight, while public-interest factors remain.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 433–439

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Atlantic Marine Construction Co. v. U.S. District Court (2013)
records.text: A forum-selection clause does not make statutorily proper venue improper; a valid clause naming another federal district is enforced through § 1404(a), with the plaintiff's forum choice and private interests given no weight and only public-interest factors left to resist transfer.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 433–439

records.title: Atlantic Marine Construction Co. v. U.S. District Court (2013)
records.text:
The Court assumed a valid clause. This case does not resolve whether every consumer, employment, or negotiated clause is valid. Keep the validity issues in Bremen and Carnival linked but distinct.

The decision was unanimous (Alito, J.); the district court had denied both the motion to dismiss and the alternative section 1404(a) transfer motion and the Fifth Circuit denied mandamus. Under the modified section 1404(a) analysis the plaintiff's choice of forum merits no weight, the private-interest factors are treated as weighing entirely in favor of the preselected forum, and the transferee court does not carry over the original forum's choice-of-law rules; a valid clause should be given controlling weight in all but the most exceptional cases.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 433–439

records.title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938)
records.text: Federal courts deciding state-law rights ordinarily follow the governing state’s statutes and authoritative court decisions, rather than inventing general federal common law. Erie rejected the contrary Swift approach. It did not decide the railroad’s liability, or eliminate distinct federal rules where the Constitution, Congress or a recognized federal interest supplies them.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938)
records.text: Where no federal constitutional or statutory law supplies the substantive rule, a federal court sitting in diversity must apply state law, including authoritative state judicial decisions as well as statutes; there is no general federal common law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 445–453

records.title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938)
records.text:
Erie is not a rule that every state procedure applies in federal court. York, Byrd, Hanna, and Shady Grove examine the later questions. Nor does it abolish specialized federal common law supported by distinct federal interests.

Tompkins, a Pennsylvania citizen, was struck by something protruding from a passing Erie train while walking on a footpath beside the tracks at night, and sued in the Southern District of New York (Erie being a New York corporation); Justice Brandeis wrote for the Court, declaring that there is no federal general common law.

Vote detail: Justice Reed concurred in part (statutory ground only); Justice Butler dissented, joined by Justice McReynolds; Justice Cardozo did not participate.

records.title: Swift v. Tyson (1842)
records.text: For a long time, federal courts ruled on general commercial questions by their own judgment and treated state court decisions only as respected opinions. That is the old approach Erie later threw out.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Swift v. Tyson (1842)
records.text: As the Court then read the Rules of Decision Act, state judicial decisions on questions of general commercial law deserve respect but do not bind federal courts, which decide such questions by their own judgment; Erie later repudiated this doctrine.

records.title: Swift v. Tyson (1842)
records.text: The course assigns Swift through the discussion in Erie. It is historical and superseded in its general-common-law approach; its commercial setting does not authorize modern federal courts to invent general contract law.

records.title: Black & White Taxicab & Transfer Co. v. Brown & Yellow Taxicab & Transfer Co. (1928)
records.text: Under the approach then prevailing under Swift v. Tyson, a federal court sitting in diversity could exercise independent judgment on a question of general common law despite contrary state decisions, and an actual reincorporation in another state to create diversity was not improper or collusive.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 446–449

records.title: Black & White Taxicab & Transfer Co. v. Brown & Yellow Taxicab & Transfer Co. (1928)
records.text:
The syllabus calls this “Black & White Taxicab.” The record is a historical comparison within Erie’s reasoning, not a current rule governing exclusive station arrangements.

Justice Holmes dissented, joined by Justices Brandeis and Stone, arguing that the common law enforced in a state is the law of that state existing by its authority and that the Swift doctrine was an unconstitutional assumption of power by the federal courts, though he would have left Swift itself standing and only stopped its spread; the majority (Butler, J., 6-3) upheld the exclusive contract with the Louisville & Nashville Railroad for the Bowling Green, Kentucky station after the Kentucky owners reincorporated in Tennessee and dissolved the Kentucky company.

records.text: If a state would throw out your claim as too late, a federal court hearing the same state claim must do the same. Calling a rule procedural does not matter if ignoring it would change who wins.

records.title: Guaranty Trust Co. v. York (1945)
records.text: A federal court in diversity may not disregard a state limitations rule that would bar recovery on the same state-created claim in state court; the test is whether ignoring the state rule would substantially change the outcome so far as legal rules determine it.

records.text:
Hanna later limits mechanical use of outcome determination: almost any missed procedural step can change an outcome. Ask what source of federal rule is involved and whether there is an actual conflict before applying York.

Guaranty Trust was indenture trustee for $30 million of Van Sweringen Corporation notes; York, who received her notes by gift in 1934 from a holder who had not accepted the exchange offer, sued in a diversity class action for breach of trust; Justice Frankfurter wrote the 'outcome-determinative' opinion, and Justice Rutledge dissented, joined by Justice Murphy.

records.text: A federal case on a state claim can be too late even if you filed on time, when the state's own rule says the clock stops only on service. Filing under the federal rule did not give the claim a longer life than Kansas allowed.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co. (1949)
records.text: In a diversity action on a state-created claim, a state rule making service an integral part of the limitations scheme governs the life of the claim; filing under Federal Rule 3 does not give the claim a longer life than state law allows.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 460–461

records.title: Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co. (1949)
records.text:
The casebook provides the historical filing and service sequence. Its core role is the distinction between federal commencement and state limitations tolling, not a universal rule that state service methods control in federal court.

The accident occurred in Kansas on October 1, 1943; Ragan filed in the District of Kansas on September 4, 1945 and served the summons on December 28, 1945, after Kansas's two-year period; the district court denied summary judgment and a verdict was entered for Ragan, the Tenth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Rutledge dissenting.

The Court's rationale was that a state-created cause of action cannot be given longer life in federal court than it would have in state court; Walker v. Armco Steel (1980) reaffirmed Ragan after Hanna, reading Rule 3 as not addressing tolling of state limitations periods.

records.title: Woods v. Interstate Realty Co. (1949)
records.text: If a state's courts would shut the door on you, you cannot walk through a federal courthouse in that state on the same state-law claim. Diversity jurisdiction gives you a different court, not a better chance to win.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 461

records.title: Woods v. Interstate Realty Co. (1949)
records.text: A litigant whom state law bars from maintaining an action in the state's courts cannot obtain a more favorable enforcement opportunity on a state-law claim by invoking diversity jurisdiction in a federal court in that state.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 461

records.title: Woods v. Interstate Realty Co. (1949)
records.text:
This is the Interstate Realty case, not Burlington Northern v. Woods. Later readings ask how an asserted federal rule or federal policy changes the analysis.

Interstate Realty, a Tennessee corporation, sued a Mississippi resident for a broker's commission on the sale of Mississippi land while doing business in Mississippi without qualifying under its statute.
