records.title: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949)
records.text: A small shareholder suing on behalf of a company had to post security for expenses under state law, and the federal court had to follow that rule. The ruling is also why some orders can be appealed right away if they decide something separate that would be lost later.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 461–462

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949)
records.text: A state statute requiring a small shareholder to post security for the corporation's expenses in a derivative suit is substantive and binds a federal diversity court; Cohen is also the origin of the collateral-order doctrine, under which the order refusing security was immediately appealable.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 461–462

records.title: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949)
records.text:
This is separate from the Contracts course’s Cohen v. Cowles Media.

Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; the district court denied the corporation's motion to require security, the Third Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed. The case is also the origin of the collateral-order doctrine: the order was immediately appealable because it conclusively determined a question separate from the merits that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment; the New Jersey statute, enacted in 1945 while the action was pending, applied to holders of less than 5 percent (or $50,000) of the stock.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 461–462

records.title: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc. (1958)
records.text: A strong federal interest in the judge-and-jury system outweighed South Carolina’s rule assigning this disputed statutory-employee issue to the judge. The state rule was not shown integral to the substantive right. Byrd received a chance to litigate the issue before a jury on remand; the Court did not decide his employee status.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc. (1958)
records.text: In diversity, a state rule on the mode of enforcing a state right that is not shown to be integral to that right yields to a strong countervailing federal interest, such as the federal judge-jury allocation, even though the outcome might differ.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc. (1958)
records.text:
The Court did not hold the state workers’ compensation immunity invalid or announce that the Seventh Amendment directly dictates every allocation in state proceedings. Dice presents a distinct question about enforcement of a federal right in state court.

Justice Brennan wrote for the Court; Byrd, a North Carolina resident, won a jury verdict against the South Carolina cooperative, the Fourth Circuit reversed and directed judgment for the cooperative, and the Supreme Court reversed and remanded for a new trial; Justices Frankfurter and Harlan dissented. The opinion describes the federal jury allocation as reflecting the influence, if not the command, of the Seventh Amendment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: Hanna v. Plumer (1965)
records.text: First ask whether a Federal Rule covers the question. If it does, and it is valid, the federal court follows it. Only when no Rule applies do you ask the Erie questions about forum shopping and unfair treatment. Serving papers on a relative at home was fine under the Rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–480

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hanna v. Plumer (1965)
records.text: When a Federal Rule actually covers the disputed issue, a federal diversity court applies it unless it exceeds the Rules Enabling Act or the Constitution; ordinary Erie analysis, guided by forum shopping and inequitable administration, applies only when no Federal Rule covers the issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–480

records.title: Hanna v. Plumer (1965)
records.text:
The scope inquiry comes first. Walker holds that Rule 3 does not answer the state limitations-tolling question, while Hanna’s service rule directly answered the service-method question. The Rules of Decision Act and the Rules Enabling Act perform different functions.

Hanna, an Ohio citizen, sued Plumer as executor of a Massachusetts decedent's estate over a car accident; Chief Justice Warren wrote the Court's opinion (Justice Harlan concurred, Justice Black concurred in the result), reframing York's outcome test by reference to the 'twin aims' of Erie (discouraging forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws) and holding that a Federal Rule within the Enabling Act and the Constitution governs regardless of contrary state law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–480

records.title: Sibbach v. Wilson & Co. (1941)
records.text: A federal rule is valid if it truly governs how courts run a case, even if it touches something personal like a physical exam. How important the interest is does not turn a procedural rule into a substantive one.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–479

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Sibbach v. Wilson & Co. (1941)
records.text: A federal rule is within the rulemaking authority Congress delegated if it genuinely regulates procedure, meaning the judicial process for enforcing substantive rights and administering remedies; the importance of the interest affected does not make a procedural rule substantive.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–479

records.title: Sibbach v. Wilson & Co. (1941)
records.text:
The assigned discussion concerns the Rule’s validity; it does not supply every aspect of the original discovery and contempt proceedings.

Sibbach was injured in Indiana and sued in federal court in Illinois, whose law did not allow court-ordered physical examinations; ordered to submit under Rule 35, she refused and was held in contempt under Rule 37, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed.

Although it upheld Rule 35, the Court (Justice Roberts, 5-4) actually reversed the contempt judgment because Rule 37 as then written did not authorize contempt for refusing a physical examination; Justice Frankfurter's dissent was joined by Justices Black, Douglas and Murphy. The majority's test, whether a rule 'really regulates procedure', is the language the Shady Grove plurality later adopted.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–479

records.title: Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. (1980)
records.text: The federal rule on starting a case did not decide when the state's time limit stopped running. With no Federal Rule on that question, the federal court followed Oklahoma's rule that the clock stops on service, not on filing.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 480–485

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. (1980)
records.text: In a diversity action on a state-law claim, Rule 3 does not govern tolling of the state statute of limitations; because no Federal Rule covers the issue, Erie requires applying the state rule that service, not filing, stops the limitations period.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 480–485

records.title: Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. (1980)
records.text:
A federal and state provision can use related vocabulary without regulating exactly the same legal consequence. Identify the precise question: commencing federal procedure, serving process, or preserving a claim against limitations.

Walker, an Oklahoma carpenter injured by a defective nail on August 22, 1975, filed in federal court on August 19, 1977 (three days before the two-year limit) but did not serve Armco until December 1, 1977, outside Oklahoma's 60-day service window; the district court dismissed, the Tenth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding Rule 3 was not sufficiently broad to control the issue and was not intended to toll state limitations periods.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 480–485

records.title: Stewart Organization, Inc. v. Ricoh Corp. (1988)
records.text: When a valid federal statute answers the question, it beats a conflicting state policy in a diversity case. The transfer statute lets a judge weigh a forum-selection clause as one important factor, so a state rule ignoring the clause could not control.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 486–492

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Stewart Organization, Inc. v. Ricoh Corp. (1988)
records.text: When a federal statute invoked in a diversity case fairly covers the disputed issue and is constitutionally valid, it governs over contrary state policy; § 1404(a) therefore controls the effect of a forum-selection clause on a motion to transfer.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 486–492

records.title: Stewart Organization, Inc. v. Ricoh Corp. (1988)
records.text: Atlantic Marine later clarifies the weight of a valid clause under § 1404. Preserve the chronology: Stewart’s historical factor discussion and Atlantic Marine’s later framework are connected, not interchangeable.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 486–492

records.title: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996)
records.text: A state's limit on how big a damages award can be applies in federal court too. The trial judge applies that standard first, and the appeals court only checks for abuse of discretion. The case involved lost photographs and a jury award of $450,000.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996)
records.text: In diversity, a state standard limiting the size of damages awards is substantive under Erie and must be applied, but by the federal district judge in the first instance, with the court of appeals reviewing only for abuse of discretion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996)
records.text:
This case illustrates why “apply state substantive law and federal procedure” requires further analysis. The labels alone do not determine which standard and which reviewing institution control.

Gasperini, a journalist, had lent 300 original slide transparencies that the Center lost; the jury awarded $1,500 per slide, the district court denied a new trial, and the Second Circuit ordered a new trial unless he accepted a remittitur to $100,000; the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J., 5–4) vacated and remanded for the district judge to apply New York's 'deviates materially' standard.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010)
records.text: Five Justices agreed that Rule 23 answered whether this suit could proceed as a class action and displaced New York’s restriction here. They divided over the Rules Enabling Act validity analysis. The Court restored the opportunity to seek certification; it did not certify the class or erase every state limit on class remedies.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 502–515

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010)
records.text: When a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure answers the same question as a state law, the Federal Rule governs in federal court if it is valid under its statutory and constitutional authorization; ordinary Erie outcome analysis does not simply override it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 502–515

records.title: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010)
records.text:
This did not certify the proposed class or erase Rule 23’s prerequisites. It also does not make every state rule affecting a class action invalid in federal court. Record the distinct scope and validity questions and the fractured reasoning.

Shady Grove treated Sonia Galvez after a car accident and took an assignment of her Allstate benefits; Allstate paid late and refused the statutory interest of 2 percent per month, worth about $500 to Shady Grove but roughly $5 million class-wide; N.Y. C.P.L.R. 901(b) bars class actions to recover statutory penalties, and the Eastern District of New York dismissed for lack of CAFA jurisdiction, with the Second Circuit affirming.

Justice Scalia's plurality asked only whether Rule 23 'really regulates procedure' (Sibbach), while Justice Stevens's controlling concurrence would hold a Federal Rule inapplicable where it would displace a state rule so intertwined with a state right or remedy that it functions to define the scope of the state-created right; Justice Ginsburg's dissent, joined by Justices Kennedy, Breyer and Alito, read Rule 23 and § 901(b) as not in conflict.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 502–515

records.title: Dice v. Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Co. (1952)
records.text: A railroad worker's release of his rights under the federal injury law is judged by federal law, even in state court. If the railroad tricked him into signing, the release fails, and the state cannot take that fraud question away from the jury.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dice v. Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Co. (1952)
records.text: Federal law governs the validity of a release of Federal Employers' Liability Act rights even in state court, and a state that provides jury trials for such negligence actions may not take the disputed question of fraudulent procurement from the jury.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Dice v. Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Co. (1952)
records.text:
Do not restate this as general incorporation of the Seventh Amendment against the states. The reasoning concerns the federal statutory right and its enforcement. It also provides a carefully bounded connection to Contracts release and misrepresentation doctrines.

Dice, a railroad fireman, alleged the railroad told him the release was merely a receipt for back pay; the trial court entered judgment notwithstanding the jury's verdict, the Ohio Court of Appeals reversed, the Ohio Supreme Court reinstated judgment for the railroad, and the U.S. Supreme Court (Black, J.) reversed.

Justice Frankfurter's separate opinion, joined by Justices Reed, Jackson and Burton, concurred in reversal on the release question but dissented from requiring the state court to send the fraud issue to the jury.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States (1943)
records.text: When the United States issues its own checks, federal law decides who bears the loss from a forged endorsement, not state law. Delay in giving notice only helps the defendant if the delay actually caused a loss.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 528–531

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States (1943)
records.text: Federal law governs the United States' rights and duties on commercial paper it issues in exercising its constitutional and statutory functions, and absent an applicable Act of Congress federal courts may fashion the governing rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 528–531

records.title: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States (1943)
records.text:
The surrounding Parnell and Kimbell Foods notes qualify automatic assumptions of federal uniformity. A federal connection does not mean every private dispute requires a newly created federal rule.

Justice Douglas wrote for the Court; a 1936 WPA check payable to Clair Barner was stolen, forged and cashed at a J. C. Penney store in Clearfield, Pennsylvania, the district court applied Pennsylvania law and ruled for the bank on the government's delay, the Third Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the rights and duties of the United States on its own commercial paper are governed by federal law fashioned by the federal courts, since applying varying state rules would create uncertainty for a nationwide program.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 528–531

records.title: Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. (1988)
records.text: A military contractor can avoid state design-defect claims if the government approved precise specifications, the equipment matched them, and the contractor warned the government of dangers it alone knew about. Otherwise the state claim could raise military costs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. (1988)
records.text: State design-defect liability for military equipment is displaced when the United States approved reasonably precise specifications, the equipment conformed to them, and the supplier warned the United States of dangers known to the supplier but not to the Government.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. (1988)
records.text:
The opinion is an example of specialized federal common law, not a general power to replace state contract or tort doctrine whenever the federal government is a customer.

Justice Scalia wrote for a 5-4 Court; Boyle's estate brought a diversity action under Virginia law against Sikorsky (a division of United Technologies), won a $725,000 jury verdict, the Fourth Circuit reversed and directed judgment for Sikorsky, and the Supreme Court vacated and remanded for application of the three-part test; Justice Brennan's dissent was joined by Justices Marshall and Blackmun.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: Gillispie v. Goodyear Service Stores (1963)
records.text: Under the old fact-pleading rules, you could not just say the defendants committed trespass, assault and confinement. Those are conclusions. You had to state the actual facts, and Gillispie was told she could amend.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 606–608

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Gillispie v. Goodyear Service Stores (1963)
records.text: Under code pleading, a complaint must state the material, essential, ultimate facts that constitute the cause of action, not merely the pleader's legal conclusions such as assault, trespass, or malicious confinement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 606–608

records.title: Gillispie v. Goodyear Service Stores (1963)
records.text:
This is a state code-pleading decision. Its vocabulary should not be silently treated as the language or full test of Federal Rule 8.

The complaint alleged that on May 5 and 6, 1959 in Alamance County the defendants trespassed on her premises, assaulted her, and had her seized, exhibited as a prisoner and jailed; four groups of defendants demurred, the trial court sustained each demurrer, and the North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed because the pleading failed to say what occurred, when, where, and who did what.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 606–608

records.title: Dioguardi v. Durning (1944)
records.text: Under the Federal Rules, a self-drafted complaint over seized tonics did not have to state facts that make out a technical cause of action. A short statement showing the plaintiff may be entitled to relief was enough to go forward.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–612

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Dioguardi v. Durning (1944)
records.text: Under the Federal Rules a complaint need only give a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief under Rule 8(a); the old formulation requiring facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action is not the governing pleading formula.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–612

records.title: Dioguardi v. Durning (1944)
records.text:
Read with the later Twombly and Iqbal decisions. Dioguardi illustrates fair construction and the limited role of pleading; the chapter does not present it as an exemption from all later sufficiency requirements.

The opinion was written by Judge Charles E. Clark, the principal draftsman of the Federal Rules; the 'home-drawn' complaint alleged that the customs collector sold the tonics at auction to another bidder at Dioguardi's own bidding price and that two cases had disappeared three weeks before the sale.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–612

records.title: Conley v. Gibson (1957)
records.text: A complaint is fine if it gives fair notice of the claim and what it rests on, and it should not be thrown out unless the plaintiff could prove nothing that would entitle them to relief. Detailed facts were not required. Twombly later retired the no-set-of-facts wording.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 612–614

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Conley v. Gibson (1957)
records.text: Under Rule 8(a)(2) a complaint needs only a short and plain statement giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds, and should not be dismissed unless it appears beyond doubt that no set of supporting facts could entitle the claimant to relief.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 612–614

records.title: Conley v. Gibson (1957)
records.text:
Historical holding and language. The no-set-of-facts phrase is not the operative Twombly–Iqbal test.

The opinion's famous (and since retired) standard: "a complaint should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts in support of his claim which would entitle him to relief"; Bell Atlantic v. Twombly (2007) declared this 'no set of facts' language to have earned its retirement.

The union, Local 28 of the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks, allegedly acquiesced in the Texas and New Orleans Railroad's May 1954 discharge of 45 Black employees who were then replaced by white workers, and ignored the members' repeated requests for help.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 612–614

records.title: Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A. (2002)
records.text: You do not have to plead the full proof framework for a job discrimination case in your complaint. Describing what happened, the dates, and the ages and nationalities of the people involved gave enough notice to proceed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 614–617

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A. (2002)
records.text: An employment discrimination complaint need not plead facts establishing a McDonnell Douglas prima facie case, which is a framework for proof and not a pleading requirement; it need only satisfy Rule 8(a)(2) by giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 614–617

records.title: Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A. (2002)
records.text: Twombly and Iqbal later govern general plausibility. This decision remains important to the distinction between plausible factual allegations and prematurely demanding a complete trial proof structure.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 614–617

records.title: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007)
records.text: A complaint needs enough facts to make your claim believable, not just labels. Showing that rival companies acted alike did not make an illegal agreement plausible, since each had its own reasons to act that way.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–628

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007)
records.text: A complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to make entitlement to relief plausible; for a Sherman Act § 1 conspiracy claim, parallel conduct plus an unsupported assertion of agreement does not suffice.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–628

records.title: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007)
records.text:
Do not substitute the summary-judgment test for this pleading inquiry. Matsushita also discusses inferences about antitrust conspiracies, but it addresses an evidentiary record at a later procedural stage.

Justice Souter wrote for a 7-2 Court; the plaintiffs were subscribers of local telephone and high-speed internet service suing the incumbent local exchange carriers under section 1 of the Sherman Act, and the opinion retired Conley v. Gibson's 'no set of facts' formulation, requiring instead enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face; Justice Ginsburg joined the Stevens dissent except as to Part IV.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–628

records.title: Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009)
records.text: Courts ignore bare conclusions in a complaint and ask whether the remaining facts make the claim plausible. Senior officials are not liable for what their subordinates did just because of their rank. The complaint had to show the officials themselves acted with discriminatory purpose.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 628–639

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009)
records.text: Under Rule 8, in all civil actions, a court disregards legal conclusions and unsupported recitations of elements and asks whether the remaining factual allegations, taken as true, plausibly support entitlement to relief.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 628–639

records.title: Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009)
records.text:
The ruling did not find the alleged abuses false and did not adjudicate every claim against every defendant. Keep the parties, required mental state, pleading posture, and possibility of amendment distinct.

Justice Kennedy wrote for a 5-4 Court; the defendants were Attorney General Ashcroft and FBI Director Mueller, the case reached the Court on interlocutory appeal from the denial of qualified immunity, and the opinion sets out the two-step method: disregard conclusory allegations not entitled to the assumption of truth, then ask whether the remaining well-pleaded facts plausibly (not merely possibly) give rise to an entitlement to relief.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 628–639

records.title: Kearns v. Ford Motor Co. (2009)
records.text: If your whole case rests on a fraud story, you must plead who, what, when and where with particularity, even if fraud is not an element of the claim. Relabeling it as an unfair business practice does not avoid the stricter rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 647–653

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Kearns v. Ford Motor Co. (2009)
records.text: When a plaintiff relies entirely on a unified fraudulent course of conduct, the claim as a whole sounds in fraud and must satisfy Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement, even if fraud is not an element of the claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 647–653

records.title: Kearns v. Ford Motor Co. (2009)
records.text:
The source distinguishes claims grounded in fraud from claims in which fraud is not an essential part of the theory. Rule 9(b) and general Rule 8 plausibility are related but separate questions.

Kearns sued under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law; the Ninth Circuit (567 F.3d 1120) affirmed dismissal of his Third Amended Complaint, holding that claims 'grounded in fraud' under those statutes, including nondisclosure claims, must plead the 'who, what, when, where, and how' of the misconduct under Rule 9(b).

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 647–653

records.title: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)
records.text: In securities fraud cases, the facts must point to intent to deceive at least as strongly as they point to an innocent explanation. A judge weighs the guilty and innocent stories together. A tie goes to the plaintiff.

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)
records.text: Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, the inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any plausible opposing inference drawn from the alleged facts, considered collectively.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 654–658

records.title: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)
records.text: This is the special statutory securities test. It should not be imported as an automatic requirement that every ordinary Rule 8 complaint establish an equally strong comparative inference.

records.title: Ziervogel v. Royal Packing Co. (1949)
records.text: Under Missouri's rules, a harm like high blood pressure that was not pleaded and did not necessarily follow from the pleaded injuries cannot be proved at trial. It does not matter that the defendant already knew about it.

records.title: Ziervogel v. Royal Packing Co. (1949)
records.text: Under the Missouri provision requiring items of special damage to be specifically stated, an injury neither pleaded nor a necessary result of a pleaded injury cannot be proved over objection, even where the defendant had actual advance knowledge of it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–661

records.title: Ziervogel v. Royal Packing Co. (1949)
records.text:
This is a state decision and a fact-specific treatment of the injuries alleged. It does not establish that every bodily injury is special damage under Federal Rule 9(g).

The collision was at Vandeventer Avenue and North Market Street in St. Louis; the petition alleged injuries to her "neck, back, spine and nervous system"; the rule stated is that special damages must be pleaded or shown to be the necessary result of the injuries already alleged.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–661

records.title: Garcia v. Hilton Hotels International, Inc. (1951)
records.text: A complaint can survive even if it is a bit messy, as long as the defendant can understand the claim. The court still ordered a clearer statement of the words said, and struck allegations about testimony at a Labor Department hearing because they were absolutely privileged.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Garcia v. Hilton Hotels International, Inc. (1951)
records.text: A complaint that shows an intended claim the defendant can reasonably understand survives a motion to dismiss even if imperfectly stated, and a conditional privilege must be raised as an affirmative defense, while an absolute privilege disclosed by the complaint bars the claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Garcia v. Hilton Hotels International, Inc. (1951)
records.text:
The assigned opinion applies the rules to the particular allegations and privilege law before the court. Its treatment of Rule 12(e) should be read with later discussion of the limited role of that motion.

Garcia, a Puerto Rico resident, sued the Delaware hotel corporation after being 'violently discharged' amid accusations of bringing prostitution to the hotel; the case was removed to the federal court for Puerto Rico, which held that a conditional (qualified) privilege is a defense the defendant must prove and cannot support dismissal, whereas statements at the labor-department hearing were absolutely privileged.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Swanson v. Citibank, N.A. (2010)
records.text: Plausibility does not mean a plaintiff has to prove the case in the complaint. It means telling a coherent story with enough specifics, here the discrimination alleged, who did it and the early-2009 transaction, to show what the claim is about.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 672–677

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Swanson v. Citibank, N.A. (2010)
records.text: To satisfy plausibility under Rule 8, a plaintiff must supply enough case-specific detail to tell a coherent story and identify the nature and grounds of the claim; plausibility is not a more-likely-than-not test.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 672–677

records.title: Ingraham v. United States (1987)
records.text: The Fifth Circuit treated this Texas damages cap as an affirmative defense. Because the government first raised it after judgment, it lost the cap’s benefit in these cases. The decision explains that particular statute’s treatment under Rule 8(c), rather than classifying every damages limit automatically.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Ingraham v. United States (1987)
records.text: A statutory limit on damages is an avoidance within Rule 8(c)'s residual clause, so it is an affirmative defense that the defendant waives by failing to raise it in a timely way before judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Ingraham v. United States (1987)
records.text:
This is a preservation ruling concerning the particular state limitation and procedural record. It is not a statement that every unpleaded defense is inevitably lost regardless of amendment, notice, or prejudice.

The consolidated FTCA cases involved a surgeon's negligent drilling into Ingraham's spine (award of $1,264,000) and a mismanaged cesarean that left Stephanie Bonds brain-damaged (awards of about $3.49 million and $750,000); the cap was the Texas Medical Liability and Insurance Improvement Act, and the court treated it as an 'avoidance' under Rule 8(c) whose purpose is to prevent unfair surprise.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Kegerise v. Susquehanna Township School District (2016)
records.text: When you answer a complaint, you must respond to each part of every allegation, admitting what is true and denying the rest. You cannot dodge by calling a paragraph a legal conclusion. Here the fix was an amended answer, not an automatic admission.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Kegerise v. Susquehanna Township School District (2016)
records.text: Under Rule 8(b) an answer must admit or deny each portion of every allegation or state a genuine lack of knowledge after reasonable inquiry, and it may not decline to respond because an allegation states a legal conclusion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Kegerise v. Susquehanna Township School District (2016)
records.text: Kegerise was the district's fired superintendent; the issue arose on her motion for judgment on the pleadings, where she attacked answers that admitted part of an allegation without denying the rest, labeled allegations 'legal conclusions' requiring no response, and claimed lack of knowledge about matters the defendants knew (M.D. Pa. 2016, 321 F.R.D. 121).

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Beeck v. Aquaslide ’N’ Dive Corp. (1977)
records.text: Aquaslide could amend its mistaken admission that it made the slide: the judge found no bad faith or unfair prejudice on this record. A separate jury then found it was not the manufacturer. Rule 15 favors amendment when justice requires, but withdrawal of an admission is not automatically allowed in every case.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–692

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Beeck v. Aquaslide ’N’ Dive Corp. (1977)
records.text: Leave to amend under Rule 15(a) is to be freely given when justice requires, and the party opposing amendment bears the burden of showing prejudice, assessed in the particular circumstances rather than assumed whenever an admission is withdrawn.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–692

records.title: Beeck v. Aquaslide ’N’ Dive Corp. (1977)
records.text:
The decision does not permit withdrawal of any admission as of right. It concerns leave to amend, the record supporting good faith, and the trial court’s management discretion.

Aquaslide's original admission of manufacture rested on inspections by three insurance investigators; its president and owner Carl Meyer later inspected the slide himself before his deposition and concluded it was a counterfeit, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed under Rule 15(a) because the plaintiffs had not shown bad faith and might still have remedies against the actual manufacturer.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–692

records.title: Moore v. Moore (1978)
records.text: A claim nobody pleaded counts as tried only if the other side knew it was being fought over and had a fair chance to respond. Evidence that merely fits a claim already in the case gives no such notice. Here custody stood but separate maintenance was reversed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Moore v. Moore (1978)
records.text: Under Rule 15(b), an unpleaded issue is tried by implied consent only if the record shows the opposing party recognized it was being litigated and had a fair chance to contest it; evidence relevant to an already pleaded issue does not establish consent.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Moore v. Moore (1978)
records.text: Father Reuben Moore filed the custody action; after trial the court orally awarded custody and child support to the mother (with visitation conditioned on a $7,500 bond) and let her file a post-trial counterclaim conforming to the evidence. The D.C. Court of Appeals held custody, child support and attorney's fees were tried by implied consent, but separate maintenance was not because the father lacked notice and an opportunity to contest it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Krupski v. Costa Crociere S.p.A. (2010)
records.text: When a plaintiff sued the wrong company and fixes it late, the question is what the company she meant to sue knew, not how careless she was. Costa Crociere should have known it was left out only because of a mix-up, so the Court reversed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 695–697

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Krupski v. Costa Crociere S.p.A. (2010)
records.text: Relation back under Rule 15(c)(1)(C) depends on what the party to be added knew or should have known within the Rule 4(m) period, not on the amending plaintiff's knowledge or her timeliness in seeking to amend.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 695–697

records.title: Krupski v. Costa Crociere S.p.A. (2010)
records.text:
Relation back has additional requirements, including notice, lack of prejudice in defending, and the relation of the amended claim to the original transaction. This case resolves the mistake inquiry; it does not eliminate the other requirements.

Justice Sotomayor wrote for the Court; Justice Scalia concurred in part, declining to rely on the Advisory Committee Notes. Krupski's ticket named Costa Cruise (the U.S. sales agent) on the front but identified Costa Crociere as the carrier; she sued Costa Cruise three weeks before the one-year limitations period ran.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 695–697

records.title: Surowitz v. Hilton Hotels Corp. (1966)
records.text: A shareholder who signs a verification in good faith, trusting careful work by advisers and lawyers, should not lose her suit because she cannot explain the complex deals herself. The rule exists to stop abusive suits, not to throw out honest ones.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–703

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Surowitz v. Hilton Hotels Corp. (1966)
records.text: The verification requirement for shareholder derivative actions does not justify dismissing a bona fide complaint because the shareholder does not personally understand it, when she verified it in good faith reliance on careful investigation by trusted advisers and counsel.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–703

records.title: Surowitz v. Hilton Hotels Corp. (1966)
records.text: The opinion concerns the derivative verification requirement before the Court, rather than a general permission to sign allegations without a reasonable factual basis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–703

records.title: Hadges v. Yonkers Racing Corp. (1995)
records.text: For sanctions requested by another party, Rule 11 requires a separate motion and the opportunity to correct or withdraw during its safe harbor, ordinarily twenty-one days. Those protections were skipped here, so the sanctions were reversed. Court-initiated sanctions follow a separate show-cause procedure and have no party-motion safe harbor.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hadges v. Yonkers Racing Corp. (1995)
records.text: Under the 1993 version of Rule 11, sanctions sought by a party require a separate motion served twenty-one days before presentation to the court, giving a safe harbor to correct or withdraw, and a lawyer may rely on objectively reasonable client information.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713

records.title: Hadges v. Yonkers Racing Corp. (1995)
records.text:
The decision illustrates both substantive and procedural limits on sanctions. It does not insulate lawyers from inquiry obligations whenever a client supplies a statement.

Hadges, a harness-racing driver whose license had been suspended and revoked, was represented by William Kunstler; the district court fined Hadges $2,000 and censured Kunstler, partly for failing to disclose a related state-court action, and the Second Circuit reversed because YRC's Rule 11 motion did not comply with the 1993 safe-harbor procedure (service 21 days before filing) and the court imposed sanctions without notice and an opportunity to respond.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713

records.title: Ellis Canning Co. v. International Harvester Co. (1953)
records.text: Under Kansas’s real-party-in-interest statute, an insurer that paid the entire loss owned the whole subrogated claim. The insured could not sue in its own name for the insurer’s benefit, so the defense survived. The court did not decide partial-payment cases or make this Kansas rule a universal procedural requirement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Ellis Canning Co. v. International Harvester Co. (1953)
records.text: Under the Kansas real-party-in-interest statute, once an insurer has fully paid a loss the subrogated claim belongs wholly to the insurer, which must bring the action in its own name; the insured cannot sue for the insurer's benefit.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Ellis Canning Co. v. International Harvester Co. (1953)
records.text:
This is a state decision; Federal Rule 17 has its own cure provisions. Partial payment can raise a different party problem because more than one person may retain an interest.

The Kansas Supreme Court held that an insured fully paid by its insurer (Potomac Insurance Co.) is not the real party in interest under the Kansas code and cannot sue in its own name 'for the use and benefit of' the insurer; the court gave no ruling on partial subrogation, where insured and insurer may each hold part of the claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Harris v. Avery (1869)
records.text: A person who was falsely imprisoned and slandered in one episode can sue for both in a single petition, even though one harms the body and the other harms reputation. What ties them together is that the accusation, the taking of the horse and the detention were one event.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–722

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Harris v. Avery (1869)
records.text: Under the Kansas code, causes of action arising from the same transaction may be joined in one petition even though they fall in different categories, such as injury to the person and injury to character.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–722

records.title: Harris v. Avery (1869)
records.text:
Federal Rule 18 later permits broad joinder of claims against an existing opposing party without this same-transaction limitation. Jurisdiction must still be established separately.

Harris demurred for misjoinder; the district court overruled the demurrer and the Kansas Supreme Court affirmed, reading the code to permit joinder of claims arising out of 'the same transaction or transactions connected with the same subject of action' and finding that the accusation, taking of the horse, arrest and four-or-five-day confinement with felons formed one transaction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–722

records.title: United States ex rel. D’Agostino Excavators, Inc. v. Heyward-Robinson Co. (1970)
records.text: If a defendant's counterclaim is closely tied to the same dispute, it must be raised in that suit, and a federal court can hear it without any separate basis for federal jurisdiction. Here claims over a private project were tied to a federal project's Miller Act suit.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–729

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: United States ex rel. D’Agostino Excavators, Inc. v. Heyward-Robinson Co. (1970)
records.text: A counterclaim is compulsory under Rule 13(a) when it bears a logical relationship to the opposing party's claim, and a compulsory counterclaim falls within ancillary federal jurisdiction without an independent jurisdictional ground.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–729

records.title: United States ex rel. D’Agostino Excavators, Inc. v. Heyward-Robinson Co. (1970)
records.text:
This predates § 1367. A present course analysis should examine the statute discussed elsewhere in the assigned chapter rather than assume every aspect of older ancillary-jurisdiction terminology supplies the statutory answer.

D'Agostino sued Heyward and its surety, Maryland Casualty Company, under the Miller Act for payments due on the Navy barracks job at the New London submarine base; Heyward counterclaimed for overpayments and extra completion costs on both the Navy job and the private Stelma plant job in Stamford, and the Second Circuit affirmed the judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–729

records.title: LASA Per L’Industria Del Marmo Societa Per Azioni v. Alexander (1969)
records.text: In a construction dispute where the supplier, subcontractor, prime contractor and architect all have claims against one another, those claims can be heard in one case if they are logically connected. If that gets messy, the judge can split the trials later.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–739

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: LASA Per L’Industria Del Marmo Societa Per Azioni v. Alexander (1969)
records.text: Under Rule 13(g) and (h), crossclaims and claims against added parties arise from the same transaction or occurrence as the original action when they are logically related to it, and Rule 42(b) separate trials can manage any resulting complexity.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–739

records.title: LASA Per L’Industria Del Marmo Societa Per Azioni v. Alexander (1969)
records.text:
The decision does not authorize any claim against anyone involved in a construction project. Identify the specific rule, the required relationship, and the independent jurisdictional basis.

LASA (Italian marble supplier) sued subcontractor Alexander, general contractor Southern Builders, its surety Continental Casualty, and the City of Memphis over unpaid marble for the Memphis city hall; Alexander and Southern Builders counterclaimed that LASA shipped the wrong marble late and short, and the Sixth Circuit held the cross-claims and the claim against the architect arose from the same transaction and fell within ancillary jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–739

records.title: Mosley v. General Motors Corp. (1974)
records.text: Plaintiffs can sue together if their claims grow out of related events and share some common question, even when their individual situations differ. An alleged general discriminatory policy was enough here, so the plaintiffs got to proceed jointly.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 743–747

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Mosley v. General Motors Corp. (1974)
records.text: Rule 20(a) permits joinder of plaintiffs when their rights to relief arise from the same transaction, occurrence, or series of logically related transactions or occurrences and a common question of law or fact will arise.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 743–747

records.title: Mosley v. General Motors Corp. (1974)
records.text:
Compare Wal-Mart carefully. Mosley addresses Rule 20 joinder of named plaintiffs; Wal-Mart addresses proof required for a very large representative class under Rule 23.

Ten employees alleging race discrimination sued General Motors and the UAW under Title VII after EEOC reasonable-cause findings; the district court severed the claims into ten separate actions, and the Eighth Circuit (497 F.2d 1330) held that an alleged companywide policy of discrimination could link the employees' claims as a series of transactions, and that differences in its effects on each plaintiff did not defeat the common question.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 743–747

records.title: Bank of California National Ass’n v. Superior Court (1940)
records.text: An absent person is not essential to a lawsuit just because the case touches them. If the court can write a decree limited to the defendants in front of it, the case can go on. Here each recipient owed a separate obligation, so the unserved beneficiaries did not have to be brought in.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–751

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Bank of California National Ass’n v. Superior Court (1940)
records.text: An absent party is indispensable only if any decree the court could render would inevitably affect that party's interest; a necessary party whose interest is separable should ordinarily be joined, but the court keeps jurisdiction to proceed without that party.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–751

records.title: Bank of California National Ass’n v. Superior Court (1940)
records.text:
Read the historical necessary/indispensable language alongside Provident Tradesmens and the modern Rule 19 sequence. An abstract label cannot replace the rule’s practical inquiry.

Sara Boyd died in 1937 leaving an estate of about $225,000; her niece Bertha Smedley sued to enforce Boyd's alleged contract to leave her the entire estate, serving only the Bank of California (executor) and St. Luke's Hospital (the residuary legatee), and the court distinguished 'necessary' parties, who should be joined if possible, from 'indispensable' parties, without whom the action cannot proceed at all.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–751

records.title: Provident Tradesmens Bank & Trust Co. v. Patterson (1968)
records.text: Whether a case must be dismissed because someone cannot be joined is a practical judgment about fairness to everyone involved, not a label you attach first. Here the judgment was to be preserved if possible, with relief shaped to protect people who were not in the case.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 752–761

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Provident Tradesmens Bank & Trust Co. v. Patterson (1968)
records.text: Under Rule 19(b), whether an action may proceed without a person who cannot be joined is a contextual judgment of equity and good conscience weighing the interests of plaintiff, defendant, absentee and public; indispensability is the conclusion of that analysis, not a label preceding it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 752–761

records.title: Provident Tradesmens Bank & Trust Co. v. Patterson (1968)
records.text:
The Court discussed, without deciding, possible effects of the owner’s failure to intervene. Do not convert that discussion into a general rule binding all nonparties who knew of a suit.

The insurer, Lumbermens Mutual Casualty Co., had refused to defend on the theory that Cionci lacked Dutcher's permission; Provident Tradesmens Bank, administrator of passenger Lynch's estate, sought a declaratory judgment that Cionci was a permitted user covered by the policy, and the jury found for the plaintiffs.

The Court identified four interests for the Rule 19(b) inquiry: the plaintiff's interest in a forum, the defendant's interest in avoiding multiple or inconsistent liability, the absent person's interest, and the public and the courts' interest in complete, consistent and efficient settlement of controversies; and it stressed that after a judgment has been rendered the balance shifts because the absent party's interest can be protected by shaping relief.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 752–761

records.title: Jeub v. B/G Foods, Inc. (1942)
records.text: A defendant who might later be held liable can bring in the party who would owe it reimbursement now, without waiting until it has paid anything. The two disputes get decided together, but nobody has to pay until state law says the time has come.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 763–766

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Jeub v. B/G Foods, Inc. (1942)
records.text: Rule 14 allows a defendant to implead a party who is or may be liable to it for the plaintiff's claim before the defendant has suffered any loss; the contingent claim is determined in the same action and enforcement is stayed until state law's conditions are met.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 763–766

records.title: Jeub v. B/G Foods, Inc. (1942)
records.text:
Impleader is for potential liability to the defending party for the plaintiff’s claim. An allegation that the third party alone owes the plaintiff on an unrelated or alternative direct claim is a different situation.

The case arose in the District of Minnesota (2 F.R.D. 238, 1942): Jeub got food poisoning from ham at a B/G restaurant, B/G impleaded the manufacturer Swift & Co., and Swift moved to vacate because B/G had suffered no loss yet; the court held Rule 14 reaches a party who 'is or may be liable' and merely accelerates the timing of a Minnesota indemnity right without altering it.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 763–766

records.title: Hancock Oil Co. v. Independent Distributing Co. (1944)
records.text: A stakeholder facing two groups that claim the same money can make them fight it out in one case, even if the stakeholder is a tenant who normally cannot question its landlord's title. Here both groups demanded the same lease royalties, so the lessees could bring everyone in.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–770

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Hancock Oil Co. v. Independent Distributing Co. (1944)
records.text: Under California's broadened interpleader statute, a disinterested tenant facing competing claims to the same lease royalties may interplead its landlord and an adverse claimant, despite the rule barring a tenant from denying the landlord's title, if it alleges facts showing a reasonable probability of competing demands.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–770

records.title: Hancock Oil Co. v. Independent Distributing Co. (1944)
records.text:
This is a state interpleader decision. Federal rule interpleader and statutory interpleader have separate jurisdiction and service requirements.

The Hopkinses leased land to Hancock Oil and Bush Oil in 1936; Independent Distributing later claimed the Hopkinses held the land in trust for it and demanded the $1,500 in accrued landowner royalties; the California Supreme Court held that the lessee's contractual obligation to pay rent is not an 'independent liability' barring interpleader and that the rule against a tenant disputing the landlord's title does not prevent the tenant from interpleading rival claimants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–770

records.title: Pan American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Revere (1960)
records.text: This 1960 trial court allowed an insurer to interplead unliquidated claims competing for its limited policy fund, even while denying liability. Later, Tashire limited the injunction’s reach: interpleader can protect allocation of the fund without forcing every accident claim against insureds and other tortfeasors into that one case.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–778

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Pan American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Revere (1960)
records.text: An insurer facing tort claims that may exceed its policy limit may interplead the claimants under Rule 22 or the interpleader statute, even though it denies liability and the claims are unliquidated, because possible multiple liability on one inadequate fund is enough.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–778

records.title: Pan American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Revere (1960)
records.text:
Read the scope of the injunction alongside State Farm v. Tashire. Interpleader over insurance money does not automatically authorize control of every related tort action.

The case arose in the Eastern District of Louisiana (Judge J. Skelly Wright) from a collision between a tractor-trailer and a school bus near Covington, Louisiana; the insurer deposited a $100,400 bond covering its $100,000 policy limit, and the court enjoined all claimants from suing elsewhere, required claims to be filed within 30 days, and ordered a joint trial on liability and damages.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–778

records.title: State Farm Fire & Casualty Co. v. Tashire (1967)
records.text: Interpleader lets a stakeholder bring rival claimants into one federal case, and it only needs two claimants from different states. But the order stopping other suits can only protect the fund, here State Farm's $20,000. It cannot pull every suit against the drivers into the case.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 778–782

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: State Farm Fire & Casualty Co. v. Tashire (1967)
records.text: Statutory interpleader under section 1335 requires only minimal diversity among adverse claimants and is available before tort claims are reduced to judgment, but the injunction it supports must be limited to protecting the interpleaded fund.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 778–782

records.title: State Farm Fire & Casualty Co. v. Tashire (1967)
records.text: Rule 22 interpleader has different jurisdictional prerequisites. Do not transfer § 1335’s minimal-diversity and service rules to Rule 22 without analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 778–782

records.title: Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel (2008)
records.text: If a foreign government with a serious claim to the disputed assets cannot be sued because of immunity, a court cannot go ahead without it by guessing it would lose. When its interests could be hurt, the case must be dismissed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel (2008)
records.text: Under Rule 19(b), when a required party is a sovereign entitled to immunity and its claims to the disputed property are not frivolous, the action must be dismissed if there is a potential for injury to the absent sovereign's interests.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel (2008)
records.text:
This is a conjunction of Rule 19, interpleader, and sovereign immunity. It does not establish that every absent claimant requires dismissal in an ordinary private interpleader.

The fund was a Merrill Lynch brokerage account (roughly $35 million) held by Arelma, S.A., a Panamanian company Marcos created; the Pimentel class of human-rights victims held a nearly $2 billion judgment against the Marcos estate and sought to attach the account, and Merrill Lynch filed the statutory interpleader naming the Republic, its Presidential Commission on Good Government, Arelma, PNB and the class.

Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court, reversing the Ninth Circuit, and Justices Stevens and Souter each concurred in part and dissented in part, preferring a remand rather than outright dismissal; the Court held that where a sovereign has a non-frivolous claim to the assets and sovereign immunity, dismissal is required under Rule 19(b) even though the claimants may be left without a forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Smuck v. Hobson (1969)
records.text: The D.C. Circuit allowed the parents to intervene for an appeal, limited to decree provisions affecting their educational interests; the individual defendants lacked an appealable interest. The practical-interest intervention analysis was a three-judge plurality, rather than a majority explanation of every Rule 24 requirement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–791

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Smuck v. Hobson (1969)
records.text: On a three-judge plurality's analysis, a person whose practical interest may be impaired and inadequately represented by existing parties can intervene under Rule 24(a)(2), even to appeal after judgment, but only to challenge decree provisions that actually affect that interest.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–791

records.title: Smuck v. Hobson (1969)
records.text:
The syllabus requires reading this material but states that class time will not be spent on intervention.

The underlying case was Hobson v. Hansen, 269 F. Supp. 401 (D.D.C. 1967), in which the district court found the D.C. schools' tracking system and other practices discriminated against black and poor children; the D.C. Circuit decided Smuck en banc in an opinion by Judge Bazelon, denying intervention to former superintendent Carl Hansen, holding that dissenting board member Carl Smuck could not appeal, but allowing twenty parents to intervene and appeal only the decree provisions restricting the board's future discretion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–791

records.title: Hansberry v. Lee (1940)
records.text: A court cannot bind people to an earlier class judgment just because the earlier suit was labelled a class action. The people in that suit must truly have represented the interests of those being bound. Here their interests conflicted, so the earlier decree could not shut out the challenge.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 804–808

records.title: Hansberry v. Lee (1940)
records.text: Due process forbids binding a person to a judgment in an earlier representative action unless the parties to that action adequately represented that person's interests; a state's labelling a suit a class action does not settle its power to bind absentees.

records.title: Hansberry v. Lee (1940)
records.text:
The holding here is about representation and preclusion. It is not the later constitutional holding concerning judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants in Shelley v. Kraemer.

Carl Hansberry (father of playwright Lorraine Hansberry) bought a home in Chicago's Washington Park, and the suit to enforce the covenant against the sale was brought in 1937; the covenant required signatures of owners of 95 percent of the frontage but only about 54 percent had signed, and the earlier suit, Burke v. Kleiman, had proceeded on a stipulation that 95 percent had signed; Justice Stone wrote for the Court, reversing the Illinois Supreme Court.

records.title: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011)
records.text: Putting many people in one class requires a shared question whose single answer would resolve a central issue for every member. Saying everyone was hurt under the same statute is not enough. These plaintiffs could not show a company-wide policy or a common way of using discretion, and individual backpay claims did not fit this kind of class.

records.title: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011)
records.text: Rule 23(a)(2) commonality requires a common contention whose resolution can resolve an issue central to every class member's claim on a classwide basis, established through rigorous analysis; individualized monetary claims such as backpay cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(2).

records.title: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011)
records.text:
Additional assigned discussion appears at printed pp. 831–833 and 849. The Court left open whether some incidental monetary relief could accompany a Rule 23(b)(2) class; it did not hold that every form of money relief is categorically unavailable. Compare Mosley’s different Rule 20 question.

The proposed class was about 1.5 million current and former female employees across roughly 3,400 stores; Justice Scalia wrote for a 5–4 majority on commonality, which "requires the plaintiff to demonstrate that the class members 'have suffered the same injury'" and that the common contention is "capable of classwide resolution."

records.text: The Ninth Circuit rejected a separate requirement to prove an administratively easy way to identify every class member. Actual Rule 23 requirements still had to be met. The opinion discussed a different approach in the Third Circuit, so its rejection of this extra hurdle should not be presented as an unqualified nationwide rule.

records.title: Briseno v. ConAgra Foods, Inc. (2017)
records.text: Rule 23 does not require class representatives to demonstrate an administratively feasible way to identify absent class members as a separate prerequisite to class certification.

records.text:
The opinion expressly identifies disagreement with the Third Circuit’s approach. This is not labeled a uniform Supreme Court rule.

The product was Wesson cooking oil labeled '100% Natural,' allegedly misleading because it contained genetically modified ingredients; the Ninth Circuit sided with the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Circuits against the Third Circuit's administrative-feasibility requirement, reasoning that such a rule would effectively bar class actions over inexpensive consumer goods where no one keeps receipts.

records.title: Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin (1974)
records.text: In a damages class action, every member you can find with reasonable effort must get individual notice. The named plaintiff normally pays for it, even if he cannot afford it. A judge cannot push 90 percent of the cost onto the defendants because the plaintiff looks likely to win.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 842–843

records.title: Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin (1974)
records.text: In a Rule 23(b)(3) class action, individual notice must be sent to all class members identifiable through reasonable effort, the representative plaintiff ordinarily bears its cost, and a court may not conduct a preliminary merits inquiry to shift that cost to defendants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 842–843

records.title: Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin (1974)
records.text:
Wal-Mart explains that Eisen’s language does not prohibit examining merits-related matters genuinely necessary to decide certification. The objection here concerned the preliminary merits inquiry used to allocate notice costs.

The Court also held that Rule 23(c)(2) requires individual notice to every class member who can be identified through reasonable effort (about 2,250,000 of the roughly six million odd-lot traders), and that 'nothing in either the language or history of Rule 23' authorizes a preliminary inquiry into the merits when deciding certification.

records.title: Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor (1997)
records.text: A settlement class has to meet the same class requirements as a litigated one, apart from worries about running a trial. A deal that looks fair does not make up for a class whose members had conflicting interests and too little in common. Here the class failed.

records.title: Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor (1997)
records.text: A class certified only for settlement must still satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b), apart from trial manageability; the fairness of the settlement under Rule 23(e) cannot substitute for predominance of common questions and adequate representation of conflicting groups within the class.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 853–860

records.title: Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor (1997)
records.text:
The opinion does not categorically prohibit mass-tort or settlement classes. It requires the class to meet the governing conditions despite the attraction of a comprehensive settlement.

Justice Ginsburg wrote for the Court (6-2, Justice O'Connor not participating); the opinion holds that settlement is relevant to certification because a court need not consider trial-manageability problems, but the other Rule 23 requirements demand undiluted, even heightened, attention in the settlement context, and that predominance is far more demanding than Rule 23(a)(2) commonality.

records.title: Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. (1999)
records.text: A class that forces everyone in, with no right to opt out, because there is not enough money to go around needs real proof that the fund is limited. Here the fund was not independently shown to be limited and conflicting claimants lacked separate representation, so the settlement could not be certified.

records.title: Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. (1999)
records.text: A mandatory limited-fund class under Rule 23(b)(1)(B) presumptively requires a fund independently shown to be insufficient for all claims, devotion of the whole fund to those claims, and inclusion and equitable treatment of the claimants, with conflicts addressed by separately represented subclasses.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 860–864

records.title: Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. (1999)
records.text:
The holding is bounded by the mandatory limited-fund theory presented. Do not merge the Rule 23(b)(1)(B) inquiry with Amchem’s Rule 23(b)(3) predominance analysis, although both decisions emphasize representation.

The vote was 7-2: Justice Souter wrote for the Court; Chief Justice Rehnquist concurred, joined by Scalia and Kennedy; Justice Breyer dissented, joined by Stevens, arguing the district court's detailed findings deserved deference and the disputed insurance asset was a genuine limited fund. The certification was under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), and the Court required that the fund be limited by more than the parties' agreement and allocated through a process addressing conflicting interests.

records.text: Before certification, Knowles could not bind absent class members by promising that the whole class would seek less than $5 million. The court therefore had to ignore that nonbinding cap and aggregate their claims for CAFA jurisdiction. His promise could limit his own demand, but not theirs.

records.title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021)
records.text: Every class member seeking individual damages needs a concrete injury. Disseminated false terrorist-related credit alerts supported standing through harm analogous to defamation; undisclosed internal alerts did not on this record. A statutory violation or unmaterialized risk alone was insufficient for damages. The Court reserved the standing showing required at certification.

records.title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021)
records.text: Every class member must have Article III standing to recover individual damages, which requires a concrete injury; a statutory violation alone does not suffice, and an unmaterialized risk of future harm does not by itself support standing for retrospective damages.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 872–873

records.title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021)
records.text:
The assigned note expressly states that the Court did not decide whether every class member must establish standing before certification. Preserve that reservation.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote for a 5–4 Court (Roberts, Alito, Gorsuch, Barrett joining); the opinion's rule is often reduced to "No concrete harm, no standing," and it held that only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a statutory violation may seek damages against a private defendant in federal court.

records.title: Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts (1985)
records.text: A state can bind out-of-state class members on money claims if they get notice, a chance to be heard, a chance to opt out and fair representation. But the state cannot apply its own law to claims with little connection to it. Kansas could not apply its law to every transaction here.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 873–882

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts (1985)
records.text: A forum may bind absent plaintiff-class members on money claims without minimum contacts if they receive the best practicable notice, a chance to be heard, a chance to opt out, and adequate representation; but it may apply its own law only to claims with sufficient forum contacts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 873–882

records.title: Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts (1985)
records.text:
On remand, the Kansas court found no relevant conflict after examining the other states’ laws and reached the same practical result. That later result did not erase the Supreme Court’s requirement to perform the choice-of-law analysis.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for the Court; the certified class of 33,000 royalty owners (more than 28,000 after opt-outs) lived in all 50 states, the District of Columbia and several foreign countries, and about 99% of the leases and 97% of the class members had no Kansas connection other than the suit; it was the defendant, Phillips, that raised the absent class members' due-process objection, and the Court allowed it standing to do so.

Rule statement: an absent plaintiff class member is bound if given adequate notice, an opportunity to be heard, a right to opt out, and adequate representation, so minimum contacts with the forum are not required; but a forum may apply its own law only if it has a significant contact or aggregation of contacts creating state interests, so the choice of law is not arbitrary or unfair.

It reversed the order striking the nationwide class allegations; it did not certify the class.

records.title: Mussat v. IQVIA, Inc. (2020)
records.text: In a nationwide Rule 23 class action under a federal statute, the named representative must establish personal jurisdiction over the defendant, but no separate showing of specific jurisdiction is required for each absent class member's claim.

records.title: Mussat v. IQVIA, Inc. (2020)
records.text:
This is a Seventh Circuit holding about a nationwide federal statutory class action. The casebook presents the broader issue as unsettled at its publication; do not label this a Supreme Court resolution. TransUnion concerns the separate Article III injury requirement.

Dr. Florence Mussat's Illinois medical practice, a professional services corporation, sued under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act over two unsolicited junk faxes lacking the required opt-out notice from IQVIA (a Delaware corporation headquartered in Pennsylvania); the Seventh Circuit reasoned that 'absent class members are not full parties to the case for many purposes,' so only the named plaintiff had to establish personal jurisdiction.
