records.title: Cooper v. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (1984)
records.text: Losing a class claim that the employer had a company-wide pattern of discrimination does not mean every worker's own claim fails, because individual decisions were never decided. The Baxter petitioners could still pursue their promotion claims but could not relitigate the pattern issue.

records.title: Cooper v. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (1984)
records.text: A class judgment binds class members under ordinary claim and issue preclusion, but only as to what was actually adjudicated: a finding of no classwide pattern or practice of discrimination does not bar class members' unadjudicated individual discrimination claims.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 886–890

records.title: Cooper v. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (1984)
records.text:
The class suit was originally an EEOC action (filed March 1977) in which Cooper and three other employees intervened and won certification of a class of Black employees; the district court found a pattern of discrimination only in pay grades 4 and 5, and the Baxter plaintiffs (who had received notice and not opted out) then filed separate individual promotion claims.

Justice Stevens wrote for the Court (Justice Marshall concurring in the judgment; Justice Powell not participating): a class judgment on a pattern-or-practice claim precludes relitigation of whether the employer engaged in a pattern of discrimination, but does not bar individual class members from proving discrete individual claims in later suits.

records.text: A state cannot insist that arbitration agreements allow class procedures, even if it calls the rule ordinary unconscionability law. That would change arbitration into something the parties did not agree to. Parties remain free to agree to class arbitration themselves.

records.title: AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion (2011)
records.text: The Federal Arbitration Act preempts a state rule, even one framed as generally applicable unconscionability, that conditions enforcement of an arbitration agreement on the availability of class procedures and so interferes with arbitration as the parties agreed to it.

records.text:
The assigned chapter discusses continuing questions about generally applicable defenses and class waivers.

The Concepcions were charged $30.22 in sales tax on phones advertised as free; the district court denied AT&T's motion to compel arbitration under California's Discover Bank rule and the Ninth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court (Scalia, J., 5-4) reversed and remanded, with Justice Thomas concurring and Justice Breyer's dissent joined by Justices Ginsburg, Sotomayor and Kagan.

records.title: Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co. (1970)
records.text: The side asking for summary judgment must first show there is nothing to try. If its own evidence leaves a gap, the motion fails even when the other side offers nothing. Here Kress did not rule out that a policeman was in the store and reached an understanding with an employee.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1013–1017

records.title: Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co. (1970)
records.text: A party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of showing the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, and if its own showing leaves a gap the motion must be denied even though the opponent offers no competent evidence in response.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1013–1017

records.title: Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co. (1970)
records.text:
Celotex later explains why Adickes does not require every defendant to affirmatively negate an element the plaintiff must prove. The comparison concerns how a movant identifies an actual absence of supporting evidence rather than ignoring material already in the record.

Justice Harlan wrote for the Court; the case is the source of the rule that the party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of showing the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, so Kress had to foreclose the possibility that a policeman was in the store, and Adickes's first count (refusal of service under a custom of segregation) went to trial and ended in a directed verdict for Kress that the Court also reversed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1013–1017

records.title: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)
records.text: A party moving for summary judgment need not prove the opponent's case false. It can point out that after enough time for discovery the opponent has no evidence on something it must prove at trial. The opponent must then show specific facts, here exposure to a Celotex product.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1017–1027

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)
records.text: After adequate time for discovery, a summary-judgment movant need not negate an element on which the opponent bears the trial burden; it may point to the absence of supporting evidence in the record, and the opponent must then designate specific facts showing a genuine issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1017–1027

records.title: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)
records.text:
The opinion quotes an earlier numbering of Rule 56. The casebook identifies the later numbering and discusses the 2010 changes. Do not describe the Supreme Court’s remand as a final finding that Catrett lacked evidence or that Celotex won the underlying case.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for a 5-4 Court (joined by White, Marshall, Powell and O'Connor); the opinion describes summary judgment as an integral part of the Federal Rules rather than a disfavored procedural shortcut, and Justice White's concurrence stressed that a movant cannot simply assert that the opponent has no evidence and must still support its motion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1017–1027

records.title: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (1986)
records.text: A judge deciding summary judgment asks whether a reasonable jury could find for the other side under the burden of proof that will apply at trial. In this libel case that meant clear and convincing proof of actual malice. The judge does not weigh evidence or decide who is telling the truth.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1027–1029

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (1986)
records.text: On summary judgment the judge asks whether the evidence, viewed favorably to the nonmovant, could support a reasonable jury verdict under the substantive burden of proof that will apply at trial, including the clear-and-convincing standard for actual malice.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1027–1029

records.title: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (1986)
records.text:
The rule is not that judges personally must be clearly convinced by the nonmovant’s evidence at summary judgment.

Justice White wrote for a 6-3 Court; Justice Brennan dissented, and Justice Rehnquist dissented joined by Chief Justice Burger, both objecting to importing the trial-stage clear-and-convincing standard into Rule 56. The plaintiffs were Liberty Lobby and its founder Willis Carto, suing columnist Jack Anderson over articles in The Investigator magazine, and the opinion is also the source of the rule that a mere scintilla of evidence is insufficient to defeat summary judgment.

records.title: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. (1986)
records.text: When an alleged conspiracy makes little economic sense, ambiguous evidence is not enough to reach trial. Conduct that fits ordinary price competition as well as a conspiracy proves nothing alone. The plaintiffs needed evidence tending to rule out that the companies acted independently.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1029–1031

records.title: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. (1986)
records.text: To survive summary judgment, an antitrust plaintiff must present evidence tending to exclude the possibility of independent action, and when the claimed conspiracy makes no economic sense the plaintiff needs more persuasive evidence than conduct equally consistent with lawful competition.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1029–1031

records.title: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. (1986)
records.text:
Do not restate this as a general rule that a plaintiff must disprove every alternative explanation, or merge it with Twombly’s earlier-stage pleading inquiry.

The decision was 5-4: Justice Powell wrote (joined by Burger, Marshall, Rehnquist and O'Connor) and Justice White dissented, joined by Brennan, Blackmun and Stevens, arguing the majority discounted the DePodwin expert report and weighed evidence that created a genuine issue for trial. The Court required evidence 'that tends to exclude the possibility' that the alleged conspirators acted independently.

records.text: A plaintiff who must prove that someone said something cannot get to a jury just by hoping the jury will disbelieve witnesses who all deny it. With no admissible proof of his own, Dyer lost on summary judgment.

records.title: Dyer v. MacDougall (1952)
records.text: Summary judgment is proper against a party who bears the trial burden, has no admissible affirmative proof, and relies only on the possibility that the demeanor of witnesses who all deny the essential fact would persuade a jury of the opposite.

records.text: If a video plainly shows what happened, a court need not accept a version of events the recording flatly contradicts. Here the recording showed a dangerous chase, so the officer's intervention was reasonable. This does not let a court ignore a plaintiff's story whenever a defendant has video.

records.title: Scott v. Harris (2007)
records.text: At summary judgment the evidence and reasonable inferences favor the nonmovant only where the dispute is genuine; a court need not adopt a version of the facts so plainly contradicted by the record that no reasonable jury could believe it.

records.title: Scott v. Harris (2007)
records.text:
The casebook’s subsequent discussion reports research finding different viewer interpretations. That discussion is commentary on the decision, not part of the holding.

Harris sued under § 1983 claiming an unreasonable Fourth Amendment seizure after Deputy Scott rammed his bumper during a roughly ten-mile high-speed chase in Georgia, leaving Harris a quadriplegic; the Court ruled 8-1 in an opinion by Justice Scalia, with Justices Ginsburg and Breyer concurring and Justice Stevens dissenting.

Rule statement: when opposing parties tell two different stories and one is blatantly contradicted by the record so that no reasonable jury could believe it, the court should not adopt that version of the facts in ruling on summary judgment; the Court also held that an officer's attempt to end a dangerous high-speed chase that threatens the lives of innocent bystanders, by forcing the fleeing motorist off the road, does not violate the Fourth Amendment even at risk of serious injury to the motorist.

records.title: Tolan v. Cotton (2014)
records.text: Even when the issue is qualified immunity, a court at summary judgment must take the injured person's evidence as true and draw reasonable inferences in that person's favor. It cannot settle genuinely disputed facts against the plaintiff to make the officer's conduct look reasonable.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1034–1035

records.title: Tolan v. Cotton (2014)
records.text: Under either prong of the qualified-immunity inquiry, a court ruling on summary judgment must credit the nonmoving party's competent evidence and draw reasonable inferences in that party's favor, and may not define the factual context by resolving genuinely disputed facts for the movant.

records.title: Tolan v. Cotton (2014)
records.text:
This is a short assigned note. It supplies a useful limit on overly broad readings of Scott: a judge may not treat ordinary disagreement in testimony as an absence of a genuine dispute.

The Supreme Court's decision was per curiam. Robert Tolan, unarmed, was shot on his parents' front porch by Sergeant Jeffrey Cotton on New Year's Eve 2008; the suit was under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for excessive force, and the summary-judgment ruling arose on the officer's qualified-immunity defense.

The Court faulted the Fifth Circuit for failing to adhere to the axiom that on summary judgment "[t]he evidence of the nonmovant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences are to be drawn in his favor."

records.text: In the Second Circuit in 1946, summary judgment was off the table when there was even the slightest doubt about the facts, especially if the outcome depended on believing a witness the jury had not seen. Here Porter's denial of copying had to be tested before a jury.

records.title: Arnstein v. Porter (1946)
records.text: Under the Second Circuit's approach in 1946, summary judgment is improper where there is the slightest doubt as to the facts, particularly where the outcome turns on the credibility of a witness whom the jury has not seen testify.

records.title: Arnstein v. Porter (1946)
records.text:
The historical slightest-doubt language is not the standard announced by the later trilogy.

Ira Arnstein sued Cole Porter claiming Porter had plagiarized his compositions; the district court granted Porter summary judgment, and the Second Circuit (Frank, J.) reversed and remanded because the circulation of Arnstein's works and the unresolved credibility of Porter's denial of access presented a genuine issue that live cross-examination before a jury should test, over Judge Clark's dissent who heard no significant musical resemblance, found the evidence of access insufficient and saw no copyright exception to Rule 56.

records.text: In a complicated antitrust case where motive and intent matter and most of the proof sits with the defendants, a judge should be slow to end it on written affidavits. Acts that are lawful alone can still be part of an unlawful scheme, and that question deserves a trial.

records.title: Poller v. Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc. (1962)
records.text: Summary judgment should be used cautiously in complex antitrust litigation where motive and intent are central, the proof lies largely with the alleged conspirators and credibility may matter; the record must be viewed favorably to the party opposing the motion.

records.title: Poller v. Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc. (1962)
records.text:
The casebook covers Poller through commentary. It does not reproduce a full factual record or every issue in the opinion.

Poller owned WCAN, a UHF station in Milwaukee; he alleged CBS conspired to cancel WCAN's network affiliation, acquire competing station WOKY, and buy WCAN's equipment at distressed prices, in a treble-damage Sherman Act suit.

The decision was 5-4: Justice Clark wrote for the Court, and Justice Harlan dissented, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Whittaker and Stewart; the majority's oft-quoted rationale is that summary procedures should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent play leading roles, the proof is largely in the hands of the alleged conspirators, and hostile witnesses thicken the plot.

The detailed underlying litigation facts are not reproduced there. The note’s later discussion of possible waiver is not a holding that parties can never consent to trial in the transferee forum.

Lexecon sued the Milberg Weiss and Cotchett firms in Illinois for malicious prosecution; the Judicial Panel transferred the case to Arizona for pretrial proceedings, and the Arizona court then transferred it to itself for trial under 1404(a). Justice Souter wrote for a unanimous Court (Justice Scalia did not join Part II-C).

records.text: When one of several consolidated cases is finally decided, the loser can appeal right away without waiting for the rest. Consolidating cases puts them together for convenience but does not erase each case's separate identity.

records.title: Hall v. Hall (2018)
records.text: When one of several cases consolidated under Rule 42(a) is finally decided, the losing party may immediately appeal that decision under section 1291, because consolidation does not merge the constituent cases or eliminate their separate identities.

records.title: Hall v. Hall (2018)
records.text: Facts: Ethlyn Hall sued her son Samuel over his handling of her Virgin Islands property (the 'trust case'), her daughter Elsa succeeded her as trustee and plaintiff, Samuel sued Elsa individually, and the cases were consolidated under Rule 42(a) and tried together; the Third Circuit dismissed Elsa's appeal from the judgment in the individual case as premature, and the Supreme Court (Roberts, C.J., unanimous) reversed, holding that a final judgment in one consolidated case is immediately appealable.

records.text: Subject-matter jurisdiction is a court’s authority to decide a category of dispute. Federal courts require an applicable grant of authority within the limits allowed by the Constitution.

Analyze each defendant and each relevant claim.

records.text: A court may need both a statute authorizing its action and constitutional permission to exercise that authority. The Constitution can allow a reach that the legislature has chosen not to grant.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 107–114

records.title: Procedural rulings and decisions on the merits
records.text: A procedural ruling decides how or whether litigation may proceed. A merits determination decides the parties’ underlying legal entitlement, although some motions can resolve that entitlement without trial.

records.text: For each case, identify the challenged motion, what facts the court could consider, which assertions were assumed rather than found, and exactly what the appellate disposition required. atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 29–36

records.title: Waiver and preservation of objections
records.text: Waiver or forfeiture can prevent a party from relying on an objection that was available earlier. The consequences depend on the kind of objection and the governing rule.

records.text: Consent can support personal jurisdiction, while the parties cannot confer missing subject-matter authority by agreement. Finality of a completed judgment raises additional questions: Capron allowed the losing plaintiff to raise the defect on direct review, but whether a subject-matter defect survives a final judgment in a later collateral attack is a separate question.

records.text: Federalism distributes judicial and lawmaking responsibilities between the national government and the states. Procedure can affect that distribution through jurisdiction, governing law, and the treatment of state-created rights.

records.text: Judicial discretion is the authority a rule or doctrine gives a judge to choose among legally permissible responses after considering relevant facts and interests. The authority remains bounded by the governing law.

records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the allegedly intentional act, its intended or known audience and location, and the forum-directed activity. Compare Calder’s publication setting with Walden’s insistence that the plaintiff’s residence or resulting harm alone cannot connect the defendant to the forum.

records.title: Contracts as forum contacts
records.text: A contract can create forum connections through the parties’ deliberate relationship, negotiations, future obligations, and performance. The existence of a contract with a forum resident is only part of the inquiry.

records.title: Long-arm authorization
records.text: A long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over persons outside the state in defined circumstances. Its interpretation determines the state-law reach before constitutional limits are applied.

records.text: A long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over persons outside the state in defined circumstances. Its interpretation determines the state-law reach before constitutional limits are applied.

records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the precise statutory provision, the conduct alleged to satisfy it, and the state court’s construction. Gray separates interpretation of the place of the tortious act from the due-process analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 107–114

records.title: Consent to personal jurisdiction
records.text: Consent supplies a basis for personal jurisdiction through an agreement, conduct in litigation, or another legally recognized submission to the court’s authority. The assigned cases examine both how consent arises and its limits.

records.text: Consent supplies a basis for personal jurisdiction through an agreement, conduct in litigation, or another legally recognized submission to the court’s authority. The assigned cases examine both how consent arises and its limits.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 194–200

records.title: Discovery of jurisdictional facts
records.text: Jurisdictional discovery develops evidence concerning facts needed to decide the court’s authority over a party. A defendant’s objection to jurisdiction does not necessarily remove the court’s power to require information needed to decide that objection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 194–197

records.text: A sanction is not a general permission to invent jurisdictional facts or confer subject-matter power. Its legal basis, notice, and relation to the withheld evidence matter.

records.text: Jurisdictional discovery develops evidence concerning facts needed to decide the court’s authority over a party. A defendant’s objection to jurisdiction does not necessarily remove the court’s power to require information needed to decide that objection.

records.text: Identify what evidence was requested, why it bears on jurisdiction, and the defendant’s response to court orders. In Insurance Corp. of Ireland, connect the sanction to the specific facts the discovery was intended to establish.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 194–197

records.title: Personal service while in the forum
records.text: Tag jurisdiction refers to personal jurisdiction based on serving an individual while the individual is physically present in the state. Burnham upheld its use on the facts before the Court, with differing reasons.

records.text: Do not automatically extend an individual-service holding to corporations or to presence procured by fraud. Tickle addresses a different problem concerning how the defendant was induced to enter the forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 223–234

records.title: Jurisdiction based on property
records.text: Property-based jurisdiction uses a defendant’s interests in property as part of the basis for adjudication. The course distinguishes disputes about the property itself from efforts to use unrelated property to obtain leverage over a person.

records.text: Internet-jurisdiction questions ask which online activities connect a particular defendant to a particular forum. The ability to access a site everywhere creates a need to identify meaningful forum-directed conduct.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 200–207

records.title: Collateral challenges to jurisdiction
records.text: A collateral challenge contests a judgment’s authority in a later proceeding rather than through ordinary review in the original action. Personal-jurisdiction choices can affect whether such a challenge remains open.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 234–237

records.title: Collateral challenges to jurisdiction
records.text: A jurisdictional defect does not imply that every final judgment can be challenged at any time by any party. The precise defect, earlier litigation, and procedural route matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 234–237

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 234–237

records.title: Finality and the binding effect of judgments
records.text: Finality limits repeated litigation after a court has entered a judgment. The course encounters it in jurisdictional challenges, class representation, and the protection of absent persons.

records.title: Constitutional adequacy of notice
records.text: Due process ordinarily asks for a reasonable method rather than a guarantee of actual receipt. Compliance with a service rule and constitutional adequacy are separate inquiries.

records.title: Constitutional adequacy of notice
records.text: Notice is the communication needed to give an affected person a meaningful opportunity to protect an interest before a court acts. Mullane evaluates whether the method is reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform interested persons.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 237–251

records.title: Constitutional adequacy of notice
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the interests affected, what addresses or other contact information are known or reasonably available, the proposed method, and any reason to know it failed. Distinguish readily identifiable people from unknown or unlocatable persons.

records.title: Service of process
records.text: Service of process is the formal delivery or legally authorized communication of the summons and complaint or equivalent initiating papers. It tells a defendant that a judicial proceeding requires a response.

records.title: Presence procured by fraud and service immunity
records.text: A court may refuse to recognize service when deception procured a defendant’s presence for that purpose. The separate doctrine of immunity can protect persons present for judicial proceedings in specified circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Presence procured by fraud and service immunity
records.text: Tickle accepted the plea’s allegations at the stage before it; it did not finally find the alleged deception. Fraud and immunity have different foundations and should not be treated as one automatic exemption.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Presence procured by fraud and service immunity
records.text: A court may refuse to recognize service when deception procured a defendant’s presence for that purpose. The separate doctrine of immunity can protect persons present for judicial proceedings in specified circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Presence procured by fraud and service immunity
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: For fraud, identify the representation, who made it, the reason for entering the forum, and the procedural stage at which the allegation is tested. For immunity, identify the person’s role and the reason for attendance, using the separate assigned notes.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 31–36

records.title: Due process in civil adjudication
records.text: Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 237–296

records.title: Due process in civil adjudication
records.text: Using the same constitutional phrase does not make the tests interchangeable. A minimum-contacts inquiry and a hearing-before-attachment inquiry address distinct concerns.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 237–296

records.title: Due process in civil adjudication
records.text: Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 237–296

records.title: Due process in civil adjudication
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Specify the governmental action and the threatened deprivation. Identify whether the dispute concerns jurisdiction, communication of the proceeding, timing of a hearing, or representation of absent persons. Apply the test developed for that problem.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 237–296

records.title: Opportunity to be heard
records.text: An opportunity to be heard allows an affected person to challenge the grounds for governmental action before an appropriate decision-maker. Timing and the form of the hearing depend on the legal setting.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Opportunity to be heard
records.text: The due-process cases do not prescribe a full trial before every temporary measure. The kind of property, prior interest, evidentiary showing, decision-maker, and available prompt review matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Opportunity to be heard
records.text: An opportunity to be heard allows an affected person to challenge the grounds for governmental action before an appropriate decision-maker. Timing and the form of the hearing depend on the legal setting.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Opportunity to be heard
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the private interest, the risk that the procedure will produce an erroneous deprivation, the usefulness of additional safeguards, and the countervailing interests. Distinguish ordinary private creditor collection from extraordinary situations requiring immediate action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Prejudgment seizure and attachment
records.text: A prejudgment remedy restricts possession or use of property before final determination of liability. Attachment, garnishment, and replevin can protect a claimant but can also harm a person before the claim is proven.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Prejudgment seizure and attachment
records.text: A bond or later damages action does not automatically eliminate the risk of erroneous deprivation. Nor does Fuentes invalidate every procedure involving provisional seizure.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Prejudgment seizure and attachment
records.text: A prejudgment remedy restricts possession or use of property before final determination of liability. Attachment, garnishment, and replevin can protect a claimant but can also harm a person before the claim is proven.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Prejudgment seizure and attachment
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify what is seized or restricted, whether the applicant already has an interest in it, who authorizes the measure, what factual showing is required, whether a bond is required, and when the affected person can contest it. Compare Sniadach, Fuentes, and Doehr with the notes on different safeguards.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 278–296
Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 22–24

records.title: Balancing the safeguards required by due process
records.text: The Mathews framework evaluates the private interest, the risk of error and value of additional safeguards, and the relevant governmental or countervailing interests. Doehr applies an adapted inquiry to a private litigant’s use of attachment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 284–294

records.title: Balancing the safeguards required by due process
records.text: This balancing framework must be applied in its procedural setting. It is not a numerical formula or a general license to dispense with required notice whenever adjudication would be convenient.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 284–294

records.title: Balancing the safeguards required by due process
records.text: The Mathews framework evaluates the private interest, the risk of error and value of additional safeguards, and the relevant governmental or countervailing interests. Doehr applies an adapted inquiry to a private litigant’s use of attachment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 284–294

records.title: Balancing the safeguards required by due process
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Describe the actual deprivation and the evidentiary reliability of the proposed procedure. Consider how notice, a judicial assessment, adversarial input, prompt review, or other safeguards would change the risk. Then identify the applicant’s urgency or existing interest.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 284–294

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction
records.text: Diversity jurisdiction permits specified civil actions between parties of different citizenship to be heard in federal court when the statutory conditions are met. The ordinary statute combines citizenship requirements with an amount in controversy.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 304–328

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction
records.text: Article III’s constitutional allowance is not identical to § 1332’s ordinary complete-diversity rule. CAFA and statutory interpleader use different conditions.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 304–328

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction
records.text: Diversity jurisdiction permits specified civil actions between parties of different citizenship to be heard in federal court when the statutory conditions are met. The ordinary statute combines citizenship requirements with an amount in controversy.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 304–328

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Determine the citizenship of every relevant party at the legally relevant time. Apply complete diversity where required, identify the amount genuinely in dispute, and check exceptions and statutory restrictions. Treat corporations, unincorporated entities, natural persons, and foreign parties under their respective rules.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 304–328

records.title: Citizenship of persons and entities
records.text: Citizenship identifies the legally relevant state or foreign affiliation of a party for diversity jurisdiction. It depends on the kind of party rather than a single universal test.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–317

records.title: Citizenship of persons and entities
records.text: Residence, a business address, or extensive operations may be insufficient. An entity’s citizenship for subject-matter jurisdiction also differs from its contacts or corporate home for personal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–317

records.title: Citizenship of persons and entities
records.text: Citizenship identifies the legally relevant state or foreign affiliation of a party for diversity jurisdiction. It depends on the kind of party rather than a single universal test.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–317

records.title: Citizenship of persons and entities
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Natural-person citizenship uses domicile in the assigned cases. A corporation has the statutory places of citizenship discussed in the text, including its principal place of business. Unincorporated associations generally require examining members’ citizenship. Verify the entity’s legal form before applying a corporate rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 305–317

records.title: Amount in controversy
records.text: The amount in controversy is the value genuinely placed in dispute for a jurisdictional statute. It is assessed by the governing legal standard and the claim at issue, rather than simply the amount eventually awarded.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–324

records.title: Amount in controversy
records.text: A small eventual recovery does not itself show that jurisdiction was absent at filing. Aggregating several claims or class members requires separate authority.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–324

records.title: Amount in controversy
records.text: The amount in controversy is the value genuinely placed in dispute for a jurisdictional statute. It is assessed by the governing legal standard and the claim at issue, rather than simply the amount eventually awarded.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–324

records.title: Amount in controversy
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the statutory threshold and excluded items, the relief sought, and whether the claim was made in good faith. Apply the legal-certainty inquiry described in A.F.A. Tours and the notes. For injunctions, specify what interest is valued and which viewpoint the relevant rule permits.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 318–324

records.title: Combining claim values for jurisdiction
records.text: Aggregation concerns when several claims may be added together to satisfy a jurisdictional amount. The answer depends on the parties and whether the claims are separate or share a common undivided interest.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 322–324

records.title: Combining claim values for jurisdiction
records.text: Procedural permission to join claims does not itself authorize adding their values for jurisdiction. Exxon addresses supplemental jurisdiction over related claims and should not be restated as unlimited aggregation.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 322–324

records.title: Combining claim values for jurisdiction
records.text: Aggregation concerns when several claims may be added together to satisfy a jurisdictional amount. The answer depends on the parties and whether the claims are separate or share a common undivided interest.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 322–324

records.title: Combining claim values for jurisdiction
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify who owns each claim and against whom it is asserted. Separate a single plaintiff’s multiple claims against one defendant from separate plaintiffs’ claims. Then check whether a special statute such as CAFA changes the ordinary treatment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 322–324

records.title: Article III standing
records.text: Standing asks whether the party invoking federal judicial power has the constitutionally required personal stake in the requested relief. The assigned discussion emphasizes concrete injury and its relationship to the challenged conduct and remedy.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 719–720
Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 872–873

records.title: Article III standing
records.text: Real party in interest, class representation, diversity, and personal jurisdiction are distinct inquiries. TransUnion expressly reserves a separate question about the timing of every class member’s standing showing before certification.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 719–720
Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 872–873

records.title: Article III standing
records.text: Standing asks whether the party invoking federal judicial power has the constitutionally required personal stake in the requested relief. The assigned discussion emphasizes concrete injury and its relationship to the challenged conduct and remedy.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 719–720
Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 872–873

records.title: Article III standing
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the plaintiff’s injury, the connection to the defendant’s conduct, and whether the requested judicial relief addresses that injury. In a damages class, apply TransUnion’s requirement to each person recovering individual damages.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 719–720
