records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction
records.text: Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 328–354

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction
records.text: A federal defense or a federal issue somewhere in the dispute is not enough by itself. Shoshone and the embedded-issue cases show why the source and nature of the claim must be examined carefully.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 328–354

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction
records.text: Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 328–354

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the claim as it appears in a properly pleaded complaint. Ask whether federal law creates the claim, and separately whether a necessary embedded federal issue meets Grable and Gunn. Confirm the particular statute, including any specialized grant.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 328–354

records.title: The well-pleaded complaint rule
records.text: The well-pleaded complaint rule looks to the plaintiff’s own claim for federal-question jurisdiction. A federal defense anticipated in the complaint ordinarily does not make a state-law claim arise under federal law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: The well-pleaded complaint rule
records.text: The rule differs from the breadth of Article III and from the merits of a federal defense. Specialized removal doctrines discussed in the notes require separate treatment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: The well-pleaded complaint rule
records.text: The well-pleaded complaint rule looks to the plaintiff’s own claim for federal-question jurisdiction. A federal defense anticipated in the complaint ordinarily does not make a state-law claim arise under federal law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: The well-pleaded complaint rule
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: State what the plaintiff must establish to obtain relief. Remove predictions about the defendant’s federal defense and the plaintiff’s response to that defense, then examine the remaining claim. Mottley’s contract-enforcement claim illustrates the distinction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 331–339

records.title: Federal issues within state-law claims
records.text: A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–354

records.title: Federal issues within state-law claims
records.text: The presence of a federal standard or the importance of the case to the litigants does not automatically satisfy the test. A hypothetical patent question in malpractice may matter greatly to the parties while lacking the required systemic significance.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–354

records.title: Federal issues within state-law claims
records.text: A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–354

records.title: Federal issues within state-law claims
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the particular federal issue and why the state claim necessarily raises it. Ask whether it is disputed, substantial to the federal system rather than merely valuable to these parties, and appropriate for federal adjudication without upsetting the intended balance. Compare Grable with Gunn.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 340–354

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: Supplemental jurisdiction allows a federal court with an authorized anchor claim to hear certain related claims that lack an independent federal jurisdictional basis. The statute imposes conditions, exclusions, and grounds for declining the additional claims.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: A joinder rule supplies procedural permission, not subject-matter jurisdiction. An absence of original jurisdiction cannot be repaired by calling every claim supplemental.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: Supplemental jurisdiction allows a federal court with an authorized anchor claim to hear certain related claims that lack an independent federal jurisdictional basis. The statute imposes conditions, exclusions, and grounds for declining the additional claims.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: First identify a claim within original federal jurisdiction. Ask whether the other claim belongs to the same Article III case or controversy. Then apply § 1367(b) where original jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, and § 1367(c)’s grounds for declining jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–379

records.title: From pendent and ancillary jurisdiction to § 1367
records.text: Pendent and ancillary jurisdiction are historical descriptions of federal authority over related claims or parties. Congress’s enactment of § 1367 provides the statutory framework emphasized in the later course materials.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–373

records.title: From pendent and ancillary jurisdiction to § 1367
records.text: An older case’s terminology does not automatically answer the statutory question. Preserve the chronology and identify the proposition for which an older decision remains useful.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–373

records.title: From pendent and ancillary jurisdiction to § 1367
records.text: Pendent and ancillary jurisdiction are historical descriptions of federal authority over related claims or parties. Congress’s enactment of § 1367 provides the statutory framework emphasized in the later course materials.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–373

records.title: From pendent and ancillary jurisdiction to § 1367
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Use Gibbs for the related-case and discretionary framework, then compare Aldinger, Kroger, and Finley for the difficulties of adding parties. Read the statute and Exxon to determine how its text changes the analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 354–373

records.title: Adding parties through supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: The pendent-party problem asks whether a related claim against or by an additional person may be heard when that person’s claim has no independent federal jurisdictional basis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–373

records.title: Adding parties through supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: Kroger’s concern with an original plaintiff’s claim against a nondiverse third-party defendant is reflected in the later statutory restrictions. Distinguish that claim from the defending party’s own derivative impleader claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–373

records.title: Adding parties through supplemental jurisdiction
records.text: The pendent-party problem asks whether a related claim against or by an additional person may be heard when that person’s claim has no independent federal jurisdictional basis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–373

records.title: Adding parties through supplemental jurisdiction
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the anchor claim, the new party’s procedural role, the joinder rule, and the statutory limitations. Compare the historical decisions with § 1367’s text rather than assuming that factual overlap alone answers the question.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 359–373

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases
records.text: When original jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, § 1367(b) restricts certain additional claims by plaintiffs and proposed plaintiffs. The role of each party and the method of joinder matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases
records.text: Do not treat every joined plaintiff or every third-party claim identically. Nor does satisfaction of one plaintiff’s amount eliminate all other jurisdictional defects.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases
records.text: When original jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, § 1367(b) restricts certain additional claims by plaintiffs and proposed plaintiffs. The role of each party and the method of joinder matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–379

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Apply § 1367(a) first. Then identify the specific claim and the listed joinder rule in subsection (b), and ask whether exercising jurisdiction would conflict with § 1332’s requirements. Exxon addresses related claims lacking the required amount while preserving the distinction from missing complete diversity.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 365–379

records.title: When a court may decline related state claims
records.text: Even when supplemental judicial power exists, the court may have grounds to decline to exercise it. The assigned materials connect that choice to state-law complexity, predominance, loss of federal claims, and other exceptional circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 356–379

records.title: When a court may decline related state claims
records.text: Power and the choice to exercise power are separate. A discretionary dismissal or remand should not be described as proof that the court never had jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 356–379

records.title: When a court may decline related state claims
records.text: Even when supplemental judicial power exists, the court may have grounds to decline to exercise it. The assigned materials connect that choice to state-law complexity, predominance, loss of federal claims, and other exceptional circumstances.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 356–379

records.title: When a court may decline related state claims
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the statutory ground and explain the effects on economy, convenience, fairness, and the state’s interest in deciding its own law. Consider the litigation’s stage and what work has already occurred.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 356–379

records.title: Removal from state to federal court
records.text: Removal transfers an eligible action from state court to federal court through a procedure authorized by Congress. It ordinarily depends on federal original jurisdiction and the removing party’s statutory role.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 379–390

records.title: Removal from state to federal court
records.text: A federal issue in a defense does not ordinarily authorize removal. The meaning of defendant matters in Shamrock Oil and Home Depot. Remand grounds and reviewability present additional questions.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 379–390

records.title: Removal from state to federal court
records.text: Removal transfers an eligible action from state court to federal court through a procedure authorized by Congress. It ordinarily depends on federal original jurisdiction and the removing party’s statutory role.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 379–390

records.title: Removal from state to federal court
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the original complaint, the party seeking removal, the jurisdictional basis, the destination federal court, and the procedural requirements. Check consent, timing, amount allegations, and special statutes. Distinguish original defendants from plaintiffs or counterclaim defendants as the cases require.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 379–390

records.title: The forum-defendant limitation
records.text: The forum-defendant rule restricts specified diversity removals when a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the forum state. It is a statutory restriction beyond the existence of diversity jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 384–385

records.title: The forum-defendant limitation
records.text: The assigned Lively discussion treats the restriction as procedural for the issue presented. CAFA has different removal provisions, so this limitation should not be transferred to that statute without checking its text.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 384–385

records.title: The forum-defendant limitation
records.text: The forum-defendant rule restricts specified diversity removals when a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the forum state. It is a statutory restriction beyond the existence of diversity jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 384–385

records.title: The forum-defendant limitation
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the basis of removal and the citizenship and service status of the relevant defendant. Then distinguish the restriction from an absence of original subject-matter jurisdiction when considering remand timing and preservation.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 384–385

records.title: Venue
records.text: Venue identifies the geographically proper court within the relevant court system. It allocates the location of litigation and is distinct from subject-matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–410

records.title: Venue
records.text: A district need not be the single best location to be a proper venue. Conversely, a defendant’s consent to personal jurisdiction does not automatically answer every statutory venue question.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–410

records.title: Venue
records.text: Venue identifies the geographically proper court within the relevant court system. It allocates the location of litigation and is distinct from subject-matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–410

records.title: Venue
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Read the applicable venue statute, identify the defendants’ relevant residences and where substantial events or property are located, and determine whether a general or special provision governs. Bates illustrates why an event’s receipt in a district can matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–410

records.title: Local actions and territorial land disputes
records.text: The historical local-action rule associated certain claims involving land with courts where the land was located. The readings examine the rule’s origins, contested rationale, and later statutory treatment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–409

records.title: Local actions and territorial land disputes
records.text: The cases arise in different jurisdictions and periods. Do not treat the older local-action doctrine as the unqualified modern federal venue rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–409

records.title: Local actions and territorial land disputes
records.text: The historical local-action rule associated certain claims involving land with courts where the land was located. The readings examine the rule’s origins, contested rationale, and later statutory treatment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–409

records.title: Local actions and territorial land disputes
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify whether the action determines title or possession or instead seeks personal damages, and distinguish subject-matter authority from venue. Compare Livingston’s historical restriction with Reasor-Hill’s rejection of denying a remedy solely on that basis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 395–409

records.title: Transfer among federal courts
records.text: Transfer moves litigation from one federal district to another under statutory authority. Different statutes address a convenient alternative to a proper venue, an improper venue, and coordinated pretrial proceedings.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–420

records.title: Transfer among federal courts
records.text: Hoffman interprets an earlier statutory formulation; the casebook discusses later consent language. Transfer can also affect the choice-of-law analysis, and an ordinary transfer and an Atlantic Marine forum-clause transfer require careful distinction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–420

records.title: Transfer among federal courts
records.text: Transfer moves litigation from one federal district to another under statutory authority. Different statutes address a convenient alternative to a proper venue, an improper venue, and coordinated pretrial proceedings.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–420

records.title: Transfer among federal courts
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the statute before evaluating destination and convenience. Under § 1404, examine eligibility, the relevant interests, and any valid forum clause. Under § 1406, address the defect in venue. Consider the distinct treatment of multidistrict proceedings under § 1407.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 410–420

records.title: Forum non conveniens
records.text: Forum non conveniens permits dismissal in favor of an available adequate alternative forum when the governing balance strongly favors litigation there. It often matters when transfer within the federal system cannot reach the alternative forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 420–439

records.title: Forum non conveniens
records.text: Less favorable substantive law does not alone make the alternative inadequate. The possibility that no meaningful remedy exists is a different question. Dismissal, transfer, and enforcement of a forum clause have related but distinct frameworks.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 420–439

records.title: Forum non conveniens
records.text: Forum non conveniens permits dismissal in favor of an available adequate alternative forum when the governing balance strongly favors litigation there. It often matters when transfer within the federal system cannot reach the alternative forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 420–439

records.title: Forum non conveniens
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify an available adequate alternative, evaluate the private and public interests, and explain the weight due the plaintiff’s forum choice. Piper considers foreign plaintiffs, an overseas accident, evidence and witnesses abroad, and the adequacy of the Scottish forum.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 420–439

records.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie
records.text: Erie addresses the law a federal court uses when adjudicating rights governed by state law. Federal jurisdiction alone does not authorize creation of a federal general common law to replace state rules of decision.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 441–480

records.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie
records.text: The statement state substance and federal procedure is a starting description, not a sufficient test. Hanna explains why the source of the federal rule changes the analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 441–480

records.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie
records.text: Erie addresses the law a federal court uses when adjudicating rights governed by state law. Federal jurisdiction alone does not authorize creation of a federal general common law to replace state rules of decision.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 441–480

records.title: Governing law in federal court: Erie
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the precise disputed rule and the competing federal source. If a valid federal statute or applicable Federal Rule governs, analyze its scope and authority. Otherwise use the assigned Erie line to consider state rights, likely forum incentives, and the relevant federal judicial interests.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 441–480

records.title: Swift, Erie, and federal general common law
records.text: Before Erie, Swift permitted federal courts to exercise independent judgment on some questions categorized as general law. Erie rejected that approach to state-law rights and required respect for state judicial decisions as well as statutes.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 445–454

records.title: Swift, Erie, and federal general common law
records.text: Erie rejects federal general common law, while the course separately studies specialized federal common law justified by particular federal interests. Those are different claims of authority.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 445–454

records.title: Swift, Erie, and federal general common law
records.text: Before Erie, Swift permitted federal courts to exercise independent judgment on some questions categorized as general law. Erie rejected that approach to state-law rights and required respect for state judicial decisions as well as statutes.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 445–454

records.title: Swift, Erie, and federal general common law
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Trace the asserted source of law in Swift, the strategic reincorporation in Black & White Taxicab, and the disputed railroad duty in Erie. Explain how federal forum choice affected the governing substantive standard.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 445–454

records.title: Outcome effects and Erie’s twin aims
records.text: The outcome inquiry asks how a difference between state and federal treatment affects the enforcement of state-created rights. Hanna relates the inquiry to discouraging forum shopping and unequal administration of law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 454–462

records.title: Outcome effects and Erie’s twin aims
records.text: Almost any procedural choice can affect who wins after a dispute arises. That observation alone does not decide whether the federal court must adopt the state practice.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 454–462

records.title: Outcome effects and Erie’s twin aims
records.text: The outcome inquiry asks how a difference between state and federal treatment affects the enforcement of state-created rights. Hanna relates the inquiry to discouraging forum shopping and unequal administration of law.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 454–462

records.title: Outcome effects and Erie’s twin aims
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the practical effect of applying the alternative rules, especially at the point parties choose a forum. York’s limitations problem is an important example. Then consider the later qualifications in Byrd and Hanna.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 454–462

records.title: State interests and the federal judge–jury allocation
records.text: Byrd examines whether a federal court should follow a state practice assigning a disputed factual issue to a judge rather than a jury. The analysis considers the state rule’s connection to substantive rights and the federal system’s interests.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: State interests and the federal judge–jury allocation
records.text: Byrd is not a general permission to disregard state law whenever federal judges prefer another practice. Explain the competing interests concretely and distinguish a promulgated Federal Rule problem.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: State interests and the federal judge–jury allocation
records.text: Byrd examines whether a federal court should follow a state practice assigning a disputed factual issue to a judge rather than a jury. The analysis considers the state rule’s connection to substantive rights and the federal system’s interests.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: State interests and the federal judge–jury allocation
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the issue to be decided, why the state assigns it to the judge, and whether that assignment is bound up with the state-created right. Then examine the federal interest in the judge–jury division and the likely outcome effect.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 462–468

records.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?
records.text: A scope inquiry asks whether the federal provision actually answers the disputed procedural question. A direct conflict requires a different analysis from a situation in which the state and federal provisions can operate together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–491

records.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?
records.text: Calling a state rule substantive does not by itself prove that a Federal Rule is inapplicable. Calling a federal provision procedural does not establish its precise scope.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–491

records.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?
records.text: A scope inquiry asks whether the federal provision actually answers the disputed procedural question. A direct conflict requires a different analysis from a situation in which the state and federal provisions can operate together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–491

records.title: Does a federal statute or Federal Rule govern?
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Define the question precisely and compare the provisions. Hanna finds an unavoidable conflict over service. Walker reads Rule 3 as not deciding when the state limitations period is tolled. Stewart examines the transfer statute. After scope, assess the federal provision’s authority under the relevant standard.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 468–491

records.title: The Rules Enabling Act
records.text: The Rules Enabling Act authorizes general federal rules of practice and procedure while limiting their effect on substantive rights. It supplies a validity inquiry for Federal Rules distinct from the ordinary Erie choice when no such Rule governs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–515

records.title: The Rules Enabling Act
records.text: Shady Grove contains divided reasoning about how the Act applies to state rights. Preserve the plurality, concurrence, and dissent rather than presenting one broad formulation as unanimous.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–515

records.title: The Rules Enabling Act
records.text: The Rules Enabling Act authorizes general federal rules of practice and procedure while limiting their effect on substantive rights. It supplies a validity inquiry for Federal Rules distinct from the ordinary Erie choice when no such Rule governs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–515

records.title: The Rules Enabling Act
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the applicable Federal Rule, its operation, and the alleged effect on substantive rights. Read Sibbach, Hanna, and the separate approaches in Shady Grove. Distinguish this statutory limit from Congress’s constitutional authority to enact a procedural statute.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 477–515

records.title: Accommodating state and federal requirements
records.text: Accommodation asks whether the relevant state and federal interests can both be respected through a particular allocation of tasks or procedure. Gasperini considers review of damages under state law and federal appellate constraints.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Accommodating state and federal requirements
records.text: Accommodation is a case-specific method of implementing the governing law, not a free-floating compromise whenever two rules disagree.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Accommodating state and federal requirements
records.text: Accommodation asks whether the relevant state and federal interests can both be respected through a particular allocation of tasks or procedure. Gasperini considers review of damages under state law and federal appellate constraints.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Accommodating state and federal requirements
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Specify the state standard, the federal institutional constraint, and which court or decision-maker can perform the required review. Explain why the proposed arrangement preserves each interest under the opinion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 492–502

records.title: Choosing which state’s law governs
records.text: Choice of law identifies which jurisdiction’s substantive law governs a claim. This is separate from whether a court has authority over the case and parties.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 517–525

records.title: Choosing which state’s law governs
records.text: Jurisdiction over the defendant or the class does not alone authorize application of the forum’s law to every transaction. A contractual choice-of-law clause also requires its own scope and validity analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 517–525

records.title: Choosing which state’s law governs
records.text: Choice of law identifies which jurisdiction’s substantive law governs a claim. This is separate from whether a court has authority over the case and parties.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 517–525

records.title: Choosing which state’s law governs
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: In a diversity action, consider the forum state’s conflicts rules as discussed with Klaxon, and account for any relevant transfer doctrine. In a nationwide class, apply Shutts’s separate constitutional limits on selecting one state’s law for all claims.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 517–525

records.title: Specialized federal common law
records.text: Specialized federal common law consists of judicially developed federal rules supported by particular federal interests or authority, rather than a general power arising from federal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 525–539

records.title: Specialized federal common law
records.text: A federal connection alone does not justify replacing all state law. The readings emphasize restrictions on judicial lawmaking and differences among the recognized settings.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 525–539

records.title: Specialized federal common law
records.text: Specialized federal common law consists of judicially developed federal rules supported by particular federal interests or authority, rather than a general power arising from federal jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 525–539

records.title: Specialized federal common law
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the federal interest and the need for displacement of state law. Then ask whether federal law should supply a distinct rule or borrow state law. Compare the government payment instrument in Clearfield with the procurement conflict and specific conditions in Boyle.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 525–539

records.title: The federal contractor defense in Boyle
records.text: Boyle recognizes a defined defense to certain state design-defect claims when imposing liability would significantly conflict with federal procurement decisions. It is a specialized federal common-law doctrine.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: The federal contractor defense in Boyle
records.text: The defense does not establish general immunity for contractors or excuse all defects. The Court’s conditions and remand posture remain central.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: The federal contractor defense in Boyle
records.text: Boyle recognizes a defined defense to certain state design-defect claims when imposing liability would significantly conflict with federal procurement decisions. It is a specialized federal common-law doctrine.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: The federal contractor defense in Boyle
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Examine government approval of reasonably precise specifications, conformity to those specifications, and disclosure of dangers known to the contractor but not the government. Explain the federal interest and actual conflict rather than relying simply on a government purchase.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 531–537

records.title: Federal rights enforced in state court
records.text: The reverse-Erie problem concerns the obligations of a state court adjudicating a federal claim. State procedure cannot be used in a way that impermissibly defeats the federal right and its protected incidents.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–546

records.title: Federal rights enforced in state court
records.text: Dice is not a general holding that the Seventh Amendment governs all state civil trials. Its analysis concerns the federal statutory right and the particular protections at issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–546

records.title: Federal rights enforced in state court
records.text: The reverse-Erie problem concerns the obligations of a state court adjudicating a federal claim. State procedure cannot be used in a way that impermissibly defeats the federal right and its protected incidents.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–546

records.title: Federal rights enforced in state court
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the federal right, the state practice, and the connection between the contested procedure and enforcement of that right. Dice examines both the validity of a release under FELA and the role of a jury in deciding the issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–546

records.title: Releases and federal statutory claims
records.text: A release purports to surrender a legal claim. When the claim arises under a federal statute, federal law may govern whether a challenged release validly extinguishes that right.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Releases and federal statutory claims
records.text: A connection to Contracts does not make ordinary state contract law the answer to every release question. State and federal sources can assign different protections to the claim being relinquished.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Releases and federal statutory claims
records.text: A release purports to surrender a legal claim. When the claim arises under a federal statute, federal law may govern whether a challenged release validly extinguishes that right.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Releases and federal statutory claims
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the underlying right, the document, the alleged misrepresentation, and the law governing the release’s validity. In Dice, the federal treatment of the allegedly fraudulent release could not be displaced by the state’s restrictive approach.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 540–544

records.title: Pleading a civil claim
records.text: A pleading states a party’s claims or responses in the form required by the applicable procedural rules. A complaint must provide a sufficient account of entitlement to relief to move the case forward.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 603–639

records.title: Pleading a civil claim
records.text: An allegation accepted as true on a motion to dismiss is not thereby established as fact for trial or summary judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 603–639

records.title: Pleading a civil claim
records.text: A pleading states a party’s claims or responses in the form required by the applicable procedural rules. A complaint must provide a sufficient account of entitlement to relief to move the case forward.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 603–639

records.title: Pleading a civil claim
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the rule and court system. State the relevant conduct, actors, injury, and basis for relief in intelligible factual terms. Apply Rule 8 plausibility to the claim, then any special particularity requirements. Distinguish those requirements from what evidence must eventually prove.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 603–639

records.title: Notice pleading and its development
records.text: Notice pleading emphasizes giving the opposing party an intelligible account of the claim and its grounds without requiring the technical formulas of older pleading systems. The assigned cases trace its development and later qualifications.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–617

records.title: Notice pleading and its development
records.text: Conley’s no-set-of-facts formulation was expressly retired in Twombly. A historical statement should remain visible as history, rather than be placed beside the later standard as if both formulations were interchangeable.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–617

records.title: Notice pleading and its development
records.text: Notice pleading emphasizes giving the opposing party an intelligible account of the claim and its grounds without requiring the technical formulas of older pleading systems. The assigned cases trace its development and later qualifications.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–617

records.title: Notice pleading and its development
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Use Dioguardi and Conley to understand the notice function, Swierkiewicz to separate evidence frameworks from pleading, and Twombly and Iqbal to identify the later plausibility requirement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 608–617

records.title: Plausibility under Rule 8
records.text: Plausibility asks whether the well-pleaded factual allegations support a reasonable inference of entitlement to relief in the context of the claim. Legal labels and recitations of elements do not supply missing facts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–639

records.title: Plausibility under Rule 8
records.text: This is not trial proof or a requirement that the plaintiff establish a probability of winning. Nor does it authorize the judge to treat well-pleaded facts as false because the judge prefers another account. The separate opinions and Swanson show substantial disagreement in application.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–639

records.title: Plausibility under Rule 8
records.text: Plausibility asks whether the well-pleaded factual allegations support a reasonable inference of entitlement to relief in the context of the claim. Legal labels and recitations of elements do not supply missing facts.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–639

records.title: Plausibility under Rule 8
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the claim’s required elements, separate conclusory statements from factual allegations, accept well-pleaded facts, and assess what those facts plausibly support. Explain why a factual detail bears on the needed inference.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 617–639

records.title: Allegations, evidentiary sufficiency, and persuasion
records.text: A claim passes through different tests as litigation proceeds. Pleading concerns sufficient allegations; the production burden concerns enough evidence for a reasonable verdict; persuasion concerns whether the factfinder is convinced under the governing standard.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1012–1017

records.title: Allegations, evidentiary sufficiency, and persuasion
records.text: Do not use a trial evidentiary checklist as an automatic pleading requirement, or assume that surviving a Rule 12 motion supplies evidence sufficient for Rule 56.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1012–1017

records.title: Allegations, evidentiary sufficiency, and persuasion
records.text: A claim passes through different tests as litigation proceeds. Pleading concerns sufficient allegations; the production burden concerns enough evidence for a reasonable verdict; persuasion concerns whether the factfinder is convinced under the governing standard.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1012–1017

records.title: Allegations, evidentiary sufficiency, and persuasion
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: For every motion, identify the stage and permissible materials. A complaint may survive dismissal and still fail after discovery. A party may produce enough evidence to reach a jury yet lose when that jury evaluates credibility and weight.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1012–1017

records.title: Particularity for fraud or mistake
records.text: Rule 9(b) requires particular circumstances for allegations of fraud or mistake. The requirement concerns the pleaded theory, not simply the title of the statute under which the party sues.

records.text: The full rule text (Rule 9) is in the supplement, PDF page 29, linked below. The casebook discussion does not make every consumer claim a fraud claim or replace the separate PSLRA requirements.
