records.title: Particularity for fraud or mistake
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the allegedly false statement or omission, the responsible actor, relevant time and setting, and how it figures in the claim. Kearns examines consumer claims founded on a course of alleged fraud. Check the rule’s different treatment of mental conditions and any additional statute.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 647–658
Rule 9. Pleading Special Matters · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 29 of 354

records.title: The PSLRA’s strong-inference requirement
records.text: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act imposes a heightened pleading requirement concerning scienter, the legally required wrongful state of mind, in the securities setting addressed by Tellabs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 654–658

records.title: The PSLRA’s strong-inference requirement
records.text: This is a specialized statutory requirement. It should not be applied automatically to every Rule 8 claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 654–658

records.title: The PSLRA’s strong-inference requirement
records.text: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act imposes a heightened pleading requirement concerning scienter, the legally required wrongful state of mind, in the securities setting addressed by Tellabs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 654–658

records.title: The PSLRA’s strong-inference requirement
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Evaluate the allegations collectively and compare the proposed inference with plausible nonculpable explanations. Under Tellabs, the inference must be cogent and at least as compelling as the competing inference.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 654–658

records.title: Specifically pleading special damages
records.text: Special-damage pleading identifies losses that require particular notice rather than being sufficiently conveyed by the ordinary consequences of the pleaded wrong. The classification depends on the governing law and the claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–663

records.title: Specifically pleading special damages
records.text: Do not infer a universal classification of all injuries or damages from one state case. The source uses the case to explore notice and the governing pleading requirement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–663

records.title: Specifically pleading special damages
records.text: Special-damage pleading identifies losses that require particular notice rather than being sufficiently conveyed by the ordinary consequences of the pleaded wrong. The classification depends on the governing law and the claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–663

records.title: Specifically pleading special damages
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: State which loss is sought, why it follows from the wrong, and whether the pleading fairly identifies it. Compare the particular injuries discussed in Ziervogel and consider whether amendment is needed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 659–663

records.title: Choosing the appropriate Rule 12 response
records.text: Rule 12 provides distinct ways to respond to a complaint, including objections to authority, legal sufficiency, excessive vagueness, and specified material within the pleading. Each motion has its own purpose and preservation rules.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–681
Rule 12. Defenses and Objections · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 33 of 354

records.title: Choosing the appropriate Rule 12 response
records.text: A Rule 12(b)(6) motion and a Rule 56 motion use different materials and assumptions. The full text of Rule 12 is in the supplement (PDF page 33), linked below.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–681
Rule 12. Defenses and Objections · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 33 of 354

records.title: Choosing the appropriate Rule 12 response
records.text: Rule 12 provides distinct ways to respond to a complaint, including objections to authority, legal sufficiency, excessive vagueness, and specified material within the pleading. Each motion has its own purpose and preservation rules.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–681
Rule 12. Defenses and Objections · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 33 of 354

records.title: Choosing the appropriate Rule 12 response
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify whether the objection concerns jurisdiction, service, venue, failure to state a claim, a required party, inability to frame a response, or matter to be struck. Garcia illustrates why a court may preserve a claim while requiring detail and removing particular allegations.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–681
Rule 12. Defenses and Objections · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 33 of 354

records.title: Privilege as a response to a pleaded claim
records.text: A privilege can protect conduct or statements that might otherwise support liability. The assigned Garcia opinion distinguishes conditional protection, which may depend on facts such as malice, from absolute protection for particular proceedings.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Privilege as a response to a pleaded claim
records.text: The privilege rules are substantive and setting-specific. Garcia’s treatment should not be generalized to every employment communication or proceeding.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Privilege as a response to a pleaded claim
records.text: A privilege can protect conduct or statements that might otherwise support liability. The assigned Garcia opinion distinguishes conditional protection, which may depend on facts such as malice, from absolute protection for particular proceedings.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Privilege as a response to a pleaded claim
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the statement, occasion, legal source of the privilege, and facts relevant to overcoming it. Determine whether the complaint itself establishes the defense or whether factual development remains necessary.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 664–669

records.title: Admissions, denials, and lack of knowledge
records.text: An answer responds to the complaint’s allegations by admitting them, denying them, or properly stating insufficient knowledge. Those responses define what remains disputed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Admissions, denials, and lack of knowledge
records.text: A defective answer can require correction. The consequences of an admission and permission to amend it depend on the procedural setting, as Beeck illustrates.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Admissions, denials, and lack of knowledge
records.text: An answer responds to the complaint’s allegations by admitting them, denying them, or properly stating insufficient knowledge. Those responses define what remains disputed.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Admissions, denials, and lack of knowledge
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Read each allegation fairly and respond to its substance. A party cannot evade a factual allegation merely by calling it a legal conclusion, and a claimed lack of knowledge must be appropriate to the information the party has.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 684–688

records.title: Affirmative defenses
records.text: An affirmative defense supplies an additional reason the defendant should avoid or limit liability even when the claim’s ordinary allegations are assumed. It performs a different role from a denial.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Affirmative defenses
records.text: Not every unpleaded defense is inevitably lost. Amendment, notice, consent, and prejudice may matter under the governing rule and cases.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Affirmative defenses
records.text: An affirmative defense supplies an additional reason the defendant should avoid or limit liability even when the claim’s ordinary allegations are assumed. It performs a different role from a denial.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Affirmative defenses
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the defense, the rule requiring notice, when it was raised, and whether omission deprived the other side of a fair opportunity to litigate. Ingraham examines a damages limitation raised only after trial.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 681–683

records.title: Amending pleadings
records.text: Amendment changes a party’s pleading as the case develops. The rules distinguish changes allowed without permission from those requiring consent or leave of court, and address the effect on timing and trial.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–699

records.title: Amending pleadings
records.text: Permission to amend does not itself establish that an otherwise late claim relates back. Nor does a change in proof automatically show consent to try a new issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–699

records.title: Amending pleadings
records.text: Amendment changes a party’s pleading as the case develops. The rules distinguish changes allowed without permission from those requiring consent or leave of court, and address the effect on timing and trial.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–699

records.title: Amending pleadings
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the stage, the proposed change, delay, good faith, prejudice, and whether the amendment would be legally futile. Beeck considers withdrawal of an admission; Krupski concerns relation back after the limitations period.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 688–699

records.title: Relation back of an amended claim or party
records.text: Relation back treats a qualifying amendment as connected to the original pleading for limitations purposes. Different provisions govern changed allegations and changed defendants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 694–699

records.title: Relation back of an amended claim or party
records.text: Krupski focuses on the correct defendant’s understanding. It does not eliminate the other conditions or equate a deliberate choice between correctly understood defendants with a mistake.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 694–699

records.title: Relation back of an amended claim or party
records.text: Relation back treats a qualifying amendment as connected to the original pleading for limitations purposes. Different provisions govern changed allegations and changed defendants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 694–699

records.title: Relation back of an amended claim or party
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the transaction described originally, the nature of the change, and the applicable route under Rule 15(c). For a changed defendant, examine timely notice, prejudice, and whether the prospective defendant knew or should have known that a mistake explained the omission.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 694–699

records.title: Issues tried by consent
records.text: An issue not stated in the pleadings may become part of the case when the parties expressly or impliedly consent to trying it. The evidence and conduct of the parties must support that conclusion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Issues tried by consent
records.text: The mere admission of evidence relevant to two issues does not automatically add an unpleaded claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Issues tried by consent
records.text: An issue not stated in the pleadings may become part of the case when the parties expressly or impliedly consent to trying it. The evidence and conduct of the parties must support that conclusion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Issues tried by consent
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify what additional issue was actually litigated and what notice the opponent had. In Moore, evidence already relevant to child-related issues did not necessarily show consent to try a separate spousal-support claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 692–694

records.title: Factual responsibility, verification, and sanctions
records.text: Certification and verification requirements attach responsibility to statements submitted to the court. Sanctions can enforce that responsibility but require the applicable substantive standard and procedural protections.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–716

records.title: Factual responsibility, verification, and sanctions
records.text: Losing a claim does not itself prove sanctionable conduct. A genuine investigation and reasonable reliance matter, and the safeguards in Hadges remain separate from the underlying merits.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–716

records.title: Factual responsibility, verification, and sanctions
records.text: Certification and verification requirements attach responsibility to statements submitted to the court. Sanctions can enforce that responsibility but require the applicable substantive standard and procedural protections.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–716

records.title: Factual responsibility, verification, and sanctions
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Distinguish derivative-action verification in Surowitz from Rule 11 certification and the court’s other sanctions authority. Identify the document, factual or legal inquiry, alleged misconduct, notice, and procedure for imposing a sanction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 699–716

records.title: Rule 11’s safe-harbor procedure
records.text: The safe-harbor mechanism gives a party an opportunity to withdraw or correct challenged material before an opponent’s Rule 11 motion is filed with the court. It is a procedural condition on that route to sanctions.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713
Rule 11. Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Sanctions · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 31 of 354

records.title: Rule 11’s safe-harbor procedure
records.text: Different sanctions mechanisms have different procedures. The full rule and its exceptions are in the supplement (Rule 11, PDF page 31), linked below; a general allegation of bad faith does not excuse identifying the correct authority.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713
Rule 11. Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Sanctions · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 31 of 354

records.title: Rule 11’s safe-harbor procedure
records.text: The safe-harbor mechanism gives a party an opportunity to withdraw or correct challenged material before an opponent’s Rule 11 motion is filed with the court. It is a procedural condition on that route to sanctions.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713
Rule 11. Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Sanctions · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 31 of 354

records.title: Rule 11’s safe-harbor procedure
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify whether sanctions are sought by a party’s motion or another authority, whether the motion was properly separated and served, and whether the required opportunity to correct was provided. Hadges illustrates why these conditions matter.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 706–713
Rule 11. Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Sanctions · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 31 of 354

records.title: Joining claims and parties
records.text: Joinder determines which claims and persons can be included in one action. Different devices govern multiple claims, counterclaims, crossclaims, additional defendants, required parties, interpleader, and intervention.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–799

records.title: Joining claims and parties
records.text: Permission to combine matters does not make all jurisdictional requirements disappear. Nor does joinder mean all issues must be tried together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–799

records.title: Joining claims and parties
records.text: Joinder determines which claims and persons can be included in one action. Different devices govern multiple claims, counterclaims, crossclaims, additional defendants, required parties, interpleader, and intervention.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–799

records.title: Joining claims and parties
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify who is asserting the claim against whom, the relevant rule, the required factual relationship, and whether joinder is optional or required. Then separately establish subject-matter jurisdiction, personal jurisdiction, service, and venue as applicable.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–799

records.title: Real party in interest
records.text: The real party in interest is the person entitled under the governing substantive law to enforce the right asserted. The inquiry can change when rights are assigned or an insurer becomes subrogated to a claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Real party in interest
records.text: This is distinct from capacity, Article III standing, and permission to join persons. Ellis Canning supplies a state-law example, not the complete federal Rule 17 procedure.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Real party in interest
records.text: The real party in interest is the person entitled under the governing substantive law to enforce the right asserted. The inquiry can change when rights are assigned or an insurer becomes subrogated to a claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Real party in interest
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the underlying right and any transfer or payment affecting who owns it. Distinguish full subrogation from partial payment. Then apply the governing procedural rule about the name in which the action proceeds and any opportunity to cure.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 717–719

records.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party
records.text: Claim joinder allows a party to assert more than one claim against an existing opposing party. Federal Rule 18 provides broad procedural permission even when claims differ in subject or legal theory.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–725

records.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party
records.text: Broad Rule 18 permission does not itself provide supplemental jurisdiction for an unrelated state claim. Earlier code cases such as Harris v. Avery used a narrower transaction framework.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–725

records.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party
records.text: Claim joinder allows a party to assert more than one claim against an existing opposing party. Federal Rule 18 provides broad procedural permission even when claims differ in subject or legal theory.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–725

records.title: Multiple claims against an opposing party
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the existing opposing-party relationship and each proposed claim. Then test jurisdiction and other independent requirements. A court can separate matters for fair or efficient trial even though they may be pleaded together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 720–725

records.title: Counterclaims against an opposing party
records.text: A counterclaim is a claim against an opposing party. Rule 13 distinguishes compulsory claims arising from the relevant transaction or occurrence from permissive claims that may be asserted without that connection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 724–735

records.title: Counterclaims against an opposing party
records.text: A claim’s procedural classification and its jurisdictional basis are separate. The pre-§ 1367 ancillary-jurisdiction cases must be read alongside the later statute.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 724–735

records.title: Counterclaims against an opposing party
records.text: A counterclaim is a claim against an opposing party. Rule 13 distinguishes compulsory claims arising from the relevant transaction or occurrence from permissive claims that may be asserted without that connection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 724–735

records.title: Counterclaims against an opposing party
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the opposing party, the factual relationship, the time the claim existed, and any applicable exception. Then examine jurisdiction. Heyward-Robinson illustrates both the breadth and the disagreement surrounding a logical-relationship approach.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 724–735

records.title: Transaction, occurrence, and related events
records.text: Transaction and occurrence connect events for particular joinder rules. The inquiry often considers their logical and factual relationship rather than requiring identical legal theories or documents.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–747

records.title: Transaction, occurrence, and related events
records.text: Similar language in different rules does not automatically create identical tests, and a useful connection for joinder does not itself establish constitutional or statutory jurisdiction.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–747

records.title: Transaction, occurrence, and related events
records.text: Transaction and occurrence connect events for particular joinder rules. The inquiry often considers their logical and factual relationship rather than requiring identical legal theories or documents.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–747

records.title: Transaction, occurrence, and related events
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: State the events, shared evidence, disputed facts, and practical relationship. Compare the linked construction dealings in Heyward-Robinson and LASA with the asserted common employment policy in Mosley. Identify which rule uses the term.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 725–747

records.title: Crossclaims against a coparty
records.text: A crossclaim is a claim against a coparty, such as one defendant’s claim against another defendant. Rule 13(g) requires the specified connection to the transaction, occurrence, or property involved in the action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–741

records.title: Crossclaims against a coparty
records.text: A crossclaim is distinct from a counterclaim against an opponent and from impleading someone not yet a party. Jurisdiction remains an additional inquiry.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–741

records.title: Crossclaims against a coparty
records.text: A crossclaim is a claim against a coparty, such as one defendant’s claim against another defendant. Rule 13(g) requires the specified connection to the transaction, occurrence, or property involved in the action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–741

records.title: Crossclaims against a coparty
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify why the parties are coparties, what relief is sought, and how the claim relates to the original dispute or a counterclaim. LASA examines connected claims among construction participants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 735–741

records.title: Permissive joinder of parties
records.text: Rule 20 permits multiple plaintiffs or defendants when the claims have the required transaction-or-series connection and share a question of law or fact. It allows related individual claims to proceed in one action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 741–747

records.title: Permissive joinder of parties
records.text: This concerns named parties. Representing absentees requires Rule 23, with its separate certification protections.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 741–747

records.title: Permissive joinder of parties
records.text: Rule 20 permits multiple plaintiffs or defendants when the claims have the required transaction-or-series connection and share a question of law or fact. It allows related individual claims to proceed in one action.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 741–747

records.title: Permissive joinder of parties
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the shared events or asserted policy and the common question. Explain both requirements separately. Mosley shows that differing employment experiences need not defeat joinder when a common discriminatory policy is alleged.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 741–747

records.title: Required parties and Rule 19
records.text: Rule 19 asks whether an absent person should be joined and, if joinder is not feasible, whether the action can fairly proceed without that person. The inquiry protects existing parties, absentees, and the interest in complete resolution.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Required parties and Rule 19
records.text: Indispensable describes the conclusion that dismissal is required after analysis. Provident rejects using the label as a substitute for examining the actual interests and possible protection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Required parties and Rule 19
records.text: Rule 19 asks whether an absent person should be joined and, if joinder is not feasible, whether the action can fairly proceed without that person. The inquiry protects existing parties, absentees, and the interest in complete resolution.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Required parties and Rule 19
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: First identify the need for the person’s participation under Rule 19(a). Then determine feasibility, including jurisdictional obstacles. If joinder is impossible, evaluate prejudice, ways to lessen it, adequacy of the judgment, and the consequences of dismissal under Rule 19(b).

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Protecting persons outside the lawsuit
records.text: A judgment ordinarily does not bind a person who was neither a party nor represented through a recognized exception. Yet litigation can still practically impair an absentee’s interests even without formally binding that person.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Protecting persons outside the lawsuit
records.text: Knowledge of litigation is not itself a universal substitute for party status or adequate representation. Do not convert a reserved issue about possible intervention consequences into an automatic rule.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Protecting persons outside the lawsuit
records.text: A judgment ordinarily does not bind a person who was neither a party nor represented through a recognized exception. Yet litigation can still practically impair an absentee’s interests even without formally binding that person.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Protecting persons outside the lawsuit
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the property, fund, or right at risk; distinguish formal preclusion from practical harm; and consider joinder, intervention, representation, or tailored relief. Provident and Hansberry address different protections for absent persons.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 747–762

records.title: Impleader and potential liability over
records.text: Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 762–766

records.title: Impleader and potential liability over
records.text: A statement that someone else, rather than the defendant, is directly liable to the plaintiff does not by itself establish the required derivative claim. Rule 14 does not create a substantive right to reimbursement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 762–766

records.title: Impleader and potential liability over
records.text: Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 762–766

records.title: Impleader and potential liability over
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the original claim and the substantive source of the proposed third party’s liability to the defendant. Show why that liability depends on or passes through the original claim. Then examine Rule 14’s procedure and the separate jurisdictional requirements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 762–766

records.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation
records.text: Interpleader allows a stakeholder facing competing demands for the same property or obligation to bring the claimants into one proceeding. It protects against inconsistent obligations while providing a process to decide entitlement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–786

records.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation
records.text: Interpleader does not combine all related liabilities into one fund. Tashire limits an injunction to the stakeholder problem rather than permitting control over every accident claim.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–786

records.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation
records.text: Interpleader allows a stakeholder facing competing demands for the same property or obligation to bring the claimants into one proceeding. It protects against inconsistent obligations while providing a process to decide entitlement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–786

records.title: Interpleader: competing demands on one obligation
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the fund or obligation, the competing claimants, and whether the stakeholder faces double payment or multiple liability. Choose between the applicable state procedure, Federal Rule 22, and statutory interpleader, then check that route’s jurisdiction and service requirements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 766–786

records.title: Federal statutory interpleader
records.text: Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–786
28 U.S.C. § 1335. Interpleader · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 150 of 354

records.title: Federal statutory interpleader
records.text: Do not import these special features into Rule 22, which requires its own ordinary subject-matter and personal-jurisdiction basis. The full text of § 1335 is in the Civil Procedure supplement (PDF page 150), linked below.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–786
28 U.S.C. § 1335. Interpleader · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 150 of 354

records.title: Federal statutory interpleader
records.text: Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–786
28 U.S.C. § 1335. Interpleader · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 150 of 354

records.title: Federal statutory interpleader
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Check the statutory amount, diversity among claimants, required deposit or bond, and the relevant service and venue provisions. Potential unliquidated claims can qualify under Tashire, but the scope of protective relief remains limited.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 773–786
28 U.S.C. § 1335. Interpleader · Civil Procedure supplement 2026–27, PDF page 150 of 354

records.title: Sovereign immunity and required parties
records.text: Sovereign immunity can prevent a state or foreign sovereign from being joined in litigation without an applicable exception or waiver. When that sovereign claims an interest in the dispute, its absence also affects the Rule 19 analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Sovereign immunity and required parties
records.text: Rule 19 remains a contextual analysis, but the immunity and sovereign interest can give dismissal unusual force. This is not a rule that every absentee has the same protection as an immune sovereign.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Sovereign immunity and required parties
records.text: Sovereign immunity can prevent a state or foreign sovereign from being joined in litigation without an applicable exception or waiver. When that sovereign claims an interest in the dispute, its absence also affects the Rule 19 analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Sovereign immunity and required parties
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the immunity, the asserted interest, whether joinder is possible, and the practical effect of a judgment without the sovereign. Pimentel shows why a court cannot resolve the sovereign’s property claim against it merely as a preliminary justification for proceeding.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 783–786

records.title: Intervention by a nonparty
records.text: Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–794

records.title: Intervention by a nonparty
records.text: The ability to intervene does not automatically impose a duty to intervene on every informed nonparty. The syllabus assigns the chapter but allocates no classroom time to intervention.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–794

records.title: Intervention by a nonparty
records.text: Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–794

records.title: Intervention by a nonparty
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the applicant’s interest, possible impairment, timeliness, and adequacy of existing representation, or the relevant basis for permissive intervention. Smuck illustrates why a government representative’s broad responsibilities may leave particular interests insufficiently represented.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 787–794

records.title: Joinder, consolidation, and separate trials
records.text: A court can coordinate related litigation or separate issues for trial without treating every procedural unit as one merged claim. These management choices seek efficiency while limiting prejudice and confusion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 794–799

records.title: Joinder, consolidation, and separate trials
records.text: A shared courtroom or pretrial process does not necessarily merge separate actions for every purpose. Jurisdiction, appealability, and substantive rights require their own analysis.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 794–799

records.title: Joinder, consolidation, and separate trials
records.text: A court can coordinate related litigation or separate issues for trial without treating every procedural unit as one merged claim. These management choices seek efficiency while limiting prejudice and confusion.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 794–799

records.title: Joinder, consolidation, and separate trials
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Distinguish joining parties and claims in one action, consolidating separate actions, ordering separate trials of issues, and multidistrict coordination. Identify the rule or statute and the effect on party rights and judgments.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 794–799

records.title: Named-party joinder and representative class actions
records.text: Joinder combines claims of persons who are individually parties. A class action allows named representatives to litigate for absentees after satisfying the requirements for legitimate representation.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–885

records.title: Named-party joinder and representative class actions
records.text: Mussat distinguishes a federal Rule 23 class from the mass action in Bristol-Myers. That distinction does not exempt every absentee from every jurisdictional requirement, as TransUnion demonstrates.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–885

records.title: Named-party joinder and representative class actions
records.text: Joinder combines claims of persons who are individually parties. A class action allows named representatives to litigate for absentees after satisfying the requirements for legitimate representation.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–885

records.title: Named-party joinder and representative class actions
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Ask whether each claimant is named and participating or belongs to an absent class. Then identify the procedural question: commonality, personal jurisdiction, standing, venue, or preclusion. The status of absentees varies with the issue.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–885

records.title: Who counts as a party for this question?
records.text: Party status is sometimes context-dependent in representative litigation. Absent class members may be bound by a judgment while receiving different treatment from named parties for other procedural requirements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–890

records.title: Who counts as a party for this question?
records.text: Mussat’s treatment of absentees for one jurisdictional purpose cannot simply be transferred to Article III injury or every other requirement.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–890

records.title: Who counts as a party for this question?
records.text: Party status is sometimes context-dependent in representative litigation. Absent class members may be bound by a judgment while receiving different treatment from named parties for other procedural requirements.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–890

records.title: Who counts as a party for this question?
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Specify the legal consequence at issue rather than relying on the label party alone. Compare standing for damages, citizenship, venue, personal jurisdiction, participation, and the preclusive scope of a class judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 883–890

records.title: Class actions
records.text: A class action allows named parties to litigate on behalf of an adequately defined group of absent persons when the requirements for representative litigation are satisfied. It can make small claims viable and resolve common issues together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 799–804

records.title: Class actions
records.text: A large number of similar claims does not alone justify certification. The full chapter includes both access benefits and risks to absent members or defendants.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 799–804

records.title: Class actions
records.text: A class action allows named parties to litigate on behalf of an adequately defined group of absent persons when the requirements for representative litigation are satisfied. It can make small claims viable and resolve common issues together.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 799–804

records.title: Class actions
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the class and representatives. Apply Rule 23(a)’s prerequisites and a category under Rule 23(b). Then address notice, opt-out rights, representation, jurisdiction, settlement if proposed, and the scope of any binding judgment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 799–804

records.title: Certification and the required showing
records.text: Certification is the court’s decision that a proposed group and its representatives satisfy the legal conditions for class treatment. It requires analysis of the applicable Rule 23 requirements, not simply acceptance of a class label.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–833

records.title: Certification and the required showing
records.text: Wal-Mart requires rigorous analysis even where an issue overlaps the merits. Eisen does not prohibit all merits-related examination necessary for certification.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–833

records.title: Certification and the required showing
records.text: Certification is the court’s decision that a proposed group and its representatives satisfy the legal conditions for class treatment. It requires analysis of the applicable Rule 23 requirements, not simply acceptance of a class label.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–833

records.title: Certification and the required showing
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Examine numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequacy, then the requested Rule 23(b) category. Identify the evidence capable of proving the shared issues and whether certification can be decided without resolving unnecessary merits questions.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–833

records.title: Commonality under Rule 23(a)(2)
records.text: Commonality requires a common contention capable of producing an answer central to the claims together. A shared label, protected status, or citation to the same statute does not necessarily supply that common answer.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–822

records.title: Commonality under Rule 23(a)(2)
records.text: Commonality and predominance are separate requirements. The Wal-Mart dissent objected that the majority demanded too much at the commonality stage.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–822

records.title: Commonality under Rule 23(a)(2)
records.text: Commonality requires a common contention capable of producing an answer central to the claims together. A shared label, protected status, or citation to the same statute does not necessarily supply that common answer.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–822

records.title: Commonality under Rule 23(a)(2)
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the disputed contention and the proof that could resolve it across the class. Explain whether a single policy, practice, or event connects the individual claims. Use Wal-Mart’s disagreement to test the proposed connection.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 810–822

records.title: Predominance in damages classes
records.text: Predominance asks whether common questions are sufficiently important and cohesive relative to individual questions for the proposed Rule 23(b)(3) treatment. It is more demanding than the presence of one shared question.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 828–834

records.title: Predominance in damages classes
records.text: Predominance is not a simple numerical count of shared and individual questions. Settlement removes trial-manageability concerns, but does not erase this separate requirement.

records.text: Predominance asks whether common questions are sufficiently important and cohesive relative to individual questions for the proposed Rule 23(b)(3) treatment. It is more demanding than the presence of one shared question.

records.title: Predominance in damages classes
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the elements requiring proof, what can be established commonly, and which issues require individual adjudication. Consider variation in causation, injury, defenses, and governing law. Amchem shows why a common interest in settlement does not replace this assessment.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 828–834

records.title: Adequate representation
records.text: Adequate representation protects absentees by requiring representatives and counsel capable of pursuing the class’s interests without disqualifying conflicts. It is central to the legitimacy of binding people who do not appear individually.

records.title: Adequate representation
records.text: A representative’s assurance of fairness does not itself resolve a fundamental allocation conflict. Subclasses with appropriate independent representation may be necessary, depending on the setting.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 804–810

records.title: Adequate representation
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify whose interests the representatives advance, any materially different groups within the class, and counsel’s ability and incentives. Hansberry addresses opposing interests; Amchem and Ortiz require structural protection for conflicting claimant groups.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 804–810

records.title: Class-wide injunctive or declaratory relief
records.text: Rule 23(b)(2) concerns a defendant’s action or refusal to act on grounds generally applicable to a class, making appropriate class-wide injunctive or corresponding declaratory relief.

records.title: Class-wide injunctive or declaratory relief
records.text: The Court did not decide that every incidental monetary remedy is categorically excluded. Individualized damages can require the different safeguards of Rule 23(b)(3).

records.text: Rule 23(b)(2) concerns a defendant’s action or refusal to act on grounds generally applicable to a class, making appropriate class-wide injunctive or corresponding declaratory relief.

records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the conduct and the remedy, and explain whether the relief operates on the class as a whole. Wal-Mart examines why the individualized backpay claims there did not fit that category.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 831–833

records.title: Identifying the class and its members
records.text: Class identification concerns whether the group is defined so that membership can be determined and the action fairly administered. The readings report disagreement about adding a separate administrative-feasibility requirement.

records.title: Identifying the class and its members
records.text: The Ninth Circuit’s approach differs from the Third Circuit approach discussed in the opinion.

records.title: Identifying the class and its members
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: State objective membership criteria and consider available proof, notice, claims administration, and the defendant’s ability to contest membership. Briseno places feasibility concerns within the express Rule 23 framework rather than adding an independent bar.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 834–840

records.title: Notice and exclusion in class actions
records.text: Class notice informs absentees about the action, their rights, and the effect of participating or remaining in the class. The required method and opportunity to opt out depend on the category and procedural stage.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 840–844

records.title: Notice and exclusion in class actions
records.text: Best practicable notice is not a guarantee that every person actually reads it. Mandatory class categories, certification notice, and settlement notice should not be collapsed into one rule.

records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the class category, whether members can be identified with reasonable effort, what the notice must communicate, who pays, and when an exclusion decision must be made. Compare Eisen’s certification-notice problem with Shutts’s protection of absent damages plaintiffs.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 840–844

records.title: Settlement classes and judicial approval
records.text: A settlement class seeks certification for resolving a controversy by an agreed compromise rather than through a class trial. Certification requirements and review of the settlement’s fairness remain distinct safeguards.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 853–869

records.title: Settlement classes and judicial approval
records.text: A beneficial compromise does not by itself create an adequately represented or cohesive class. Amchem and Ortiz examine different certification categories and should retain their separate tests.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 853–869

records.title: Settlement classes and judicial approval
records.text: A settlement class seeks certification for resolving a controversy by an agreed compromise rather than through a class trial. Certification requirements and review of the settlement’s fairness remain distinct safeguards.

records.title: Settlement classes and judicial approval
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Apply Rule 23(a) and the relevant Rule 23(b) category, identifying any conflicts and need for subclasses. Then evaluate the settlement under the applicable approval procedure. Explain which manageability concerns disappear because no trial is planned and which protections remain.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 853–869

records.title: Mandatory limited-fund classes
records.text: A limited-fund class addresses a situation where separate claims could exhaust a genuinely insufficient fund and impair other claimants’ recovery. Mandatory treatment requires strong justification because class members lack the ordinary damages-class opt-out choice.

records.title: Mandatory limited-fund classes

records.text: Identify and substantiate the fund’s limit, compare it with the competing claims, and examine inclusion and equitable treatment of the affected claimants. Ortiz rejects relying solely on the parties’ negotiated contribution as proof of a limited fund.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 860–864

records.text: Class litigation raises separate questions about subject-matter jurisdiction, Article III injury, personal jurisdiction, and venue. The relevance of absent members differs among these inquiries.

records.title: Jurisdiction in representative litigation
records.text: Certification cannot supply missing jurisdiction, and one decision about absentees’ status cannot be generalized to every requirement.

records.text: Class litigation raises separate questions about subject-matter jurisdiction, Article III injury, personal jurisdiction, and venue. The relevance of absent members differs among these inquiries.

records.text: Identify the jurisdictional basis and the particular requirement. Compare ordinary diversity with CAFA, TransUnion’s concrete-injury requirement for individual damages, Shutts’s protection of absent plaintiffs, and Mussat’s treatment of defendant contacts.

records.text: A properly conducted class judgment can bind absentees, but its preclusive scope depends on the claims and issues actually resolved and on legitimate representation.

records.text: A loss on a class-wide theory is not necessarily a finding that no class member suffered an individual wrong. Inadequate representation also raises an independent barrier to binding absentees.

records.title: Issue preclusion within the assigned materials
records.text: Issue preclusion prevents relitigation of a qualifying issue actually litigated and necessarily determined in an earlier action. It differs from a broader bar on relitigating the same claim.

records.title: Class-action waivers and arbitration
records.text: A class waiver restricts the use of representative or aggregate proceedings, often through an agreement requiring individual arbitration. Its effect can depend on federal arbitration law and the applicable contract defenses.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 890–894

records.text: Preemption occurs when controlling federal law displaces a conflicting state rule. The course encounters it in arbitration, jurisdictional characterization, and enforcement of federal rights.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 890–894

records.text: An ordinary federal defense generally does not itself create federal-question jurisdiction. Do not confuse preemption on the merits with the special removal doctrines discussed in the jurisdiction notes.

records.title: Summary judgment under Rule 56
records.text: Summary judgment decides a claim or defense without trial when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It examines an evidentiary record rather than only a complaint.

records.title: The burden of producing evidence
records.text: The production burden requires enough evidence to permit a reasonable factfinder to decide an issue for the party who must prove it. At summary judgment, the movant also has an initial procedural responsibility to support the motion.

records.text: A bare assertion that the opponent has no evidence is insufficient. Meeting the production threshold also does not guarantee persuasion at trial.

records.text: The persuasion burden determines how convincingly a party must establish its claim or defense to the factfinder. The assigned discussion distinguishes preponderance, clear and convincing evidence, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

records.title: The trial standard of proof
records.field: sections.How to work through the question
records.text: Identify the applicable standard for the particular issue. Under Anderson, use it to ask whether a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant; do not replace the jury by deciding whether the judge personally believes the evidence.

atlasSources.label: Civil Procedure casebook, printed pp. 1027–1029

records.title: Reasonable inferences and credibility
records.text: An inference is a conclusion drawn from evidence about an unobserved or disputed fact. At summary judgment, reasonable favorable inferences belong to the nonmovant, while credibility and weight generally remain for trial.

records.title: Reasonable inferences and credibility
records.text: Favorable treatment does not require accepting an account no reasonable factfinder could believe. That limit should not become an excuse to choose the movant’s witnesses in an ordinary genuine dispute.

records.text: The judge determines governing law and whether the evidence meets legal sufficiency requirements; the jury generally decides genuinely disputed facts, credibility, and the weight of evidence in a jury case. The allocation can also become a federal-state question.

records.text: Forum shopping is choosing a court in light of advantages that the forum’s rules, governing law, or procedures may offer. It becomes legally significant when a doctrine seeks to prevent particular incentives or unfair differences.

records.title: 28 U.S.C. § 1332 — diversity and CAFA
records.text:
Determine the citizenship of every relevant party at the legally relevant time. Apply complete diversity where required, identify the amount genuinely in dispute, and check exceptions and statutory restrictions. Treat corporations, unincorporated entities, natural persons, and foreign parties under their respective rules.

Under § 1332(a) the amount in controversy must exceed $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and diversity must be complete: no plaintiff may share a state of citizenship with any defendant (Strawbridge). A corporation is a citizen of every State and foreign state in which it is incorporated and of the State or foreign state where it has its principal place of business (§ 1332(c)(1)). The Class Action Fairness Act, § 1332(d), gives original jurisdiction over class actions with at least 100 proposed class members, more than $5,000,000 in controversy in the aggregate, and minimal diversity (any class member diverse from any defendant), subject to the local-controversy and home-state exceptions.

records.title: 28 U.S.C. § 1406 — improper venue
records.text: When venue is improper, § 1406(a) lets the court dismiss or, if it is in the interest of justice, transfer the case to any district in which it could have been brought. Under § 1406(b) a venue defect is waived if not timely objected to. Contrast § 1404(a), which transfers from a proper venue for convenience; Atlantic Marine holds a forum-selection clause does not make venue improper, so § 1406 is the wrong vehicle for enforcing it.

records.title: Cargo of the Brig Aurora v. United States (1813)
records.text: Congress can pass a law that switches back on when a future event happens, and let the President announce that the event occurred. The ship owner lost because he could not prove the cargo was American.

records.title: Cargo of the Brig Aurora v. United States (1813)
records.text: Congress may exercise its legislative discretion to revive an earlier law either expressly or conditionally, making its operation depend on a future event that the President is to declare by proclamation.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 45–47 · physical PDF pp. 4–6

records.title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark (1892)
records.text: If Congress sets out the condition and what follows from it, the President only has to announce that the condition is met. That is fact-finding, not lawmaking. Also, a signed and filed bill stands even if the journals suggest it passed differently.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 47–52 · physical PDF pp. 6–11

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark (1892)
records.text: Congress does not delegate legislative power when it sets a contingency and its legal consequence and leaves the President to find and proclaim the contingency, any discretion over duration being execution of the law; and a duly authenticated enrolled act cannot be impeached by legislative journals.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 47–52 · physical PDF pp. 6–11

records.title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark (1892)
records.text:
Justice Harlan wrote for the Court and, quoting the Ohio Supreme Court, stated the governing line verbatim: "The true distinction ... is between the delegation of power to make the law, which necessarily involves a discretion as to what it shall be, and conferring authority or discretion as to its execution, to be exercised under and in pursuance of the law."

The same decision announced the enrolled-bill rule: a bill signed by the Speaker and President of the Senate and approved by the President is conclusive evidence of its passage, so courts will not look behind it to the journals.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 47–52 · physical PDF pp. 6–11

records.title: United States v. Grimaud (1911)
records.text: Congress can write the broad rules and let an agency fill in the details, such as permits for grazing sheep in forest reserves. Breaking those rules can be a crime because Congress itself made it one and set the penalty.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 52–56 · physical PDF pp. 11–15

records.reviewStatus: Inventory only; see explanation-audit.json for actual review.

records.title: United States v. Grimaud (1911)
records.text: Once Congress has legislated and indicated its will, it may authorize an administrator to fill in the details within the defined statutory field, and violation of such regulations may be punished as a crime when Congress itself makes the violation an offense and fixes the penalty.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 52–56 · physical PDF pp. 11–15

records.title: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States (1928)
records.text: Congress can let the President adjust tariff rates as long as it gives a clear goal to follow. Here the goal was to make up the difference in production costs between foreign and domestic goods, and that was enough guidance.

records.title: Trump v. Slaughter (2026)
records.text:
The assigned Shane & Bruff supplement is in added-sources (Class 11 - Slaughter Supplement.html); its notes and questions are carried below. The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court (5-4) denied the administration’s request to stay the order in Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook’s favor, stressing the Federal Reserve’s unique historical status.

Questions the editors pose:
• Should Justice Kavanaugh have heeded Judge Kavanaugh's insights and argued for a bright-line differentiation between single-headed and multimember agencies under Article II?
• What would have been the advantages or disadvantages of giving Congress the choice between a single director removable at will and multimember leadership protected against at-will discharge?
• If historical rootedness can save a regulatory agency like the Fed from Article II challenge, why were the precedents for agency independence cited in Slaughter insufficient?
• Don't the Sinking Fund Commission, the Mint Board, the Revolutionary War Debt Commission, and even the First and Second National Banks of the United States, establish a historical tradition of creating independent administrative structures in contexts that 'require some measure of nonpartisan administration'?
• Might not equally compelling concerns counsel exceptions for agencies protecting the integrity of investment markets or the safety of nuclear energy?
• If functionalism is what is driving the Supreme Court's Federal Reserve exception, is the Court threatening to 'pass the line which circumscribes the judicial department, and to tread on legislative ground'?
• Would Perkins also cover an agency economist, statistician, epidemiologist, or other professional, whose advice may influence the making of policy, as long as they have 'no power to render a final decision on behalf of the United States unless permitted to do so by other Executive officers'?
• Do the implications of Slaughter for inferior officers depend upon whether there actually exist civil servants who exercise 'policymaking or administrative authority' but may still be considered 'inferior'? Who might such officers be?
• Would default rules allowing multimember commissions to act as long as any duly qualified members are present be good policy?
• Should there be a judicial remedy to prevent presidents from firing all of a commission's members? What would such a remedy look like?
• What if the revisionist historical work is sufficient to at least cast significant doubt on the soundness of unitarian originalism?
• Should changes in historical understanding weaken the case for stare decisis as applied to cases that relied on a questionable historical narrative to justify their outcomes?
• Does the very nature of historical investigation, which tends to surface more nuance and ambiguity than bright-line consensus, mean that courts should generally treat separation of powers disputes as political, rather than justiciable?
• Do you think Story was alarmist or prescient in his anxiety about an unlimited removal power?

Key line: Applying this intelligible principle test to congressional delegations, our jurisprudence has been driven by a practical understanding that in our increasingly complex society, replete with ever changing and more technical problems, Congress simply cannot do its job absent an ability to delegate power under broad general directives. (Justice Blackmun)

Citation: 488 U.S. 361 (1989).

records.title: INS v. Chadha (1983)
records.text: The House could not reverse Chadha’s deportation suspension through a one-House veto. That change to legal rights outside Congress was legislative and required passage by both chambers and presentment to the President, subject to the Constitution’s express exceptions. Presentment does not always require the President’s signature: a veto can be overridden.

records.text: An enabling statute is legislation that creates or authorizes an agency’s powers, purposes, and jurisdiction.

records.title: Enabling statutes and the source of agency power
records.text:
An agency must identify statutory authority for the action it takes. Congress may specify exact factual triggers and outcomes, or permit judgment under broader standards. The statute supplies both an operational instruction and a claimed source of democratic legitimacy. Grimaud illustrates how a general forest-protection policy can support detailed use regulations while leaving punishment to Congress.

The editors caution that describing Congress as principal and the agency as agent simplifies a more complicated relationship: agencies can develop initiatives and seek legislative support, while Congress can enact highly specific requirements or broader delegations under different political conditions. More administrative discretion does not necessarily mean more regulation. Statutory authorization, the validity of the delegation, and the legality of a particular exercise are separate questions.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 45–52 · physical PDF pp. 4–11

records.title: Conditional legislation and executive fact-finding
records.text:
Begin by identifying the consequence Congress fixed, the condition that activates it, and the discretion involved in determining that condition. Brig Aurora accepts revival of trade restrictions when the President proclaims the relevant foreign-policy event. Field applies the idea to reciprocal trade treatment and tariffs that Congress itself specified.

The difficult question is whether the apparent condition embeds an unresolved policy choice. Field’s separate opinion treats judgments of unreasonable foreign treatment and the just duration of a suspension as legislative, while the majority treats them as administration. The category supplies an analytical distinction; the label fact-finding does not resolve how much discretion the statute actually grants.

records.title: Policy choices and administrative details
records.text:
Grimaud uses the need for local and seasonal forest-management judgments to explain why Congress may authorize implementing rules. The responsibility to choose the governing subject, goal, and legal consequences remains central to that explanation. Gorsuch’s Gundy dissent would place greater weight on the distinction between Congress’s policy decisions and an administrator’s details.

The post-Gundy note asks whether the category can be applied consistently. Deciding whether a worker is an employee may require factual findings, legal interpretation, and a policy choice affecting a large workforce at once. An account that calls every consequential judgment a detail risks making the limit empty; an account that permits only facts devoid of judgment would threaten much ordinary administration. These are questions posed by the editors, not additional holdings of Gundy.

records.title: The intelligible-principle test
records.text:
Identify the delegated task by interpreting the whole statute, then assess the guidance Congress imposed. Hampton names the formulation and upholds bounded tariff adjustments. Schechter rejects an exceptionally broad economic code-making power with little meaningful guidance. Yakus, Whitman, and the Gundy plurality illustrate the willingness to accept substantial discretion when statutory purposes, defined subjects, and standards constrain it.

A statute need not mechanically dictate every outcome. Whitman explains that the amount of acceptable discretion varies with the breadth of the authority, and that voluntary agency restraint cannot repair a constitutional failure by Congress. Gundy also shows the importance of opinion alignment: the judgment sustained the statute, but only four Justices joined Kagan’s full statutory and constitutional explanation.

records.title: Assessing the scope as well as the specificity of a delegation
records.text:
Guidance concerns the criteria an administrator must use; scope concerns the regulated parties, activities, and range of legal obligations the administrator may impose. Whitman expressly recognizes that a broader delegation calls for greater guidance. Coglianese’s assigned argument uses this distinction to reconcile Schechter with later cases sustaining broadly worded standards.

On that account, authority over nearly every industry and economic practice differs from authority over air pollution even when both have economy-wide consequences. Coglianese acknowledges difficulty fitting Panama Refining into the explanation. The dimensional approach is an attributed scholarly interpretation of the cases, not a separately adopted universal test.

records.title: Agency self-restraint and a defective delegation
records.text:
Whitman distinguishes interpretation of the power Congress actually granted from an agency’s discretionary choice to exercise only part of that power. Courts determine whether the statute supplies sufficient guidance. If Congress left a constitutionally impermissible legislative choice open, the agency cannot cure the problem by choosing its own limiting rule.

Amalgamated Meat Cutters describes subsidiary administrative standards as supporting accountability and consistency under a validly construed statute. That practical role does not establish that administrative rulemaking can repair an unconstitutional transfer of legislative power. The comparison therefore requires attention to whether the statutory guidance already exists.

records.text: Constitutional avoidance favors an available statutory reading that avoids serious constitutional doubt.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 71 · physical PDF pp. 28–28

records.title: Constitutional avoidance in defining delegated power
records.text:
The technique operates through interpretation before invalidation. Amalgamated Meat Cutters resists the union’s claim that Congress authorized arbitrary and unfair administration, relying on statutory purpose and constitutional concerns. Whitman supplies a limit: a court may choose only among readings the text can reasonably bear.

A constitutional concern cannot justify inserting cost consideration into a provision that unambiguously directs a health-based standard. Separately determine the plausible statutory readings, the constitutional difficulty, and whether the proposed reading genuinely resolves it. An explanation should identify which step is doing the work rather than use avoidance as a conclusion.

records.title: Administrative discretion and legal and political accountability
records.text:
Legal accountability may come from statutory standards, required reasons, administrative procedures, and judicial review. Political accountability may come from elections, appointment and removal, legislative oversight, and renewed authorization. Their effectiveness depends on timing, information, institutional capacity, and the distribution of responsibility.

Amalgamated Meat Cutters relies on temporary authorization and review but is followed by doubts about how an emergency program could actually be supervised. Gorsuch’s Gundy dissent worries that delegation lets Congress and the Executive exchange blame. Mashaw argues that discretion can make government responsive to presidential elections when new legislation is hard to enact. Arthrex emphasizes visible responsibility through superior review of agency adjudication, while its dissenters emphasize expertise and protection against political interference. These mechanisms involve different institutional tradeoffs.

records.title: The Appointments Clause and permissible appointing actors
records.text:
The default method is presidential nomination and appointment with Senate advice and consent. Congress may by law vest appointment of inferior officers in the President alone, courts of law, or department heads. The initial classification asks whether the position is an office rather than employment; the next asks whether the officer is principal or inferior.

Buckley excludes congressional leaders and an additional House confirmation requirement from the permitted methods for officials exercising significant federal authority. Freytag addresses what qualifies as a court of law or department. Morrison permits interbranch appointment where the arrangement does not impair constitutional functions or create an incongruity between judicial work and the appointment responsibility. Senate consent to an appointment is by simple majority; the two-thirds requirement applies to treaties, not appointments.

records.title: Officers and employees
records.text: An officer exercises significant authority under federal law; an employee is a lesser functionary whose position does not carry the constitutional office status at issue.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 150–154 · physical PDF pp. 80–84

records.title: Officers and employees
records.text:
Buckley connects officer status with significant administration and enforcement of public law. Freytag emphasizes an office established by law and substantial adjudicative duties, including discretion over testimony, evidence, and discovery; Lucia applies the comparison to SEC administrative law judges. A continuing legally defined role and the actual authority it carries are therefore central inquiries.

The exact border remains unsettled in the assigned account. The note contrasts a broader originalist proposal covering ongoing statutory duties with the Court’s significant-authority approach, and points out historical complications involving deputies and apparently ministerial officials. Congress’s label for a position alone does not answer the constitutional question.

records.title: Principal and inferior officers
records.text:
Morrison considers removal by a higher official, limited duties, limited jurisdiction, and temporary tenure. Edmond centers on direction and supervision by Senate-confirmed officers, including administrative control and executive appellate review. Arthrex holds that final patent adjudications insulated from principal-officer review were incompatible with the appointment method used for the administrative patent judges.

These decisions should be compared on their actual institutional arrangements. Neither Edmond nor Arthrex announces an exclusive criterion covering every office, and Arthrex expressly limits its supervision discussion to the adjudicative context presented. Being lower on an organizational chart is relevant but does not alone establish that constitutionally sufficient supervision exists.

records.title: New duties that are germane to an existing office
records.text: Germane duties are responsibilities sufficiently related to an existing office that assigning them does not require a new constitutional appointment.

atlasSources.label: lrs-september(2).pdf · printed pp. 154–155 · physical PDF pp. 84–85

records.title: New duties that are germane to an existing office
records.text:
Shoemaker permits already commissioned engineering officers to take related park-development responsibilities. Weiss applies the principle to commissioned military officers assigned judicial duties within the military justice system. The inquiry concerns the relationship between the old office and the added functions.

This doctrine also protects the appointments process against circumvention. Congress can define and enlarge an office’s duties, but a purported assignment of unrelated responsibilities to a known incumbent may function as selection for a new office. The assigned cases uphold related duties; they do not authorize Congress to fill any new office by attaching it to a chosen person’s existing job.
