records.title: Vermont Yankee, statutory interpretation, and administrative common law
records.text:
The historical introduction describes judicial efforts to require limited trial-type procedures in technically complex rulemakings. Mobil Oil reasoned that an adversarial opportunity was necessary to create evidence substantial enough for rate review even without formal rulemaking. Vermont Yankee rejected general judicial authority to add preferred procedures, but retained review of the rule’s support. The notes ask whether challenging deficient evidence differs meaningfully from demanding more opportunities to test it.

In American Radio Relay League, the D.C. Circuit required fuller disclosure of staff studies under Portland Cement. Then-Judge Kavanaugh accepted binding circuit precedent but argued separately that the requirement lacked a basis in § 553’s text and conflicted with Vermont Yankee. He also criticized the cumulative procedural and substantive demands imposed through expanding arbitrary-and-capricious review. His criticism did not erase the panel’s holding.

Ronald Levin defends evolving APA interpretation as a response to the transformation of agency rulemaking. He points to Supreme Court recognition of logical outgrowth, review on an administrative record, and responses to significant comments despite spare statutory language. His account treats the boundary between interpretation and extra-statutory procedure as contested. The reading also notes that agencies themselves may choose oral workshops and additional participation. Distinguishing Congress’s requirements, judicial interpretation, constitutional minima, and voluntary agency choices prevents the debate from collapsing into an absolute ban on every procedure beyond § 553’s literal words.

records.text:
Key line: But where a specific duty is assigned by law, and individual rights depend upon the performance of that duty, it seems equally clear that the individual who considers himself injured, has a right to resort to the laws of his country for a remedy. (Chief Justice Marshall)

Citation: 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803).

Cornell LII Wex on this case (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/marbury_v_madison_(1803)): Marbury v. Madison (1803) was the U.S. Supreme Court case that established the Supreme Court’s power of judicial review. (Read the opinion here). After President John Adams lost the 1800 election, but before he left office, he appointed Marbury as a justice of the peace and signed the commission. Soon thereafter, Thomas Jefferson became President of the United States and refused to allow Secretary of State James Madison to deliver the commission to Marbury. Marbury sued Madison in the Supreme Court to get his commission via a writ of mandamus. Under Justice John Marshall, the Court specifically held that the provision in the 1789 Act granting the Supreme Court the power to issue a writ of mandamus was unconstitutional. More importantly, however, Marshall’s opinion established that the Supreme Court has the authority, under the Supremacy Clause and Article III, § 2 of the Constitution, to review legislative or executive acts and find them unconstitutional, i.e., the power of judicial review. The Court also delineated the limits of the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction, namely, stating that political questions are not reviewable by the federal courts. It also described the limitations on federal courts’ jurisdiction set forth in Article III of the Constitution. While Marbury v. Madison limited federal court’s jurisdiction, it cemented the Court’s status as the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution.  lawsuits-court

records.title: National-security detention and administrative constitutionalism
records.text: The assigned Hamdi and Boumediene comparison shows the difficulty of designing procedures when physical liberty and claimed national-security necessities both carry great weight.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 469–470 · physical PDF pp. 40–41

records.title: National-security detention and administrative constitutionalism
records.text:
The AUMF authorized detention in the setting discussed by Hamdi, but did not itself define every status criterion or hearing procedure. The source places the government’s interest in detaining actual security threats against the detainee’s basic interest in freedom from physical confinement. It describes the divided Court’s use of Mathews to fashion procedural protection, without reproducing the full opinions or each proposed safeguard.

The subsequent narrative describes creation of combatant status review tribunals, a disclaimer of privately enforceable benefits in the establishing order, congressional procedural changes, and restrictions on judicial review. It presents Boumediene as testing whether the combination of tribunal procedures and limited review adequately protected detainees.

Adrian Vermeule’s accompanying observation is that agencies often decide what procedural details constitutional standards require when statutes leave them open, sometimes without meaningful later judicial review. The editors label this administrative constitutionalism. It describes who practically interprets the Constitution during implementation, while leaving the content of constitutional obligations to substantive analysis.

records.title: Study problem: presidential cost priorities and bilingual-education duties
records.text: Test the difference between directing a lawful choice and replacing the criterion Congress required.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-1-100(2).pdf · printed pp. 269–270 · physical PDF pp. 25–26

records.title: Study problem: presidential cost priorities and bilingual-education duties
records.text:
The classroom hypothetical asks what follows if a bilingual-education statute directs an agency to select the educationally most effective program regardless of expense, while the President directs use of the most cost-effective program regardless of educational efficacy. Start with the enacted criterion and identify the factual or policy discretion it leaves. A supervisory instruction that selects within that discretion differs from an instruction that changes the controlling criterion.

Marbury and Kendall support enforcing a lawful mandatory duty; they do not eliminate the need to identify which choices the statute actually settles. Wirt and Taney expose the further institutional question of who may direct discretion assigned to a subordinate. Sierra Club and the OLC regulatory-review memorandum add the possibility of presidential advice or coordination while preserving the officer’s duty to meet the statute. This is a casebook problem, not a decided case.

records.title: Study problem: can a legislature disclaim the property it creates?
records.text: Compare substantive eligibility criteria, a no-entitlement clause, and statutory hearing procedures before deciding whether due process applies.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 484–487 · physical PDF pp. 55–58

records.title: Study problem: can a legislature disclaim the property it creates?
records.text:
The notes ask whether a legislature can prescribe mandatory eligibility criteria while declaring that the law creates no property interest under the Fourteenth Amendment. Identify first whether the operative criteria actually confine administrative discretion. Then determine what the disclaimer is about: unconditional receipt, conditional program funding, or the constitutional effect of individually enforceable eligibility standards.

Barry found no mandatory shelter entitlement and therefore did not need to give the disclaimer independent effect. Weston found mandatory welfare rights and interpreted the federal disclaimer in context. Arnett then presents a distinct question: may a legislature define the substantive right as including only the procedural protections it chose? Rehnquist’s plurality answered in that direction; Powell and Blackmun, joined in rejecting that rationale by the dissenters, treated constitutional procedure as an independent guarantee. These are questions for comparing sources, not a categorical assertion that every disclaimer succeeds or fails.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 484–487 · physical PDF pp. 55–58

records.title: Study problem: a defective record after Vermont Yankee
records.text: A challenger must distinguish an actual defect in a rule’s evidentiary justification from a preference for additional procedures that might reveal a defect.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 702–706 · physical PDF pp. 124–128

records.title: Study problem: a defective record after Vermont Yankee
records.text:
Assume participants wanted cross-examination of a technical study and the agency refused. One proposed argument is that a better hearing might have produced a better record. Another identifies a concrete unresolved flaw in the study that leaves the final rule inadequately supported. The notes ask how these arguments differ after Vermont Yankee.

The decision bars courts from routinely adding preferred procedural devices to § 553, but leaves review of the rule’s justification intact. The substantive argument therefore requires identifying a real deficiency, while an abstract demand for extra procedures may only hypothesize one. Nova Scotia and American Radio Relay raise the adjacent question whether disclosing the critical study is already part of statutory meaningful comment. Kavanaugh and Levin offer opposing accounts of that interpretive boundary. This is a casebook problem, not a decided case.

records.title: Administrative adjudication: varied decisions and layered procedural law
records.text: Administrative adjudication includes high-profile licensing and security decisions, mass benefits systems, and routine permits; no single hearing model fits every determination.

atlasSources.label: lrs-october-1-100(2).pdf · printed pp. 325–328 · physical PDF pp. 48–51

records.title: Administrative adjudication: varied decisions and layered procedural law
records.text:
Adjudication encompasses decisions about particular people, organizations, and situations across a wide range of public programs. The introduction places prominent decisions such as security-clearance revocation and aircraft grounding beside high-volume benefits, immigration, and licensing determinations and routine permits. Public salience is an unreliable measure of the aggregate importance of these decisions.

Procedure comes from several layers: the Constitution, the APA, the organic statute, and agency regulations. The APA’s definitions make adjudication a residual category after rulemaking, but that classification does not automatically require a courtroom-style hearing. Sections 553(c) and 554(a) use separate on-the-record triggers to invoke formal procedures. Congress may supply special hearing regimes, and agencies fill many procedural gaps through regulations. Informal adjudication can involve applications, investigation, negotiation, inspection, and settlement rather than a single evidentiary event.

The editors identify a persistent institutional tension. Individual adversarial process can improve fairness and protect against error, while mass administration requires coherent and workable management. Agencies are also frontline interpreters of procedural constitutional requirements because many disputes never reach courts. The chapter therefore separates the forum’s constitutional permissibility, action classification, statutory hearing requirements, and due-process minima instead of assuming that the label adjudication answers all four.

records.title: Hard-look review and the rulemaking record

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 575–591 · physical PDF pp. 1–17

records.title: Hard-look review and the rulemaking record
records.text:
Hard-look review is judicial examination of whether agency reasoning connects the record, the governing statute, and the choice made. The automobile-safety materials trace its development from APA §§ 553(c) and 706 as broad policy decisions increasingly received direct, pre-enforcement review. A statement of basis and purpose must disclose how the agency handled major issues; an agency need not answer every observation or use a trial’s findings format.

The record in informal rulemaking can include studies, comments, and other material without a trial-type hearing. Its existence does not trigger §§ 556–557. Contemporary explanatory materials can make the rationale intelligible, but the notes warn against relying on later litigation rationalizations or expecting the reviewing court to assemble a rationale itself. The statutory and institutional settings matter: APA review of an agency’s delegated choices demands explanations beyond the minimal constitutional rationality inquiry applied to legislation.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 575–591 · physical PDF pp. 1–17

records.title: Technology-forcing rules and uncertainty
records.text: A technology-forcing rule requires performance that industry may be able to achieve through further development; the agency must explain the prediction.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 613–619 · physical PDF pp. 39–45

records.title: Technology-forcing rules and uncertainty
records.text:
Mashaw and Harfst argue that demanding a presently demonstrable factual basis can impede a statutory program designed to induce future innovation. Their account of NHTSA attributes part, but not all, of its retreat from ambitious standards toward recalls to litigation and the burden of defending predictions. They question the assumption that a remand is a modest intervention: staff reassignment, new leadership, and elapsed time can transform or end a project. They also argue that agencies may present artificially linear explanations of a more experimental decision process. These are attributed institutional critiques, rather than holdings.

The contrasting diesel-emissions decision shows how review can accommodate uncertainty. EPA had to identify the remaining engineering tasks, answer theoretical objections, and give plausible reasons for believing industry could solve the problems within the available lead time. It did not have to supply every engineering solution. Existing prototypes, recent progress, candidate materials, and manufacturers’ projections supported its prediction about trap-oxidizers. The distinction is between an explained prediction suited to the statute’s forward-looking task and unsupported confidence.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 613–619 · physical PDF pp. 39–45

Secretary Coleman’s proposal asks how safety, consumer choice, equity among belt users and nonusers, innovation, and market incentives should interact. A sound analysis first identifies the statutory factors and then tests the evidence and explanation; a preference alone does not answer an objection that the agency ignored its mandate.

records.title: Guidance: policy statements and interpretive rules
records.text: Guidance includes statements of enforcement policy and explanations of existing law; whether notice and comment is required depends on the statement’s legal character and operation.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 626–631 · physical PDF pp. 51–56

records.title: Guidance: policy statements and interpretive rules
records.text:
APA § 553(b)(A) excepts interpretive rules and general policy statements from ordinary notice and comment. Guidance communicates an agency’s interpretation or intended exercise of discretion and can help field personnel and regulated people predict the agency’s position. Publication and disclosure obligations can still apply; exemption from notice and comment does not mean an agency may keep adopted guidance secret.

Pacific Gas describes a policy statement as a tentative announcement whose underlying policy remains open to challenge when applied. Community Nutrition complicates that account: an FDA action level could function as a binding norm by limiting the agency’s own enforcement discretion, even though the agency would still need to prove adulteration in court. Mandatory language, exemptions from an announced norm, and actual practice can reveal binding effect. Regulatory beneficiaries may be harmed by a safe harbor and have no later enforcement proceeding in which to contest it.

The distinction for interpretive rules is related but different. Such a rule explains an existing statute or legislative rule; the inquiry asks whether that existing law supplies the duty or whether the agency is exercising delegated lawmaking power to add one. The materials caution that the tests remain contested and cannot be reduced to a document’s label.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 650–656 · physical PDF pp. 75–81

records.title: Interpretive rules and new legal duties
records.text:
American Mining Congress identifies indicators of legislative action: without the new rule, the agency would lack a sufficient legal basis for enforcement, or the new rule repudiates an existing legislative rule. The notes state that later D.C. Circuit law abandoned publication in the Code of Federal Regulations as a decisive indicator. Absence of an indicator does not settle every case.

Paralyzed Veterans sustained an explanation that wheelchair sightlines had to extend over standing spectators because the interpretation was fairly encompassed by the existing requirement of comparable sightlines. Hoctor rejected an eight-foot big-cat fence requirement as a policy selection that could not be derived by interpreting a general secure-containment rule. Numeric specificity may signal such selection, but the court expressly declined to classify every numerical interpretation as legislative.

Perez rejected the separate rule that an agency must use notice and comment whenever it changes a prior interpretation of its regulation. Section 553 exempts interpretive rules without that carveout. Perez did not resolve the broader, contested boundary between interpretation and legislation. The Paralyzed Veterans change-of-interpretation rule is gone; the question whether a purported interpretation adds a new duty survives.

atlasSources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 660–664 · physical PDF pp. 85–89

records.title: Guidance reform: participation, judicial review, and regulatory beneficiaries
records.text:
Elliott proposes treating an agency’s unpromulgated policy as nonbinding and requiring fresh justification when the agency applies it. The agency could choose between the expense of legislative rulemaking and later case-specific justification. Franklin criticizes this approach because deregulatory guidance may produce no enforcement case in which beneficiaries could contest it. Mendelson also emphasizes that informal processes and enforcement litigation often give regulated parties greater access than beneficiaries. These are competing proposals, not a single judicial test.

Parrillo’s empirical account describes voluntary participation in guidance, including draft publication, stakeholder meetings, and advisory committees. He distinguishes the FDA’s broad guidance procedures from OMB’s narrower economically significant category and explains why guidance consultations generally require lighter analysis and response than legislative rulemaking. Participation can improve information and legitimacy but uses time and staff. Broad procedural mandates can leave documents indefinitely in draft; parties may nevertheless follow them, obscuring whether the agency endorses the text or remains internally divided. Raso’s cited work questions the assumption that agencies systematically choose guidance to evade procedure.

records.title: APA § 553(b)(B): good cause and alternative rulemaking sequences
records.text:
The agency must state its good-cause finding and brief reasons when it issues the rule; counsel cannot first invoke the exception during later litigation. The notes describe different appellate approaches to review of that finding. Time constraints, emergencies, and technical or predetermined changes can support the respective rationales, but classification is subject to review.

Direct final rulemaking conditions an anticipated uncontroversial rule on the absence of adverse comments and promises withdrawal if opposition appears. Interim final rulemaking gives a rule immediate effect while inviting later comments and possible revision. Those procedures have different justifications and consequences. The GAO figures in the reading concern its 2003–2010 sample and do not measure every guidance document.

Hickman and Thomson identify risks that an operative interim rule can harden agency commitment or discourage comments. The materials contrast categorical invalidation of a later rule, acceptance of a completed later notice-and-comment process, and the intermediate judicial open-mind test. Little Sisters rejects that additional procedural test for the final rule; it does not hold that every invocation of good cause for an interim rule is valid.

records.title: The framework for judicial review under the APA
records.text:
The APA supplies an authorization and framework for review; a separate statute supplies subject-matter jurisdiction. Section 702 addresses who may challenge agency action, § 703 the form and venue, § 704 the actions reviewable, and § 706 the reviewing court’s task. Injunctions and declarations are conventional remedies. Agency-specific statutes can create review routes with their own form, timing, and conditions.

Scope of review concerns the intensity and kind of examination. Legal interpretation, factfinding, discretionary policy, and procedural compliance present different questions, even when joined in one case. The introduction explains the institutional tension between enforcing legal limits and preserving the responsibilities assigned to administrators and elected institutions. The assigned questions ask who should be able to enforce public duties and how legal, political, technical, and equitable concerns affect the timing and intensity of review.

records.title: The administrative record and contemporaneous reasons
records.text:
Overton Park’s record requirement affects agency organization: officials anticipating review must assemble information and explain decisions in a way a court can examine. The remand history also shows that record-based review applies when an agency later refuses approval; the Sixth Circuit ultimately rejected a demand that the Secretary identify a particular alternative route before refusing the park route. The editors question how a model of explicit findings captures intergovernmental bargaining and evolving planning.

Chenery’s principle protects the agency’s delegated responsibility: a reviewing court should not adopt a new policy rationale that the agency never selected. Additional explanation may clarify an existing rationale, but supplying a distinct new ground ordinarily requires new agency action. Regents applies that distinction to an agency official’s later memorandum as well as a lawyer’s litigation argument. Department of Commerce adds a distinct issue: an explanation can be facially plausible yet contrived. Exceptional evidence of pretext may justify inquiry beyond the record, while disagreement with policy alone does not warrant routine exploration of motives.

records.title: Substantial evidence, contrary evidence, and standards of review
records.text:
Section 706(2)(E) expressly applies to formal proceedings and other statutorily specified on-the-record hearings; organic statutes may also prescribe substantial-evidence review. Universal Camera requires attention to contrary evidence and examiner findings, while preserving the agency’s authority to choose between fairly conflicting accounts.

The notes illustrate different problems. Allentown Mack upheld the Board’s reasonable-doubt policy but rejected its evidentiary application after important contrary evidence was disregarded. Biestek rejected a categorical rule that a vocational expert’s refusal to disclose supporting data always prevents the testimony from being substantial evidence; reliability remains contextual. Dickinson v. Zurko required the APA approach to agency review rather than importing court-to-court clearly-erroneous review based on an uncertain historical exception. The verbal distinction can be subtle without becoming meaningless.

ADAPSO’s D.C. Circuit approach equates the required quantum of factual support under substantial evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review, while locating that support in different kinds of administrative records. Safe Extensions applied that reasoning to an informal FAA decision treating competing runway-light products differently without supporting evidence. The notes also identify organic-statute decisions that distinguish the standards. The conceptual problem asks whether later judicial convergence can be reconciled with the understanding of the APA’s drafters; it does not assume that historical meaning has already settled the answer.

records.title: Enforcement priorities, resources, and disclosure
records.text:
The introductory materials contrast judicial protection from unlawful coercion with requests that courts stimulate enforcement for regulatory beneficiaries. An agency must allocate staff and money among more possible violations than it can pursue. The FDA examples show that priority-setting can reflect expected health benefits, public anxiety, political attention, and demands generated by emergencies. The historical inspector and budget figures illustrate this constraint and are not presented as current agency staffing.

Disclosure of enforcement criteria promotes predictability and voluntary compliance, but can weaken deterrence or expose compromises that the public finds disturbing. The FDA’s publication of food-contaminant action levels illustrates both effects. The NLRB examples distinguish broad discretion whether to prosecute from a refusal based on a mistaken legal deadline. The SEC no-action cases raise another institutional issue: attaching review only when agency leadership explains or approves a staff choice may discourage internal review and reason-giving.

The packet begins with the final page of a tribal-recognition discussion whose case caption appears outside the supplied assigned range. That passage explains that an agency’s own regulations may supply judicially manageable criteria even in a traditionally political area; merely promulgating a regulation does not suffice if its terms lack usable standards. No case identity or omitted factual history is inferred.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1050–1060 · physical PDF pp. 67–77

records.title: APA § 701(a): preclusion and commitment to discretion
records.text:
Statutory preclusion under § 701(a)(1) asks whether Congress intended to foreclose review. Commitment to discretion under § 701(a)(2) asks whether the governing law supplies meaningful standards for assessing the decision. Possession of some discretion does not itself eliminate review for abuse: Overton Park found enforceable limits, while Chaney identified a presumptively unreviewable category of enforcement refusals.

A statute’s mandatory language and specific enforcement conditions can rebut Chaney’s presumption, as the assigned Dunlop account illustrates. The notes preserve unresolved concerns about a general policy amounting to abdication of statutory responsibilities and explain why merely labeling conduct categorical does not automatically establish reviewability. They distinguish the agency’s choice of remedy after enforcement, which can receive particularly deferential review, from whether review is available at all.

United States v. Texas (2023) illustrates overlap with standing: the Court rejected states’ attempt to compel more immigration arrests under Article III, using institutional concerns similar to those associated with nonreviewability. That standing ruling is a separate threshold doctrine and must not be treated as simply another application of § 701(a)(2).

records.title: Review of petitions for rulemaking: APA §§ 553(e) and 555(e)
records.text:
Section 553(e) permits interested persons to petition for issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule. Section 555(e) generally requires a brief statement of grounds when an agency denies a covered request. Massachusetts v. EPA treats the denial in its statutory setting as reviewable, while distinguishing enforcement refusal and preserving substantial administrative discretion.

American Horse Protection v. Lyng illustrates a developed record: the agency had studied a tentative rule, held meetings, prepared amendments, and acknowledged an apparent inconsistency with later research before declining to proceed. The court remanded for explanation. Later note cases show the limits: absence of applicable standards can still defeat review; where review occurs it may be very deferential, though a failure to address a central safety matter on an empty record can warrant intervention.

The editors pose a statutory question rather than concealing it: a petition can seek to initiate a proceeding rather than arise within one, and the text of § 555(e) refers to requests connected with agency proceedings. They weigh this concern against the broad APA definition of action, including denials and failures to act. A reason-giving obligation does not automatically settle standing, finality, reviewability, or entitlement to a particular substantive rule.

records.title: APA § 706(1): discrete action legally required
records.text:
Norton requires both discreteness and legal obligation. Identifying a mandatory broad statutory goal does not identify a discrete step that the agency must perform. Conversely, identifying a precise desirable step does not establish that the law requires it. A statutory deadline for a decision can support compulsion even though the agency retains authority to decide its substance.

The land-planning notes distinguish challenges to concrete actions inconsistent with an adopted plan from demands to enforce the plan’s projections. They report later agency efforts to describe plans as strategic and aspirational, illustrating how review doctrines can influence agencies’ drafting and planning practices. Finality, ripeness and exhaustion are separate timing limits. The Farmworker Justice Fund v. Brock (D.C. Cir. 1987) opinion, which had ordered OSHA to act on a field-sanitation standard, was withdrawn as moot once OSHA issued the standard.

records.title: Problem: Can the meaning of evidentiary review evolve?
records.text: Kenneth Culp Davis described a shift from treating substantial evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review as materially different to treating their evidentiary demands as equivalent. The note asks whether a modern court may follow that later understanding if the original understanding differed. A response should separate the historical claim, the statutory text and structure, the role of precedent, and the institutional reasons for convergence. The question remains an interpretive problem in the assigned text.

records.text: An agency changing policy must acknowledge the change, explain its reasons, and address contrary prior findings and serious reliance when they matter.

records.title: Changing agency policy and reliance interests
records.text:
Fox permits policy change without a categorical requirement to prove the new policy superior in court. The agency must nevertheless account for the circumstances of change: its own contrary factual findings and serious reliance on its prior position can require a fuller explanation. Regents applies that principle even where an earlier memorandum disclaimed substantive rights; the disclaimer bears on the strength of reliance and does not excuse failing to consider it.

The notes distinguish several inquiries. Political supervision can influence policy within the statutory mandate, while pressure to consider forbidden factors remains problematic. Constitutional review remains available independently of APA reason-giving, as the later Fox fair-notice decision illustrates. Whether a court is assessing an agency’s process or reweighing its policy can be difficult at the boundary; the editors present that institutional concern without discarding the legal obligation to provide reasons.

records.title: Persuasive weight of agency interpretations under Skidmore
records.text:
The inquiry evaluates the interpretation’s thoroughness, reasoning, consistency, relevant expertise, and other features that make it persuasive. The agency’s official responsibilities may produce knowledge useful to judges and litigants, even where the interpretation did not emerge from a formal adversarial adjudication. An agency interpretation does not become controlling merely because the agency issued it. Skidmore illustrates the distinction with the Administrator’s assessment of fire-hall employees’ sleeping, eating, and other on-call time. (Printed 930–932.)

Loper Bright retains this source of guidance while requiring independent statutory interpretation. Its majority specifically notes the potential value of interpretations adopted near enactment and maintained over time. The assigned notes ask whether that emphasis narrows or simply elaborates the broader Skidmore formulation; they do not resolve that question. Courts also must distinguish persuasive interpretation from an agency’s exercise of actual delegated policy discretion. (Printed 945, 963.)

Kisor adds a separate comparison. Chief Justice Roberts regarded many circumstances justifying deference to an agency’s own regulation as similar to circumstances making the agency persuasive, but explicitly maintained the difference between persuasion and a conditional obligation to defer. A study answer should identify the relevant source of law and the review method before applying a generic label such as “deference.” (Printed 995–996.)

records.title: The historical Chevron framework and its limits
records.text:
The first step asked whether Congress had directly answered the precise issue. Courts used traditional interpretive tools to identify that answer and rejected contrary agency constructions. The second step applied when statutory silence or ambiguity remained: a permissible agency reading could govern even if the court preferred another reading. Chevron’s own dispute concerned EPA’s plantwide definition of stationary source. The casebook situates this formulation in the opinion’s context and explains that its later doctrinal influence exceeded the Court’s initially modest treatment of the case. (Printed 933–935.)

Later decisions determined the framework’s domain and effects. Mead asked whether Congress had delegated authority to act with the force of law and whether the agency interpretation exercised it; sufficiently formal procedures often signaled that authority. Brand X permitted a qualifying agency interpretation to displace an earlier judicial reading that had not found the statute unambiguous. King v. Burwell withheld deference on a question of extraordinary significance and independently adopted the agency’s interpretation. These examples show distinct threshold, precedent, and significance questions. (Printed 936–938.)

Loper Bright rejected the premise that ambiguity alone establishes delegation and required the court’s best interpretation. The assigned notes distinguish cases previously resolved at Chevron step one, discretionary policy choices under flexible grants, and former step-two disputes in which an agency had selected a permissible reading different from the court’s best one. The methodological change is clearest in that last category. Earlier decisions upholding specific agency actions remain subject to statutory stare decisis. (Printed 952–953, 963–966.)

records.title: Independent judicial interpretation after Loper Bright
records.text:
A reviewing court first asks whether the challenged action falls within the statute’s authority. Under Loper Bright’s reading of APA § 706, the court uses traditional interpretive tools to reach the best statutory reading. It may draw on an agency’s informed interpretation, but statutory ambiguity alone does not transfer the choice of meaning to the agency. The majority treats this as the legal task Congress assigned to reviewing courts. (Printed 943–949, 953.)

The court must separately identify discretion that the statute actually confers. An express instruction for the agency to define a term, an authorization to fill details, or language allowing a reasonable or appropriate policy choice can grant real decisionmaking room. The court identifies its extent and tests whether the agency exercised it through reasoned decisionmaking. This preserves the separate operation of State Farm review over policy choices within the statutory boundaries. (Printed 945–946, 950, 963–964.)

The opinions disagree about both history and institutional capacity. Kagan maintains that some ambiguities leave policy choices that agencies are better equipped and more accountable to make, and that § 706 does not command de novo review. The majority responds that expertise can inform a court and that legal interpretation remains judicial even in technical disputes. The majority’s statutory holding leaves constitutional questions about legislatively specified standards of review for further analysis; Thomas’s concurrence would impose a constitutional restriction as well. (Printed 949–960, 961–963.)

records.title: Finding and reviewing delegated agency discretion
records.text: Delegated discretion is a range of choices that Congress has authorized an agency to make within statutory boundaries.

records.title: Finding and reviewing delegated agency discretion
records.text:
The reviewing court determines the legal boundaries of that range. Loper Bright identifies express delegations to define terms, authority to fill details, and flexible standards such as reasonable or appropriate as examples of statutes that can authorize agency choices. The agency must then choose within the range and give the reasoned explanation required by the APA. The court’s independent interpretation of the boundary coexists with deferential review of the agency’s permitted policy judgment. (Printed 945–946, 950.)

This distinction explains both continuity and change after Chevron. The earlier doctrine presumed delegation from unresolved ambiguity more broadly. Loper Bright requires an independent legal finding that the statute actually assigns discretion. The casebook’s proposed framework suggests that clear statutory answers and genuine open-ended policy grants may produce continuity, while former step-two choices between alternative legal meanings change decisionmaker. The authors present that as an analytical framework, not as a holding quantifying how many cases will change. (Printed 963–964.)

West Virginia adds the requirement of clear authorization for the extraordinary power at issue there. Kisor separately addresses interpretations of agency regulations and requires a contextual inquiry into whether deference is justified. Kavanaugh’s Kisor concurrence describes a reasonable policy choice within an open-ended regulation as a State Farm issue. These doctrines interact, but a classification as agency discretion does not itself establish the scope of the statute, the validity of a regulation, or the adequacy of the reasons given. (Printed 972–975, 999–1000.)

records.title: The major questions doctrine
records.text:
West Virginia describes a contextual trigger involving the history and breadth of the claimed authority and its economic and political significance. Novel assertions under long-existing or ancillary provisions, transformative regulatory consequences, and a poor fit with the agency’s customary responsibilities can prompt the inquiry. The majority required more than a plausible textual basis for EPA’s generation-shifting program and found the necessary clear authorization absent. These are contextual considerations rather than a numerical threshold for how much money, novelty, or controversy makes a question major. (Printed 972–975.)

The assigned materials trace two different uses. King v. Burwell withheld Chevron deference but independently upheld the challenged interpretation. West Virginia applied a narrowing construction and rejected the agency’s program. The casebook then compares student debt relief, OSHA’s broad workplace vaccination-or-testing standard, healthcare-facility vaccination, and the CDC eviction moratorium. The healthcare case illustrates that a consequential action can receive different treatment depending on its statutory and institutional setting. (Printed 937–938, 966, 980–982.)

A separate entry explains the competing justifications. Roberts refers to both separation of powers and likely congressional intent; Gorsuch links the requirement to nondelegation; Barrett understands it as ordinary contextual inference; Kagan challenges a special clear-statement requirement that narrows Congress’s broad language. Those positions should remain attributed. The readings do not supply one uncontested explanation of the doctrine’s legitimacy or exact boundaries. (Printed 977–983.)

records.title: Competing rationales for major questions review
records.text: The assigned opinions disagree whether major questions review protects a constitutional allocation of power, draws a contextual inference about delegation, or improperly narrows broad statutory language.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 973–983 · physical PDF pp. 29–39

records.title: Competing rationales for major questions review
records.text:
Justice Gorsuch’s West Virginia concurrence, summarized in the notes, treats the doctrine as a clear-statement principle supporting Article I’s placement of legislative power in Congress. He links it to nondelegation and to narrow constructions that avoid constitutionally doubtful transfers of power. The authors ask whether that logic should make its reach track the underlying nondelegation concern, including Gorsuch’s attention to coercion of private conduct. They ask how a benefits case such as student loan relief fits that account. (Printed 982.)

Justice Barrett’s Biden v. Nebraska concurrence gives a different explanation. She treats the scale of the delegation as part of ordinary communicative context: what would a principal reasonably be understood to authorize an agent to do? She expresses concern about strong substantive canons that displace a statute’s natural meaning. Constitutional structure is part of context in her approach, while a separate clear-statement rule to enforce nondelegation goes further than her justification. (Printed 982–983.)

Justice Kagan’s West Virginia dissent argues that broad language can deliberately enable important regulatory action in response to unforeseen problems. On her reading, the earlier cases involved mismatches between agency expertise, claimed power, and statutory structure. EPA’s regulation of power-plant pollution presented no comparable mismatch. She therefore objects to a separate clear-authorization hurdle. The majority instead reads the same precedents as a distinct approach for extraordinary assertions of power. A careful analysis identifies the precise claimed delegation and evaluates how each rationale treats it. (Printed 973–980.)

records.title: Auer deference after Kisor
records.text: Kisor permits deference to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of its own genuinely ambiguous regulation only after the court establishes demanding legal and institutional prerequisites.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 989–1002 · physical PDF pp. 45–58

records.title: Auer deference after Kisor
records.text:
The court must first exhaust ordinary interpretive tools. Text that is difficult or disputed is not automatically genuinely ambiguous. The agency’s reading must then fall within the reasonable interpretive range that remains. Finally, the court examines the interpretation’s authority, substantive expertise, fairness, considered character, and effect on settled expectations. A convenient litigation position, post hoc rationalization, or unfair surprise can defeat deference. These requirements come from Part II-B, joined by five Justices. (Printed 990–992, 1000.)

The inquiry attends to how the agency speaks. An interpretation need not be issued by the agency head, but must come from actors and procedures understood to establish its authoritative position. A new brief generally does not suffice; the opinion explains the exceptional posture in Auer, where a nonparty agency responded to the Court’s request and the circumstances supported treating its view as considered. A single Board adjudicator’s ruling in Kisor raised an authority question requiring examination on remand. (Printed 991–992.)

Kisor’s defense based on expertise, authorial knowledge, political accountability, and the APA received four votes, while the operative limits and stare decisis ground received five. Roberts distinguished persuasive weight from conditional deference. Gorsuch challenged compatibility with §§ 706 and 553 and constitutional judicial responsibility. The packet’s later notes preserve these disagreements and discuss tension with Loper Bright without treating the two source types as governed by one identical rule. (Printed 993–1002.)

records.title: Statutory interpretation and regulatory interpretation
records.text: The identity of the text matters: Loper Bright addresses statutes enacted by Congress, while Kisor addresses an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations.

records.title: Statutory interpretation and regulatory interpretation
records.text:
The statutory-review question concerns what legal authority Congress supplied. Loper Bright requires independent interpretation while respecting actual delegations and persuasive agency guidance. The regulatory-review question concerns the meaning of a rule made under that authority. Kisor retains conditional Auer deference when a regulation remains genuinely ambiguous and the agency’s reading satisfies the additional prerequisites. The casebook notes treat both as operative and emphasize that Roberts and Kavanaugh distinguished them in Kisor. (Printed 995–996, 1000–1001.)

There is a genuine theoretical tension. Kagan’s four-Justice discussion in Kisor reads § 706 as compatible with deferential interpretation and relies on pre-APA practice. Loper Bright’s majority reads the APA as requiring independent statutory judgment. The authors suggest possible explanations grounded in statutory language or historical practice, practical overlap between Kisor and persuasion, and the possibility of a future challenge. They present alternatives for analysis, not a later overruling. (Printed 1000–1001.)

The final problem asks whether a regulation could expressly entrust future interpretive rules with defining its ambiguous terms, drawing an analogy to an express statutory delegation recognized in Loper Bright. The question raises the agency’s authority to delegate interpretive control, § 553’s procedural distinction, § 706 review, and the separation-of-powers criticism of joining prescription with interpretation. The reading leaves the hypothetical unresolved. (Printed 1002.)

records.title: Questions of law, fact, and mixed application
records.text:
The distinction becomes especially consequential when legal interpretation receives independent review while factfinding and policy choices receive deferential review. Loper Bright’s majority characterizes Gray v. Powell and NLRB v. Hearst Publications as factbound applications within particular delegations. Kagan questions whether that characterization can separate them from much statutory interpretation, because applying a broad statutory category often defines its meaning. (Printed 942–943, 958–959, 965.)

The notes use John Dickinson’s 1927 analysis to challenge the idea of a fixed natural boundary. In his account, policy choices about judicial control can influence whether a court describes an issue as law or fact. This is an attributed scholarly criticism. It does not erase the governing review provisions, nor establish that every classification is arbitrary. It asks the reader to explain what the court is reviewing and why the assigned standard follows. (Printed 965–966.)

Identify the disputed proposition before naming the review standard. Whether herring vessels must carry observers differs from whether the statute permits requiring payment. Whether an employee remained on call differs from how compensable time is defined and applied. Whether an agency has statutory power to regulate differs from whether its chosen policy is supported and reasonably explained. Skidmore, Loper Bright, and the historical Gray/Hearst discussion make these distinctions concrete. (Printed 930–932, 939–950.)

records.title: Stare decisis after a change in interpretive method
records.text:
The majority says that earlier agency-action holdings, including Chevron’s Clean Air Act holding, remain subject to statutory stare decisis. Their use of Chevron alone does not supply the special justification needed to overrule them. At the same time, the Court overrules the general interpretive framework on grounds of poor statutory reasoning, unworkability, and unreliable or destabilizing reliance. Kagan argues for stronger adherence because Congress can correct statutory decisions and actors operated against the framework for decades. (Printed 951–960.)

The notes identify a difficult question about the content of an earlier holding. Brand X distinguished a judicial finding of one permissible reading from a finding that a statute has only one allowable meaning. After Loper Bright, a court’s best reading might differ from the agency interpretation previously upheld as permissible. Whether and how the older holding controls requires analysis; the text does not resolve every possible configuration. (Printed 936–937, 966.)

Kisor provides a comparison. Its five-Justice stare decisis discussion retained a long series of regulatory-interpretation precedents and emphasized settled regulatory constructions. The different outcomes in Kisor and Loper Bright should be assessed through the stated considerations and the source being interpreted, while preserving the disputes among the Justices over the significance of history, workability, and reliance. (Printed 994–1001.)

records.title: Scientific uncertainty and quantitative risk assessment
records.text: The Benzene notes explain why regulatory risk assessment combines incomplete empirical evidence with assumptions and policy judgment.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 984–986 · physical PDF pp. 40–42

records.title: Scientific uncertainty and quantitative risk assessment
records.text:
Evidence that a substance increases cancer incidence at high exposures may not establish the risk at lower current exposures. Long latency can make direct observation impractical. A dose-response curve projects relationships between exposure and harm, but constructing it may require assumptions about thresholds, animal-to-human differences, background illness, actual exposure, and interactions among substances. The supplied discussion notes that benzene experiments and exposure data did not provide a complete empirical answer. (Printed 985.)

The authors describe quantitative risk assessment as a continuing tool because regulators need decisions despite uncertainty and lack better alternatives. They characterize Benzene as making the method effectively obligatory in later health-regulation disputes. The question then often becomes whether a particular assessment is plausible, adequately supported, and reasonably explained. Their cited Hodgson and American Petroleum Institute decisions recognize the role of policy judgment at the limits of scientific knowledge while retaining review for arbitrary or capricious action. (Printed 985–986.)

This reading supports a distinction between statutory authority, required findings, evidence, and policy choice. A court may independently determine that the statute requires a finding of significant risk, while assessing the agency’s technical judgment through the appropriate review framework. Uncertainty does not itself prove either that regulation is legally forbidden or that any protective measure is authorized.

records.title: What the assigned empirical studies say about Chevron
records.text:
Eskridge and Baer’s study examined 1,014 Supreme Court cases from the 1983 through 2005 Terms involving agency statutory interpretations. The quoted account reports express Chevron use in 8.3 percent and no identifiable deference regime in 53.6 percent. The authors describe a continuum of approaches rather than a uniform doctrinal revolution. A later analysis by Salmanowitz and Spamann proposed that the parties’ and amici’s presentation of Chevron helped explain whether the Court discussed it. These are reports of particular datasets and arguments, not current measurements. (Printed 964–965.)

The notes report that Barnett and Walker’s study of circuit opinions from 2003 through 2013 found fidelity to Chevron, and list other studies with differing results about whether review frameworks affected outcomes. The source also identifies work on Chevron’s gradual rise in lower courts. Supreme Court docket selection, whether a study counts all relevant cases or only those citing a doctrine, the time window, and the outcome being measured can change what an empirical claim means. (Printed 965.)

The casebook states that, at the time of its writing, it lacked empirical work measuring Loper Bright’s effect. That statement is part of the assigned historical source. The study takeaway is to preserve each claim’s court level, dates, denominator, and measure rather than convert the notes into an unsupported forecast.

records.title: The disputed history of judicial respect for agency interpretation
records.text:
The nineteenth-century account separates common-law damages actions against officers from proceedings for mandamus or injunction. In damages suits, an officer could invoke statutory authority as a defense, and errors could expose the officer to liability. Courts also gave weight to contemporaneous official constructions. In prerogative-writ proceedings, review depended partly on whether the official duty was discretionary or ministerial. Decatur v. Paulding refused mandamus concerning an executive duty involving judgment, while explaining that an ordinary court suit presenting statutory meaning would not bind the Court to the department’s reading. (Printed 928–929.)

The twentieth-century survey identifies both respect for consistent agency practice and a judicial capacity to reject unpersuasive constructions. Burnet emphasized that inconsistency reduced the weight due an executive reading. Gray, Dobson, and Hearst gave particular attention to expert application and mixed questions. Skidmore then articulated persuasion-based factors. Friendly’s later Pittston discussion described analytically conflicting lines of Supreme Court decisions, leaving lower courts to decide which applied. (Printed 929–932.)

Loper Bright’s majority reads this history as a tradition of independent legal interpretation with confined exceptions for delegated factbound questions. Its dissent emphasizes practices around the APA’s enactment that permitted deference and disputes reading § 706 to prohibit a standard already in use. The course account should identify both the form of proceeding and the level of generality at which a historical case is described. The authors’ survey and the Justices’ historical claims are evidence of a disagreement rather than a single settled historical narrative. (Printed 940–944, 957–959, 961–963.)

records.title: The separation-of-powers critique of interpreting an agency’s own rules
records.text:
Justice Scalia’s separate opinion in Decker, reproduced in the notes, argues that letting an agency authoritatively interpret its own language joins prescription and interpretation and encourages vague rules followed by potentially retroactive clarification. The notes identify John Manning’s earlier academic version of this structural critique. This is an attributed challenge to Auer, not the holding of the Kisor majority. (Printed 1001–1002.)

Sunstein and Vermeule’s response, as characterized by the editors, rejects the premise that agency interpretation unlawfully expands power. Kagan’s four-Justice Kisor discussion treats agency activities taking legislative or adjudicative form as exercises of executive authority under a statutory plan and emphasizes the courts’ retained reviewing role. Gorsuch disputes the statutory and constitutional sufficiency of those limits. The disagreement involves both institutional power and the practical consequences of interpretation without notice and comment. (Printed 994, 997–1002.)

The final express-delegation hypothetical asks whether an agency could write a regulation authorizing later interpretive rules to define its terms. That question tests whether an explicit instruction resolves only an implied-delegation problem or also confronts limits arising from the APA and constitutional structure. The source poses the problem and leaves the answer open.

records.title: Article III standing
records.text:
Article III standing determines whether the particular claimant has the personal stake needed for a federal court to exercise judicial power over a particular claim and requested remedy. The course text organizes the inquiry into injury in fact, causation, and redressability. Injury must be concrete and particularized and actual or imminent. Causation asks whether the injury is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct. Redressability asks whether a favorable judicial decision is likely to address that injury. The claimant must satisfy each element; the presence of an important public question does not establish them.

The procedural stage matters. Pleading may support a plausible allegation; summary judgment requires evidence supporting standing. Lujan examines affidavits and testimony about future visits to endangered-species habitats. Laidlaw examines actual losses of recreational use connected to ongoing unlawful discharges. Standing must also support each form of relief sought: an injury that supports one remedy does not automatically support another.

Keep constitutional standing separate from the statutory question whether Congress authorized this claimant to sue and from the merits of the legal challenge. ADAPSO rejected an approach that required a plaintiff to prove a legally protected interest before obtaining judicial review. The zone-of-interests inquiry remains an additional question about the statutory scheme. A plaintiff who clears the threshold may still lose on the merits. The cases also distinguish standing at the beginning of a suit from later mootness.

records.title: Concrete and particularized injury
records.text:
An injury in fact is a concrete effect on the claimant, rather than a request to vindicate the general interest in lawful government. Particularization asks how the claimant is affected; concreteness asks whether the asserted harm has sufficient substance. An injury may be widespread and still concrete. Akins allows voters to challenge the denial of useful campaign information, while Sierra Club requires members actually affected by the development of Mineral King.

Environmental plaintiffs must identify their own relationship to the affected place or resource. Lujan rejects indefinite intentions to revisit distant habitats at the summary-judgment stage. Laidlaw accepts evidence that reasonable concerns about ongoing permit violations impaired identified members’ use of a particular river. Those decisions turn on the nature and evidentiary support of the asserted personal injury. They do not make a general interest in environmental protection sufficient.

Congress can recognize legally protected interests, but the assigned TransUnion and Spokeo notes explain a constitutional limit: a statutory violation alone does not automatically create a concrete injury. Tangible harms readily qualify; intangible harms can qualify by a sufficiently close relationship to traditionally recognized injuries. The cases leave contested boundaries between legislative creation of rights and Article III’s independent demands.

records.title: Causation and redressability in challenges to agency action
records.text:
Causation requires a sufficiently supported connection between the challenged action and the plaintiff’s injury. Redressability connects the requested remedy to a likely improvement in that injury. Challenges to government regulation of someone else often raise difficulty because independent actors intervene between the government’s decision and the claimant’s harm. The court must examine that chain rather than assume that invalidating an agency decision necessarily changes third-party conduct.

Akins recognizes that lawful agency reconsideration can supply redress even when the agency might reach the same ultimate result through a valid exercise of discretion. Laidlaw holds that a civil penalty payable to the Treasury can redress the plaintiffs’ future injuries by deterring violations that were ongoing when suit began. That rationale does not authorize penalties for wholly completed violations lacking a continuing or imminent threat. Massachusetts v. EPA accepts a contribution to reducing climate risk, rather than requiring a complete solution to global warming; the dissent disputes the link between the requested regulation and loss of particular coastal land.

The standard must be applied to the injury actually alleged and the remedy actually sought. The fact that a defendant’s conduct has broad social effects does not by itself establish or defeat traceability or redressability. The assigned fragment on Bennett also emphasizes that evidentiary demands differ at dismissal and summary judgment.

records.title: Congressional creation of rights and standing
records.text:
A statutory authorization to sue identifies who Congress wishes to place in court and what legal interests the statute protects. It does not by itself settle whether a federal claimant has a concrete injury. The course develops this boundary through Havens Realty, Akins, Raines, Spokeo, and TransUnion. Havens recognizes the denial of truthful housing information as a statutory injury to a tester. Akins recognizes voters’ concrete inability to obtain campaign information. Raines rejects legislators’ challenge despite a statute expressly authorizing congressional plaintiffs.

The distinction between constitutional and nonconstitutional restrictions affects Congress’s power. In Brown Group, Congress could authorize a union to recover individual damages because the requirement that members participate personally was prudential, once Article III standing otherwise existed. In contrast, Congress could not remove the constitutional need for an actual member with a qualifying injury in a representative suit.

Cass Sunstein’s assigned commentary argues for broad legislative power to create novel interests, including informational and environmental interests. The casebook contrasts that proposal with later decisions requiring concrete harm independent of the mere existence of a cause of action. Treat Sunstein’s proposal as a contested theory, and analyze the governing case, statutory language, asserted injury, and requested relief separately.

records.title: Associational standing
records.text:
Associational standing allows an organization to represent injured members without proving a separate injury to the organization itself. The Hunt test, as explained in UAW v. Brock, asks whether members could sue in their own right, whether the protected interests relate to the association’s purposes, and whether individual participation is required by the claim or relief. In Brock, a union could litigate a common legal interpretation while state authorities retained responsibility for individual benefit determinations.

The third requirement reflects practical and prudential concerns. Brown Group holds that Congress can authorize a union damages action that would otherwise require individual participation. The first requirement implements Article III: a representative association still needs at least one member with standing for the claim. The assigned SFFA note rejects additional operational scrutiny of a genuine voluntary membership organization that identifies and represents members in good faith.

Distinguish an association’s representation of members from injury to the association’s own operations. Havens recognizes an organizational claim where alleged racial steering directly impaired the organization’s housing counseling and referral services. FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024) distinguishes that interference from an organization’s choice to spend money investigating or opposing a policy; those expenditures alone do not establish injury. Conflicts among members also require care: National Maritime holds that disagreement alone does not defeat representative standing, while preserving concerns about organizational procedures, intervention, adequate representation, and a union’s duty of fair representation.

records.title: State plaintiffs and special solicitude
records.text:
A state may sue based on its own property, its governmental authority, or its asserted responsibility for residents’ welfare. These interests must be identified because they supply different explanations for a state’s presence in court. Massachusetts v. EPA emphasizes state-owned coastal land, sovereign powers surrendered to the federal government, and a statutory avenue for challenging EPA’s rejection of a rulemaking petition. Its special-solicitude language accompanies that particular combination.

The majority accepts partial reduction of the risk to Massachusetts, even though domestic regulation cannot solve global warming. Chief Justice Roberts’s dissent rejects a relaxed state standard and disputes proof connecting the requested motor-vehicle regulation to loss of coastal land. The casebook describes several readings of the majority: protection of procedural rights, recognition of increased risk, or a distinct role for sovereign states. These are interpretive alternatives, not interchangeable holdings.

Later assigned notes qualify the concept. California v. Texas rejects state standing for inadequate causation, and United States v. Texas distinguishes challenges to immigration-enforcement discretion from the rulemaking petition in Massachusetts. Biden v. Nebraska recognizes Missouri’s injury through its state instrumentality MOHELA, over a dissent questioning the absent entity’s separate status. These examples show that identifying the particular plaintiff, injury, government action, and remedy remains necessary.

records.title: Zone of interests under the APA
records.text:
The zone-of-interests inquiry asks whether the interest the plaintiff seeks to protect falls within the interests of the statutory provision invoked. ADAPSO formulates the test alongside injury in fact. NCUA applies it generously: the plaintiff need not show that Congress specifically intended to benefit that particular plaintiff, but there must be a supported relationship between the statute’s protected interests and the interest harmed. The banking competitors qualified because the common-bond limitation constrained the customer markets credit unions could serve.

The level of generality matters. NCUA’s dissent argues that describing the interest as limiting markets converts any incidental competitive benefit into statutory protection. Air Courier illustrates a limiting result: protecting postal revenues and public postal service did not place employees’ job interests within the relevant monopoly statute. The source also cautions against assembling unrelated statutory provisions into a broad subject area to evade the test.

The later notes apply the inquiry in different settings. Thompson treats targeted retaliation against an employee as within Title VII’s protective purposes. Patchak treats neighboring land-use interests as within a statute governing federal land acquisition for tribes. Twin Rivers requires an indirect claimant’s interest to align systematically with the statutory beneficiaries and rejects paper manufacturers’ challenge to electronic disclosure. The assigned cases use historical terminology such as prudential standing.

records.title: Mootness and voluntary cessation
records.text:
Mootness asks whether an actual controversy remains after filing. Standing asks whether the plaintiff could properly invoke the court’s authority when the suit began. Laidlaw distinguishes the two because a defendant could otherwise stop a challenged practice while litigation proceeds and remain free to resume it after dismissal.

Under the assigned voluntary-cessation discussion, a defendant asserting mootness bears the heavy burden of making it absolutely clear that the alleged wrongdoing cannot reasonably be expected to recur. The Court reversed the Fourth Circuit, which had held the case moot because civil penalties could not redress the plaintiffs; it held that compliance and closure did not moot the case unless Laidlaw carried the heavy voluntary-cessation burden, and it left those factual questions for remand. Its standing analysis relied on violations ongoing when the complaint was filed and on the deterrent effect of civil penalties.

The casebook also identifies the capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception. The supplied printed 1229 fragment discusses an agency’s continuing defense of generation-shifting authority, but the preceding page is outside the supplied assignment. That fragment supports a limited illustration that a government’s continuing assertion of disputed authority can bear on recurrence; it does not provide the entire West Virginia mootness analysis.

records.title: Procedural rights and concrete interests
records.text:
A person accorded a procedural right to protect a concrete interest may challenge the failure to follow that procedure without proving that the procedure will certainly produce a different substantive outcome. The assigned Lujan footnote example concerns a resident beside a proposed dam who seeks the environmental analysis required before licensing. The claimant’s connection to the site supplies the concrete interest; the omitted procedure relates to protecting it.

Massachusetts v. EPA uses a procedural-right analysis in reviewing denial of a rulemaking petition. The casebook questions how far that reasoning extends because the cited Clean Air Act provision concerns judicial review and venue. It therefore does not treat every avenue of judicial review as automatically eliminating ordinary standing requirements.

Spokeo and TransUnion reinforce the independent need for concrete harm. A statutory procedure and authorization to sue are significant, but they do not entitle every person to federal adjudication merely because a procedure was violated. Analyze the actual interest, the connection between procedure and harm, and the remedy sought.

records.title: Citizen suits and private enforcement
records.text:
A citizen-suit provision gives specified private claimants a statutory route to enforce regulatory law. Under the Clean Water Act provision described in Laidlaw, a person with an adversely affected interest must provide advance notice, and diligent prosecution by EPA or the state can bar a citizen suit. Courts can award injunctions and civil penalties payable to the Treasury. The claimant still needs constitutional standing for each remedy.

Laidlaw supports penalties where their deterrent effect is likely to reduce the claimant’s exposure to ongoing or future violations. It distinguishes suits seeking only to punish wholly past violations. Its treatment of the state settlement also matters: the district court found that a prosecution arranged with assistance from Laidlaw had not been diligent enough to bar the private suit.

The opinions debate separation of powers. Justice Scalia argues that private penalty suits can displace executive enforcement judgment and confer disproportionate bargaining power. The majority emphasizes the deterrent relationship to concrete injury and the government’s statutory capacity to prosecute or intervene. Kennedy’s concurrence expressly reserves that issue.

records.title: APA §702: Persons entitled to judicial review
records.text:
Section 702 supplies the general statutory gateway quoted in ADAPSO and NCUA. Its two formulations address a person suffering a legal wrong because of agency action and a person adversely affected or aggrieved within the meaning of a relevant statute. The pre-1970 account treated those formulations through existing legal-right and special-review doctrines. ADAPSO reoriented the analysis toward injury in fact and the zone of interests.

The statutory language does not settle every threshold. Article III requires the claimant’s personal stake, and the relevant regulatory statute shapes the zone of interests. ADAPSO warns against requiring proof of the merits as a condition of standing. NCUA nevertheless requires a relationship between the interests the statute arguably protects and those the plaintiff asserts. The editorial discussion questions whether ADAPSO’s framework follows directly from APA language or reflects an additional constitutional and judicial construction. Those competing explanations should remain distinct.

records.title: How did ADAPSO change access to review?
records.text:
The casebook’s ADAPSO notes draw on M. Elizabeth Magill’s account of earlier public actions and Peter Shane’s discussion of §702. They question the opinion’s claim to simply advance a preexisting expansion in standing. The injury-in-fact and zone-of-interests formulas were new, and a test that expands general APA review might simultaneously constrain suits under specific review provisions that formerly required neither direct injury nor beneficiary status.

Shane offers a possible textual account: being affected or aggrieved could support an injury requirement, and the phrase within the meaning of a relevant statute could support the statutory zone. On that reconstruction, the criteria need not originate in Article III. The notes do not say the Court actually adopted that reconstruction. They emphasize that assessing whether the decision widened standing overall requires uncertain assumptions about earlier doctrine and its hypothetical future development. The course account should therefore preserve the distinction between the decision’s result for data-processing competitors and broader contested claims about judicial access.

records.title: Cass Sunstein on informational standing after Akins
records.text: Sunstein reads Akins as supporting substantial congressional power to create enforceable interests; the casebook contrasts that theory with later concrete-injury decisions.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1178–1181 · physical PDF pp. 121–124

records.title: Cass Sunstein on informational standing after Akins
records.text:
In Informational Regulation and Informational Standing: Akins and Beyond, Sunstein first acknowledges a narrow reading: Akins might protect informational injury especially because it directly serves voting. Sunstein then argues for a broader account in which the law substantially defines which interests count as injury. If Congress may create rights to information, he asks why it cannot create interests in preservation of species, pristine land, clean air, or other public goods.

His examples explore whether Congress could create property-like interests even for citizens who never visit a particular environmental site. The argument emphasizes legislative choice, the value people assign to a resource’s existence, and statutory design capable of creating novel enforceable interests. These are scholarly proposals and interpretations, rather than holdings that all such statutes would be constitutional.

The editors follow the excerpt with FECA decisions applying informational standing and then with TransUnion’s insistence on independently concrete harm. Raines also shows that explicit congressional authorization is not always sufficient. Reading those materials together preserves the live disagreement over how much freedom Congress has to define the injury that permits federal adjudication.

records.title: Peter Shane on Bennett and the procedural stage
records.text:
The assigned page begins in the middle of Shane’s discussion of Bennett v. Spear. The available text explains how a Fish and Wildlife Service biological opinion constrained another agency’s options and how the Bureau’s prior reservoir practice supported an inference of redress. A unanimous finding of standing in that setting suggested that indirect causation and redressability need not always be fatal.

Shane also acknowledges a substantial qualification: Bennett arose at dismissal on the complaint, while Lujan evaluated proof at summary judgment. That difference affects what the plaintiff must establish and how the comparison should be understood.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1229 · physical PDF pp. 145–145

records.title: Daniel Farber’s place-based theory of standing
records.text:
The casebook briefly summarizes Daniel Farber’s A Place-Based Theory of Standing. Drawing together Massachusetts v. EPA and Laidlaw, Farber proposes that a plaintiff should be able to challenge environmental violations involving a specific area if the plaintiff shows an appropriate relationship to that area.

This is a scholarly simplification of a difficult field. It highlights the practical importance of a claimant’s connection to a place, which also appears in Sierra Club, Lujan, and Laidlaw. The supplied paragraph does not specify every boundary of an appropriate relationship or reproduce the article’s complete argument. It therefore supports a comparative reading and a question about doctrinal coherence, rather than a substitute for the courts’ actual injury, causation, and redressability requirements.
