records.text: The notes distinguish expertise, federalism, public-nuisance, and representational accounts of why states might receive special treatment.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1241–1243 · physical PDF pp. 157–159

records.title: Competing explanations of state standing after Massachusetts v. EPA
records.text:
The assigned notes present several explanations that should remain attributed. Freeman and Vermeule interpret Massachusetts as reflecting concern that political appointees displaced EPA expertise and suggest strategic use of federalism to obtain a decisive vote. The editors expressly describe that proposed account of judicial motivation as speculative.

Merrill argues, in earlier scholarship, for state attorneys general’s authority to bring public-nuisance suits, analogizing public civil enforcement to criminal prosecution; the note limits his proposal to states’ own courts. Percival responds that surrender of sovereign powers on joining the Union supplies a continuing reason to let states challenge out-of-state environmental harms despite later standing doctrines. Watts and Wildermuth distinguish proprietary, quasi-sovereign, and sovereign interests, and tie the last category to limits federal regulation places on states’ authority to govern.

The editors also consider the representative credentials of elected state attorneys general in comparison with self-appointed private public-interest plaintiffs, citing Mank. Each explanation offers a different rationale and potential scope. Later notes on rejected state suits, MOHELA, and immigration enforcement show that special solicitude is not a universal exemption.

records.title: Generalized grievances and differentiated interests
records.text: A broadly shared injury can support standing when it is sufficiently concrete and tied to the claimant; a general demand for lawful government ordinarily cannot.

records.title: Generalized grievances and differentiated interests
records.text:
The assigned materials distinguish an injury shared by many people from an abstract interest in governmental compliance. Sierra Club requires the organization or members to use the affected area. Akins recognizes useful campaign information as a concrete interest even though the same disclosure would benefit many voters. Widely distributed harm therefore does not alone decide standing.

The notes contrast Richardson’s challenge to secrecy of the CIA budget and Schlesinger’s challenge to congressional members holding military-reserve commissions with a contractor denied equal opportunity to compete in Northeastern Florida. They ask whether the doctrinal distinctions reflect the type of legal right, congressional authorization, or the constitutional provision’s structural character. These are editorial questions about coherence; the questions themselves are not additional holdings.

Raines adds a related limit for legislators’ abstract institutional injuries. A student should identify precisely how the claimant is personally affected, what provision protects the asserted interest, and why the requested remedy would matter to that claimant. Simply labeling an injury political, informational, environmental, or widespread will not perform that analysis.

records.title: Third-party standing and its relationship to associations
records.text:
The casebook identifies three considerations for third-party rights claims: injury to the plaintiff from denial of the other person’s rights, an obstacle to that person’s independent assertion, and an appropriate representative relationship. It contrasts physicians permitted to challenge Medicaid exclusions affecting patients in Singleton with a pediatrician denied standing as doctor, parent, and defender of the unborn in Diamond.

Associational standing supplies a more developed route for organized groups representing members, with the Hunt requirements explained in Brock. The doctrines overlap in representational concerns but have distinct formulations. The question also appears in Newport News, where an administrator sought to litigate a claimant’s benefits determination, and in the dissent to Biden v. Nebraska, where Missouri sued despite MOHELA’s absence. Identifying whose injury and whose legal right are at issue is the necessary starting point.

records.text: Whether setting aside agency action differs from enjoining its implementation is disputed.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1259 · physical PDF pp. 169–169

records.title: APA remedies: Setting aside, vacatur, and injunctions
records.text:
APA §706 directs reviewing courts to hold unlawful and set aside agency action that violates specified standards. Section 703 identifies available forms of judicial proceeding, including declaratory judgments and prohibitory or mandatory injunctions. Courts have often described relief using set aside, vacate, and enjoin with little differentiation.

Whether “set aside” in § 706 means vacatur of the rule for everyone or only relief for the parties, and how that relates to injunctions and universal relief, is a live dispute (see CIC Services v. IRS (2021) and National Mining Association v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (D.C. Cir. 1998)).

records.title: Study questions: Personal injury and public information
records.text:
The casebook asks why a Black housing tester’s statutory right to truthful information supports a claim while a citizen’s interest in CIA-budget information under a constitutional provision did not support Richardson’s suit. It also compares contractors’ equal opportunity to compete with a taxpayer’s interest in an informed electoral process. Analyze the interest asserted, the relevant text, the claimant’s relation to it, and whether Congress expressly authorized review.

A second question follows Sunstein’s discussion: if Congress can create an enforceable informational interest, how far can it recognize interests in preservation of distant landscapes or endangered species? State Sunstein’s argument and then test it against the assigned TransUnion and Spokeo limits. The notes frame this as a disputed question.

records.title: Study questions: What work does special solicitude do?
records.text:
Identify each possible basis in Massachusetts: the state’s ownership of coastal land, the sovereign powers displaced by the Union, the statutory route for review of a rulemaking petition, and a reduction in future climate risk. Explain what each contributes to injury, causation, or redressability. Then assess Roberts’s objection that the remedy must address the particular land injury actually identified.

Use the assigned later cases to test the proposed rule. California v. Texas rejects an unsupported causal link; United States v. Texas distinguishes enforcement discretion; Biden v. Nebraska divides over the relationship between a state and its instrumentality. Explain which reading of Massachusetts survives each comparison.

atlasSources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1253–1259 · physical PDF pp. 163–169

records.title: Study questions: How broadly should the statutory interest be defined?
records.text:
NCUA identifies an interest in limiting credit-union customer markets. Its dissent identifies the provision’s internal cooperative and financial-stability purposes. Explain why the chosen level of description matters and what evidence in the statutory text and operation supports each account.

Apply both approaches to Air Courier’s postal employees, the hypothetical stenographer harmed by omitted on-the-record hearings, and Twin Rivers’s paper companies. Then explain why Thompson and Patchak satisfied the test under the supplied descriptions. Distinguish injury in fact from membership in the statutory zone at every step.

records.title: RLCC § 9 — standard terms and the parol-evidence rule
records.text:
Section 9 is one sentence. It works by denying the standard term the status the parol-evidence rule depends on: the term is not treated as a final expression on that subject, so there is no integration to discharge the business's prior affirmation or promise.

Comment 1 states the reason. Standard terms are not a jointly drafted memorial of a negotiated agreement, so there is less reason to let them override what the consumer was told. It describes § 9 as a corollary of § 7 (deception) and § 8 (affirmations and promises are part of the contract and cannot be negated by standard terms).

Read with Restatement (Second) §§ 209–216 and UCC § 2-202 from the same assignment: those ask whether a writing is integrated; § 9 answers that question against the business for a standard term that conflicts with its own earlier statement.

records.title: RLCC § 8 — affirmations and promises that are part of the contract
records.text:
(a) The business's own affirmation or promise becomes part of the contract when it creates a reasonable expectation, in a consumer who is the intended audience, that the subject matter will have a particular attribute.

(b) A third party's affirmation or promise of that kind (1) becomes part of the contract between the business and the consumer if the business knew or reasonably should have known of it and the consumer could reasonably have believed the business intended to stand behind it; and (2) binds the third party itself to the consumer, even without a direct transaction, if the third party has an appreciable financial interest in the contract.

(c) Standard contract terms that purport to negate or unreasonably limit obligations arising under (a) and (b) are not enforceable.

records.title: RLCC § 6 — unconscionability
records.text: An unconscionable consumer contract or term is unenforceable; substantive and procedural unconscionability are weighed on a sliding scale as of the time of contracting, and a sufficiently high degree of one can be enough in appropriate circumstances.

atlasSources.label: RLCC § 6. Unconscionability · Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts (Official Text 2024), PDF page 106 of 197

records.title: RLCC § 6 — unconscionability
records.text:
(a) An unconscionable contract or term is unenforceable.

(b) Two factors, judged when the contract is made: substantive unconscionability (a fundamentally unfair or unreasonably one-sided contract or term) and procedural unconscionability (unfair surprise, or the absence of meaningful choice for the consumer). More of one means less of the other is needed, and in appropriate circumstances a sufficiently high degree of one is sufficient.

(c) A term is substantively unconscionable if its effect is to (1) unreasonably exclude or limit the business's liability or the consumer's remedies for death or personal injury, or for loss caused by the business's intentional or negligent act or omission; (2) unreasonably expand the consumer's liability or the business's remedies or enforcement powers on the consumer's breach; or (3) unreasonably limit the consumer's ability to pursue or express a complaint or seek reasonable redress.

(d) A term is procedurally unconscionable if a reasonable consumer in the circumstances is not aware of it, or does not understand or appreciate its implications, and so does not meaningfully account for it in deciding to contract. Relevant factors: the consumer's legal and financial sophistication, the complexity of the term or agreement, pressure tactics and manipulation by the business, and the process by which the term was introduced.

records.title: Restatement § 302 — intended and incidental beneficiaries
records.text:
Section 302 replaces the older creditor-beneficiary and donee-beneficiary categories with one test. A beneficiary is intended if recognising a right to performance is appropriate to effectuate the parties' intention and either (a) the performance will satisfy an obligation of the promisee to pay money to the beneficiary or (b) the circumstances indicate that the promisee intends to give the beneficiary the benefit of the performance. Subsection (2) defines an incidental beneficiary as any beneficiary who is not intended; an incidental beneficiary has no right to enforce.

The two limbs keep the two older cases on the map: Lawrence v. Fox (the promise to pay the promisee's creditor) falls under (1)(a), and Seaver v. Ransom (the promise to make a gift to a relative) under (1)(b). The Sisney cases apply the intended-beneficiary test to a public contract.

records.title: UCC § 2-209 — modification, rescission and waiver
records.text: For a sale of goods, parties can change their contract without exchanging new consideration, but good faith and applicable writing requirements still matter. records.title: UCC § 2-209 — modification, rescission and waiver
records.text:
Subsection (1) drops the pre-existing-duty rule for sales of goods: a modification needs no consideration. Subsection (2) lets a signed agreement exclude modification or rescission except by a signed writing, but a merchant's form imposing that requirement on a non-merchant must be separately signed by the other party. Subsection (3) keeps the statute of frauds in play if the contract as modified falls within it. Subsections (4) and (5) deal with waiver: an attempted modification that fails (2) or (3) can still operate as a waiver, and a waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract can be retracted by reasonable notification that strict performance will be required, unless retraction would be unjust because the other party has materially changed position in reliance on the waiver.

The section is the Code's answer to Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico: instead of policing modifications by the consideration doctrine, the Code's comments test them for good faith. Section 1-303(f) separately recognizes course of performance as evidence of waiver or modification, subject to § 2-209. The deletion footnote on the Selections page concerns the preceding § 2-208, not § 2-209.

records.title: UCC §§ 1-303 and 2-202 — course of dealing, usage of trade and the final writing
records.text:
Section 1-303 (formerly § 1-205, with course of performance moved in from § 2-208) defines the three sources: a course of performance is repeated performance under the contract that the other side accepts without objection; a course of dealing is the parties' conduct in earlier transactions; a usage of trade is a practice observed so regularly in a place, vocation or trade that parties expect it to be observed, and its existence and scope are proved as facts. Subsection (d) makes all three relevant to the meaning of the agreement and lets them give particular meaning to, supplement or qualify its terms. Subsection (e) orders them when they cannot be reconciled: express terms first, then course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade. That hierarchy is subject to subsection (f): course of performance can show waiver or modification of an inconsistent term, subject to § 2-209. Subsection (g) requires notice before evidence of a usage is admitted against a party, to prevent unfair surprise.

Section 2-202 applies this to the parol-evidence rule for sales of goods: terms in a writing intended as a final expression may not be contradicted by a prior agreement or a contemporaneous oral agreement, but may be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing or usage of trade, and by consistent additional terms unless the writing was intended as a complete and exclusive statement. Columbia Nitrogen, Nanakuli and Frigaliment show how far a usage can go in reading a written term.

records.title: UCC § 2-716 — buyer's right to specific performance or replevin
records.text: Specific performance may be decreed where the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, on such terms as to price, damages and other relief as the court deems just; a buyer may also replevy goods identified to the contract when cover is unavailable.

atlasSources.label: UCC § 2-716. Buyer's Right to Specific Performance or Replevin · Contracts Selections (Farnsworth et al., 2021), PDF page 412 of 713

records.title: UCC § 2-716 — buyer's right to specific performance or replevin
records.text:
Subsection (1) states the test: specific performance may be decreed where the goods are unique 'or in other proper circumstances'. The second phrase allows relief beyond goods labelled unique; inability to obtain substitutes can show why damages are inadequate. It does not make specific performance automatic whenever a seller breaches. Subsection (2) lets the decree carry terms as to payment of the price, damages or other relief. Subsection (3) gives the buyer a right of replevin for goods identified to the contract when cover cannot be had after reasonable effort, circumstances indicate that effort would be unavailing, or the goods were shipped under reservation and the security interest has been satisfied or tendered; for consumer goods the right vests when the buyer acquires a special property in the goods.

Morris v. Sparrow and the notes on personal-service contracts show the older equity limits that the section relaxes for sales of goods.

records.title: compare preparation with expressly invited commencement
records.text: Ever-Tite’s form invited commencement and the assigned conclusion includes loading and transport. White’s conduct was ambiguous and private under a different proposal.

records.title: preserve conflicting views of bid reliance
records.text: Learned Hand in James Baird rejected promissory estoppel as a basis for holding a subcontractor's bid open; Traynor in Drennan uses § 90 reliance to give the general contractor a protected opportunity to accept. The two holdings conflict, and Restatement (Second) § 87(2) follows Drennan.

records.title: language determines the statutory formation route
records.text: Dorton’s form was not sufficiently conditional under its test. C. Itoh’s expressly conditional form blocked formation by writings but performance triggered subsection (3).

records.title: compare materiality without universalizing arbitration treatment
records.text: Dorton remands a fact-dependent arbitration question. Bayway describes a New York per se rule for arbitration while rejecting the analogy to its limited tax clause.

records.title: additional terms differ from conflicting terms
records.text: Bayway applies subsection (2)’s material-alteration exception to an addition. Northrop confronts the separate textual problem of terms that conflict with the offer.

records.title: distinguish a limited sale tax from later back taxes
records.text: The scope, timing, custom, and ability to avoid liability differ. Bayway also leaves the independent-hardship issue open while the quoted Union Carbide analysis rejects it.

records.title: similar exclusions arise through different routes
records.text: C. Itoh excludes an unmatched clause from a subsection (3) conduct contract. Northrop applies a knockout approach to different terms after a subsection (1) acceptance.

records.title: preserve disagreement about the formation event
records.text: Hill treats later retention as initial acceptance. Klocek assumes an earlier contract on the record and applies proposal-and-assent analysis. The two decisions also differ in law, proof, and procedure.

records.title: compare notice before conduct is called assent
records.text: Specht asks whether downloading communicated agreement to hidden terms. Hill relies on a chance to inspect and return before retention becomes acceptance under its approach.

records.title: compare proof of agreement to an arbitration term
records.text: Each requires a supported account of assent to the disputed term. Their interfaces, formation sequences, and applicable state-law analyses differ.

records.title: different obstacles to reliance-based relief
records.text: Cohen sustains estoppel after a constitutional remand. Tolosa requires a particular exception to a statutory writing barrier. A reliance theory must address the actual obstacle to enforcement.

records.title: one basis of enforcement
records.text: The first chapter treats bargains as an enforcement basis before examining reliance and restitution.

records.title: another basis examined by the chapter
records.text: The source develops enforcement through induced reliance without necessarily finding consideration.

records.title: requires a separate form inquiry when applicable
records.text: An enforcement basis does not by itself establish compliance with an applicable writing requirement.

records.title: Contracts application: a remedial baseline
records.text: A reliance interest measures loss; the presence of that interest and the elements authorizing relief are different inquiries.

records.title: distinguishes expenditure from benefit transferred
records.text: An expense can reduce the claimant’s position without enriching the defendant.

records.title: expressed through the bargain requirement
records.text: The chapter’s account of section 71 asks whether the performance or promise was sought and given in exchange.

records.title: distinguishes equal value from legal sufficiency
records.text: The notes use section 79 after identifying a genuine exchange, rather than as a substitute for finding one.

records.title: permits other motives alongside a bargain
records.text: A transaction can be induced by generosity while still involving the exchange the parties requested.

records.title: uses a statutory variable-quantity framework
records.text: Section 2-306 supplies the goods-contract framework for output, requirements, and exclusive dealings; the linked Selections preserve the separately assigned text.

records.title: compares reasonable and best efforts
records.text: The Wood notes invite comparison with the provision while preserving the difference between licensing and goods.

records.title: organizes the reliance elements and remedy
records.text: The two versions reproduced in the casebook should be distinguished rather than blended.

records.title: separates a liability basis from a measure
records.text: The same word appears in the remedy chapter and in the later introduction to recovery without a promise.

records.title: clarifies historical action labels
records.text: The historical names do not replace an explanation of the basis for recovering a benefit.

records.title: develops the pre-existing assent hub
records.text: The newly sourced cases examine how context gives words and conduct their legal meaning.

records.title: identifies the first commitment
records.text: Find a manifestation inviting assent that would conclude the bargain before classifying the response.

records.title: identifies the invited response
records.text: Acceptance must answer the actual offer, not merely show interest in doing business.

records.title: limits withdrawal without completing the sale
records.text: The pre-existing irrevocability concept is refined through the distinct option routes in this assignment.

records.title: protects beginning invited performance
records.text: Section 45 concerns performance-only offers and a protected opportunity to complete.

records.title: addresses recitals and preparatory reliance
records.text: The source discussions concern two different option bases and do not make all reliance an acceptance.

records.title: includes a merchant firm-offer route
records.text: The goods provision provides a distinct exception to ordinary revocability, with its full predicates in SEL.

records.title: contrasts two signed-offer provisions
records.text: The reproduced New York text excepts the UCC merchant offer while providing another route beyond it.

records.title: separates older tests from the reproduced amendments
records.text: The 2023 publication expressly dates the amendment and enactment discussion.

records.title: controls access to automatic incorporation
records.text: The subsection (2) between-merchants rule differs from the nonmerchant proposal route.

records.title: adds timing to the acceptance analysis
records.text: Dispatch and receipt rules operate after identifying valid communications and a still-open acceptance power.

records.title: explains performance after a counteroffer
records.text: The traditional treatment of a qualified response can make later performance adoption of that response.

records.title: explains the commercial problem behind the section
records.text: Conflicts in standard terms may coexist with agreement on the transaction-specific terms.

records.title: requires separate inquiries
records.text: The chapter’s organization distinguishes creation of an obligation from incorporation of a disputed clause.

records.title: tests the proviso to subsection (1)
records.text: A qualifying condition can prevent writings alone from forming the contract.

records.title: examines one incorporation exception
records.text: Materiality is one exception among others and its proof depends on the relevant legal approach.

records.title: includes one of three approaches
records.text: Northrop uses the knockout approach for its state-law prediction while describing alternatives.

records.title: makes formation timing decisive
records.text: Whether the earlier transaction already created a contract changes how later terms are analyzed.

records.title: compares the purposes and effects of writing
records.text: Evidence and caution are different possible functions from a substantive substitute for consideration.

records.title: provides a comparative form rule
records.text: The quoted Convention provision takes a different approach within its own sphere.

records.title: develops promise, prediction, description, and commendation
records.text: The notes contrast a jeweler’s specific statement of diamond quality with general commendation.

records.title: develops promise, prediction, description, and commendation
records.text: The notes ask when assurances in medical treatment should receive contract consequences.

records.title: develops promise, prediction, description, and commendation
records.text: A township granted industrial tax abatements after a plant presentation about new investment and continued employment, subject to favorable demand. General Motors later planned to transfer production.

records.title: develops expectation interest
records.text: The notes separate losses, transfers, and profits before assessing a remedy.

records.title: develops expectation interest
records.text: The problem varies the promised improvement, the actual worsening, expenses, and pain across three operations. Its baseline includes $20,000 of promised enhancement, $10,000 deterioration, $3,000 pain per operation, and specified doctor and hospital charges.

records.title: develops expectation interest
records.text: The notes contrast sunk expenditures, promised profits, alternative opportunities, and the value of a payment returned.

records.title: develops restitution as a remedial interest
records.text: The book uses recovery of $156 million paid for lease rights to show restitution’s distinct perspective.

records.title: develops specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text: The notes ask whether affection for a particular dog supports specific relief.

records.title: develops specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text: A cannery’s time-sensitive supply need can make ordinary market damages inadequate.

records.title: develops specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text: The text distinguishes restraining competing performances from compelling personal service.

records.title: develops specific performance and adequacy of damages
records.text: Remedies concerning people’s labor raise different problems from transfer of goods.

records.title: develops punitive damages and independent torts
records.text: The historical notes discuss attempts to obtain tort remedies for conduct connected with contractual relations.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: The notes use family arrangements to test whether an act is the agreed price of a promise.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: The notes ask how the timing of research participation and a promised benefit affects consideration.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: The editors compare public-gift limitations with ordinary bargain analysis.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: The chapter traces how older forms helped shape the bargain requirement.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: The notes refine the Hamer analysis through several different questions.

records.title: develops consideration
records.text: An employer accelerates an employee’s enjoyment of a retirement-related benefit in connection with an undertaking not to compete.

records.title: develops forbearance of claims and settlement
records.text: The notes compare a promise made in exchange for forbearance of a paternity claim that later evidence undermined.

records.title: develops forbearance of claims and settlement
records.text: The notes examine the tradeoff between settling uncertainty and protecting bad-faith assertions.

records.title: develops past action and the requirement of exchange
records.text: The assigned page begins the moral-obligation case concerning care given before a later promise.

records.title: develops past action and the requirement of exchange
records.text: A benefactor’s completed contribution and a later assurance about an institution’s name raise the timing problem associated with past consideration.

records.title: develops illusory promises and constrained discretion
records.text: The consideration-and-interpretation unit supplies several ways to identify a real obligation.

records.title: develops illusory promises and constrained discretion
records.text: A family arrangement concerning a farm and testamentary plans includes a promise associated with mortgage payments and possible changes in the family.

records.title: develops formalities and substitutes for consideration
records.text: The notes preserve historical disagreement over whether form or commercial context should replace consideration.

records.title: develops formalities and substitutes for consideration
records.text: A written and notarized memorandum promises $50,000 in recognition of assistance already rendered.

records.title: develops charitable subscriptions and reliance
records.text: The named memorial subscription is treated as an exchange involving an implied college undertaking.

records.title: develops charitable subscriptions and reliance
records.text: The notes compare a donor’s papers and a promised charitable payment.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: Land improvements and assurances during a gratuitous bailment appear in the history of reliance protection.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: The assigned boundary page reports an appellate concern that job-related stress and continued service had been overlooked in evaluating reliance.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: The problem reports different treatment of a negligent-undertaking claim and a promise-based claim concerning removal of abusive material.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: The wording changes to § 90 bear both on who may rely and on what relief follows.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: The book returns to Cohen for a different doctrinal purpose.

records.title: develops promissory estoppel
records.text: The editor’s account of the later trial adds facts and a different damages figure.

records.title: develops restitution as an independent basis of liability
records.text: The assigned page introduces emergency medical services to an unconscious accident victim and reports a reversal and remand.

records.title: develops restitution as an independent basis of liability
records.text: The restitution introduction distinguishes several reasons a benefit may be retained unjustly.

records.title: develops objective interpretation of assent
records.text: The watch-and-check example involves a transaction understood as a frolic by both parties.

records.title: develops objective interpretation of assent
records.text: The book’s advertisement example tests what a reasonable audience would understand as a serious commercial commitment.

records.title: develops objective interpretation of assent
records.text: The notes present a different electronic arrangement involving an installation technician and a laptop.

records.title: develops objective interpretation of assent
records.text: The introductory quotations disagree about the place of actual intention.

records.title: develops social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text: The duck-hunting ride example tests whether a social arrangement is a contractual exchange.

records.title: develops social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text: The note distinguishes ordinary contractual capacity from automatic consequences of a domestic status.

records.title: develops social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text: The chapter places context beside outward wording and formal reservation.

records.title: develops social and professional contexts of legal commitment
records.text: Balfour is the leading case on domestic arrangements made without intent to create legal relations.

records.title: develops preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text: The notes identify evidence bearing on whether an unsigned or informal agreement is already binding.

records.title: develops preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text: An agreement about how to negotiate differs from a promise to complete the ultimate deal.

records.title: develops preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text: The notes contrast a fully settled bargain awaiting formalization with a binding obligation to negotiate remaining terms.

records.title: develops preliminary agreements and reservations of a signed writing
records.text: The editors use the controversy to illustrate how a preliminary arrangement can affect claims involving another participant.

records.title: develops offer and the power of acceptance
records.text: The assigned range reaches the beginning of a land-sale correspondence case.

records.title: develops offer and the power of acceptance
records.text: The salt quotation illustrates the difference between inviting orders and committing to fill any responsive order.

records.title: develops offer and the power of acceptance
records.text: The notes put classic offer analysis beside consumer settings and noncontract remedies.

records.title: develops advertisements, quotations, catalogs, and offers
records.text: The note contrasts an unsuccessful ordinary contract claim with a statutory remedy for advertising.

records.title: develops auction formation and reserve terms
records.text: The auction discussion uses a land transaction to compare reserve rules.

records.title: develops auction formation and reserve terms
records.text: The assigned page contains the end of a discussion of a mistakenly advertised automobile price.

records.title: develops rewards
records.text: The claimant acted without knowing of the reward and could not rely on that act as acceptance of it.

records.title: develops acceptance and invited method
records.text: A statement acknowledging an order may have a different meaning from a statement accepting it.

records.title: develops acceptance and invited method
records.text: The cases distinguish further negotiation, private preparation, specified approval, and invited performance.

records.title: develops acceptance and notification
records.text: The reward advertisement invited performance without advance notification of acceptance.

records.title: develops acceptance and notification
records.text: The note requires notice when the offeror would not promptly learn of the offeree’s completed act.

records.title: develops beginning performance and mere preparation
records.text: Preparing to fill an order did not on the facts described amount to acceptance.

records.title: develops beginning performance and mere preparation
records.text: The form invited written approval or commencement of performance; the assigned conclusion treats loading and transporting materials as commencement.

records.title: develops silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
records.text: Retention of eel skins after repeated similar accepted shipments could have contractual significance.

records.title: develops silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
records.text: A longstanding order-and-production practice gave significance to the supplier’s response to new orders.

records.title: develops silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
records.text: The silence materials require attention to the relationship preceding the apparent offer.

records.title: develops contract formation and civil-rights claims
records.text: A remand examined whether a salon contract had formed before discriminatory refusal of service.

records.title: develops lapse and reasonable time
records.text: An offer made during a conversation ordinarily expires with that conversation.

records.title: develops lapse and reasonable time
records.text: A reward advertised during an emergency was held no longer open several years later.

records.title: develops lapse and reasonable time
records.text: A reward concerning possible future bank robberies could be understood as continuing.

records.title: develops lapse and reasonable time
records.text: The notes compare long delays in accepting public land dedications.

records.title: develops revocation
records.text: A withdrawal need not employ a technical revocation formula.

records.title: develops revocation
records.text: The opening presents a written land offer; later assigned notes discuss the distinction between a stated deadline and enforceable irrevocability.

records.title: develops option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text: Different events terminate or protect the power to accept in different ways.

records.title: develops option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text: The notes preserve the difference between protecting an opportunity to accept and binding both parties to performance.

records.title: develops option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text: The introductory note presents Learned Hand’s rejection of reliance-based irrevocability for this bargain offer.

records.title: develops option contracts and protected acceptance periods
records.text: Using and listing a subcontractor’s bid did not necessarily accept it or create reciprocal estoppel.

records.title: develops scope of article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text: A sale and installation of bowling equipment was analyzed as predominantly a goods transaction.

records.title: develops scope of article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text: The note describes separating goods and nongoods aspects of the sale of a radio station.

records.title: develops scope of article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text: The diving-board dispute illustrates looking at the goods aspect that gives rise to the claim.

records.title: develops scope of article 2 and mixed transactions
records.text: The editors describe Article 2 reasoning about shingles in a roof-installation transaction.

records.title: develops mailbox rule and overtaking communications
records.text: The note traces the common-law mailbox rule to the posted acceptance of a wool offer.

records.title: develops mailbox rule and overtaking communications
records.text: The assigned page introduces reinstatement of a lapsed policy through a directed payment and reports the court’s conclusion that coverage existed at death.

records.title: develops mirror-image rule and counteroffers
records.text: A signed return accompanied by a condition about furnishings operated as a counteroffer.

records.title: develops mirror-image rule and counteroffers
records.text: An inquiry about a different proposed plea did not necessarily reject the offer already made.

records.title: develops last-shot analysis
records.text: Repeated performance under conflicting labor-supply forms produced a disputed inference about the governing terms.

records.title: develops expressly conditional acceptance
records.text: Dorton’s notes preserve competing readings and a reported later rejection of the broad Roto-Lith approach.

records.title: develops ucc § 2-207 — formation and unmatched terms
records.text: The chapter organizes the statute around formation by writings, formation by conduct, and determination of terms.

records.title: develops material alteration
records.text: Unexpected back-tax liability illustrates a materially altering allocation distinct from Bayway’s transaction-specific tax.

records.title: develops material alteration
records.text: The notes identify recurring settings for a material-alteration dispute.

records.title: develops material alteration
records.text: The materiality notes compare types of clause and kinds of evidence.

records.title: develops different terms and the three § 2-207 approaches
records.text: The notes juxtapose the Code’s default terms with firms’ strategies for avoiding unwanted boilerplate.

records.title: develops different terms and the three § 2-207 approaches
records.text: The notes separate the statutory ambiguity, judicial role, and commercial incentives.

records.text: The two principal opinions give competing significance to ProCD’s box-term formation analysis.

records.text: The note reports adoption of a retention-based formation account.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Subject-matter jurisdiction is a court’s authority to decide a category of dispute. Federal courts require an applicable grant of authority within the limits allowed by the Constitution.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Personal jurisdiction is a court’s authority to bind a particular person or entity through its judgment. It concerns the defendant’s relationship to the forum or a separate recognized basis for submitting to that authority.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A court may need both a statute authorizing its action and constitutional permission to exercise that authority. The Constitution can allow a reach that the legislature has chosen not to grant.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A procedural ruling decides how or whether litigation may proceed. A merits determination decides the parties’ underlying legal entitlement, although some motions can resolve that entitlement without trial.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Waiver or forfeiture can prevent a party from relying on an objection that was available earlier. The consequences depend on the kind of objection and the governing rule.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A precedent’s contribution depends on what the court decided, the facts and posture before it, and which reasoning commanded the necessary votes. A dissent or concurrence can illuminate a dispute without becoming the holding of the Court.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Federalism distributes judicial and lawmaking responsibilities between the national government and the states. Procedure can affect that distribution through jurisdiction, governing law, and the treatment of state-created rights.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Procedural design affects whether parties can obtain a meaningful decision and what obtaining one costs. The course repeatedly examines the tradeoff between access to proof and protection against costly, weakly supported litigation.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Judicial discretion is the authority a rule or doctrine gives a judge to choose among legally permissible responses after considering relevant facts and interests. The authority remains bounded by the governing law.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The territorial approach associated with Pennoyer linked a state court’s authority to service, consent, domicile-related settings, and property within its territory. It provides the historical starting point for the course’s personal-jurisdiction sequence.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Domicile connects a person to a state through residence and the legally relevant intention to make it a home. In the readings it matters both to citizenship for diversity and to certain bases of judicial authority.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Minimum contacts describe the forum connections needed to make an assertion of personal jurisdiction compatible with the due-process standard developed in International Shoe. The inquiry examines the quality, nature, and legal significance of the connections.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Purposeful availment concerns conduct by which a defendant deliberately engages with a forum and invokes the benefits or protections associated with that activity. Some contexts describe purposeful direction of conduct toward the forum.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Specific jurisdiction requires an appropriate connection between the defendant’s forum activity and the particular litigation. The assigned cases describe claims that arise out of or relate to those contacts.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The fairness inquiry evaluates whether exercising jurisdiction is reasonable in light of the burdens and interests identified in the personal-jurisdiction cases. It operates within the governing jurisdictional framework.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Specific jurisdiction is authority to decide a claim connected to the defendant’s forum contacts. It is claim-linked, so the relationship among defendant, forum, and litigation must be identified.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: General jurisdiction permits a court to hear claims against a defendant without requiring those claims to arise from forum activity. For a corporation, the assigned cases focus on whether it is essentially at home in the forum.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The stream-of-commerce problem asks when a manufacturer’s distribution of a product through others supplies a sufficient connection to the state where litigation is brought. It is especially difficult when the manufacturer does not directly sell to the ultimate forum customer.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The effects cases examine when intentional conduct directed toward a forum supplies a jurisdictional connection even though the actor worked elsewhere. The defendant’s connection to the forum remains essential.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A contract can create forum connections through the parties’ deliberate relationship, negotiations, future obligations, and performance. The existence of a contract with a forum resident is only part of the inquiry.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over persons outside the state in defined circumstances. Its interpretation determines the state-law reach before constitutional limits are applied.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Consent supplies a basis for personal jurisdiction through an agreement, conduct in litigation, or another legally recognized submission to the court’s authority. The assigned cases examine both how consent arises and its limits.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: An agreement identifies where the parties will litigate covered disputes.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Jurisdictional discovery develops evidence concerning facts needed to decide the court’s authority over a party. A defendant’s objection to jurisdiction does not necessarily remove the court’s power to require information needed to decide that objection.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Tag jurisdiction refers to personal jurisdiction based on serving an individual while the individual is physically present in the state. Burnham upheld its use on the facts before the Court, with differing reasons.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Property-based jurisdiction uses a defendant’s interests in property as part of the basis for adjudication. The course distinguishes disputes about the property itself from efforts to use unrelated property to obtain leverage over a person.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Internet-jurisdiction questions ask which online activities connect a particular defendant to a particular forum. The ability to access a site everywhere creates a need to identify meaningful forum-directed conduct.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A collateral challenge contests a judgment’s authority in a later proceeding rather than through ordinary review in the original action. Personal-jurisdiction choices can affect whether such a challenge remains open.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Finality limits repeated litigation after a court has entered a judgment. The course encounters it in jurisdictional challenges, class representation, and the protection of absent persons.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Notice is the communication needed to give an affected person a meaningful opportunity to protect an interest before a court acts. Mullane evaluates whether the method is reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform interested persons.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Service of process is the formal delivery or legally authorized communication of the summons and complaint or equivalent initiating papers. It tells a defendant that a judicial proceeding requires a response.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A court may refuse to recognize service when deception procured a defendant’s presence for that purpose. The separate doctrine of immunity can protect persons present for judicial proceedings in specified circumstances.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: An opportunity to be heard allows an affected person to challenge the grounds for governmental action before an appropriate decision-maker. Timing and the form of the hearing depend on the legal setting.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A prejudgment remedy restricts possession or use of property before final determination of liability. Attachment, garnishment, and replevin can protect a claimant but can also harm a person before the claim is proven.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The Mathews framework evaluates the private interest, the risk of error and value of additional safeguards, and the relevant governmental or countervailing interests. Doehr applies an adapted inquiry to a private litigant’s use of attachment.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Diversity jurisdiction permits specified civil actions between parties of different citizenship to be heard in federal court when the statutory conditions are met. The ordinary statute combines citizenship requirements with an amount in controversy.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Citizenship identifies the legally relevant state or foreign affiliation of a party for diversity jurisdiction. It depends on the kind of party rather than a single universal test.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The amount in controversy is the value genuinely placed in dispute for a jurisdictional statute. It is assessed by the governing legal standard and the claim at issue, rather than simply the amount eventually awarded.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Aggregation concerns when several claims may be added together to satisfy a jurisdictional amount. The answer depends on the parties and whether the claims are separate or share a common undivided interest.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Standing asks whether the party invoking federal judicial power has the constitutionally required personal stake in the requested relief. The assigned discussion emphasizes concrete injury and its relationship to the challenged conduct and remedy.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The well-pleaded complaint rule looks to the plaintiff’s own claim for federal-question jurisdiction. A federal defense anticipated in the complaint ordinarily does not make a state-law claim arise under federal law.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Supplemental jurisdiction allows a federal court with an authorized anchor claim to hear certain related claims that lack an independent federal jurisdictional basis. The statute imposes conditions, exclusions, and grounds for declining the additional claims.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Pendent and ancillary jurisdiction are historical descriptions of federal authority over related claims or parties. Congress’s enactment of § 1367 provides the statutory framework emphasized in the later course materials.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The pendent-party problem asks whether a related claim against or by an additional person may be heard when that person’s claim has no independent federal jurisdictional basis.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: When original jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, § 1367(b) restricts certain additional claims by plaintiffs and proposed plaintiffs. The role of each party and the method of joinder matter.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Even when supplemental judicial power exists, the court may have grounds to decline to exercise it. The assigned materials connect that choice to state-law complexity, predominance, loss of federal claims, and other exceptional circumstances.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Removal transfers an eligible action from state court to federal court through a procedure authorized by Congress. It ordinarily depends on federal original jurisdiction and the removing party’s statutory role.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The forum-defendant rule restricts specified diversity removals when a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the forum state. It is a statutory restriction beyond the existence of diversity jurisdiction.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Venue identifies the geographically proper court within the relevant court system. It allocates the location of litigation and is distinct from subject-matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The historical local-action rule associated certain claims involving land with courts where the land was located. The readings examine the rule’s origins, contested rationale, and later statutory treatment.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Transfer moves litigation from one federal district to another under statutory authority. Different statutes address a convenient alternative to a proper venue, an improper venue, and coordinated pretrial proceedings.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Forum non conveniens permits dismissal in favor of an available adequate alternative forum when the governing balance strongly favors litigation there. It often matters when transfer within the federal system cannot reach the alternative forum.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Erie addresses the law a federal court uses when adjudicating rights governed by state law. Federal jurisdiction alone does not authorize creation of a federal general common law to replace state rules of decision.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Before Erie, Swift permitted federal courts to exercise independent judgment on some questions categorized as general law. Erie rejected that approach to state-law rights and required respect for state judicial decisions as well as statutes.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The outcome inquiry asks how a difference between state and federal treatment affects the enforcement of state-created rights. Hanna relates the inquiry to discouraging forum shopping and unequal administration of law.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Byrd examines whether a federal court should follow a state practice assigning a disputed factual issue to a judge rather than a jury. The analysis considers the state rule’s connection to substantive rights and the federal system’s interests.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A scope inquiry asks whether the federal provision actually answers the disputed procedural question. A direct conflict requires a different analysis from a situation in which the state and federal provisions can operate together.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The Rules Enabling Act authorizes general federal rules of practice and procedure while limiting their effect on substantive rights. It supplies a validity inquiry for Federal Rules distinct from the ordinary Erie choice when no such Rule governs.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Accommodation asks whether the relevant state and federal interests can both be respected through a particular allocation of tasks or procedure. Gasperini considers review of damages under state law and federal appellate constraints.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Choice of law identifies which jurisdiction’s substantive law governs a claim. This is separate from whether a court has authority over the case and parties.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Specialized federal common law consists of judicially developed federal rules supported by particular federal interests or authority, rather than a general power arising from federal jurisdiction.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Boyle recognizes a defined defense to certain state design-defect claims when imposing liability would significantly conflict with federal procurement decisions. It is a specialized federal common-law doctrine.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The reverse-Erie problem concerns the obligations of a state court adjudicating a federal claim. State procedure cannot be used in a way that impermissibly defeats the federal right and its protected incidents.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A release purports to surrender a legal claim. When the claim arises under a federal statute, federal law may govern whether a challenged release validly extinguishes that right.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A pleading states a party’s claims or responses in the form required by the applicable procedural rules. A complaint must provide a sufficient account of entitlement to relief to move the case forward.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Notice pleading emphasizes giving the opposing party an intelligible account of the claim and its grounds without requiring the technical formulas of older pleading systems. The assigned cases trace its development and later qualifications.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Plausibility asks whether the well-pleaded factual allegations support a reasonable inference of entitlement to relief in the context of the claim. Legal labels and recitations of elements do not supply missing facts.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A claim passes through different tests as litigation proceeds. Pleading concerns sufficient allegations; the production burden concerns enough evidence for a reasonable verdict; persuasion concerns whether the factfinder is convinced under the governing standard.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Rule 9(b) requires particular circumstances for allegations of fraud or mistake. The requirement concerns the pleaded theory, not simply the title of the statute under which the party sues.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act imposes a heightened pleading requirement concerning scienter, the legally required wrongful state of mind, in the securities setting addressed by Tellabs.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Special-damage pleading identifies losses that require particular notice rather than being sufficiently conveyed by the ordinary consequences of the pleaded wrong. The classification depends on the governing law and the claim.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Rule 12 provides distinct ways to respond to a complaint, including objections to authority, legal sufficiency, excessive vagueness, and specified material within the pleading. Each motion has its own purpose and preservation rules.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A privilege can protect conduct or statements that might otherwise support liability. The assigned Garcia opinion distinguishes conditional protection, which may depend on facts such as malice, from absolute protection for particular proceedings.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: An answer responds to the complaint’s allegations by admitting them, denying them, or properly stating insufficient knowledge. Those responses define what remains disputed.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: An affirmative defense supplies an additional reason the defendant should avoid or limit liability even when the claim’s ordinary allegations are assumed. It performs a different role from a denial.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Amendment changes a party’s pleading as the case develops. The rules distinguish changes allowed without permission from those requiring consent or leave of court, and address the effect on timing and trial.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Relation back treats a qualifying amendment as connected to the original pleading for limitations purposes. Different provisions govern changed allegations and changed defendants.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: An issue not stated in the pleadings may become part of the case when the parties expressly or impliedly consent to trying it. The evidence and conduct of the parties must support that conclusion.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Certification and verification requirements attach responsibility to statements submitted to the court. Sanctions can enforce that responsibility but require the applicable substantive standard and procedural protections.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The safe-harbor mechanism gives a party an opportunity to withdraw or correct challenged material before an opponent’s Rule 11 motion is filed with the court. It is a procedural condition on that route to sanctions.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Joinder determines which claims and persons can be included in one action. Different devices govern multiple claims, counterclaims, crossclaims, additional defendants, required parties, interpleader, and intervention.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: The real party in interest is the person entitled under the governing substantive law to enforce the right asserted. The inquiry can change when rights are assigned or an insurer becomes subrogated to a claim.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Claim joinder allows a party to assert more than one claim against an existing opposing party. Federal Rule 18 provides broad procedural permission even when claims differ in subject or legal theory.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A crossclaim is a claim against a coparty, such as one defendant’s claim against another defendant. Rule 13(g) requires the specified connection to the transaction, occurrence, or property involved in the action.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Rule 20 permits multiple plaintiffs or defendants when the claims have the required transaction-or-series connection and share a question of law or fact. It allows related individual claims to proceed in one action.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Rule 19 asks whether an absent person should be joined and, if joinder is not feasible, whether the action can fairly proceed without that person. The inquiry protects existing parties, absentees, and the interest in complete resolution.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A judgment ordinarily does not bind a person who was neither a party nor represented through a recognized exception. Yet litigation can still practically impair an absentee’s interests even without formally binding that person.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Interpleader allows a stakeholder facing competing demands for the same property or obligation to bring the claimants into one proceeding. It protects against inconsistent obligations while providing a process to decide entitlement.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Sovereign immunity can prevent a state or foreign sovereign from being joined in litigation without an applicable exception or waiver. When that sovereign claims an interest in the dispute, its absence also affects the Rule 19 analysis.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A court can coordinate related litigation or separate issues for trial without treating every procedural unit as one merged claim. These management choices seek efficiency while limiting prejudice and confusion.

records.title: falls within this question

records.title: falls within this question
records.text: A class action allows named parties to litigate on behalf of an adequately defined group of absent persons when the requirements for representative litigation are satisfied. It can make small claims viable and resolve common issues together.

records.title: falls within this question

Small examines a statute through domestic context and competing uses of legislative history. Both accounts show why the domain of a broad word requires explanation. Evidence of commercial agreement and evidence of congressional meaning have different legal roles; neither case makes the other course’s interpretive test controlling.

records.title: Whose context informs meaning?
records.text: The Contracts account addresses evidence of the parties’ agreement, including commercial practice and the governing jurisdiction’s treatment of extrinsic evidence. Katzmann addresses the institutional production of statutes and the value he attributes to legislative materials. Both require an explanation of why particular context bears on disputed language. Contract parol-evidence rules do not supply a test for using legislative history; the source, institutional setting, and competing interpretive theories differ.

records.title: Read a provision within its legal structure
records.text: The LRS treatment of statutory structure considers how neighboring provisions and the whole enactment bear on meaning. UCC § 2-207 separates formation, the treatment of additional terms, and contracts established by conduct into distinct subsections. That organization supplies a concrete comparison for reading legal text in context.

records.title: Notice supports a meaningful opportunity to participate
records.text: Mullane requires notice reasonably calculated in the circumstances to inform interested parties. Mathews addresses the procedural safeguards appropriate to disability-benefit termination. Read together, the two cases raise separate questions about whether a person can learn of the proceeding and what opportunity to respond is required. The comparison does not suggest that balancing under Mathews erases Mullane’s notice requirement.

records.title: Compare the timing and form of a hearing
records.text: Fuentes examines prejudgment seizure of household goods and the opportunity to contest the deprivation. Mathews examines termination of disability benefits and the sufficiency of written procedures followed by a later evidentiary hearing. The comparison asks how the private interest, risk of error, and government burden shape procedure. A civil creditor’s seizure and an agency benefits decision involve different facts and procedural systems; neither case makes a single hearing format appropriate for every deprivation.

records.title: Promises and agency changes give reliance different consequences
records.text: Drennan limits revocation of a subcontractor’s bid in light of foreseeable justified reliance in that setting. Fox explains that an agency changing policy must address serious reliance interests and contrary prior factual findings when those features require a fuller explanation. Fox did not hold that broadcasters had proved promise-based liability. Its analysis creates no contract, automatic damages remedy, or irrevocable regulatory policy.

records.title: Different sources of protection for reliance
records.text: Drennan addresses a general contractor’s reliance on a subcontractor’s bid and the resulting limitation on revocation in that setting. Administrative review requires an agency changing policy to address serious reliance interests when the governing reasoned-decisionmaking analysis demands it. These accounts show why a decisionmaker should identify the reliance and the rule that gives it legal significance. Agency reliance review does not import promissory estoppel or make every prior policy irrevocable.
