records.text: The FTC Act removal provision upheld in Humphrey's Executor is the provision held unconstitutional in Slaughter.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Wiener extends the Humphrey's Executor reasoning about adjudicatory bodies to a statute silent on removal, so the FTC tenure provision is the natural comparison.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Arthrex turns on whether APJs appointed by the Secretary of Commerce exercised authority reserved to presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed principal officers.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The decision applies the text of Article II, § 2, cl. 2 distinguishing principal from inferior officers.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Weiss asks whether assigning judicial duties to commissioned officers requires a second Appointments Clause appointment.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Black's opinion rests on Article I vesting lawmaking in Congress and denies the President a lawmaking role; useful cross-reference for exam analysis of separation of powers.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Universal Camera is the source of the 'substantial evidence on the record as a whole' formulation this concept applies to administrative hearing evidence.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Vermont Yankee bars judicially imposed procedures while preserving substantive review of the rule's justification, which is the space hard-look review occupies.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Nova Scotia's demand that the agency answer significant comments and disclose its data is a canonical hard-look application.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court's reasoning depends on classifying the incentive-charge proceeding as rulemaking rather than adjudication (the Londoner/Bi-Metallic line).

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Thompson reads Title VII's 'person aggrieved' by reference to the APA § 702 zone-of-interests test.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Twin Rivers applies the § 702 'adversely affected or aggrieved' zone-of-interests requirement to a petition for review.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The case sorts Hunt's three prongs into Article III requirements and prudential requirements Congress can abrogate.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority held the states lacked Article III standing because a party has no judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution or nonprosecution of another.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court relied on the Executive's enforcement discretion (the Heckler v. Chaney tradition) in explaining why nonenforcement priorities are not a suitable object of suit.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court first rejected the government's argument that the case was moot or that the states lacked standing because EPA had disavowed enforcing the Clean Power Plan.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Yakus is the wartime-emergency benchmark for how broad a delegation can be while remaining sufficiently specific.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The protected-interest question in Weston is the first step of the procedural due process framework.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Barry applies the protected-interest threshold of the procedural due process framework to shelter allocation.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority refuses to adjudicate because no rule can say how much partisanship is too much, while the dissent answers that ordinary legal standards of intent, effect and justification are enough.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court reads the Elections Clause’s allocation to state legislatures and Congress as relevant to its rejection of partisan gerrymandering claims for lack of manageable judicial standards. It expressly preserves federal judicial review of racial gerrymandering and one-person-one-vote claims.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The political question doctrine, like standing, flows from Article III's limit of federal courts to cases and controversies 'of a Judiciary Nature.'

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Roberts warns that the unelected and politically unaccountable federal judiciary would assume 'an extraordinary and unprecedented role' if it reallocated political power between the parties.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority points to bills introduced in Congress and to state reforms as the proper channel; Kagan replies that bills that never become law are no remedy when the beneficiaries of gerrymanders control the legislature.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Earl reads the wills statutes by the purpose of their makers and asks what the legislature would have said had the case been put to it, extending or restraining the words to match that intention.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority relies on Blackstone's rule that a statute's general words do not reach collateral consequences manifestly contradictory to common reason, illustrated by the manor of Dale and the Bologna barber.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Gray's dissent holds the court to the letter of a statute that regulates wills 'with comprehensive particularity' and treats the missing exception as a matter for the legislature alone.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The opinion states the canon that a thing within the intention of the makers is within the statute though not within the letter, and applies common-law maxims against profiting from one's own wrong as background rules.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Earl explains the gap by the drafting condition that lawmakers 'could not set down every case in express terms,' while Gray reads the same silence as a deliberate and complete legislative scheme.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority resolves the case on dictionary definitions and the mechanics of the trigger and refuses to rewrite the text to serve a broader purpose that Congress did not enact.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The dissent relies on the NRA president's 1934 hearing testimony and the House and Senate Reports as evidence of contemporaneous meaning, while the majority decides without them.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The dissent's presumption against ineffectiveness argues that a text's manifest purpose must not be defeated by easy evasion; the majority answers that a law is not useless because it draws a line more narrowly than one of its purposes might suggest.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The en banc Fifth Circuit resolved the ambiguity it found in section 5845(b) in Cargill's favor under the rule of lenity; the Supreme Court found the text clear and did not need lenity.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: ATF's Rule reinterpreting a criminal statute, after more than 10 contrary classifications, exceeded the agency's statutory authority, so the challenge under the APA succeeded.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority fixes the meaning of "weapon" as of 1968 with dictionaries and ordinary usage, treating the word as an artifact noun whose intended function can be clear before assembly.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The starter-gun parenthetical and the "designed to" and "readily converted" clauses are read together so that each clause does work, which is how the Court both defines "weapon" and calibrates "readily."

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Both the plaintiffs and the dissent invoke lenity because the Act carries criminal penalties, but the majority holds that lenity has no role where text, context, and structure decide the case.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: ATF issued the rule under section 926(a), and Justice Jackson's concurrence frames the whole case as a question of whether the agency stayed within the boundaries Congress drew in section 921(a)(3).

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The plaintiffs asked the Court to narrow the definition through constitutional avoidance, and the majority declined because avoidance applies only when the text is genuinely ambiguous.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court relies on a committee report, a floor colloquy between the Act's author and a committee chairman, a rejected floor amendment, and a conference manager's statement, ranking each as evidence of what Congress meant.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Marshall treats the question as what Congress intended for AEC-regulated materials, and lets that intent control over the literal breadth of "radioactive materials."

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court of Appeals' plain-meaning ruling is the foil: the unqualified words of section 1362(6) would cover all radioactive materials, and the Court says that reading contributes little once the history is consulted.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court expects a clear indication of legislative intent before reading the FWPCA to alter the AEA's pervasive regulatory scheme, so the later statute is not read to displace the earlier one.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The FWPCA's state permit programs and stricter state limits are contrasted with the AEA's exclusive federal control to show that the two schemes were not meant to overlap.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court requires a clear and manifest congressional intention before one statute displaces another and finds none in section 7, while the dissent argues the later and more specific NLRA should repeal the FAA to the extent of any conflict.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The catchall "other concerted activities" is read in light of the specific terms about organizing and bargaining that precede it; the dissent objects that the canon should not narrow deliberately broad language.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The case stages competing canons: harmony and the presumption against implied repeal on one side, the later-in-time and specific-over-general rules on the other, with each side claiming its canon fits.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Gorsuch refuses to consult legislative history, saying it is not the law, while Ginsburg builds her reading on the NLRA's history and the 1924 hearings on the FAA.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority infers from the NLRA's detailed regulation of every other section 7 activity that Congress did not silently protect class procedures, and treats express FAA overrides in other statutes as a benchmark.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Holmes grounds lenity in fair warning: a criminal prohibition must be stated in words the common world understands, so a court does not extend it to conduct the words do not plainly describe.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The general phrase "any other self-propelled vehicle" takes its meaning from the preceding list of automobiles, trucks, wagons and motor cycles, all of which run on land.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court reads the enacted words in their ordinary sense and refuses to expand them on speculation that Congress would have used broader language had it thought of airplanes.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Holmes notes that airplanes were never mentioned in the reports or debates, treating that silence as confirming rather than supplying the statute's meaning.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: McBoyle shows two canons pointing the same way, ordinary meaning reinforced by the list, and states the policy behind lenity as fair notice rather than tenderness to defendants.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority reads "communication" in section 2(10) in light of its listed neighbors, notice, circular, advertisement and letter, and confines it to public documents; Thomas replies that the canon applies only to words of doubtful meaning.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Kennedy anchors the meaning of "prospectus" in section 10, which requires registration-statement contents, and carries that meaning into section 12 under the rule that identical words in one act mean the same thing.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority treats "prospectus" as a 1933 term of art for a document soliciting the public, which explains the partial circularity of the statutory definition and the no-reliance remedy.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Both sides claim the text: the majority reads the whole act and the list in context, while the dissents insist the enacted definition in section 2(10) controls over structure and extrinsic meaning.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The opinions disagree about when a canon may be invoked, with Thomas charging that the majority used noscitur a sociis to manufacture ambiguity rather than resolve it.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The court states the canon in full and applies it to confine "other dangerous weapon" to stabbing weapons like the daggers, dirks and stilettos that precede it.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Section 750.226, which expressly covers "a pistol or other firearm" carried with unlawful intent, shows the legislature had already placed long guns in a different offense, confirming the narrow reading of section 750.227.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The court tests the broad reading against its consequences: treating rifles as concealed weapons would make felons of weekend hunters who have no unlawful intent.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The decision narrows a criminal statute to its enumerated weapons and leaves any broader regulation of long guns to the legislature, though the court does not invoke lenity by name.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The case shows a canon doing real work against a plain-meaning argument that "dangerous weapon" simply means any dangerous weapon.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority treats avoidance as decisive: with the text and history in equipoise, the Court adopts the reading that keeps FACA away from the President's Article II nomination power.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Brennan rejects the literal reading of "utilized" because it would reach consultations with the NAACP, an American Legion post or a political party; Kennedy answers that none of that is patently absurd.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The Court relies on Executive Order 11007, the Conference Report and the unexplained insertion of "or utilized" to narrow the word, while Kennedy calls the account one-sided and unauthoritative.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority follows Holy Trinity, holding that the ABA Committee is within the letter of FACA but not within its spirit as revealed by the statute's purposes.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Kennedy's concurrence argues that the plain language should be the starting and stopping point and that reading in a narrower meaning amends the statute by judicial interpretation.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The President's power to federalize the Guard exists only on the terms of § 12406(3), and the Court refused to let inherent Article II protective authority substitute for the statutory condition the Government could not satisfy.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Section 12406(3) is conditional legislation triggered by a presidential finding of inability; the majority tested the legal premise of that finding while Alito, citing Martin v. Mott, argued the President's judgment of the exigency is conclusive.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The majority read "execute the laws" in § 12406(3) together with the Posse Comitatus Act and applied the presumption that the same phrase carries the same meaning in related statutes; Alito answered that the presumption is not conclusive.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The opinions clash over consistent-usage, the ordinary meaning of "unable" (literal incapacity, substantial impairment, or legal barrier), and whether the Court may add an unwritten condition to the enacted text.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The case arrived on an emergency application to stay a temporary restraining order, referred by the Circuit Justice to the full Court, decided on supplemental letter briefs without argument, and framed throughout as likely conclusions at a preliminary stage.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The opinion lists the signals of a delegation to speak with the force of law, statutory grants of rulemaking or adjudicative power and agency practice that treats its output as binding, and finds none for 10,000 unpublished letters a year from 46 offices.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Classification ruling letters were placed with the policy statements, manuals, and enforcement guidelines of Christensen v. Harris County: interpretive output that lacks the force of law and therefore cannot bind a reviewing court.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Scalia’s Mead dissent predicted ossification of judicial statutory readings under Skidmore. Loper Bright now requires independent judicial interpretation of statutes, informed by persuasive agency reasoning, while respecting actual delegations of discretion. Kisor separately governs deference to an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The first question is whether a Federal Rule, read by its plain meaning, answers the question in dispute; here Rule 8 and section 6853 both address what a plaintiff must supply about the merits at the outset.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: A Rule that answers the question governs if it really regulates procedure under Sibbach, and the substantive nature or purpose of the displaced state law makes no difference to that inquiry.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: When a valid Federal Rule answers the disputed question, Berk uses Hanna’s governing-rule analysis rather than the unguided Erie outcome-and-twin-aims inquiry. Rule scope and validity must still be established.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Rule 8(a)(2)'s short and plain statement is a ceiling on merits information as well as a floor, so a state cannot require evidence such as an expert affidavit to accompany the complaint.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Rule 12(b)(6) tests whether the complaint states a claim. Under Rule 12(d), outside material not excluded by the court triggers conversion to summary judgment with a fair opportunity to respond. Justice Jackson’s Berk concurrence, joined by Justices Kagan and Sotomayor, used Rules 12 and 56 as its distinct conflict analysis.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Rule 56(c) allows judgment only where no genuine issue of material fact exists, and a contested question of a taxpayer's primary purpose is not such a case.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: On Cross’s disputed 1964 tax-deduction record, the taxpayers’ purpose and credibility required testing at trial. The court did not resolve the competing inferences about the trip’s primary purpose on the affidavits and deposition.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Cross rejected resolving disputed purpose and witness credibility on this summary-judgment record. A court may draw reasonable inferences favorable to the nonmovant, but may not choose among genuine competing factual accounts or weigh credibility.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Cross distinguished the ordinary duty to respond to a supported motion because, on this 1964 record, the disputed material facts depended on the taxpayers’ own credibility and the government sought cross-examination. Read its caution alongside the later Rule 56 cases.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The case reads the 1964 text of Rule 56(c) and shows the pre-Celotex reluctance to resolve state-of-mind questions on the papers.

records.title: Contrast

records.text: Complete diversity asks whether any plaintiff shares citizenship with any defendant.

records.title: Contrast
records.text: Section 1335 interpleader requires only minimal diversity, unlike the complete diversity Strawbridge requires under the general diversity statute.

records.title: Cited by

records.title: Reaffirmed by
records.text: Twombly reaffirmed Swierkiewicz: no heightened fact pleading of a prima facie case.

records.title: Tension
records.text: Iqbal's screen for conclusory allegations sits uneasily with Swierkiewicz's lenient pleading rule.

records.text: The plurality read a significant-risk threshold into the statute, which avoided an unbounded delegation of power to the Secretary.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Justice Rehnquist's concurrence argued that the statute, read as the Secretary read it, gave no intelligible principle and so was an invalid delegation.

records.title: Contrast
records.text: At the emergency stay stage on the same day, Biden v. Missouri allowed the CMS vaccine requirement for Medicare and Medicaid providers to take effect pending litigation, while NFIB stayed OSHA's broader workplace mandate. The statutory authority and regulated risks differed.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Scalia’s separate opinion in Decker criticized combining agency rulemaking and interpretation as a separation-of-powers problem. Kisor later debated that critique and retained Auer deference with limits; Scalia’s criticism preceded Kisor.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The critique goes to the foundation of Auer deference: whether an agency should have the last word on what its own regulation means.

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept
records.text: Katzmann's chapter on Congress and the lawmaking process is where this concept is drawn from:  the division of labor and drafting conditions.

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept
records.text: Katzmann's discussion of purposivism, textualism and legislative history is where this concept is drawn from:  purposivism.

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept

records.title: Casebook notes on the concept

records.title: Applies

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Arlington Central construes the IDEA fee provision and holds that it does not authorize recovery of expert fees.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The hypotheticals are the panel's own test of the government's proposed immunity rule in Raila.

records.title: Illustrates
records.text: Comparing injuries whose differences have nothing to do with the statute is a way of testing an interpretation by its anomalous results.

records.title: Analogy
records.text: Riggs and Holy Trinity are the two classic cases that read a statute by its purpose against the apparent breadth of its words.

records.title: Distinguishes
records.text: American Horse distinguishes Heckler v. Chaney: a refusal to begin rulemaking is less like a nonenforcement decision and is reviewable, though under a deferential standard.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The note introduces the enforcement-discretion questions that Heckler v. Chaney answers.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Section 553(b)(B) is the good-cause exception to the notice-and-comment requirement of § 553.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Remand without vacatur is one option within the debate over setting aside, vacatur and injunctions.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The framework note orients the reader to the APA § 701 limits on review.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The framework note orients the reader to § 702, which says who may challenge agency action.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The framework note orients the reader to the standard of review, including hard-look review.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The framework note orients the reader to the standards of review, including substantial evidence.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Akins holds that an injury shared by many people can still be concrete and particularized, which limits the generalized-grievance bar.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Bennett holds that the zone of interests is set by the provision allegedly violated, and that the Endangered Species Act's citizen-suit clause ('any person') negates the zone-of-interests test for those claims.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Bennett shows how a citizen-suit provision opens review to private plaintiffs enforcing a public statute.

records.title: Extends
records.text: State Farm v. Dole is the sequel to the State Farm rescission case and concerns the amended passive-restraint rule.

records.title: Applies
records.text: Brock applies the three-factor Mathews balance to a temporary reinstatement order and finds that the employer must receive notice and an opportunity to respond.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Goldberg treats welfare benefits as a statutory entitlement protected by due process, the shift away from the right–privilege distinction.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: OSHA submitted its ethylene-oxide rule to OMB for review under E.O. 12,291; the D.C. Circuit declined to decide whether that review was lawful.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The challenge to OMB’s role in the ethylene-oxide rule arose under E.O. 12,291, and the court left the question undecided.

records.title: Applies
records.text: Bell Aerospace relies on Wyman-Gordon and Chenery II in holding that the Board may make new policy through adjudication, unless that is an abuse of discretion or violates the statute.

records.title: Applies
records.text: Bell Aerospace applies Chenery II: the choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies primarily within the agency’s discretion.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The plurality and concurrence discuss Chenery II on choosing adjudication over rulemaking and on the futility of a remand.

records.title: Extends
records.text: Bowsher builds on Chadha: Congress may not retain control over the execution of the laws except through legislation.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Chadha applies Article I’s vesting of legislative power: legislative action needs bicameral passage and presentment.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Humphrey’s Executor upheld the FTC Act’s term and removal provisions set out in this rule entry.

records.title: Applies
records.text: Lucia applies Freytag's officer test to SEC administrative law judges point for point: a continuing office established by law plus the power to take testimony, conduct trials, rule on evidence and enforce discovery; SEC ALJs have more independent effect because their initial decisions can become final without further review.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Kagan’s four-Justice plurality read § 20913(d) as requiring registration of pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible. Alito concurred in the judgment under the existing nondelegation approach, producing the vote to reject the constitutional challenge.

records.title: Distinguishes
records.text: Weiss assumes without deciding that Shoemaker's germaneness test governs and finds judicial duties germane to a commissioned officer's office; it distinguishes Shoemaker because Congress in Weiss did not select particular individuals for the new duties.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: Peevyhouse limits recovery to diminution in value where the breached term is incidental and the cost of performance is grossly disproportionate to the benefit.

records.title: Contrast
