records.title: Applies
records.text: Trident applies Pacific Gas despite Judge Kozinski’s criticism: California law requires preliminary consideration of offered context even when the writing looks clear. The evidence must still make the proposed meaning reasonably susceptible and support a genuine dispute to avoid summary judgment.

records.title: Contrast
records.text: Greenfield's New York textual approach contrasts with Pacific Gas's California contextual approach to extrinsic evidence.

records.title: Contrast
records.text: W.W.W. Associates excludes outside evidence used to create ambiguity in a complete, clear New York agreement. Pacific Gas requires preliminary consideration of context under California law to decide whether the words are reasonably susceptible to the proposed meaning.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: W.W.W. bars extrinsic evidence offered to create an ambiguity in, or to add to or vary, a complete and unambiguous writing.

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The merger clause and the negotiated, complete writing made the written terms control over the buyer's account of the negotiations.

records.title: Extends
records.text: Subsection (3) is the route to a contract when the writings do not form one but the parties' conduct recognizes it.

records.title: Contrast
records.text: Northrop’s predicted Illinois approach knocks out conflicting terms even when the writings form a contract. Under § 2-207(3), a conduct-only contract instead contains agreed written terms and Code supplements. The routes are distinct, and courts disagree about different terms under subsection (2).

records.title: Bears on
records.text: The problem turns on whether conduct under subsection (3) establishes a contract and which terms it carries.

records.title: consumer-contract rule
records.text: Section 9 limits the parol-evidence rule's discharging effect when a standard term conflicts with the business's earlier affirmation or promise.

records.title: denies finality
records.text: Under § 9 the conflicting standard term is not a final expression on its subject.

records.title: assigned source
records.text: Assignment 13 lists Restatement of Consumer Contracts §§ 8, 9.

records.title: corollary of
records.text: Comment 1 to § 9 calls it a corollary of §§ 7 and 8.

records.title: limits standard terms
records.text: Section 8(c) makes unenforceable a standard term that negates or unreasonably limits an affirmation or promise that became part of the contract.

records.title: assigned source
records.text: Assignment 17 lists Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 8.

records.title: assigned source
records.text: Assignment 13 lists Restatement of Consumer Contracts §§ 8, 9.

records.title: consumer-contract rule
records.text: Section 6 states the two-factor test with an express sliding scale and lists terms that are substantively unconscionable.

records.title: assigned source
records.text: Assignment 18 lists Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 6.

records.title: non-disclaimable in consumer contracts
records.text: Section 4(a) states the duty of good faith and fair dealing as non-disclaimable in a consumer contract.

records.title: assigned source
records.text: Assignment 16 lists Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 4.

records.title: section entry
records.text: § 4 has its own entry.

records.title: section entry
records.text: § 6 has its own entry.

records.title: section entry
records.text: § 8 has its own entry.

records.title: section entry
records.text: § 9 has its own entry.

records.title: states the duty
records.text: Section 205 is the Restatement's statement of the duty of good faith and fair dealing that this concept collects.

records.title: governs discretion
records.text: The duty of good faith in performance is the standard the cases apply to a party's exercise of contractual discretion.

records.title: related later duty
records.text: Wood v. Lucy implied a reasonable-efforts promise that supplied consideration. Section 205 later states the distinct general duty of good faith in performance and enforcement.

records.title: applied in
records.text: Market Street Associates reads the duty of good faith in performance that § 205 states.

records.title: states the test
records.text: Section 302 states the intended-beneficiary test that this concept collects.

records.title: codifies as § 302(1)(a)
records.text: A promise whose performance pays the promisee's debt to the beneficiary makes the beneficiary intended under § 302(1)(a).

records.title: codifies as § 302(1)(b)
records.text: A promise meant to give the beneficiary the benefit of the performance makes the beneficiary intended under § 302(1)(b).

records.title: sales-of-goods rule
records.text: Section 2-209 governs modification, rescission and waiver of contracts for the sale of goods.

records.title: counterpoint
records.text: Alaska Packers refused a modification for want of consideration; § 2-209(1) removes that requirement for sales of goods.

records.title: compare
records.text: New York's § 5-1103 reaches a similar result for written modifications outside the Code.

records.title: states the power
records.text: Section 2-302 gives the court the power to refuse or limit enforcement of an unconscionable contract or clause.

records.title: applied in
records.text: Williams v. Walker-Thomas treated § 2-302 as persuasive and supplied the test the section leaves open.

records.title: consumer-contract counterpart
records.text: Consumer Restatement § 6 supplies a consumer-specific sliding-scale test and specified examples. UCC § 2-302 grants enforcement remedies without defining the substantive test.

records.title: defines and ranks
records.text: Section 1-303 defines trade usage and supplies a hierarchy when terms cannot reasonably be reconciled. Course of performance may also show waiver or modification, subject to § 2-209.

records.title: defines
records.text: Section 1-303(b) defines a course of dealing as conduct in the parties' earlier transactions.

records.title: sales-of-goods rule
records.text: Section 2-202 states the parol-evidence rule for sales of goods and lets usage and dealing explain or supplement a final writing.

records.title: applied in
records.text: Columbia Nitrogen required admission of usage and dealing evidence to explain or supplement the writing under former §§ 1-205 and 2-202, subject to reasonable consistency. It ordered retrial rather than deciding that the buyer owed nothing.

records.title: applied in
records.text: Nanakuli used usage of trade and course of performance to read a price-protection practice into a written supply contract.

records.title: sales-of-goods rule
records.text: Section 2-716 states when a buyer of goods may have specific performance or replevin.

records.title: compare
records.text: Morris v. Sparrow ordered specific performance of a unique horse under equity's adequacy test; § 2-716 reaches unique goods and other proper circumstances.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Follow three related questions: requested forbearance, promises implied from the bargain, and surrender of a disputed claim. These state decisions supply different applications; the Restatement states a proposed common framework rather than enacting one national rule.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Consideration is a bargained-for performance or return promise (Restatement (Second) § 71), and courts do not weigh its adequacy. They imply good-faith or reasonable-efforts duties to keep promises from being illusory, and count a surrendered claim that was doubtful or honestly believed (§ 74).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Detriment, not benefit: giving up a lawful freedom at the promisor's request is consideration whether or not the promisor gains anything.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: An exclusive agent's implied promise of reasonable efforts keeps the deal from being illusory and supplies consideration (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Giving up a claim that proves invalid is consideration if it was asserted with an honest and reasonable belief in its validity (Maryland).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: A purchase conditioned on the buyer's satisfaction is not illusory, because he must judge satisfaction honestly and in good faith (California).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Second Restatement: consideration is a bargained-for exchange (§ 71), and a surrendered claim counts if doubtful or honestly believed (§ 74).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: Iowa adopts § 74: a claim later shown invalid still supports a settlement if it was doubtful or the claimant honestly believed it might be valid.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Consideration: from legal detriment to bargain and implied promises
records.text: A requirements contract has consideration even before the buyer has any requirements: § 2-306 binds it to buy its good-faith needs (Missouri law).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: Wood supplies an implied efforts promise; the UCC and Restatement then state broader performance duties. Later cases police different kinds of discretion. Singapore is a comparison, while Ginsberg adds a federal preemption limit rather than rejecting good faith generally.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: In these authorities, good faith controls performance, enforcement and contractual discretion, with scope set by the applicable jurisdiction and express terms. UCC § 1-304 states a goods-contract obligation; Restatement § 205 states a common-law formulation. Ng Giap is a Singapore comparison, and Ginsberg concerns airline-law preemption.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: Cardozo reads a duty of reasonable efforts into an exclusive agency: courts supply the obligation the business arrangement implies.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: For goods, § 2-306(2) imposes best efforts in exclusive dealing unless otherwise agreed; subsection (1) separately measures output or requirements by good faith and limits disproportionate quantities.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: Best efforts does not demand ruinous losses, but a brewer may not neglect the brand it promised to promote to raise its overall profit (New York law).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: The Second Restatement states a duty of good faith in performance and enforcement. It is persuasive common-law authority; a jurisdiction must adopt or apply the proposition.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: Posner: good faith forbids deliberately exploiting the other side's oversight about its contract rights, though it does not require altruism.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: A party must actually exercise a discretion it promised to exercise, and not arbitrarily, but good faith adds no duty the contract excludes (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: Singapore declines to imply a general duty of good faith in law; a term is implied in fact only where necessary.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Good faith, efforts and discretion in performance
records.text: The Airline Deregulation Act preempts this state-imposed covenant claim because it relates to airline prices, routes or services and enlarges voluntarily assumed obligations; ordinary contractual promises remain a separate question.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: The line moves from an unenforced gift to reliance-based enforcement, then branches into commercial offers, negotiations and limits on remedies. Cosby is a due-process comparison in criminal law, not a civil contract holding adopting § 90.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: The Restatement § 90 formulation requires a promise, expected and actual reliance, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement; relief may be limited as justice requires. These state cases show different applications and limits, including at-will expectations and Texas’s writing requirement. Cosby concerns a separate due-process route.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: A promise of a home to a relative is a gratuity: her costly move in reliance on it does not make it enforceable (Alabama).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: Equitable estoppel bars the no-consideration defense when the promisor induced the promisee to give up her job in reliance on his note (Nebraska).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: First Restatement § 90: a promise one should expect to induce definite and substantial action, which does, binds if only enforcement avoids injustice.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: Traynor carries § 90 into commerce: a subcontractor's bid becomes irrevocable once the general contractor relies on it in bidding (California).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: A pension promise binds under § 90 because the employee retired in reliance on it, though her past service was no consideration (Missouri).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: Wisconsin applies § 90 to failed franchise negotiations: reliance losses are recoverable though the promises were too indefinite for a contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: The Second Restatement omits “definite and substantial,” permits a remedy limited as justice requires, and excuses proof of induced reliance for charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements. Adoption varies by jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: Reliance on an at-will assurance earns reliance damages, such as a lost sale price, not the profits the relationship would have brought (Indiana law).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: After the Supreme Court held the First Amendment no bar, Minnesota enforces a reporter's promise of source confidentiality by promissory estoppel.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: Texas: promissory estoppel avoids the statute of frauds for loan agreements only if the lender promised to sign a writing that satisfies it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Promissory estoppel: reliance as a ground for enforcing promises
records.text: A separate criminal-law branch: Pennsylvania enforces a prosecutor’s unconditional nonprosecution assurance after detrimental reliance affecting self-incrimination. This is due process, not an ordinary § 90 contract holding.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: Start with revocability, then separate three exceptions: beginning the invited performance, a statutory firm offer, and detrimental reliance. Baird and Drennan are competing approaches; California did not overrule the Second Circuit.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: These sources distinguish an option supported by consideration, beginning invited performance, statutory signed offers and reliance-based options. UCC § 2-205’s no-consideration protection is capped at three months and contains a separate-signature condition for the offeree’s form; § 87(2) is a Restatement approach whose adoption must be checked by jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: A promise to hold an offer open, given without consideration, does not bind; the offeror may revoke, and word from a third party is enough notice.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: For an offer inviting performance rather than a return promise, beginning or tendering the invited performance protects an opportunity to complete it. The offeror’s duty remains conditional on completion; preparation alone is a separate question.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: Learned Hand: a supplier's bid used in a contractor's bid stays revocable, and promissory estoppel does not hold an offer that sought a bargain.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: New York: a signed written offer that states it is irrevocable binds for the stated period, or a reasonable time, without consideration.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: A merchant’s signed assurance to hold a goods offer open needs no consideration for the stated or reasonable time, capped at three months under § 2-205. An assurance on the offeree’s form must be separately signed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: Reliance makes an offer irrevocable: a subcontractor's bid binds for a reasonable time once the general contractor used it in a winning bid.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Irrevocable offers: firm offers and reliance
records.text: The Second Restatement follows Drennan’s reliance rationale: foreseeable substantial reliance before acceptance can bind an offer as an option to the extent necessary to avoid injustice, not automatically for every use of a bid.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: The recurring question is what objectively communicates commitment in the manner the offer invites. Advertisements, private preparations and approvals illustrate different formation settings; they are not successive universal exceptions.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: Assent is judged objectively, by what a reasonable person in the other party's position would understand from words and conduct. An advertisement is usually an invitation, but one that is definite and leaves nothing to negotiate is an offer. Acceptance is an outward commitment to the offered terms, made in the manner the offer invites; unless the offer clearly says otherwise, any reasonable manner will do (UCC § 2-206, Restatement (Second) § 30). An acceptance by performance generally needs notice when the offeror would not otherwise learn of it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: Acceptance needs an outward act put in the course of communication to the offeror; private preparations to perform are not enough (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: The offeror controls the manner: an order that makes home-office approval the acceptance needs no separate notice of that approval (Texas).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: Unless the offer clearly says otherwise, acceptance may be made in any reasonable manner, including a prompt promise to ship or prompt shipment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: Assent is read from outward words and acts as a reasonable person would take them; a secret intent to joke does not undo a signed sale (Virginia).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: An advertisement that is clear, definite and leaves nothing open is an offer; the store cannot add a 'women only' rule after acceptance (Minnesota).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Offer and acceptance: assent judged from the outside
records.text: An acceptance must be an unequivocal commitment; a reply showing readiness while asking for more information is not one (North Dakota).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: Keep formation separate from terms. Section 2-207(1) asks whether the writings form a contract; (2) addresses additional terms; (3) governs a contract recognized by conduct. Northrop treats conflicting terms, and Bayway treats an additional term.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: Section 2-207 separates formation, additional terms and performance-based agreements. A definite and seasonable acceptance may form a contract unless expressly conditional; between merchants subsection (2) has three exceptions. Northrop predicts Illinois’s knockout approach to different terms. State enactments and interpretations must be checked for the transaction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: The mirror-image rule: a reply that varies the offer's terms is a counteroffer that rejects the offer, which cannot later be revived.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: For sales of goods the Code drops the mirror-image rule: an acceptance can form a contract though it adds or changes terms.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: An acceptance is expressly conditional only if it clearly says the offeree will not proceed without assent to its terms; 'subject to' is not enough.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: When forms do not form a contract but both sides perform, § 2-207(3) supplies the terms the writings share plus Code gap-fillers.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: Different terms in offer and acceptance knock each other out and Code gap-fillers replace them: the majority rule, predicted for Illinois.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Battle of the forms under § 2-207
records.text: Between merchants an additional term enters unless § 2-207(2) excludes it: the offer limits acceptance, the addition materially alters the deal, or timely objection occurs. Bayway assigns the material-alteration burden to the party opposing inclusion.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: Notice, assent and fairness are distinct questions. Hill and Klocek take different approaches to terms delivered with goods. Later online cases examine screen design or amendments of an existing agreement, rather than overruling those formation models.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: The cases distinguish reasonable notice, objective assent, fairness and later amendment. Hill and Klocek represent different approaches to box terms; Specht and Meyer evaluate actual screen design. Anderson decides remaining pre-amendment claims on its notice record and retroactivity analysis, without deciding the dismissed later claims.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: A liability limit printed on a claim check binds only with reasonable notice and assent; taking the ticket is not assent as a matter of law (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: A non-negotiated forum clause in a form ticket is enforceable if reasonable and fundamentally fair; notice of the clause was conceded.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: Terms in the box: following ProCD, a seller may invite acceptance by keeping the goods, so enclosed terms bind a buyer who does not return them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: The buyer ordinarily is the offeror, so terms shipped in the box are proposals under § 2-207 that bind a consumer only on express assent.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: Online terms bind only if the screen reasonably shows they exist and that clicking means assent; terms hidden below a download button did not.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: Inquiry notice suffices: a clear sign-up screen linking the terms binds a user who registers, without an 'I agree' box (California law).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Notice and assent to standard and online terms
records.text: On this record, website posting and continued use did not give sufficient notice of an arbitration amendment. A separate retroactivity analysis excludes the remaining pre-amendment claims; post-amendment claims had been dismissed by stipulation.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: Separate a final contract with open terms from a contract to negotiate and from reliance on negotiation promises. The UCC, state decisions and French law supply different routes to liability; failure to reach a final deal does not itself establish any of them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: Open terms can coexist with intended agreement and a sufficiently certain remedy under the UCC. Liability for a promise to negotiate and promissory estoppel are separate routes with their own elements and remedies. The cases apply or predict particular states’ law; Article 1112 supplies a French-law comparison.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: Leaving the price and how long it would run for later agreement makes an unenforceable agreement to agree; the court will not supply them (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: A sale of goods does not fail for open terms if the parties meant to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: Reliance in negotiations: Wisconsin awards reliance losses on promises made during franchise talks that were too indefinite for a contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: A letter of intent with an express promise to negotiate in good faith can itself be an enforceable contract (Pennsylvania law predicted).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: When parties meant to stay bound and their pricing mechanism fails, a court may set a reasonable price and supervise continued performance (Ohio).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: New York promissory estoppel yields reliance damages, including attributable overhead, when talks never produced the contemplated contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: A lender's promise to consider a loan modification, inducing the borrower to default, can support promissory estoppel (Massachusetts law predicted).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Incomplete bargains and liability in negotiations
records.text: France codifies good faith in negotiations: fault in negotiating yields damages, but never the benefits expected from the unmade contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: Track consideration first, then ask separately whether the modification was voluntary and made in good faith. Removing the consideration requirement under a statute does not remove the defenses of duress or other invalidity.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: The selected common-law cases distinguish lack of new consideration from economic duress. UCC § 2-209 removes the consideration requirement for a good-faith goods modification; New York’s statute addresses signed written modifications; Restatement § 89 states a fair-modification approach. Applicable enactments and state adoption matter.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: A promise of extra pay for work the promisees were already bound to do lacks consideration and does not bind.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: New York: a signed written agreement to modify or discharge a contract does not fail for lack of consideration.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: Parties may rescind and replace a deal in one transaction; an owner who freely gives up the old price after unforeseen rock is bound (New Hampshire).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: An agreement modifying a sales contract needs no consideration; the Code's comments police modifications by a test of good faith instead.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Modification and the pre-existing duty rule
records.text: A separate validity limit: even a modification with consideration is voidable for economic duress when threatened withholding leaves no timely substitute or adequate breach remedy. This does not loosen the pre-existing-duty rule.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: The UCC supplies a judicial power; later decisions explain meaningful choice and oppressive terms in their jurisdictions. The FAA cases add a federal preemption boundary for arbitration defenses, rather than abolishing unconscionability.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: The selected state cases examine choice, surprise and one-sided terms, with California’s sliding-scale approach. Concepcion adds an FAA preemption limit against demanding class arbitration. General contract defenses remain, but their application and other federal constraints must be checked in the relevant setting.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: The Code lets a court refuse to enforce a contract or clause it finds unconscionable when made, without defining the term.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: Courts may refuse to enforce a contract unconscionable when made: absence of meaningful choice plus terms unreasonably favorable to the other side.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: California: adhesion terms bind unless outside reasonable expectations or unduly oppressive; one side's own ally cannot be sole arbitrator.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: California applies a sliding scale of procedural and substantive unconscionability and refuses a one-sided mandatory employment arbitration agreement.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: Oklahoma applies the two-part test: a hidden, one-sided litter clause the buyers could not understand is unconscionable as a matter of law.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: The FAA preempts a state rule, framed as unconscionability, that conditions arbitration agreements on the availability of class procedures.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Unconscionability
records.text: After Concepcion, unconscionability remains a general defense to arbitration, and several one-sided terms can defeat the whole agreement (California).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: Integration and interpretation are different inquiries, and reformation for mutual mistake is another route. California and New York/Pennsylvania develop competing approaches; a later decision in one does not supersede the other. The CISG is a separate regime.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: The California cases permit provisional consideration of extrinsic evidence and collateral agreements under their respective tests. W.W.W. and Greenfield illustrate New York’s stricter treatment of a complete, clear writing; Gianni supplies a Pennsylvania example. The CISG comparison follows Article 8 rather than a domestic parol-evidence rule.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: Where the writing is complete on a subject, an oral term the parties would naturally have put in it is barred, even as a separate deal (Pennsylvania).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: New York: a prior oral term is provable only if collateral in form, consistent with the writing, and not one the parties would ordinarily put in it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: The rule does not bar reformation: a term left out by mutual mistake may be proved and written back in (Pennsylvania).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: California admits a collateral oral term the parties might naturally have made separately, unless the writing was meant as the whole bargain.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: Extrinsic evidence is admissible whenever relevant to a meaning the words are reasonably susceptible to, however plain the writing looks (California).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: Under Pacific Gas even an unambiguous clause must be opened to extrinsic evidence; the Ninth Circuit applies the rule while criticizing it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: New York's answer: extrinsic evidence may not be used to create an ambiguity in a complete, clear and unambiguous writing.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: New York again reads the writing on its face: silence about a use does not make a clear, unconditional transfer of ownership ambiguous.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: The parol evidence rule and plain meaning
records.text: Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause binds only if both parties meant it to; negotiations count under Article 8.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: The line explains how context enters a written sales agreement. Admission without facial ambiguity does not eliminate the express-terms priority when a reasonable reconciliation is impossible; usage can restrict remedies as well as expand obligations.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: Under UCC §§ 1-303 (formerly 1-205) and 2-202, usage of trade, course of dealing and course of performance explain or supplement a writing without any finding of ambiguity, but express terms prevail where the two cannot reasonably be read together. Whether a usage binds a party new to the trade remains a question of fact.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: Trade usage may give seemingly plain words or figures a special trade meaning, with no prior finding of ambiguity (Oregon).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: The 1952 Code’s §§ 1-205 and 2-202 admit dealing and trade usage to explain or supplement a writing. Revised Article 1 combines context rules in § 1-303: express terms generally prevail, but course of performance can show waiver or modification under §§ 1-303(f) and 2-209.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: The party claiming the narrower meaning of an ambiguous term must prove it, and a usage binds a newcomer only if known or so general as to be presumed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: Under the Code, usage and dealing come in without ambiguity unless irreconcilable with the express terms; a merger clause must expressly negate them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: Trade usage and course of performance can qualify an express posted-price term with price protection if reasonably consistent with it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Trade usage, course of dealing and course of performance
records.text: Usage can cut the other way: an unrebutted trade usage supplied an exclusive repair-or-refund remedy as part of the agreement.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Distinguish silence, half-truths, misleading opinions and a specific disclaimer of reliance. Florida home-sale law and Massachusetts caveat emptor are jurisdictional branches; a rule from one is not an overruling of the other.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: These cases distinguish silence, misleading half-truths, superior-knowledge opinions and specific reliance disclaimers. Johnson adopts a Florida home-sale disclosure duty; it does not overrule Massachusetts’s Swinton. Speakers applies Illinois fraud law and Psenicska applies New York’s disclaimer doctrine.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: A buyer need not disclose market news equally open to both sides, but neither party may say or do anything to mislead the other.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Caveat emptor: a seller's silence about a known hidden defect is not actionable without a false statement, half-truth or duty to speak (Massachusetts).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Opinions can be actionable misrepresentations when the speaker has superior knowledge or the parties are unequal in judging the subject (Florida).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Half-truths: one who speaks on a subject must disclose what is needed to keep the statement from misleading; Swinton is distinguished (Massachusetts).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Florida abandons caveat emptor for home sales: a seller must disclose known facts, not readily observable, that materially affect value.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: Aspirational sales talk is puffery, not fraud, and Illinois promissory fraud needs a scheme to defraud beyond one broken promise.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Misrepresentation and the duty to disclose
records.text: New York: a specific disclaimer of reliance on statements about the very matter at issue bars a claim of fraudulent inducement.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Distinguish an express condition from a constructive condition and a promise. Divisibility, waiver and substantial performance avoid different kinds of forfeiture; none automatically excuses a clearly stated express condition.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Express conditions, constructive conditions, waiver, divisibility and forfeiture relief remain distinct. The selected cases contrast substantial performance with a failed express financing condition and an ambiguous pay-when-paid clause. They do not establish one national rule for every payment-risk clause.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Mansfield: the order of performance follows the parties' evident sense; giving security was a condition precedent to the sale of the business.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: An express condition of personal satisfaction is enforced: a buyer who reserved the right to reject a portrait he disliked need not pay (Michigan).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Divisibility limits forfeiture: where the price is set per unit, the performer recovers for each unit fully delivered (Pennsylvania).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Waiver: an owner who kept paying without asking for the architect's certificates cannot invoke their absence against final payment (Pennsylvania).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: Substantial performance limits forfeiture for an innocent, trivial construction deviation where the requirement is treated as a promise or constructive condition. It does not generally replace strict compliance with an unmistakable express condition.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: An express condition must occur as stated: a mortgage commitment above the agreed rate fails it, whatever substitute the seller offers (Connecticut).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Conditions and the avoidance of forfeiture
records.text: An ambiguous pay-when-paid clause fixes a time for payment, not a condition; shifting the owner's credit risk needs clear words (Florida).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Impossibility and frustration concern events after formation; mutual mistake concerns an erroneous assumption at formation. Each asks separately who bore the risk. Cases from England and different states illustrate branches rather than one national progression.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: The cited cases distinguish later impossibility or frustration from mutual mistake at formation and examine allocation of risk. Added cost or reduced profitability alone is insufficient in the cases shown. A particular force-majeure clause or modern event requires its own jurisdictional and source analysis.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Where performance depends on a particular thing, its destruction without fault excuses both sides: the law implies a condition.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: A builder's absolute promise binds despite unforeseen soil; hardship short of impossibility is no excuse (Minnesota).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Mistake at formation: a sale may be avoided when both parties erred about the substance of the thing, not merely its quality (Michigan).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Frustration of purpose: when the shared foundation of the deal fails, the parties are discharged though performance is still possible.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: California accepts frustration but confines it: the event must be unforeseeable and destroy nearly all the value of the return performance.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Impracticability needs an unexpected event, a risk not allocated by agreement or custom, and real impracticability; extra cost alone did not suffice.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Excuse: impossibility, frustration and mistake
records.text: Arizona rescinds for a mutual mistake about a basic assumption (Restatement (Second) § 152) but limits the buyer to restitution, not reliance costs.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value
records.text: The dispute is which measure protects the promised performance without unreasonable waste. New York, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Oklahoma weigh different facts and doctrines; Groves and Peevyhouse are competing approaches, not a sequence of overrulings.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value
records.text: The selected jurisdictions choose between completion cost and diminution in value using the promised purpose, proportionality, deliberate breach and waste. Groves and Peevyhouse illustrate contrasting approaches; English loss-of-amenity damages supply another comparison. Restatement § 348(2) states a framework rather than a uniform enactment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value
records.text: When replacing innocent defective work would cost far more than the value it adds, the measure is diminution in value (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value
records.text: Minnesota awards the cost of the promised grading for a deliberate breach, though it far exceeds the value the work would add to the land.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value
records.text: Repair cost for defects reasonably fixable; diminution in value where the fix would mean tearing out work, as with the misplaced wall (Wisconsin).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Cost to complete or diminution in value

records.text: Read foreseeability, avoidability and certainty as separate restrictions on expectation damages. The Kenford decisions add New York-specific contemplation requirements; Fera addresses proof of a new business’s lost profits in Michigan.

records.title: Limits on damages: foreseeability, certainty and avoidable loss
records.text: Foreseeability, reasonable certainty and avoidable loss impose separate limits. Fera permits proof of a new business’s profits in Michigan; the Kenford decisions impose New York’s contemplation and certainty requirements. The proper formulation depends on the governing law and claim.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Limits on damages: foreseeability, certainty and avoidable loss
records.text: Recoverable losses arise naturally from breach or were within both parties' contemplation when contracting; uncommunicated special losses are out.

records.text: Avoidable loss: after a clear repudiation the other party may not keep performing and charge the cost; recovery is costs to date plus profit.

records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Expectation protects the bargain, reliance protects the changed position and restitution restores a benefit. The injured party’s restitution and a breaching party’s recovery are separate branches; disgorgement is an exceptional remedy, not ordinary contract damages.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: The cases distinguish expectation, reliance and restitution, including separate restitution questions for the injured party and the party in breach. Naval Institute rejects automatic recovery of the breacher’s gains. Restatement (Third) §§ 38–39 propose restitution/disgorgement formulations; they do not themselves supersede a court holding.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Expectation: the value of the promised result minus the value of what was delivered; pain the operation would have caused anyway is not compensated.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects

records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Contract damages compensate: punitive damages are unavailable even for a malicious breach unless a tort is pleaded and proved (Wisconsin).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: On a doctor's promise of a result, the patient recovers expenses, worsening, and pain and distress beyond what the treatment entailed, items the court found recoverable on either a reliance or an expectation measure.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Restitution for the injured party: a subcontractor who quits after a material breach recovers the value conferred, not reduced by its losing bargain.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Ordinary contract damages measure the plaintiff's loss; the breacher's gains count only insofar as they track that loss.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Expectation, reliance and restitution: which interest the remedy protects
records.text: Colorado allows disgorgement for a conscious, substantial breach where damages are inadequate, less profits due to the breacher's own contribution.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: The common question is whether money adequately protects the promised performance. The UCC relaxes the unique-goods formulation, but adequacy and equitable discretion remain. A negative injunction for services differs from compelling the service itself.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: Damages remain the default; specific performance or an injunction issues when damages are inadequate (land, unique goods, or 'other proper circumstances' under UCC § 2-716), weighed against the burden of supervising it. Courts still will not order personal services, though they may enforce a reasonable promise not to work elsewhere.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: Equity will not compel a singer to perform, but it will enjoin her breach of an express promise not to sing elsewhere during the engagement.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: A buyer of goods may obtain specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances. Inability to obtain substitutes can support relief beyond a uniqueness label; damages’ adequacy and equitable discretion still matter.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: A horse trained by the buyer has unique value to him, so equity orders its delivery despite the usual rule for chattels (Arkansas).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: On this record the used jet was not shown to be unique, and a higher replacement price does not make damages inadequate, so specific performance under § 2-716 fails.

records.title: Specific performance and injunctions
records.text: Posner: an injunction against breach of an exclusivity covenant is proper when damages are inadequate, judged by the costs and benefits of each remedy.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: American cases test a stipulated amount as compensation rather than punishment, with jurisdiction-specific formulations. The Swiss penalty rule is a comparative branch and does not change American law.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: The American cases enforce compensation reasonably tied to loss and reject penalties, using jurisdiction-specific tests. Wasserman’s gives negotiated commercial clauses a presumption in New Jersey. The Swiss decision applies a different penalty regime with judicial reduction of an excessive amount.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: A fixed sum is liquidated damages, not a penalty, if harm was hard to estimate at formation and the sum was a reasonable forecast (South Dakota).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: A formula paying full revenue without deducting the costs the promisee saves is a penalty; Posner questions the rule but applies it (Illinois law).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: New Jersey tests reasonableness in all the circumstances and presumes a clause between commercial equals valid; the challenger bears the burden.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Liquidated damages and penalties
records.text: The assigned translated Swiss decision permits judicial reduction of excessive contractual penalties. This comparative account does not establish the rule in an American jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: The line moves from creditor and family-beneficiary cases to the Restatement’s intended/incidental distinction. Government contracts receive additional scrutiny. The two Sisney decisions contrast an incidental public benefit with an expressly protected class.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: Restatement § 302 organizes intended and incidental beneficiaries by the contracting parties’ intention; its acceptance depends on the jurisdiction. The government-contract cases require more than a public benefit. The two Sisney decisions apply that distinction to different agreements.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: New York lets a creditor of the promisee sue the promisor on a promise made for his benefit, though he was no party and gave no consideration.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: Donee beneficiaries: a niece may enforce a promise made to her dying aunt for her benefit; closeness of kinship is not a strict limit (New York).

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: A city's water-supply contract benefits the public only incidentally; a resident may sue only if it promised compensation to individuals (New York).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: The Second Restatement replaces its creditor/donee terminology with intended and incidental beneficiaries, conditioned on the contracting parties’ intention. It proposes a framework; it does not enact a uniform state rule.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: South Dakota presumes against private enforcement of government contracts; an inmate is incidental to the State's food-service contract.

records.title: Third-party beneficiaries
records.text: The same day: a settlement that expressly covers every Jewish inmate who asks for kosher meals is enforceable by a member of that class.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Shoe replaces the territorial approach for absent defendants; later cases separate purposeful contacts, claim relatedness and fairness. Asahi and Nicastro leave competing contact theories. Fuld is a separate federal Fifth Amendment branch, not a relaxation of state-court due process.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: For state-court specific jurisdiction, distinguish purposeful contacts, a claim that arises out of or relates to them, and fairness. Ford rejects strict causation on its market-and-injury facts; Asahi and Nicastro leave divided stream-of-commerce reasoning. Fuld separately validates a targeted federal statute under the Fifth Amendment while reserving broader federal limits.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Power runs with territory: a personal judgment needs in-state service or a voluntary appearance, so an absent nonresident is out of reach.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Minimum contacts replace physical presence: suit is allowed if it does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: A single contract with a substantial connection to the forum supports a suit on that contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Purposeful availment: the defendant must itself reach into the forum; the unilateral acts of others do not count.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Stream of commerce in a state court: a component maker can be sued where its product, sold through ordinary distribution, causes injury.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Acquiescing in a child's move to the forum is not purposeful availment, so the parent cannot be sued there for support.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Foreseeable travel of a product is not enough; the defendant's own conduct must make suit there foreseeable, as when it serves that market.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Two steps, contacts then fairness: a long-term franchise deal aimed at a forum company is a contact even without physical entry.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Eight Justices agree the remaining foreign indemnity suit is unreasonable. No majority chooses between awareness and additional forum-directed conduct as the stream-of-commerce contact test.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Six Justices reject jurisdiction, with no five-Justice rationale: four require state targeting; two concur on the isolated-sale record and decline a broader rule. The three dissenters take a broader market approach.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: Relatedness is claim by claim: nonresidents' claims need their own link to the forum, and the sliding-scale approach is rejected.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: 'Arise out of or relate to' needs no strict causation: a maker that cultivates a market for a model can be sued where it injures.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Specific personal jurisdiction: from territorial power to minimum contacts
records.text: A separate federal-statute branch: the Fifth Amendment does not import the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts test. This targeted terrorism statute is valid; the Court leaves the outer limits and a separate reasonableness requirement open.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: Read Calder through the defendant’s own suit-related connection to the forum, as Walden later requires. Zippo is a district-court Internet framework; accessibility or interactivity alone does not establish the required claim-related targeting.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: Effects in the forum count only through the defendant's own conduct expressly aimed at the forum itself, not through the plaintiff's ties to it (Calder as read in Walden). A website's reach or interactivity is not enough unless the claim-related conduct was directed at the forum.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: Regular magazine sales in a state support a libel suit there, even for nationwide damages and though the plaintiff has no ties to it.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: Effects test: individuals whose alleged intentional tort was aimed at the forum, knowing the harm would be felt there, can be sued there.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: A sliding scale for websites: knowing online business with forum residents supports jurisdiction; a passive site does not.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: The defendant's own conduct must connect him to the forum itself; an injury the plaintiff feels there is not enough, even for torts.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction for conduct aimed at the forum: libel, torts and the Internet
records.text: After Walden, a website's reach and interactivity in a state do not support a libel suit unless the story or site was aimed there.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: This line concerns contacts-based jurisdiction over unrelated claims. Perkins supplies the exceptional home-like setting; Goodyear and Daimler narrow the ordinary test. Mallory preserves a separate consent route and decided the Due Process Clause challenge only.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: Contacts-based all-purpose jurisdiction ordinarily requires the corporation to be at home, with Perkins illustrating an exceptional setting. Mallory preserves Pennsylvania’s express registration-consent route against the Due Process Clause challenge; the Commerce Clause objection was not decided in that opinion.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: Continuous and substantial activity in a state may justify suit there even on claims unrelated to that activity.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: A foreign company run from an Ohio office during wartime may be sued there on unrelated claims; due process permits it.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: Purchases, training trips and a single negotiating visit are not the continuous and systematic contacts needed for unrelated claims.

records.title: General personal jurisdiction: from continuous business to 'at home'
records.text: 'At home' means place of incorporation and principal place of business, save an exceptional case; heavy in-state business is not enough.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent
records.text: Separate domicile, voluntary presence, property and consent. Shaffer rejects unrelated property as a shortcut; Burnham preserves tag service on an individual, with divided reasoning. Szukhent concerns effective service through an appointed agent, not a general due-process ruling.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent
records.text: Shaffer subjects property-based jurisdiction to Shoe; Burnham sustains voluntary in-state personal service on an individual, with no majority rationale. Domicile and valid consent remain distinct routes. Szukhent upholds appointed-agent service with actual prompt notice; Mallory decides the express registration statute’s due-process issue only.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent
records.text: Jurisdiction rests on in-state service, voluntary appearance, or local property seized at the outset; consent and status cases are reserved.

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent

records.title: Personal jurisdiction without contacts: presence, domicile, property and consent

records.title: Notice and hearing before property is taken

records.title: Erie: which law a federal court applies
records.text: Ask first whether valid federal law covers the disputed issue. This line follows the no-direct-conflict branch: state substantive law, outcome effects, Hanna’s twin aims and countervailing federal interests. The companion Rules timeline handles direct collisions.

records.title: Erie: which law a federal court applies
records.text: Where no Federal Rule or statute covers the issue, a federal court applies the state rule if disregarding it would encourage forum shopping or produce inequitable administration of the laws (Hanna's twin aims), giving weight to strong federal interests such as the jury's role (Byrd) and accommodating both systems where it can (Gasperini).

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: There are two questions: does federal law answer the disputed question, and is it valid? A Federal Rule must satisfy the Rules Enabling Act and Constitution; a federal statute follows its own constitutional authority. Shady Grove splits on the Rule-validity analysis.

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: A valid Federal Rule governing the disputed question controls, subject to the Rules Enabling Act’s substantive-rights limitation and the Constitution. records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: A valid Federal Rule that covers the issue applies even if the outcome differs; Erie's twin-aims test does not decide Rules cases.

records.text: No direct collision: Rule 3 does not govern state tolling, so Ragan stands and state service law applies.

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: A federal rule broad enough to collide with state law controls: an appellate sanctions rule displaces a mandatory state penalty.

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: The same test for federal statutes: § 1404(a) covers a forum clause's effect on transfer, so state hostility to the clause yields.

records.title: Federal Rules and statutes against state law
records.text: Five Justices let the Rule 23 class proceed despite New York’s penalty-class bar. No majority adopts one validity test: Scalia’s plurality reads procedure categorically; Stevens asks whether the state rule defines substantive rights.

records.text: The majority finds Rule 8, reinforced by Rule 12, incompatible with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement. Jackson agrees with the judgment through Rules 3 and 12 while rejecting the majority’s Rule 8 collision analysis.
