records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Erie rejects general federal common law, not every federal rule fashioned by courts. Clearfield, Dice and Boyle involve different federal interests; Bank of America and Rodriguez identify the boundary when an asserted federal interest is insufficient.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Federal courts make federal common law only where needed to protect uniquely federal interests, such as the United States' own rights or federal procurement where state law significantly conflicts (Clearfield, Boyle, Rodriguez); otherwise state law governs. Federal statutory rights carry their own federal rules into state court (Dice).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: No federal general common law: federal courts may not make their own rules for ordinary state-law disputes.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Federal law governs the United States' rights on its own commercial paper, and courts may fashion that law absent a statute.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Federal law decides whether a release of FELA rights is valid even in state court, and a state that uses juries cannot take the fraud issue from one.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Clearfield stops where the United States' rights are not at stake: private disputes over government paper follow state law.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: A uniquely federal interest plus a significant conflict displaces state tort law: the defense for military contractors.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal common law after Erie
records.text: Federal common law only where needed to protect uniquely federal interests; a judge-made rule for dividing tax refunds falls.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Rule 8 is the baseline; Twombly and Iqbal replace Conley’s dismissal formula with plausibility. Tellabs applies a separate securities statute, and Kearns concerns Rule 9(b); neither creates a heightened rule for every complaint.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Twombly and Iqbal require sufficient factual allegations for plausibility under Rule 8, rather than labels or a probability showing. Rule 9(b) and the PSLRA impose distinct heightened requirements; Kearns and Tellabs apply those respective regimes. Swanson illustrates the Seventh Circuit’s application of ordinary plausibility.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: The Federal Rules replace the code's 'facts constituting a cause of action' with a short and plain statement showing a right to relief.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: An inartful, home-drawn complaint survives because it shows some claim; the old cause-of-action formula no longer governs.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Fair notice is enough: dismiss only if it appears beyond doubt that no set of facts could support relief.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Code pleading holds out: North Carolina still demands the ultimate facts, not labels such as 'assault' and 'trespass'.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: No heightened pleading outside Rule 9(b): a discrimination complaint need not plead the facts of a prima facie case.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Plausibility replaces 'no set of facts': parallel conduct plus a bare assertion of agreement does not state a conspiracy.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Under the PSLRA's heightened standard, the inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any innocent one.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Plausibility governs every civil action: set aside legal conclusions, then ask whether the remaining facts plausibly show liability.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Rule 9(b) reaches any claim that rests on a unified course of fraudulent conduct, even when fraud is not an element.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: What a complaint must say: from code facts to plausibility
records.text: Plausibility is not probability: a coherent, case-specific story of what happened, who did it and why it is unlawful suffices.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Keep permission to amend, issues tried by consent and relation back distinct. The 1991 amendment changes Schiavone’s notice deadline. Krupski then focuses the mistake inquiry on the proposed defendant’s understanding.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Leave to amend is freely given unless the opponent shows real prejudice, bad faith or futility; an unpleaded issue is tried by consent only if the opponent knew it was being tried. An amendment changing the defendant relates back if it arises from the same conduct, transaction or occurrence and, within the Rule 4(m) period, the new party had notice and knew or should have known it would have been sued but for a mistake (Krupski).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Theory of the pleadings: a complaint framed as conversion fails as conversion and cannot be saved as a claim in contract.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Rule 15 lets parties amend freely, conform pleadings to the evidence tried, and relate amendments back to the original filing.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Leave to amend is freely given; the opponent must show actual prejudice, which is not presumed when an admission is withdrawn.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Trial by consent of an unpleaded issue requires that the opponent knew it was being tried; evidence relevant to pleaded issues is not consent.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Relation back for a new defendant required notice within the limitations period itself, not the added time for service.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Notice to the new defendant within the time allowed for service now suffices, so a misnamed party can be substituted after limitations runs.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Amending the pleadings: from the theory of the pleadings to relation back
records.text: Relation back turns on what the new defendant knew or should have known, not on the plaintiff's knowledge or diligence.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: Surowitz concerns derivative-complaint verification, not a Rule 11 sanctions holding. The remaining steps follow Rule 11’s successive versions: objective inquiry in 1983, discretionary deterrence and a motion safe harbor in 1993, then applications.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: A signature certifies, after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, that the paper has a proper purpose and that its legal contentions and factual claims have support (Rule 11(b)). Sanctions are discretionary and limited to what deters; a party's motion must allow a 21-day safe harbor, and a court acting on its own must first give notice and a chance to respond.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: A separate starting point in derivative verification: good-faith reliance on an adviser’s investigation sustains the shareholder’s verification. This is not a holding that subjective good faith defeats modern Rule 11 sanctions.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: Rule 11 gains teeth: signers owe an objective duty of reasonable inquiry, and courts must sanction violations.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: Under the 1983 rule a represented party who signs a paper owes an objective duty of inquiry; relying on counsel is no excuse.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: The 1993 rule makes sanctions discretionary, aims them at deterrence, and gives a 21-day safe harbor to withdraw a challenged paper.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: A party's sanctions motion must honor the safe harbor, and a lawyer may rely on objectively reasonable information from the client.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Responsibility for filings: verification and Rule 11
records.text: The district court applies Rule 11 to invented citations and knowing falsehoods or conscious avoidance after warnings. Its bad-faith requirement addresses court-initiated sanctions in that circuit; the party-motion route has a separate safe harbor.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Osborn describes Article III’s broad ceiling; § 1331 has a narrower statutory reach. The well-pleaded complaint and creation tests give the ordinary route, while Smith, Grable and Gunn address the exceptional state-law claim containing a federal issue.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: A case arises under federal law when federal law creates the claim and the federal question appears in the well-pleaded complaint, not in a defense (American Well, Mottley). A state claim qualifies only if it necessarily raises a federal issue that is disputed, substantial to the federal system, and fit for federal decision without upsetting the federal-state balance (Grable, Gunn).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Article III reaches any case in which a federal question forms an ingredient, the broad constitutional ceiling.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Congress grants general federal-question jurisdiction in words like Article III's, later read far more narrowly.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: A suit Congress authorizes is not for that reason one arising under federal law when local rules and custom decide it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Well-pleaded complaint rule: the federal question must appear in the plaintiff's own claim, not in an anticipated defense.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Holmes's creation test: a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: A state-law claim can arise under federal law when it necessarily turns on a substantial federal question.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Artful pleading: a plaintiff cannot defeat removal by dressing a claim that is really federal in state-law words.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: A federal standard embedded in a state tort claim is not substantial enough when Congress gave no private federal remedy.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: No federal cause of action is required: the federal issue must be necessarily raised, disputed, substantial, and fit the federal-state balance.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Federal-question jurisdiction: arising under
records.text: Substantial means important to the federal system as a whole; a malpractice claim about a patent case stays in state court.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Distinguish power to hear related claims from discretion to retain them. Gibbs concerns pendent claims; Aldinger, Kroger and Finley concern additional parties. Section 1367 combines the routes but retains diversity restrictions; Royal Canin concerns deleting federal claims by amendment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Section 1367(a) covers related claims within the same Article III case, including added parties, subject to the exact diversity restrictions in (b) and discretion in (c). Exxon permits certain below-amount claims with complete diversity. Royal Canin concerns a removed complaint properly amended to eliminate every federal question, not merely dismissal of the federal claims.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Pendent jurisdiction begins narrow: a court may decide a second ground for the same cause of action, not a separate state claim.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Common nucleus of operative fact: related state claims may be heard with a substantial federal claim, at the court's discretion.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Compulsory counterclaims, read by logical relationship, fall within ancillary jurisdiction without a basis of their own.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Pendent parties: a court must ask whether Congress negated jurisdiction over them; a county excluded from § 1983 stays out.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: A plaintiff cannot use ancillary jurisdiction to sue a nondiverse third-party defendant; complete diversity would be evaded.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: No pendent-party jurisdiction without express authorization from Congress, which prompted § 1367.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: Congress codifies supplemental jurisdiction over the whole case or controversy, with limits in diversity cases and room to decline.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: In diversity, one plaintiff's qualifying claim carries co-plaintiffs and class members below the amount, but not nondiverse parties.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Supplemental jurisdiction: from pendent and ancillary claims to § 1367
records.text: When a plaintiff amends away every federal claim after removal, supplemental jurisdiction ends with it and the case is remanded.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Separate constitutional minimal diversity from statutory complete diversity, citizenship and amount. Exxon addresses supplemental claims below the amount threshold. CAFA is a separate statutory route with exclusions, not a replacement of § 1332(a).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Ordinary § 1332(a) uses complete diversity and an amount exceeding $75,000; natural-person state citizenship requires U.S. citizenship and domicile. Exxon addresses related below-amount claims. CAFA supplies a separate qualifying-class route with minimal diversity, an amount exceeding $5 million and statutory size, exception and exclusion provisions.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Each holder of a joint interest must be able to sue or be sued in federal court, the root of the complete-diversity rule.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Complete diversity is a reading of the statute: Article III needs only minimal diversity, so Congress may use it, as in interpleader.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Each class member with a separate claim must meet the amount in controversy; one qualifying claim cannot carry the rest.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Citizenship means domicile, which persists until a new home is taken with intent to remain, and is tested when suit is filed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: The amount claimed in good faith controls unless it is legally certain the claim is smaller, and the plaintiff gets a chance to show it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: CAFA permits qualifying classes with minimal diversity, an aggregate amount exceeding $5 million and ordinarily at least 100 members, subject to statutory exclusions and exceptions. Ordinary § 1332(a) complete diversity remains.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Through § 1367 one plaintiff's qualifying claim carries others below the amount, but a single nondiverse plaintiff still defeats jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Diversity jurisdiction: complete diversity and the amount in controversy
records.text: Complete diversity missing at removal is not cured by wrongly dismissing the nondiverse defendant; the merits judgment is vacated.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: Separate who may remove from how removal is accomplished. CAFA relaxes several procedural restrictions, but Home Depot still limits its use to defendants to the original complaint. Amount allegations and class stipulations address other removal questions.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: Only a defendant to the original plaintiff's claim may remove (§ 1441(a), § 1453(b)). CAFA lets any such defendant remove a qualifying class action without the others' consent, and a notice of removal needs only a plausible allegation of the amount in controversy, with proof required only if it is contested.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: Removal statutes are read strictly: a plaintiff who faces a counterclaim is still a plaintiff and cannot remove.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: CAFA lets any defendant remove a class action without the others' consent, even a forum citizen, and drops the one-year limit.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: A named plaintiff's stipulation cannot hold a class below CAFA's amount, because before certification it does not bind the class.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: A notice of removal needs only a plausible allegation of the amount, with evidence only if challenged; no presumption against CAFA removal.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Removal: who may move a case to federal court
records.text: Only the original defendant may remove: a third-party counterclaim defendant cannot, under § 1441(a) or CAFA.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: A court’s adjudicatory power, an element of the claim and a procedural deadline have different consequences. Arbaugh’s clear-statement approach concerns federal statutory limits; Lacks illustrates a state-law distinction. Enbridge shows that nonjurisdictional does not mean extendable.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: A defect in subject-matter jurisdiction can be raised by any party at any time, even by the party who chose the court, but a requirement is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly says so (Arbaugh). Other limits, such as removal procedure and deadlines, can be waived or forfeited, yet may still be mandatory and closed to equitable tolling (Lively, Enbridge).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: Jurisdiction cannot be conferred by choice: even the plaintiff who picked federal court wins reversal when the record fails to show it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: A state high court holds that a missed statutory element, here divorce residency, does not strip the court of power or void its judgment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: Clear-statement rule: a limit is jurisdictional only if Congress says so; Title VII's employee count is an element of the claim.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: Removal in breach of the forum-defendant rule is a waivable defect: the plaintiff must object within 30 days, and the court cannot remand on its own.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Jurisdictional or not: why the label matters
records.text: Nonjurisdictional is not the same as flexible: the 30-day removal deadline cannot be equitably tolled.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: Venue selects the proper district; it is separate from subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. The local-action decisions are historical and interstate comparisons. Congress’s 2011 revision removes that distinction for ordinary federal venue.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: Federal venue lies in a district where any defendant resides if all reside in the same state, or where a substantial part of the events or of the property at issue is located, with a fallback district if neither exists (§ 1391(b)); since 2011 it is decided without regard to whether the action is local or transitory.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: Local actions: a trespass to land must be sued where the land lies, even if the defendant can be found elsewhere.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: A state court rejects the local-action rule so that a wrongdoer cannot escape every court for harm to land in another state.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: After the 1990 amendment venue lies wherever a substantial part of the events occurred, as where a collection notice was received.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Venue: from local actions to where the events happened
records.text: Congress restates § 1391 and provides that venue is set without regard to whether an action is local or transitory.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: Section 1404 transfers among federal districts; forum non conveniens ordinarily dismisses in favor of a foreign or state forum. The 2011 consent amendment qualifies Hoffman. Multidistrict pretrial transfer and enforcement of a forum clause add separate statutory questions.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: Section 1404(a) moves a case between federal districts for convenience to any district where it might have been brought or to which all parties consent, and a valid forum clause controls in all but unusual cases (Atlantic Marine). Dismissal for forum non conveniens remains for foreign or state forums, with less deference to a foreign plaintiff (Piper).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: Section 1404(a) lets a federal court transfer a case for convenience instead of dismissing it for forum non conveniens.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: Transfer only to a district where the plaintiff could have sued when the case began; the defendant's consent cannot add one.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: Forum non conveniens: a foreign plaintiff's choice gets less deference, and less favorable foreign law is ordinarily not decisive.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: A multidistrict pretrial court must return each case for trial; it cannot use § 1404(a) to keep cases for itself.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: The 2011 venue act lets courts transfer to any district all parties consent to, undoing Hoffman's limit.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Transfer and forum non conveniens
records.text: A valid forum clause is enforced by § 1404(a) transfer, or by forum non conveniens for a non-federal forum, not by dismissal for improper venue.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: First determine whether the clause is valid and applicable; then determine how to enforce it. Bremen and Carnival arose in admiralty. Stewart selects § 1404 in diversity, and Atlantic Marine gives a valid clause controlling weight in that transfer analysis.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: Bremen and Carnival test clause validity in admiralty. In the federal transfer setting, Stewart selects § 1404 and Atlantic Marine gives a valid, applicable clause controlling weight absent exceptional public-interest circumstances. That enforcement analysis does not itself resolve every contract-formation or validity defense.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: A freely negotiated forum clause is prima facie valid in admiralty, enforced unless unreasonable or unjust, or tainted by fraud or overreaching.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: In a diversity case § 1404(a), not state law, governs a clause's effect on transfer; the clause is a significant factor in the balance.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: A clause in a non-negotiated form ticket is enforceable if reasonable and fundamentally fair; lack of bargaining does not void it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Forum-selection clauses
records.text: A valid clause controls transfer in all but unusual cases: the plaintiff's choice and private interests get no weight.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Separate certification requirements, the constitutional ability to bind absentees, notice and individual standing. Arbitration limits and personal-jurisdiction questions are additional branches. Briseno and Mussat state circuit holdings rather than nationwide Supreme Court rules.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Rule 23 prerequisites and an appropriate (b) category, adequate representation and applicable notice/exclusion rules govern certification and binding effect. TransUnion requires standing to recover damages. Briseno and Mussat address additional circuit-specific questions; arbitration agreements add a distinct FAA branch.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Absent members are bound by a class judgment only if the parties to the suit adequately represented their interests.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: The 1966 rewrite replaces the true/hybrid/spurious categories with Rule 23(a) and (b), including notice and exclusion rights for (b)(3) damages classes. It reforms procedure rather than merely codifying Hansberry.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Individual notice to every reasonably identifiable (b)(3) member, at the plaintiff's cost, with no merits preview to shift that cost.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: A class judgment precludes only what it decided: losing a pattern-or-practice claim does not bar members' individual claims.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Absent plaintiffs can be bound without minimum contacts if they get notice, a chance to opt out and adequate representation.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: A settlement class must still satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b); a fair deal cannot replace predominance and adequate representation.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: A mandatory limited-fund class needs a fund shown to be truly limited, all of it devoted to the claims, and equitable treatment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: The FAA preempts California’s rule conditioning arbitration on class procedures. That removes this state-law obstacle to the agreement; it is not a holding that every class waiver is valid under every applicable defense.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Commonality needs a common question whose answer drives the case; individual backpay claims cannot proceed in a (b)(2) class.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: The Ninth Circuit rejects a separate administrative-feasibility test: Rule 23's listed requirements already deal with identifying members.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: The Seventh Circuit holds that a federal Rule 23 action under a federal statute needs personal jurisdiction for the named plaintiff, without a separate showing for each absentee. This is a circuit holding, not a Supreme Court resolution of every class setting.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Class actions: binding the absent members
records.text: Every class member who seeks damages must have standing; a statutory violation without concrete harm is not enough.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Follow the movant’s initial showing, the opponent’s evidentiary response and the trial burden of proof. The 1986 decisions permit judgment without a genuine jury issue; Scott does not authorize ordinary credibility weighing, and Tolan preserves the favorable view of disputed evidence.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Summary judgment is proper when, viewing the evidence for the nonmovant, no reasonable jury could find for that party under the trial burden of proof (Anderson); a movant without the burden may point to missing evidence (Celotex). Courts may not resolve genuine disputes for the movant (Tolan) unless the record blatantly contradicts one side (Scott).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Summary judgment is improper if there is the slightest doubt about the facts, especially when a witness's credibility is at stake.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: The hope that a jury will disbelieve the other side's witnesses is not evidence; a party with the burden needs proof of its own.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Summary judgment should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent matter and the proof lies with the other side.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: When the facts turn on the motive and credibility of the movant's own witnesses, the opponent may test them by cross-examination at trial.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: The movant must foreclose any genuine issue; if its own showing leaves a gap, the motion fails even without a response.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Evidence as consistent with lawful competition as with conspiracy cannot carry an implausible conspiracy claim to a jury.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: A dispute is genuine only if a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the burden of proof that applies at trial.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: After adequate time for discovery, a movant without the trial burden may identify the absence of evidence on an essential element without negating it. Only after that initial showing must the opponent identify a genuine jury issue.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: A court need not accept a version of events that the record, such as a video, so blatantly contradicts that no jury could believe it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
records.text: Courts must still credit the nonmovant's evidence and may not resolve genuine disputes for the movant, even in qualified-immunity cases.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: The same-transaction formulations operate in different rules: compulsory counterclaims, crossclaims and permissive party joinder. Rule 20 also requires a common question. Procedural permission to join does not itself supply subject-matter jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: Rules 13 and 20 use related but different transaction tests; permissive party joinder also needs a common question of law or fact. Rules 20(b), 21 and 42(b) manage prejudice and complexity. Procedural joinder does not dispense with an independent or supplemental jurisdictional basis.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: Under the code, claims arising from one transaction may be joined though they fall in different categories, such as false imprisonment and slander.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: 'Transaction' is a flexible word: a counterclaim arises from it when logically related to the claim, though the facts differ.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: Crossclaims and claims against added parties arise from the same transaction when logically related, with separate trials to manage them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: A counterclaim logically related to the claim is compulsory under Rule 13(a), and it comes within ancillary jurisdiction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
records.text: Plaintiffs may join when their claims arise from a series of logically related events and share a common question, as with a company-wide policy.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: Apply Rule 19(a) before Rule 19(b). If joinder is required but infeasible, practical prejudice and available remedies determine whether to proceed; Temple stops at the first question, while Pimentel gives sovereign immunity special weight.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: Rule 19(a) first asks whether an absentee is required; if joinder is not feasible, Rule 19(b) weighs prejudice, ways to lessen it, the adequacy of a judgment without the absentee and the plaintiff's alternatives to decide whether the case goes on. Joint tortfeasors are not required parties (Temple), and an immune sovereign with a real stake can compel dismissal (Pimentel).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: An absentee is indispensable only if any decree would inevitably affect its interest; separable interests let the court proceed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: The rewritten Rule 19 drops fixed labels for a two-step test: who should be joined, then whether to go on without them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: Indispensability is the conclusion of a practical weighing of everyone's interests in equity and good conscience, not a label applied first.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: Joint tortfeasors are permissive parties, not required ones, so Rule 19(b) is never reached for them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
records.text: Where an immune sovereign with a nonfrivolous claim cannot be joined and could be harmed, the action must ordinarily be dismissed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: Separate Rule 22 interpleader, which needs ordinary jurisdiction, from statutory interpleader under § 1335. The latter has a fund/deposit requirement and minimal diversity. Hancock is a California comparison; Tashire confines the injunction to protection of the stake.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: A stakeholder facing competing claims to one fund may interplead under Rule 22, with ordinary jurisdiction, or under § 1335, with minimal diversity among claimants and nationwide service, even when the claims are unliquidated and not yet reduced to judgment. Interpleader protects the fund; it does not force every related claim into one court (Tashire).
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: Statutory interpleader requires adverse claimants with minimal diversity, a stake worth at least $500, and deposit of the stake or a qualifying bond. The 1936 Act broadens access; these conditions still matter.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: A disinterested tenant may interplead its landlord and a rival claimant despite the rule that a tenant may not deny the landlord's title.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: An insurer may interplead tort claimants whose claims may exceed its policy limit, though it denies liability and the claims are unliquidated.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
records.text: Minimal diversity suffices and interpleader may come before judgment, but it protects only the fund and cannot force all claims into one court.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Distinguish finding a statutory contingency from filling administrative details and exercising delegated discretion. The 1935 invalidations are exceptions to the intelligible-principle approach. Benzene and Gundy contain separate rationales, not majority decisions replacing that test.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: The intelligible-principle approach governs the selected majority decisions; Benzene and Gundy show competing rationales and proposals for stricter limits. FCC v. Consumers’ Research (2025) independently confirms sufficient congressional guidance and retained FCC control of the private administrator. That decision is checked in the audit trail but has no separate atlas brief here.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Congress may make a law's revival turn on a fact the President finds and proclaims; that is not a transfer of lawmaking.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: When Congress names the contingency and its consequence, the President who finds the fact acts as its agent, not as a lawmaker.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Congress may let an administrator fill in details by rule and make breaking those rules a crime that Congress itself defines and punishes.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: The test is named: a delegation is valid if Congress lays down an intelligible principle to which the delegate must conform.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: First invalidation: Congress let the President ban hot-oil shipments without stating a policy, a standard or the findings required.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Power to write binding codes for whole industries, guided only by general recovery aims, is an unconstitutional transfer of lawmaking.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Wartime price control stands: standards need only be definite enough for a court to tell whether Congress's will was obeyed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: A three-judge court upholds the wage-price freeze: text, purpose, history and implied limits can supply the standard; breadth alone is no defect.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: A plurality reads the OSH Act narrowly to avoid a sweeping delegation; Justice Rehnquist alone would hold the delegation unconstitutional.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: The Sentencing Commission passes the intelligible-principle test; only Scalia objects to lawmaking by a body with no other power to exercise.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: An agency cannot cure a standardless delegation by limiting itself; 'requisite to protect the public health' is a sufficient principle.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
records.text: Four Justices uphold the delegation after narrowing SORNA by interpretation. Alito supplies the fifth vote under existing doctrine while inviting reconsideration; three dissenters propose a stricter approach. No majority replaces the intelligible-principle test.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: Congress may legislate and oversee, but appointing or controlling officials who execute the law is a different act. Chadha concerns legislative effect outside Congress; Bowsher and FEC v. NRA concern control through officers rather than a legislative veto.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: Congress controls execution by passing laws through both Houses and presentment, by funding and oversight, and through the Senate's roles in confirmation and impeachment; it may not veto by resolution or appoint or remove (other than by impeachment) officers who execute the law.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: The Senate may not share in removing an executive officer; a statute making removal depend on its consent is invalid.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: Congress may not appoint officers who enforce the law; officials it names may only gather information and investigate, as a committee could.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: A one-House veto is lawmaking: once it delegates, Congress may alter the delegate's power only by bicameral passage and presentment.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: Congress may not keep removal power, short of impeachment, over an officer who executes the law, because removal brings control.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
records.text: The D.C. Circuit holds that Congress's own agents may not sit on an enforcement agency, even as nonvoting members.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Read each holding against the officer’s functions and structure. Myers bars Senate control, Humphrey’s protected the historical FTC, and later cases cut back insulation. Slaughter changes that precedent in 2026; Cook addresses the Federal Reserve separately at the stay stage.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Slaughter holds the FTC’s executive-power commissioners removable at will and overrules Humphrey’s to that extent; it leaves the Federal Reserve and non-Article III courts aside. Cook separately denies a stay and requires statutory removal process for a Fed Governor. Inferior-officer and adjudicative settings must not be generalized from the FTC holding.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: When Congress vests an inferior officer's appointment in a department head, it may also restrict that officer's removal.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: The President's power to remove officers he appoints with Senate consent is his alone; Congress may not make it depend on the Senate.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Congress may protect members of a quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial commission such as the FTC from removal except for cause.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: The President may not remove a member of an adjudicatory body like the War Claims Commission merely to put his own appointee in its place, even when the statute says nothing about removal.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Congress may not keep for itself the power to remove an officer who executes the law; impeachment is its only removal tool.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: The test turns functional: a good-cause limit on an inferior officer is valid unless it impedes the President's constitutional duties.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Two layers of for-cause protection between the President and officers who exercise executive power violate Article II.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: A lone agency head wielding significant executive power may not be shielded; exceptions stay with multimember bodies and some inferior officers.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Seila’s single-director rule reaches the FHFA. Because the officer was properly appointed, the unconstitutional removal restriction does not automatically invalidate past actions; retrospective relief requires compensable harm caused by the restriction.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: Humphrey's Executor overruled: FTC commissioners exercise executive power and must be removable at will; the Federal Reserve is reserved.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential removal power
records.text: The Court denies a stay of Cook’s preliminary protection: removal is reviewable and the statute requires notice and an opportunity to respond. It treats the Federal Reserve’s history separately and leaves the precise definition of cause open.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Officer status, principal-versus-inferior status and the permissible appointing authority are separate questions. Shoemaker and Weiss address new duties for an already appointed officer; Noel Canning addresses the separate recess-appointment route.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: A continuing position exercising significant federal authority is an office. Principal officers ordinarily require presidential nomination and Senate consent; Congress may vest an inferior officer’s appointment in the President alone, a court of law or a department head. Edmond and Arthrex concern supervision and review; recess appointments follow a separate clause.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Congress may add duties germane to an existing office without requiring a fresh appointment of the officer who holds it.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Anyone exercising significant authority under federal law is an officer, appointed only as Article II allows; Congress may not appoint.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: An independent counsel, removable for cause and limited in duties, jurisdiction and tenure, is an inferior officer whom a court may appoint.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Tax Court special trial judges are officers, not employees, and the Tax Court is a 'Court of Law' that may appoint them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Assuming Shoemaker's germaneness principle applies, commissioned officers need no second appointment to serve as military judges, a duty germane to their office.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: Inferior officers are those directed and supervised by Senate-confirmed officers; significant authority marks an officer, not a principal one.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: The recess route is bounded: the Senate is in session when it says it is, and a break of under ten days is presumptively too short.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: SEC administrative law judges are officers under Freytag, so appointment by staff was invalid; the cure is a new hearing before another official.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
records.text: An inferior officer may not issue final decisions that no principal officer can review; the PTO Director must be able to review the Board.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Distinguish a specific statutory duty, implied executive authority and action inconsistent with Congress. Youngstown’s holding rejects the seizure; Jackson’s three categories come from his concurrence and inform Dames & Moore’s narrower foreign-affairs holding.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Courts sort presidential action by Justice Jackson's Youngstown framework: power is greatest with Congress's authorization, uncertain where Congress is silent (where long acquiescence can count), and weakest against its will. Statutes granting emergency powers are read for their stated predicates.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Political discretion belongs to the executive, but a specific legal duty on which a person's rights depend can be enforced in court.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Where Congress has said how a law is to be executed, executive instructions cannot authorize more or shield the officer who obeys them.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: The duty to execute the laws implies no power to dispense with them; a court may compel an officer's ministerial duty by mandamus.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Executive duties may be implied from the Constitution and general statutes, such as protecting a federal judge, not only from express laws.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Without a statute specifically authorizing the suit, but resting on Congress's commerce and postal legislation, the national government may sue in equity to stop forcible obstruction of interstate commerce and the mails.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Long executive practice known to Congress and left undisturbed implies its consent, here to the President's withdrawal of public lands.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: The steel seizure fails: power must come from statute or the Constitution; Jackson's concurrence sorts action by Congress's will.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: Jackson's categories become a spectrum: congressional acquiescence supports suspending claims, though the President has no plenary settlement power.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
records.text: At the stay stage, the Guard statute likely requires lawful authority to use the regular military, which an asserted protective power did not supply.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: Skidmore persuasion and historical Chevron deference to statutes are different routes. Loper Bright rejects ambiguity-based Chevron deference while respecting genuine delegations and prior holdings. Kisor concerns an agency’s own regulation, a separate interpretive branch.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: Courts decide what a statute means for themselves (Loper Bright), giving an agency's view the weight its reasoning earns and policing any discretion Congress expressly delegated; earlier Chevron-based holdings keep their stare decisis effect, and Kisor's narrowed Auer deference still governs an agency's reading of its own regulations.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: When Congress leaves an agency to apply a term like 'producer' to particular facts, a reasoned application after a fair hearing stands.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: The Board's application of 'employee' is accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: Agency interpretations do not bind courts but carry weight from their care, reasoning, consistency and power to persuade.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: Two steps: if Congress spoke to the precise question, that controls; if the statute is silent or ambiguous, a permissible agency reading wins.

records.text: Step zero: Chevron applies only where Congress gave power to act with the force of law and the agency used it; otherwise Skidmore.

records.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
records.text: A court's earlier reading yields to a later reasonable agency reading unless the court held that the statute was unambiguous.

records.text: A question of deep economic and political significance is not implicitly left to the agency; the Court reads the statute itself.

records.text: Chevron overruled: under APA § 706 courts decide what statutes mean independently, honoring real delegations and giving agency views Skidmore weight.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: These cases restrict extraordinary assertions of agency authority, but do not invalidate every large program. Biden v. Missouri is a statutory-authorization contrast. Benzene and the emergency cases must be read with their plurality or interim posture.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: When an agency claims power of vast economic and political significance, it must point to clear congressional authorization, not merely a plausible reading of general words. Justices still differ on whether the doctrine is a substantive clear-statement rule or, as Justice Barrett puts it, ordinary reading of text in context.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: Absent a clear mandate, the plurality will not read the OSH Act to give the agency unprecedented power over American industry.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: In extraordinary cases courts hesitate to find an implicit delegation over a large part of the economy; Congress had not given the FDA power to regulate tobacco products as customarily marketed.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: A question of deep economic and political significance was not left to the IRS; the Court decides it by reading the whole statute.
records.reviewStatus: Reviewed in timeline pass; scope recorded in its audit.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: A nationwide eviction moratorium needs clear authorization; a general disease-control power read with its narrow examples does not give it.

records.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
records.text: A vaccine-or-test mandate for large employers is a general public-health measure, not an occupational standard Congress clearly authorized.
